In contrast, the nervous systems of natural animals exhibit great heterogeneity in both their elements and patterns of interconnection. This heterogeneity is crucial to the flexible generation of behavior which is essential for survival in a complex, dynamic environment. It may also provide powerful insights into the design of artificial neural networks. In this paper, we describe a heterogeneous neural network for controlling the wa1king of a simulated insect. paragraphs: This paper explores a neural controller whose elements and connection patterns are deliberately heterogeneous. The motivation comes from animal nervous systems, where diverse components support flexible behavior in changing environments. The authors apply that idea to controlling a simulated insect’s walking, drawing on biological studies of insect locomotion.

The controller produces a variety of statically stable gaits at different speeds. These changes can be obtained simply by varying the sustained activity of one cell. A single control signal therefore influences the coordinated behavior of the larger network, allowing different walking patterns to arise from the same architecture.

The simulated controller also adapts to perturbations as a consequence of its design. This links the organization of the network to both gait generation and responses to disturbance. The paper’s contribution is a concrete example of how differences among neural elements and their connections can support behavioral flexibility. Its stated findings concern the simulated insect, where the designed interactions produce multiple stable walking patterns and adaptive responses.
summary.tldr: A heterogeneous neural controller gives a simulated insect multiple stable gaits and adaptive responses to disturbances.

title: Heterogeneous Neural Networks for Adaptive Behavior in Dynamic Environments

abstract: The brain represents the skin surface as a topographic map in the somatosensory cortex. This map has been shown experimentally to be modifiable in a use-dependent fashion throughout life. We present a neural network simulation of the competitive dynamics underlying this cortical plasticity by detailed analysis of receptive field properties of model neurons during simulations of skin co(cid:173) activation, cortical lesion, digit amputation and nerve section.

We present a neural network simulation of the competitive dynamics underlying this cortical plasticity by detailed analysis of receptive field properties of model neurons during simulations of skin co(cid:173) activation, cortical lesion, digit amputation and nerve section.

paragraphs: The paper studies how the brain's representation of the skin can change with experience and injury. The somatosensory cortex contains a topographic map of the skin surface, and experiments have shown that this map remains modifiable throughout life. The authors use a neural network simulation to investigate competitive dynamics underlying this plasticity.

Their analysis focuses on the receptive fields of individual model neurons: the regions of sensory input to which those neurons respond. Following these properties provides a way to connect the behavior of model cells with changes in the larger sensory representation. The map is thus examined through the responses of the units that compose it.

The simulations cover skin co-activation, cortical lesions, digit amputation, and nerve section. Together, these conditions examine competition under changes in sensory activity and disruptions to the represented system. The contribution is a computational investigation of representational plasticity across these conditions, using detailed receptive-field analysis to study how competitive neural dynamics relate to a modifiable cortical map.
summary.tldr: A neural simulation investigates competitive dynamics behind changes in cortical skin maps through detailed receptive-field analysis.

title: Neural Network Simulation of Somatosensory Representational Plasticity

abstract: This srudy has demonstrated how artificial neural networks (ANNs) can be used to characterize seismic sources using high-frequency regional seismic data. We have taken the novel approach of using ANNs as a research tool for obtaining seismic source information, specifically depth of focus for earthquakes and ripple-fire characteristics for economic blasts, rather than as just a feature classifier between earthquake and explosion populations. Overall, we have found that ANNs have potential applications to seismic event characterization and identification, beyond just as a feature classifier. In future studies, these techniques should be applied to actual data of regional seismic events recorded at the new regional seismic arrays. The results of this study indicates that an ANN should be evaluated as part of an operational seismic event identification system.

paragraphs: This paper investigates neural networks as tools for characterizing seismic sources using high-frequency regional seismic data. The intended outputs describe properties of an event, extending the task beyond deciding whether a recorded signal belongs to an earthquake or an explosion. The focus is on extracting information about the source that produced the observations.

The authors examine earthquake depth of focus and ripple-fire characteristics of economic blasts. These are different kinds of source information, but both make the network useful as a research tool for interpreting seismic events. The approach therefore treats neural processing as a means of recovering descriptive properties from seismic signals.

The study reports potential applications to event characterization and identification beyond feature classification. The authors recommend applying the techniques to actual regional-event data recorded at new seismic arrays and evaluating an ANN as part of an operational identification system. Those recommendations place the findings at a promising research stage, with application to the stated regional data and operational evaluation presented as subsequent work.
summary.tldr: Neural networks show promise for estimating earthquake depth and blast characteristics from regional seismic signals.

title: Lg Depth Estimation and Ripple Fire Characterization Using Artificial Neural Networks

abstract: We analyse the effects of analog noise on the synaptic arithmetic during MultiLayer Perceptron training, by expanding the cost func(cid:173) tion to include noise-mediated penalty terms. Predictions are made in the light of these calculations which suggest that fault tolerance, generalisation ability and learning trajectory should be improved by such noise-injection. Extensive simulation experiments on two distinct classification problems substantiate the claims. The re(cid:173) sults appear to be perfectly general for all training schemes where weights are adjusted incrementally, and have wide-ranging implica(cid:173) tions for all applications, particularly those involving "inaccurate" analog neural VLSI.

paragraphs: The paper examines how analog noise in synaptic computations affects multilayer-perceptron training. It treats noise as something that can change the learning process in useful ways. The authors analyze this by expanding the cost function to include penalty terms produced by the noise.

The calculations predict improvements in fault tolerance, generalization, and the path learning takes through parameter space. Connecting noise to additional penalties gives a reason for these effects: noisy training changes the effective objective being optimized. The approach therefore ties the behavior of imperfect computation to the mathematical criterion guiding learning.

Extensive simulations on two distinct classification problems support the predicted benefits. The authors suggest that the results apply broadly to training schemes that adjust weights incrementally, while the reported experiments provide evidence on those two problems. They emphasize implications for analog neural VLSI, where arithmetic inaccuracies are especially relevant. The work makes such inaccuracies part of the training analysis and identifies circumstances in which they can be beneficial.
summary.tldr: Analysis and simulations show that noise during multilayer-perceptron training can improve fault tolerance, generalization, and learning behavior.

title: Synaptic Weight Noise During MLP Learning Enhances Fault-Tolerance, Generalization and Learning Trajectory

paragraphs: This paper presents a method for training neural-network weights through approximate gradient descent. It estimates the gradient using finite differences, which infer the effect of a change by perturbing the system and observing the resulting difference. The goal is to obtain useful learning directions with computational and hardware requirements suited to neural implementations.

The method exploits a stochastic relationship between perturbing weights and perturbing neurons. This allows it to achieve the reported O(N³) computational complexity associated with node perturbation while avoiding access to hidden or internal neuron activity. That combination matters when internal signals are difficult to expose in a physical neural circuit.

The authors also describe the method as retaining weight perturbation's optimal hardware requirements for training VLSI neural networks. Its contribution is therefore a particular tradeoff: obtain the computational advantage of neuron-level perturbation through changes applied at the weights, without requiring internal activity measurements. The paper connects an approximation used for learning to the practical question of what information a hardware training system must access.
summary.tldr: A perturbation-based training method matches node perturbation's computational complexity without needing access to hidden-neuron activity.

title: Summed Weight Neuron Perturbation: An O(N) Improvement Over Weight Perturbation

abstract: We study the asymptotic properties of the sequence of iterates of weight-vector estimates obtained by training a multilayer feed for(cid:173) ward neural network with a basic gradient-descent method using a fixed learning constant and no batch-processing. In the one(cid:173) dimensional case, an exact analysis establishes the existence of a limiting distribution that is not Gaussian in general. For the gen(cid:173) eral case and small learning constant, a linearization approximation permits the application of results from the theory of random ma(cid:173) trices to again establish the existence of a limiting distribution. We study the first few moments of this distribution to compare and contrast the results of our analysis with those of techniques of stochastic approximation.

paragraphs: The paper examines the long-run behavior of neural-network weights trained by gradient descent with a fixed learning constant and without batch processing. Its object of study is the sequence of weight estimates produced during training. The authors ask whether this sequence has a limiting statistical distribution and what properties that distribution has.

For the one-dimensional case, they provide an exact analysis establishing that a limiting distribution exists. That distribution need not be Gaussian, so a bell-shaped description is not generally justified. For the general case, the analysis assumes a small learning constant and uses a linear approximation. Results from random-matrix theory then establish a limiting distribution within that approximate treatment.

The authors examine the first few moments of the resulting distribution, quantities describing features such as its location and spread. They use these to compare their analysis with stochastic-approximation techniques. The contribution is a distributional account of long-run training behavior under a fixed learning constant, with a clear distinction between the exact one-dimensional result and the approximate analysis of the general setting.
summary.tldr: Fixed-step gradient training can approach a limiting weight distribution that is not generally Gaussian.

title: Asymptotics of Gradient-based Neural Network Training Algorithms

abstract: Planning and learning at multiple levels of temporal abstraction is a key problem for artificial intelligence. In this paper we summarize an approach to this problem based on the mathematical framework of Markov decision processes and reinforcement learning. Current model-based reinforcement learning is based on one-step models that cannot represent common-sense higher-level actions, such as going to lunch, grasping an object, or flying to Denver. This paper generalizes prior work on temporally abstract models [Sutton, 1995] and extends it from the prediction setting to include actions, control, and planning. We introduce a more general form of temporally abstract model, the multi-time model, and establish its suitability for planning and learning by virtue of its relationship to the Bellman equations. This paper summarizes the theoretical framework of multi-time models and illustrates their potential advantages in a grid world planning task.

paragraphs: Useful actions often extend over time: grasping an object or traveling somewhere cannot naturally be described as a single immediate transition. This paper addresses how an agent can learn and plan with actions at multiple temporal levels. Its starting point is the difficulty of expressing such higher-level actions through conventional one-step models.

The authors introduce multi-time models within the framework of Markov decision processes and reinforcement learning. They generalize earlier work on temporal abstraction from prediction to actions, control, and planning. This extends the purpose of an abstract model from describing what may happen over time to supporting choices about what an agent should do.

The theoretical justification comes from the models' relationship to Bellman equations, which connect values across decisions. That relationship establishes their suitability for planning and learning. A grid-world planning task illustrates their potential advantages. The contribution is a formal way to reason over extended actions while retaining the mathematical connection between predictive models and decision-making.
summary.tldr: Multi-time models extend reinforcement-learning models to temporally extended actions while preserving a theoretical connection to Bellman-based planning.

title: Multi-time Models for Temporally Abstract Planning

abstract: We have developed and tested an analog/digital VLSI system that mod(cid:173) els the coordination of biological segmental oscillators underlying axial locomotion in animals such as leeches and lampreys. In its current form the system consists of a chain of twelve pattern generating circuits that are capable of arbitrary contralateral inhibitory synaptic coupling. Each pattern generating circuit is implemented with two independent silicon Morris-Lecar neurons with a total of 32 programmable (floating-gate based) inhibitory synapses, and an asynchronous address-event inter(cid:173) connection element that provides synaptic connectivity and implements axonal delay. We describe and analyze the data from a set of experi(cid:173) ments exploring the system behavior in terms of synaptic coupling.

paragraphs: Animals such as leeches and lampreys coordinate oscillations along their bodies to produce axial locomotion. This paper develops and tests an analog/digital chip system for modeling the coordination of the segmental oscillators underlying that movement. Its focus is how connections among pattern-generating circuits shape the behavior of the connected system.

The implementation contains a chain of twelve pattern generators. Each generator uses two independent silicon Morris-Lecar neurons and a total of 32 programmable inhibitory synapses based on floating-gate technology. The system supports arbitrary contralateral inhibitory coupling, allowing the researchers to configure inhibitory connections across opposite sides rather than study only one fixed connection arrangement.

An asynchronous address-event interconnection element supplies synaptic connectivity and implements axonal delay. These features make connection structure and delayed signaling part of the physical model. The authors report and analyze experiments exploring behavior under different synaptic coupling arrangements. The contribution is a tested hardware platform for examining how coordinated locomotor activity depends on interactions between segmental neural oscillators.
summary.tldr: A programmable neuromorphic chip models how coupled segmental neural oscillators coordinate axial locomotion.

title: A Neuromorphic VLSI System for Modeling the Neural Control of Axial Locomotion

abstract: Imagine that you wish to classify data consisting of tens of thousands of ex(cid:173) amples residing in a twenty thousand dimensional space. How can one ap(cid:173) ply standard machine learning algorithms? We describe the Parallel Prob(cid:173) lems Server (PPServer) and MATLAB*P. In tandem they allow users of networked computers to work transparently on large data sets from within Matlab. This work is motivated by the desire to bring the many benefits of scientific computing algorithms and computational power to machine learning researchers. We demonstrate the usefulness of the system on a number of tasks. For example, we perform independent components analysis on very large text corpora consisting of tens of thousands of documents, making minimal changes to the original Bell and Sejnowski Matlab source (Bell and Se(cid:173) jnowski, 1995). Applying ML techniques to data previously beyond their reach leads to interesting analyses of both data and algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the difficulty of applying familiar machine-learning algorithms to datasets containing many examples and very many dimensions. The authors introduce the Parallel Problems Server and MATLAB*P, which together let users work on large datasets from within Matlab using networked computers. The goal is to make scientific-computing resources accessible through a familiar interactive environment.

The systems are designed to make this larger-scale computation transparent to the user. This matters for researchers who already have working Matlab implementations: access to additional computational power is more useful when existing algorithm code can remain largely recognizable. The contribution concerns the computational environment supporting machine learning as well as the applications it enables.

The authors demonstrate several tasks, including independent component analysis on text corpora containing tens of thousands of documents. That example requires only minimal changes to the original Matlab implementation. It illustrates how the system can extend the reach of existing methods and make previously inaccessible data available for examining both the datasets and the behavior of the algorithms.
summary.tldr: PPServer and MATLAB*P enable large-scale machine learning from Matlab, including text analysis with minimal changes to existing code.

title: The Parallel Problems Server: an Interactive Tool for Large Scale Machine Learning

abstract: The recent introduction of the 'relevance vector machine' has effec(cid:173) tively demonstrated how sparsity may be obtained in generalised linear models within a Bayesian framework. Using a particular form of Gaussian parameter prior, 'learning' is the maximisation, with respect to hyperparameters, of the marginal likelihood of the data. This paper studies the properties of that objective func(cid:173) tion, and demonstrates that conditioned on an individual hyper(cid:173) parameter, the marginal likelihood has a unique maximum which is computable in closed form. It is further shown that if a derived 'sparsity criterion' is satisfied, this maximum is exactly equivalent to 'pruning' the corresponding parameter from the model.
originalAbstract: The recent introduction of the 'relevance vector machine' has effec(cid:173) tively demonstrated how sparsity may be obtained in generalised linear models within a Bayesian framework. Using a particular form of Gaussian parameter prior, 'learning' is the maximisation, with respect to hyperparameters, of the marginal likelihood of the data. This paper studies the properties of that objective func(cid:173) tion, and demonstrates that conditioned on an individual hyper(cid:173) parameter, the marginal likelihood has a unique maximum which is computable in closed form. It is further shown that if a derived 'sparsity criterion' is satisfied, this maximum is exactly equivalent to 'pruning' the corresponding parameter from the model.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes why sparse models can emerge from the Bayesian learning approach used by the relevance vector machine. In this framework, generalized linear model parameters have a particular Gaussian prior, and learning adjusts hyperparameters to maximize the marginal likelihood of the observed data.

The authors study the structure of that optimization objective. When considering an individual hyperparameter with the others fixed, they show that the marginal likelihood has a unique maximum that can be calculated in closed form. This gives a precise characterization of an individual adjustment within the larger learning problem; it does not establish a unique joint optimum for all hyperparameters.

They also derive a sparsity criterion. When that condition holds, the corresponding maximum is exactly equivalent to removing the associated model parameter. This explains pruning as a consequence of the marginal-likelihood objective under a stated condition. The analysis therefore links sparse solutions to the mathematical behavior of the learning criterion, making the removal of a parameter an explicit optimization result.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes individual hyperparameter optima in sparse Bayesian learning and derives a condition under which an optimum removes a model parameter.

title: Analysis of Sparse Bayesian Learning

abstract: In contrast to standard statistical learning theory which studies uniform bounds on the expected error we present a framework that exploits the specific learning algorithm used. Motivated by the luckiness framework [8] we are also able to exploit the serendipity of the training sample. The main difference to previous approaches lies in the complexity measure; rather than covering all hypothe(cid:173) ses in a given hypothesis space it is only necessary to cover the functions which could have been learned using the fixed learning algorithm. We show how the resulting framework relates to the VC, luckiness and compression frameworks. Finally, we present an application of this framework to the maximum margin algorithm for linear classifiers which results in a bound that exploits both the margin and the distribution of the data in feature space.

paragraphs: The paper develops a framework for bounding prediction error that accounts for the particular learning algorithm being used. Standard uniform analyses consider an entire hypothesis space. Here, the authors also seek to exploit favorable properties of the training sample, following the idea of learning-theoretic luckiness.

The main change is in the complexity measure. Instead of covering every hypothesis in a chosen space, the analysis needs to cover only functions that the fixed learning algorithm could have produced. This makes the algorithm’s possible outputs part of the mathematical assessment of complexity. The framework therefore connects the error analysis more directly to the procedure that actually selects a predictor.

The authors explain how this approach relates to VC, luckiness, and compression frameworks. They then apply it to maximum-margin learning for linear classifiers. The resulting bound incorporates both the margin and the distribution of data in feature space. Its significance is that the guarantee can reflect more of the learning situation than the hypothesis space alone, including the algorithm and favorable sample geometry.
summary.tldr: Algorithmic luckiness bounds prediction error using the learner’s possible outputs and favorable sample properties, including margin and data geometry.

title: Algorithmic Luckiness

abstract: The structural similarity of neural networks and genetic regulatory networks to digital circuits, and hence to each other, was noted from the very beginning of their study [1, 2]. In this work, we propose a simple biochemical system whose architecture mimics that of genetic regulation and whose components allow for in vitro implementation of arbitrary circuits. We use only two enzymes in addition to DNA and RNA molecules: RNA polymerase (RNAP) and ribonuclease (RNase). We develop a rate equation for in vitro transcriptional networks, and derive a correspondence with general neural network rate equations [3]. As proof-of-principle demonstrations, an associative memory task and a feedforward network computation are shown by simulation. A difference between the neural network and biochemical models is also highlighted: global coupling of rate equations through enzyme saturation can lead to global feedback regulation, thus allowing a simple network without explicit mutual inhibition to perform the winner-take-all computation. Thus, the full complexity of the cell is not necessary for biochemical computation: a wide range of functional behaviors can be achieved with a small set of biochemical components.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a biochemical system for implementing circuits outside cells using DNA, RNA, and just two enzymes: RNA polymerase and ribonuclease. Its architecture resembles genetic regulation. The aim is to show how a small collection of biochemical components can support computational behaviors associated with neural networks.

The authors develop rate equations for the transcriptional networks and derive a correspondence with general neural-network rate equations. Simulations demonstrate an associative-memory task and a feedforward computation as proofs of principle. These results connect the proposed chemistry to recognizable computations, with the demonstrations specifically taking place in simulation.

The biochemical model also has a distinctive interaction: enzyme saturation can couple the equations globally. This shared coupling can create feedback regulation that allows a simple network to perform winner-take-all computation without explicit mutual inhibition. The paper therefore identifies both a correspondence with neural-network dynamics and an additional computational role for biochemical coupling. Its broader argument is that varied biochemical computation need not require the full complexity of a cell.
summary.tldr: A minimal transcriptional circuit model reproduces neural-network computations in simulation and can use enzyme saturation for winner-take-all behavior.

title: Neural Network Computation by In Vitro Transcriptional Circuits

abstract: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) is a well-known scheme for feature extraction and dimension reduction. It has been used widely in many ap- plications involving high-dimensional data, such as face recognition and image retrieval. An intrinsic limitation of classical LDA is the so-called singularity problem, that is, it fails when all scatter matrices are singu- lar. A well-known approach to deal with the singularity problem is to apply an intermediate dimension reduction stage using Principal Com- ponent Analysis (PCA) before LDA. The algorithm, called PCA+LDA, is used widely in face recognition. However, PCA+LDA has high costs in time and space, due to the need for an eigen-decomposition involving the scatter matrices. In this paper, we propose a novel LDA algorithm, namely 2DLDA, which stands for 2-Dimensional Linear Discriminant Analysis. 2DLDA over- comes the singularity problem implicitly, while achieving efﬁciency. The key difference between 2DLDA and classical LDA lies in the model for data representation. Classical LDA works with vectorized representa- tions of data, while the 2DLDA algorithm works with data in matrix representation. To further reduce the dimension by 2DLDA, the combi- nation of 2DLDA and classical LDA, namely 2DLDA+LDA, is studied, where LDA is preceded by 2DLDA. The proposed algorithms are ap- plied on face recognition and compared with PCA+LDA. Experiments show that 2DLDA and 2DLDA+LDA achieve competitive recognition accuracy, while being much more efﬁcient.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a difficulty in linear discriminant analysis, a method for extracting features and reducing dimension: classical LDA fails when all its scatter matrices are singular. Applying principal component analysis first is a common workaround, but the resulting PCA+LDA procedure can require substantial time and memory because of its matrix eigendecomposition.

The proposed 2DLDA changes the data representation. It operates directly on matrices, while classical LDA uses vectorized data. The authors state that this formulation implicitly overcomes the singularity problem while improving efficiency. They also study 2DLDA+LDA, in which the matrix-based method first reduces dimension and conventional LDA then reduces it further.

Both methods are evaluated for face recognition against PCA+LDA. The reported experiments show competitive recognition accuracy with much greater efficiency. The result highlights data representation as a practical design choice: working with matrix-form observations changes the computation enough to improve efficiency while retaining competitive accuracy in the tested recognition setting.
summary.tldr: Matrix-based 2DLDA addresses LDA's singularity problem and achieves competitive face-recognition accuracy with much greater efficiency than PCA+LDA.

title: Two-Dimensional Linear Discriminant Analysis

abstract: The Variational Bayesian framework has been widely used to approximate the Bayesian learning. In various applications, it has provided computational tractability and good generalization performance. In this paper, we discuss the Variational Bayesian learning of the mixture of exponential families and provide some additional theoretical support by deriving the asymptotic form of the stochastic complexity. The stochastic complexity, which corresponds to the minimum free energy and a lower bound of the marginal likelihood, is a key quantity for model selection. It also enables us to discuss the effect of hyperparameters and the accuracy of the Variational Bayesian approach as an approximation of the true Bayesian learning.

This paper develops additional theoretical support for its use with mixtures of exponential-family distributions. Its focus is the behavior of a quantity called stochastic complexity.

The authors derive an asymptotic form of stochastic complexity for these mixture models. The abstract connects this quantity with minimum free energy and a lower bound on marginal likelihood, and identifies it as central to model selection. An asymptotic expression provides a way to analyze that selection quantity in the limiting regime studied.

The result also allows discussion of how hyperparameters affect the variational approach and how accurately it approximates full Bayesian learning. These are linked questions because model selection and approximation quality both depend on the behavior of the underlying Bayesian calculation. The contribution is theoretical: it supplies an analytical basis for examining the variational method, its settings, and its relationship to the Bayesian learning procedure it approximates.
summary.tldr: An asymptotic analysis of stochastic complexity supports model selection and assessment of variational Bayesian learning for exponential-family mixtures.

title: Variational Bayesian Stochastic Complexity of Mixture Models

abstract: Accurate short-term wind forecasts (STWFs), with time horizons from 0.5 to 6 hours, are essential for efficient integration of wind power to the electrical power grid. Physical models based on numerical weather predictions are currently not competitive, and research on machine learning approaches is ongoing. Two major challenges confronting these efforts are missing observations and weather-regime induced dependency shifts among wind variables at geographically distributed sites. In this paper we introduce approaches that address both of these challenges. We describe a new regime-aware approach to STWF that use auto-regressive hidden Markov models (AR-HMM), a subclass of conditional linear Gaussian (CLG) models. Although AR-HMMs are a natural representation for weather regimes, as with CLG models in general, exact inference is NP-hard when observations are missing (Lerner and Parr, 2001). Because of this high cost, we introduce a simple approximate inference method for AR-HMMs, which we believe has applications to other sequential and temporal problem domains that involve continuous variables. In an empirical evaluation on publicly available wind data from two geographically distinct regions, our approach makes significantly more accurate predictions than baseline models, and uncovers meteorologically relevant regimes.

paragraphs: The paper addresses wind forecasting over horizons of half an hour to six hours, a task relevant to incorporating wind power into the electrical grid. It focuses on two difficulties: observations may be missing, and relationships between wind measurements at different locations can change with the weather regime. A useful forecasting model therefore needs to accommodate incomplete records and changing dependencies.

The authors use auto-regressive hidden Markov models to represent these regimes and their associated temporal behavior. These models belong to the conditional linear Gaussian family. Although they offer a natural way to describe weather regimes, exact inference with missing observations is computationally hard. The paper introduces a simple approximate inference method to make this approach practical.

On publicly available wind data from two geographically distinct regions, the approach produces significantly more accurate forecasts than the evaluated baselines. It also identifies regimes with meteorological relevance. These findings support the value of modeling changing weather conditions explicitly, while the authors suggest that the inference method may also apply to other temporal problems involving continuous variables.
summary.tldr: A regime-aware wind forecasting model uses approximate inference to handle missing data and improves predictions in two regional evaluations.

title: Auto-Regressive HMM Inference with Incomplete Data for Short-Horizon Wind Forecasting

abstract: This paper is concerned with rank aggregation, which aims to combine multiple input rankings to get a better ranking. A popular approach to rank aggregation is based on probabilistic models on permutations, e.g., the Luce model and the Mallows model. However, these models have their limitations in either poor expressiveness or high computational complexity. To avoid these limitations, in this paper, we propose a new model, which is defined with a coset-permutation distance, and models the generation of a permutation as a stagewise process. We refer to the new model as coset-permutation distance based stagewise (CPS) model. The CPS model has rich expressiveness and can therefore be used in versatile applications, because many different permutation distances can be used to induce the coset-permutation distance. The complexity of the CPS model is low because of the stagewise decomposition of the permutation probability and the efficient computation of most coset-permutation distances. We apply the CPS model to supervised rank aggregation, derive the learning and inference algorithms, and empirically study their effectiveness and efficiency. Experiments on public datasets show that the derived algorithms based on the CPS model can achieve state-of-the-art ranking accuracy, and are much more efficient than previous algorithms.

paragraphs: Rank aggregation combines several input orderings into a single ranking. Probabilistic approaches describe how rankings arise, but the paper identifies a tension in existing models between expressive power and computational cost. Its proposed CPS model aims to describe a broad range of ranking behavior while keeping learning and prediction manageable.

The model builds a permutation through a sequence of stages and uses a coset-permutation distance to describe ranking differences. Different permutation distances can induce this distance, giving the model flexibility. Computational efficiency comes from decomposing the permutation probability across stages and from the efficient computation of most of the associated distances. These two design choices address expressiveness and cost together.

Experiments on public datasets show that the resulting algorithms can achieve leading ranking accuracy while being much faster than previous algorithms. The reported contribution is therefore a flexible probabilistic representation accompanied by practical learning and inference procedures.
summary.tldr: The CPS model combines flexible ranking distances with stagewise probabilities to support accurate and efficient supervised rank aggregation.

title: A New Probabilistic Model for Rank Aggregation

abstract: We present a new online learning algorithm that extends the exponentiated gradient to infinite dimensional spaces. Our analysis shows that the algorithm is implicitly able to estimate the $L_2$ norm of the unknown competitor, $U$, achieving a regret bound of the order of $O(U \log (U T+1))\sqrt{T})$, instead of the standard $O((U^2 +1) \sqrt{T})$, achievable without knowing $U$. For this analysis, we introduce novel tools for algorithms with time-varying regularizers, through the use of local smoothness. Through a lower bound, we also show that the algorithm is optimal up to $\sqrt{\log T}$ term for linear and Lipschitz losses.

paragraphs: Online learning algorithms make decisions sequentially and measure performance against a competitor chosen for comparison. This paper extends exponentiated gradient to infinite-dimensional spaces. A central challenge is adapting to the size of the unknown competitor, measured by its L2 norm, without needing that size as an input to the algorithm.

The analysis shows that the algorithm implicitly estimates this norm. Its regret bound depends roughly on the norm times a logarithmic factor and the square root of the number of rounds. This improves the dependence on competitor size over the standard bound available without knowing the norm, which contains a quadratic dependence on that quantity.

To establish the result, the authors develop tools for analyzing regularizers that change over time, using local smoothness. They also prove a lower bound showing that the algorithm is optimal up to a square-root logarithmic factor in the number of rounds for linear and Lipschitz losses. The contribution combines adaptation to an unknown competitor with a guarantee that remains meaningful in infinite-dimensional settings.
summary.tldr: An infinite-dimensional exponentiated-gradient algorithm adapts to an unknown competitor norm and achieves near-optimal regret guarantees.

title: Dimension-Free Exponentiated Gradient

abstract: Dirichlet process mixture of Gaussians (DPMG) has been used in the literature for clustering and density estimation problems. However, many real-world data exhibit cluster distributions that cannot be captured by a single Gaussian. Modeling such data sets by DPMG creates several extraneous clusters even when clusters are relatively well-defined. Herein, we present the infinite mixture of infinite Gaussian mixtures (I2GMM) for more flexible modeling of data sets with skewed and multi-modal cluster distributions. Instead of using a single Gaussian for each cluster as in the standard DPMG model, the generative model of I2GMM uses a single DPMG for each cluster. The individual DPMGs are linked together through centering of their base distributions at the atoms of a higher level DP prior. Inference is performed by a collapsed Gibbs sampler that also enables partial parallelization. Experimental results on several artificial and real-world data sets suggest the proposed I2GMM model can predict clusters more accurately than existing variational Bayes and Gibbs sampler versions of DPMG.

paragraphs: A cluster can have a skewed shape or several peaks, making a single Gaussian an inadequate description. The paper explains that a Dirichlet process mixture of Gaussians can then split a relatively well-defined cluster into several extra clusters. It proposes a model that separates the flexibility needed within a cluster from the identification of clusters themselves.

The infinite mixture of infinite Gaussian mixtures assigns a whole Dirichlet process Gaussian mixture to each cluster. These individual mixtures are linked through a higher-level Dirichlet process prior that determines the centers of their base distributions. This hierarchy allows a cluster's distribution to be represented by multiple Gaussian components.

Inference uses a collapsed Gibbs sampler that permits partial parallelization. Experiments on artificial and real-world datasets suggest more accurate cluster prediction than the tested variational Bayes and Gibbs-sampling versions of the standard model. The findings support the proposed distinction between a meaningful cluster and the Gaussian components needed to describe its internal shape, particularly for skewed and multimodal cluster distributions.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical mixture model lets each cluster contain multiple Gaussian components, improving flexibility for skewed and multimodal cluster shapes.

title: The Infinite Mixture of Infinite Gaussian Mixtures

abstract: We consider the problem of finding clusters in an unweighted graph, when the graph is partially observed. We analyze two programs, one which works for dense graphs and one which works for both sparse and dense graphs, but requires some a priori knowledge of the total cluster size, that are based on the convex optimization approach for low-rank matrix recovery using nuclear norm minimization. For the commonly used Stochastic Block Model, we obtain \emph{explicit} bounds on the parameters of the problem (size and sparsity of clusters, the amount of observed data) and the regularization parameter characterize the success and failure of the programs. We corroborate our theoretical findings through extensive simulations. We also run our algorithm on a real data set obtained from crowdsourcing an image classification task on the Amazon Mechanical Turk, and observe significant performance improvement over traditional methods such as k-means.

paragraphs: Finding groups in a graph becomes harder when only part of the graph is observed. This paper studies that problem for unweighted graphs using convex optimization methods associated with low-rank matrix recovery. Both proposed programs use nuclear norm minimization to recover structure from incomplete graph information.

The two programs have different scopes. One handles dense graphs. The other handles both sparse and dense graphs but needs some prior knowledge of the total cluster size. Under the Stochastic Block Model, the authors derive explicit bounds involving cluster size, sparsity, the amount of observed data, and the regularization parameter. These bounds characterize when the programs succeed or fail.

Extensive simulations support the theoretical analysis. The authors also apply their algorithm to data from an image classification task crowdsourced through Amazon Mechanical Turk, reporting substantial improvement over traditional methods such as k-means. The combination of explicit recovery bounds and empirical evaluation helps connect the optimization approach to the practical question of how much incomplete graph information can still support clustering.
summary.tldr: Two convex methods recover clusters from partially observed graphs, with explicit success and failure bounds under the Stochastic Block Model.

title: Graph Clustering With Missing Data: Convex Algorithms and Analysis

abstract: In this paper we propose a framework for supervised and semi-supervised learning based on reformulating the learning problem as a regularized Fredholm integral equation. Our approach fits naturally into the kernel framework and can be interpreted as constructing new data-dependent kernels, which we call Fredholm kernels. We proceed to discuss the noise assumption" for semi-supervised learning and provide evidence evidence both theoretical and experimental that Fredholm kernels can effectively utilize unlabeled data under the noise assumption. We demonstrate that methods based on Fredholm learning show very competitive performance in the standard semi-supervised learning setting."

Our approach fits naturally into the kernel framework and can be interpreted as constructing new data-dependent kernels, which we call Fredholm kernels. We proceed to discuss the noise assumption" for semi-supervised learning and provide evidence evidence both theoretical and experimental that Fredholm kernels can effectively utilize unlabeled data under the noise assumption. paragraphs: The paper proposes a common framework for supervised learning and semi-supervised learning, where labeled and unlabeled data are used together. Its starting point is to rewrite the learning problem as a regularized Fredholm integral equation. This gives a mathematical formulation that fits within kernel methods while changing how the learning problem is represented.

The same approach can be understood as constructing new kernels that depend on the data. The authors call these Fredholm kernels. This interpretation connects the integral-equation formulation to the kernel framework, making the construction of a data-dependent kernel the bridge between the mathematical reformulation and its use for learning.

For semi-supervised learning, the authors examine a condition they call the noise assumption. They provide both theoretical and experimental evidence that Fredholm kernels can use unlabeled data effectively under that assumption. They also report very competitive performance in the standard semi-supervised setting. The findings therefore link the value of unlabeled data to a stated assumption and support the proposed formulation with both analysis and experiments.
summary.tldr: Fredholm kernels recast learning through regularized integral equations and can exploit unlabeled data under the paper's noise assumption.

title: Learning with Fredholm Kernels

abstract: We present a unified framework for learning continuous control policies usingbackpropagation. It supports stochastic control by treating stochasticity in theBellman equation as a deterministic function of exogenous noise. The productis a spectrum of general policy gradient algorithms that range from model-freemethods with value functions to model-based methods without value functions.We use learned models but only require observations from the environment insteadof observations from model-predicted trajectories, minimizing the impactof compounded model errors. We apply these algorithms first to a toy stochasticcontrol problem and then to several physics-based control problems in simulation.One of these variants, SVG(1), shows the effectiveness of learning models, valuefunctions, and policies simultaneously in continuous domains.

The productis a spectrum of general policy gradient algorithms that range from model-freemethods with value functions to model-based methods without value functions.We use learned models but only require observations from the environment insteadof observations from model-predicted trajectories, minimizing the impactof compounded model errors. paragraphs: This paper develops a common backpropagation framework for learning policies that choose continuous actions. A central challenge is incorporating randomness into the calculation of how policy changes affect future value. The authors handle this by expressing stochasticity in the Bellman equation as a deterministic function of external noise.

That representation produces a family of policy-gradient algorithms spanning different uses of learned models and value functions. At one end are model-free methods with value functions; at the other are model-based methods without them. Although the framework uses learned models, it requires observations from the environment rather than observations along trajectories predicted by those models, reducing the impact of model errors accumulating across simulated steps.

The algorithms are evaluated on a toy stochastic control problem and several physics-based control problems in simulation. One variant, SVG(1), demonstrates the effectiveness of learning a model, value function, and policy simultaneously in continuous domains. The contribution is both a unifying way to derive these algorithms and evidence that the combined learning strategy can work in the simulated tasks considered.
summary.tldr: Stochastic value gradients unify continuous-control policy learning through backpropagation while reducing reliance on model-predicted trajectories.

title: Learning Continuous Control Policies by Stochastic Value Gradients

abstract: Matrix completion problems have been widely studied under special low dimensional structures such as low rank or structure induced by decomposable norms. In this paper, we present a unified analysis of matrix completion under general low-dimensional structural constraints induced by {\em any} norm regularization.We consider two estimators for the general problem of structured matrix completion, and provide unified upper bounds on the sample complexity and the estimation error. Our analysis relies on generic chaining, and we establish two intermediate results of independent interest: (a) in characterizing the size or complexity of low dimensional subsets in high dimensional ambient space, a certain \textit{\modified}~complexity measure encountered in the analysis of matrix completion problems is characterized in terms of a well understood complexity measure of Gaussian widths, and (b) it is shown that a form of restricted strong convexity holds for matrix completion problems under general norm regularization. Further, we provide several non-trivial examples of structures included in our framework, notably including the recently proposed spectral $k$-support norm.

paragraphs: Matrix completion estimates missing entries by exploiting structure in the underlying matrix. Much existing analysis focuses on particular structures, such as low rank or those expressed by decomposable norms. This paper develops a common analysis for low-dimensional structural constraints induced by any norm regularization.

The authors study two estimators and derive unified upper bounds on sample complexity and estimation error. Their analysis uses generic chaining to handle the complexity of the relevant structured sets. One intermediate result relates a modified complexity measure arising in matrix completion to Gaussian width, a more established way to quantify the size of such sets.

A second intermediate result establishes a form of restricted strong convexity for matrix completion under general norm regularization. Together, these tools support guarantees across multiple structural choices within one framework. The examples include the spectral k-support norm. The contribution is a reusable theoretical account of how structural constraints affect data requirements and estimation accuracy, extending beyond the special norm classes previously emphasized.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis bounds sample complexity and estimation error for matrix completion under structural constraints induced by any norm.

title: Unified View of Matrix Completion under General Structural Constraints

abstract: The Jaccard index is a standard statistics for comparing the pairwise similarity between data samples. This paper investigates the problem of estimating a Jaccard index matrix when there are missing observations in data samples. Starting from a Jaccard index matrix approximated from the incomplete data, our method calibrates the matrix to meet the requirement of positive semi-definiteness and other constraints, through a simple alternating projection algorithm. Compared with conventional approaches that estimate the similarity matrix based on the imputed data, our method has a strong advantage in that the calibrated matrix is guaranteed to be closer to the unknown ground truth in the Frobenius norm than the un-calibrated matrix (except in special cases they are identical). We carried out a series of empirical experiments and the results confirmed our theoretical justification. The evaluation also reported significantly improved results in real learning tasks on benchmarked datasets.

paragraphs: The Jaccard index measures similarity between pairs of data samples. Missing observations make those similarities difficult to estimate, and errors accumulate across the matrix of pairwise comparisons. This paper begins with a Jaccard matrix approximated from incomplete data and improves it by enforcing structural requirements on the matrix.

The proposed calibration uses alternating projections to satisfy positive semidefiniteness and other constraints. Its focus is the similarity matrix itself, whereas conventional approaches first fill in missing data and then calculate similarities. Enforcing matrix-level requirements gives the method a direct way to improve the object that subsequent learning tasks will use.

The authors prove that calibration brings the matrix closer to the unknown true matrix in Frobenius norm, except for special cases where calibration leaves it unchanged. This guarantee compares the calibrated estimate with its uncalibrated starting point. Empirical experiments support the theoretical result, and benchmark learning tasks show significantly improved outcomes. Together, these findings connect a matrix-level error guarantee to practical benefits in downstream learning.
summary.tldr: Calibrating an incomplete-data Jaccard matrix to satisfy structural constraints improves its Frobenius-distance accuracy, except when it remains unchanged.

title: Estimating Jaccard Index with Missing Observations: A Matrix Calibration Approach

abstract: Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and Belief Propagation (BP) are the most popular algorithms for computational inference in Graphical Models (GM). In principle, MCMC is an exact probabilistic method which, however, often suffers from exponentially slow mixing. In contrast, BP is a deterministic method, which is typically fast, empirically very successful, however in general lacking control of accuracy over loopy graphs. In this paper, we introduce MCMC algorithms correcting the approximation error of BP, i.e., we provide a way to compensate for BP errors via a consecutive BP-aware MCMC. Our framework is based on the Loop Calculus (LC) approach which allows to express the BP error as a sum of weighted generalized loops. Although the full series is computationally intractable, it is known that a truncated series, summing up all 2-regular loops, is computable in polynomial-time for planar pair-wise binary GMs and it also provides a highly accurate approximation empirically. Motivated by this, we, first, propose a polynomial-time approximation MCMC scheme for the truncated series of general (non-planar) pair-wise binary models. Our main idea here is to use the Worm algorithm, known to provide fast mixing in other (related) problems, and then design an appropriate rejection scheme to sample 2-regular loops. Furthermore, we also design an efficient rejection-free MCMC scheme for approximating the full series. The main novelty underlying our design is in utilizing the concept of cycle basis, which provides an efficient decomposition of the generalized loops. In essence, the proposed MCMC schemes run on transformed GM built upon the non-trivial BP solution, and our experiments show that this synthesis of BP and MCMC outperforms both direct MCMC and bare BP schemes.

paragraphs: Belief propagation often gives fast, useful inference in graphical models, but its accuracy is generally uncontrolled on graphs containing loops. Markov chain Monte Carlo has an exact probabilistic foundation but can mix extremely slowly. This paper combines them by using MCMC to correct errors remaining after a belief-propagation calculation.

Both schemes operate on transformed graphical models built from a nontrivial belief-propagation solution. Experiments show that the combined approach outperforms direct MCMC and uncorrected belief propagation. The contribution uses the initial approximation to organize subsequent sampling around its remaining error.
summary.tldr: The paper builds MCMC samplers around belief-propagation solutions to estimate and correct their loop-related approximation errors.

title: Synthesis of MCMC and Belief Propagation

abstract: Scalable and effective exploration remains a key challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). While there are methods with optimality guarantees in the setting of discrete state and action spaces, these methods cannot be applied in high-dimensional deep RL scenarios. As such, most contemporary RL relies on simple heuristics such as epsilon-greedy exploration or adding Gaussian noise to the controls. This paper introduces Variational Information Maximizing Exploration (VIME), an exploration strategy based on maximization of information gain about the agent's belief of environment dynamics. We propose a practical implementation, using variational inference in Bayesian neural networks which efficiently handles continuous state and action spaces. VIME modifies the MDP reward function, and can be applied with several different underlying RL algorithms. We demonstrate that VIME achieves significantly better performance compared to heuristic exploration methods across a variety of continuous control tasks and algorithms, including tasks with very sparse rewards.

paragraphs: Exploration becomes difficult when reinforcement learning involves high-dimensional observations or continuous actions. Methods with optimality guarantees in discrete settings do not directly carry over to these scenarios, and simple action-randomization heuristics are common. VIME proposes a more directed objective: seek experiences that provide information about the environment's dynamics.

The method represents the agent's beliefs about those dynamics with a Bayesian neural network and uses variational inference for a practical implementation. Exploration is driven by information gain about that belief. VIME incorporates this objective by modifying the reward function, allowing it to work with several different underlying reinforcement learning algorithms.

The authors evaluate VIME across continuous control tasks and multiple learning algorithms, including tasks where external rewards are very sparse. They report significantly better performance than the heuristic exploration methods compared. These findings support information gain as a useful exploration signal in the tested settings. The contribution combines that principle with an implementation designed to handle continuous state and action spaces efficiently.
summary.tldr: VIME rewards information gain about environment dynamics, improving exploration over tested heuristics across continuous control tasks, including sparse-reward tasks.

title: VIME: Variational Information Maximizing Exploration

abstract: We introduce a hierarchical model which allows to estimate a group-average piecewise-geodesic trajectory in the Riemannian space of measurements and individual variability. This model falls into the well defined mixed-effect models. The subject-specific trajectories are defined through spatial and temporal transformations of the group-average piecewise-geodesic path, component by component. Thus we can apply our model to a wide variety of situations. Due to the non-linearity of the model, we use the Stochastic Approximation Expectation-Maximization algorithm to estimate the model parameters. Experiments on synthetic data validate this choice. The model is then applied to the metastatic renal cancer chemotherapy monitoring: we run estimations on RECIST scores of treated patients and estimate the time they escape from the treatment. Experiments highlight the role of the different parameters on the response to treatment.

paragraphs: Repeated measurements can follow a shared pattern over time while differing across individuals in both their values and their timing. This paper models such data when measurements lie in a Riemannian space. Its population trajectory is piecewise geodesic: it consists of connected path segments that respect the geometry of the measurement space.

The hierarchical mixed-effects model describes each subject through spatial and temporal transformations of that group-average path, applied component by component. This gives individual trajectories a common reference while allowing differences in their progression. Because the model is nonlinear, the authors estimate its parameters with the Stochastic Approximation Expectation-Maximization algorithm and validate that choice using synthetic data.

The application concerns monitoring chemotherapy in metastatic renal cancer. Using patients' RECIST scores, the authors estimate when patients escape from treatment and examine how different parameters relate to treatment response. The work provides a framework for representing shared and individual progression jointly, with the medical application illustrating how timing differences can become quantities of interest.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical geometric model learns shared progression and individual timing differences, with an application to chemotherapy response monitoring.

title: Learning spatiotemporal piecewise-geodesic trajectories from longitudinal manifold-valued data

abstract: Hypergraph partitioning is an important problem in machine learning, computer vision and network analytics. A widely used method for hypergraph partitioning relies on minimizing a normalized sum of the costs of partitioning hyperedges across clusters. Algorithmic solutions based on this approach assume that different partitions of a hyperedge incur the same cost. However, this assumption fails to leverage the fact that different subsets of vertices within the same hyperedge may have different structural importance. We hence propose a new hypergraph clustering technique, termed inhomogeneous hypergraph partitioning, which assigns different costs to different hyperedge cuts. We prove that inhomogeneous partitioning produces a quadratic approximation to the optimal solution if the inhomogeneous costs satisfy submodularity constraints. Moreover, we demonstrate that inhomogenous partitioning offers significant performance improvements in applications such as structure learning of rankings, subspace segmentation and motif clustering.

paragraphs: Hypergraph clustering partitions vertices into groups when a single hyperedge can connect several vertices. A common objective measures the normalized cost of splitting these hyperedges across clusters. The paper challenges the assumption that every way of splitting a particular hyperedge should incur the same cost, because different subsets may have different structural importance.

The proposed inhomogeneous hypergraph partitioning method assigns different costs to different cuts of the same hyperedge. This lets the clustering objective distinguish between ways of separating a group of connected vertices. The distinction matters whenever the identities of the separated subsets carry information that a uniform cutting cost would discard.

The authors prove a quadratic approximation guarantee when the cut costs satisfy submodularity constraints. That guarantee is conditional on the specified cost structure. They also demonstrate significant performance improvements in learning structures from rankings, subspace segmentation, and motif clustering. These applications support the practical value of encoding more detail in hyperedge costs, while the analysis establishes a guarantee for an identified class of such costs.
summary.tldr: Allowing different cuts of a hyperedge to have different costs improves clustering, with an approximation guarantee under submodularity constraints.

title: Inhomogeneous Hypergraph Clustering with Applications

abstract: We examine a class of embeddings based on structured random matrices with orthogonal rows which can be applied in many machine learning applications including dimensionality reduction and kernel approximation. For both the Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform and the angular kernel, we show that we can select matrices yielding guaranteed improved performance in accuracy and/or speed compared to earlier methods. We introduce matrices with complex entries which give significant further accuracy improvement. We provide geometric and Markov chain-based perspectives to help understand the benefits, and empirical results which suggest that the approach is helpful in a wider range of applications.

We introduce matrices with complex entries which give significant further accuracy improvement. We provide geometric and Markov chain-based perspectives to help understand the benefits, and empirical results which suggest that the approach is helpful in a wider range of applications.

paragraphs: The paper investigates embeddings built from structured random matrices whose rows are orthogonal. These transformations can serve applications such as dimensionality reduction and kernel approximation. The main question is how the combination of matrix structure and orthogonality affects the accuracy and computational speed of those representations.

For the Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform and the angular kernel, the authors show that suitable matrix choices provide guaranteed improvements in accuracy, speed, or both compared with earlier methods. They also introduce matrices with complex-valued entries and report significant additional accuracy improvements. The guarantee therefore concerns selected constructions and the stated applications, rather than every structured random matrix.

The authors develop geometric and Markov-chain-based perspectives to explain the benefits. Empirical results further suggest that the approach may be helpful across a wider range of applications. The paper thus combines targeted guarantees, new matrix constructions, and explanatory viewpoints, while distinguishing the proven improvements in specific settings from the broader usefulness suggested by experiments.
summary.tldr: Selected structured random orthogonal embeddings improve accuracy or speed in dimensionality reduction and kernel approximation.

title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Structured Random Orthogonal Embeddings

abstract: We propose a principled method for gradient-based regularization of the critic of GAN-like models trained by adversarially optimizing the kernel of a Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). We show that controlling the gradient of the critic is vital to having a sensible loss function, and devise a method to enforce exact, analytical gradient constraints at no additional cost compared to existing approximate techniques based on additive regularizers. The new loss function is provably continuous, and experiments show that it stabilizes and accelerates training, giving image generation models that outperform state-of-the art methods on $160 \times 160$ CelebA and $64 \times 64$ unconditional ImageNet.

paragraphs: The paper examines generative models trained by adversarially optimizing the kernel of Maximum Mean Discrepancy, or MMD. In this setting, the critic shapes the comparison used to train the generator. The authors show that controlling the critic's gradient is essential for obtaining a sensible loss function, making regularization a central design issue.

They introduce a principled method that enforces gradient constraints exactly through analytical means. Existing techniques discussed in the abstract instead use additive regularizers to approximate this control. The proposed constraints come at no additional cost relative to those approximate techniques, and the resulting loss function is provably continuous.

Experiments show more stable and faster training. The resulting image generators outperform state-of-the-art methods on CelebA at 160-by-160 resolution and unconditional ImageNet at 64-by-64 resolution. The contribution links a mathematical property of the training objective to observed optimization improvements and generation performance. Its exactness claim concerns the analytical gradient constraints, while the training and image-quality improvements are supported by the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: Exact analytical gradient constraints give MMD-based adversarial models a continuous loss and improve training and image generation in experiments.

title: On gradient regularizers for MMD GANs

abstract: Real-world applications often naturally decompose into several sub-tasks. In many settings (e.g., robotics) demonstrations provide a natural way to specify the sub-tasks. However, most methods for learning from demonstrations either do not provide guarantees that the artifacts learned for the sub-tasks can be safely recombined or limit the types of composition available. Motivated by this deficit, we consider the problem of inferring Boolean non-Markovian rewards (also known as logical trace properties or specifications) from demonstrations provided by an agent operating in an uncertain, stochastic environment. Crucially, specifications admit well-defined composition rules that are typically easy to interpret. In this paper, we formulate the specification inference task as a maximum a posteriori (MAP) probability inference problem, apply the principle of maximum entropy to derive an analytic demonstration likelihood model and give an efficient approach to search for the most likely specification in a large candidate pool of specifications. In our experiments, we demonstrate how learning specifications can help avoid common problems that often arise due to ad-hoc reward composition.

paragraphs: Many practical tasks consist of smaller tasks that must later be combined. Demonstrations can communicate those pieces, but learned rewards do not always provide clear rules for combining them safely. This paper learns logical specifications from demonstrations, using representations with well-defined and typically interpretable composition rules.

The specifications are Boolean, non-Markovian rewards: they describe whether an entire sequence of behavior satisfies a condition, rather than assigning a reward based only on the current state. The authors formulate their inference as maximum a posteriori estimation in a stochastic environment. A maximum-entropy principle yields an analytic model of how likely a demonstration is under a candidate specification.

An efficient search procedure then identifies the most likely specification from a large candidate collection. Experiments demonstrate how these learned specifications can avoid common problems caused by ad-hoc reward composition. The approach matters because it makes the meaning of a learned sub-task explicit in a form that supports composition, connecting imitation from examples with a structured account of what successful behavior requires.
summary.tldr: The method infers composable logical task specifications from demonstrations through Bayesian inference and a maximum-entropy likelihood.

title: Learning Task Specifications from Demonstrations

abstract: Semi-supervised learning (SSL) provides a powerful framework for leveraging unlabeled data when labels are limited or expensive to obtain. SSL algorithms based on deep neural networks have recently proven successful on standard benchmark tasks. However, we argue that these benchmarks fail to address many issues that SSL algorithms would face in real-world applications. After creating a unified reimplementation of various widely-used SSL techniques, we test them in a suite of experiments designed to address these issues. We find that the performance of simple baselines which do not use unlabeled data is often underreported, SSL methods differ in sensitivity to the amount of labeled and unlabeled data, and performance can degrade substantially when the unlabeled dataset contains out-of-distribution examples. To help guide SSL research towards real-world applicability, we make our unified reimplemention and evaluation platform publicly available.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses unlabeled examples alongside a smaller labeled dataset. Its appeal is strongest when obtaining labels is costly, but strong benchmark performance may leave practical questions unanswered. This paper examines how established deep semi-supervised methods behave under evaluation conditions designed to address issues that arise in real applications.

The authors first build a unified reimplementation of widely used techniques, providing a common platform for comparison. Their experiments find that simple methods using no unlabeled data often perform better than reported comparisons suggest. They also find that semi-supervised methods respond differently to changes in the quantities of labeled and unlabeled examples.

A further finding is that performance can deteriorate substantially when the unlabeled pool contains out-of-distribution examples. This makes the composition of the available data an important part of evaluating the value of semi-supervised learning. The paper's contribution is an empirical assessment of these factors together with a publicly released implementation and evaluation platform. Its findings encourage comparisons that account for baseline strength, data quantity, and the relevance of unlabeled examples.
summary.tldr: A unified evaluation shows that semi-supervised learning results depend on baseline strength, data quantities, and whether unlabeled examples fit the task.

title: Realistic Evaluation of Deep Semi-Supervised Learning Algorithms

abstract: We propose in this paper a general framework for deriving loss functions for structured prediction. In our framework, the user chooses a convex set including the output space and provides an oracle for projecting onto that set. Given that oracle, our framework automatically generates a corresponding convex and smooth loss function. As we show, adding a projection as output layer provably makes the loss smaller. We identify the marginal polytope, the output space's convex hull, as the best convex set on which to project. However, because the projection onto the marginal polytope can sometimes be expensive to compute, we allow to use any convex superset instead, with potentially cheaper-to-compute projection. Since efficient projection algorithms are available for numerous convex sets, this allows us to construct loss functions for a variety of tasks. On the theoretical side, when combined with calibrated decoding, we prove that our loss functions can be used as a consistent surrogate for a (potentially non-convex) target loss function of interest. We demonstrate our losses on label ranking, ordinal regression and multilabel classification, confirming the improved accuracy enabled by projections.

paragraphs: Structured prediction requires choosing outputs with internal organization, such as rankings or collections of labels. This paper provides a framework for constructing loss functions from a geometric description of those outputs. The user selects a convex set containing the output space and supplies a procedure for projecting onto that set; the framework then produces a convex, smooth loss.

The authors prove that adding a projection at the output layer makes the loss smaller. They identify the convex hull of the output space, called the marginal polytope, as the best set for projection. Because that projection can be expensive, the framework also accepts larger convex sets whose projections may be cheaper to compute.

The theoretical guarantee links these losses to a target loss that may be nonconvex: combined with calibrated decoding, they provide a consistent surrogate. Experiments on label ranking, ordinal regression, and multilabel classification confirm accuracy improvements from projections. The framework thus connects available projection algorithms with trainable losses while exposing a choice between the preferred geometry and computational convenience.
summary.tldr: Projection procedures generate smooth convex losses for structured prediction, with conditional consistency guarantees and demonstrated accuracy improvements.

title: Structured Prediction with Projection Oracles

abstract: Achieving robustness to distributional shift is a longstanding and challenging goal of computer vision. Data augmentation is a commonly used approach for improving robustness, however robustness gains are typically not uniform across corruption types. Indeed increasing performance in the presence of random noise is often met with reduced performance on other corruptions such as contrast change. Understanding when and why these sorts of trade-offs occur is a crucial step towards mitigating them. Towards this end, we investigate recently observed trade-offs caused by Gaussian data augmentation and adversarial training. We find that both methods improve robustness to corruptions that are concentrated in the high frequency domain while reducing robustness to corruptions that are concentrated in the low frequency domain. This suggests that one way to mitigate these trade-offs via data augmentation is to use a more diverse set of augmentations. Towards this end we observe that AutoAugment, a recently proposed data augmentation policy optimized for clean accuracy, achieves state-of-the-art robustness on the CIFAR-10-C benchmark.
