paragraphs: Training an image model to withstand one kind of corruption can make it less reliable on another. This paper examines that tradeoff through the frequency content of image changes. High frequencies describe rapidly varying image patterns, while low frequencies describe more slowly varying structure. This perspective helps organize robustness gains and losses that otherwise appear to be separate effects.

The authors study Gaussian data augmentation and adversarial training. They find that both improve robustness to corruptions concentrated at high frequencies while reducing robustness to corruptions concentrated at low frequencies. The result identifies a shared pattern across these two training approaches, rather than treating robustness as a single property that improves uniformly.

These observations suggest that a more diverse collection of augmentations could help mitigate the tradeoff. The authors also report that AutoAugment achieves state-of-the-art robustness on CIFAR-10-C despite being optimized for accuracy on clean images. That finding supports the value of augmentation diversity, while the frequency analysis explains why gains against one family of corruptions need not extend to others.
summary.tldr: Frequency analysis reveals why Gaussian augmentation and adversarial training can improve robustness to some image corruptions while worsening it for others.

title: A Fourier Perspective on Model Robustness in Computer Vision

abstract: In correlation clustering, we are given $n$ objects together with a binary similarity score between each pair of them. The goal is to partition the objects into clusters so to minimise the disagreements with the scores. In this work we investigate correlation clustering as an active learning problem: each similarity score can be learned by making a query, and the goal is to minimise both the disagreements and the total number of queries. On the one hand, we describe simple active learning algorithms, which provably achieve an almost optimal trade-off while giving cluster recovery guarantees, and we test them on different datasets. On the other hand, we prove information-theoretical bounds on the number of queries necessary to guarantee a prescribed disagreement bound. These results give a rich characterization of the trade-off between queries and clustering error.

In this work we investigate correlation clustering as an active learning problem: each similarity score can be learned by making a query, and the goal is to minimise both the disagreements and the total number of queries. On the one hand, we describe simple active learning algorithms, which provably achieve an almost optimal trade-off while giving cluster recovery guarantees, and we test them on different datasets. paragraphs: Correlation clustering groups objects using pairwise judgments of whether they are similar or dissimilar. A disagreement occurs when a clustering separates a similar pair or places a dissimilar pair together. The usual objective is to minimize these disagreements. This paper adds a second concern: obtaining the pairwise judgments can itself be costly.

The authors treat similarity information as something an algorithm must actively request. Instead of assuming that every pairwise score is already available, their algorithms choose queries while constructing a clustering. The goal is therefore to balance the quality of the resulting groups against the amount of information collected.

The paper provides simple active learning algorithms with provable, almost optimal tradeoffs and guarantees concerning cluster recovery, alongside tests on different datasets. It also establishes information-theoretic lower bounds on the queries needed to guarantee a chosen disagreement level. These two sides clarify both what the algorithms can achieve and how much querying is fundamentally necessary. The contribution is a characterization of the cost of information in clustering, not merely a procedure that asks fewer questions.
summary.tldr: Adaptive similarity queries yield provably near-optimal tradeoffs between clustering disagreements and the cost of collecting pairwise information.

title: Correlation Clustering with Adaptive Similarity Queries

abstract: We study the problem of minimizing a strongly convex, smooth function when we have noisy estimates of its gradient. We propose a novel multistage accelerated algorithm that is universally optimal in the sense that it achieves the optimal rate both in the deterministic and stochastic case and operates without knowledge of noise characteristics. The algorithm consists of stages that use a stochastic version of Nesterov's method with a specific restart and parameters selected to achieve the fastest reduction in the bias-variance terms in the convergence rate bounds.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of minimizing a strongly convex, smooth function when we have noisy estimates of its gradient. We propose a novel multistage accelerated algorithm that is universally optimal in the sense that it achieves the optimal rate both in the deterministic and stochastic case and operates without knowledge of noise characteristics. The algorithm consists of stages that use a stochastic version of Nesterov's method with a specific restart and parameters selected to achieve the fastest reduction in the bias-variance terms in the convergence rate bounds.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization when the function being minimized is smooth and strongly convex, but its gradients may be noisy. The challenge is to make rapid progress while controlling the effects of unreliable gradient estimates. An algorithm suited to exact gradients also needs to handle noise without letting that noise undermine its convergence.

The proposed method organizes accelerated optimization into multiple stages. Each stage uses a stochastic version of Nesterov’s method, with a particular restart scheme and carefully chosen parameters. These choices target the bias and variance terms in the convergence bounds: the method coordinates progress toward the optimum with control over the contribution from gradient noise.

The central result is optimal convergence rates in both deterministic and stochastic settings, without requiring knowledge of the noise characteristics. Here, “universally optimal” refers to these two settings within the stated smooth, strongly convex problem class. The contribution is a staged acceleration strategy that achieves the appropriate rate whether gradients are exact or noisy.
summary.tldr: A multistage accelerated optimizer achieves optimal rates for smooth, strongly convex objectives with or without gradient noise, without knowing the noise characteristics.

title: A Universally Optimal Multistage Accelerated Stochastic Gradient Method

abstract: We study the safe reinforcement learning problem with nonlinear function approximation, where policy optimization is formulated as a constrained optimization problem with both the objective and the constraint being nonconvex functions. For such a problem, we construct a sequence of surrogate convex constrained optimization problems by replacing the nonconvex functions locally with convex quadratic functions obtained from policy gradient estimators. We prove that the solutions to these surrogate problems converge to a stationary point of the original nonconvex problem. Furthermore, to extend our theoretical results, we apply our algorithm to examples of optimal control and multi-agent reinforcement learning with safety constraints.

For such a problem, we construct a sequence of surrogate convex constrained optimization problems by replacing the nonconvex functions locally with convex quadratic functions obtained from policy gradient estimators. We prove that the solutions to these surrogate problems converge to a stationary point of the original nonconvex problem. Furthermore, to extend our theoretical results, we apply our algorithm to examples of optimal control and multi-agent reinforcement learning with safety constraints.

paragraphs: This paper treats safe reinforcement learning as policy optimization subject to a constraint. With nonlinear function approximation, both the objective and the constraint can be nonconvex, making the optimization problem difficult. The aim is to develop an update procedure with a convergence result for this constrained setting.

The method builds a sequence of simpler optimization problems. At each stage, local convex quadratic functions replace the original nonconvex functions, using information obtained from policy gradient estimators. Each surrogate problem retains a constrained form, so the procedure addresses the objective and constraint together while working with local approximations that are more manageable to optimize.

The authors prove that solutions of these surrogate problems converge to a stationary point of the original problem. Stationarity is the stated guarantee; the abstract does not claim a globally optimal policy. They also apply the algorithm to optimal control and multi-agent reinforcement learning examples with safety constraints, extending the presentation from a convergence argument to concrete constrained decision-making settings.
summary.tldr: Local convex quadratic surrogate problems yield a policy optimization method with convergence to a stationary point of the original safety-constrained problem.

title: Convergent Policy Optimization for Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The novel nature of SARS-CoV-2 calls for the development of efficient de novo drug design approaches. In this study, we propose an end-to-end framework, named CogMol (Controlled Generation of Molecules), for designing new drug-like small molecules targeting novel viral proteins with high affinity and off-target selectivity. CogMol combines adaptive pre-training of a molecular SMILES Variational Autoencoder (VAE) and an efficient multi-attribute controlled sampling scheme that uses guidance from attribute predictors trained on latent features. To generate novel and optimal drug-like molecules for unseen viral targets, CogMol leverages a protein-molecule binding affinity predictor that is trained using SMILES VAE embeddings and protein sequence embeddings learned unsupervised from a large corpus. We applied the CogMol framework to three SARS-CoV-2 target proteins: main protease, receptor-binding domain of the spike protein, and non-structural protein 9 replicase. The generated candidates are novel at both the molecular and chemical scaffold levels when compared to the training data. CogMol also includes insilico screening for assessing toxicity of parent molecules and their metabolites with a multi-task toxicity classifier, synthetic feasibility with a chemical retrosynthesis predictor, and target structure binding with docking simulations. Docking reveals favorable binding of generated molecules to the target protein structure, where 87--95\% of high affinity molecules showed docking free energy $<$ -6 kcal/mol. When compared to approved drugs, the majority of designed compounds show low predicted parent molecule and metabolite toxicity and high predicted synthetic feasibility. In summary, CogMol can handle multi-constraint design of synthesizable, low-toxic, drug-like molecules with high target specificity and selectivity, even to novel protein target sequences, and does not need target-dependent fine-tuning of the framework or target structure information.

paragraphs: CogMol designs candidate drug-like molecules while considering several desired properties together, including target binding and selectivity. Its generator uses a variational autoencoder trained on SMILES, a textual representation of molecules. Predictors operating on the learned molecular representations guide sampling toward candidates with the requested combination of attributes.

To address previously unseen protein targets, the framework combines molecular representations with protein sequence representations learned without supervision. A binding affinity predictor connects these two descriptions. The authors apply the framework to three SARS-CoV-2 proteins and report candidates that differ from the training data in both their complete molecular structures and their underlying chemical scaffolds.

summary.tldr: CogMol combines controlled molecular generation and computational screening to design candidates for unseen protein targets under multiple property constraints.

title: CogMol: Target-Specific and Selective Drug Design for COVID-19 Using Deep Generative Models

abstract: The Empirical Revenue Maximization (ERM) is one of the most important price learning algorithms in auction design: as the literature shows it can learn approximately optimal reserve prices for revenue-maximizing auctioneers in both repeated auctions and uniform-price auctions. However, in these applications the agents who provide inputs to ERM have incentives to manipulate the inputs to lower the outputted price. We generalize the definition of an incentive-awareness measure proposed by Lavi et al (2019), to quantify the reduction of ERM's outputted price due to a change of m>=1 out of N input samples, and provide specific convergence rates of this measure to zero as N goes to infinity for different types of input distributions. By adopting this measure, we construct an efficient, approximately incentive-compatible, and revenue-optimal learning algorithm using ERM in repeated auctions against non-myopic bidders, and show approximate group incentive-compatibility in uniform-price auctions.

paragraphs: Empirical Revenue Maximization learns auction reserve prices from observed samples. Its usefulness becomes more complicated when the people supplying those samples can benefit from changing them. A bidder may influence the learning data to push a future price downward, so evaluating price quality alone does not capture how the algorithm behaves with strategic participants.

The paper extends a measure of incentive awareness to quantify how much the output price can fall when someone changes m out of N samples. It establishes rates at which this measure approaches zero as the sample count grows, with different rates for different input distributions. These results describe how manipulation opportunities diminish in the analyzed settings.

The authors then use this measure to build an efficient learning algorithm for repeated auctions with bidders who consider future consequences. They establish approximate incentive compatibility and revenue optimality, and also show approximate group incentive compatibility for uniform-price auctions. The contribution connects statistical price learning with explicit guarantees about strategic behavior.
summary.tldr: The paper quantifies strategic manipulation of learned auction prices and uses the resulting bounds to establish approximate incentive guarantees.

title: A Game-Theoretic Analysis of the Empirical Revenue Maximization Algorithm with Endogenous Sampling

abstract: Graphical models are widely used in science to represent joint probability distributions with an underlying conditional dependence structure. The inverse problem of learning a discrete graphical model given i.i.d samples from its joint distribution can be solved with near-optimal sample complexity using a convex optimization method known as Generalized Regularized Interaction Screening Estimator (GRISE). But the computational cost of GRISE becomes prohibitive when the energy function of the true graphical model has higher order terms. We introduce NeurISE, a neural net based algorithm for graphical model learning, to tackle this limitation of GRISE. We use neural nets as function approximators in an Interaction Screening objective function. The optimization of this objective then produces a neural-net representation for the conditionals of the graphical model. NeurISE algorithm is seen to be a better alternative to GRISE when the energy function of the true model has a high order with a high degree of symmetry. In these cases NeurISE is able to find the correct parsimonious representation for the conditionals without being fed any prior information about the true model. NeurISE can also be used to learn the underlying structure of the true model with some simple modifications to its training procedure. In addition, we also show a variant of NeurISE that can be used to learn a neural net representation for the full energy function of the true model.

paragraphs: Discrete graphical models describe joint probability distributions through relationships among variables. Learning them from independent, identically distributed samples can be statistically efficient with the GRISE estimator, yet computationally expensive when the model’s energy function contains higher-order interactions. NeurISE is introduced to address that computational obstacle.

NeurISE places neural network function approximators inside an Interaction Screening objective. Optimizing this objective produces neural representations of conditional distributions. The authors find it a better alternative to GRISE when the true energy function combines high-order interactions with substantial symmetry. In those cases, it discovers compact, correct conditional representations without being supplied prior information about the true model.

The paper also describes training modifications for learning the underlying dependency structure and a variant that represents the full energy function with a neural network. The contribution therefore covers several aspects of model recovery. Its stated advantage is especially relevant to the high-order, highly symmetric setting, where representing interactions through neural functions can alleviate the computational burden of the earlier approach.
summary.tldr: NeurISE uses neural networks within Interaction Screening to learn compact graphical-model representations, particularly for high-order interactions with strong symmetry.

title: Learning of Discrete Graphical Models with Neural Networks

abstract: Can we predict how well a team of individuals will perform together? How should individuals be rewarded for their contributions to the team performance? Cooperative game theory gives us a powerful set of tools for answering these questions: the characteristic function and solution concepts like the Shapley Value. There are two major difficulties in applying these techniques to real world problems: first, the characteristic function is rarely given to us and needs to be learned from data. Second, the Shapley Value is combinatorial in nature. We introduce a parametric model called cooperative game abstractions (CGAs) for estimating characteristic functions from data. CGAs are easy to learn, readily interpretable, and crucially allows linear-time computation of the Shapley Value. We provide identification results and sample complexity bounds for CGA models as well as error bounds in the estimation of the Shapley Value using CGAs. We apply our methods to study teams of artificial RL agents as well as real world teams from professional sports.

paragraphs: Predicting team performance and assigning credit to individuals are related problems. Cooperative game theory describes a team's performance through a characteristic function and offers contribution measures such as the Shapley Value. Applying these tools is difficult because the characteristic function usually must be learned from observations, and computing Shapley Values involves combinatorial complexity.

The paper introduces cooperative game abstractions, or CGAs, as a parametric model for learning characteristic functions. The proposed representation is interpretable and easy to learn, while allowing Shapley Values to be computed in linear time. It therefore connects estimation of team performance with an efficient way to allocate individual credit within the learned model.

The authors provide identification results, sample complexity bounds, and bounds on errors in the resulting Shapley Value estimates. These results address both learning the model and understanding the reliability of its contribution estimates. Applications cover teams of artificial reinforcement learning agents and professional sports teams, bringing the same modeling framework to computational and real-world teamwork.
summary.tldr: Cooperative game abstractions learn interpretable models of team performance and enable linear-time Shapley Value computation.

title: Evaluating and Rewarding Teamwork Using Cooperative Game Abstractions

abstract: The profile of a sample is the multiset of its symbol frequencies. We show that for samples of discrete distributions, profile entropy is a fundamental measure unifying the concepts of estimation, inference, and compression. Specifically, profile entropy: a) determines the speed of estimating the distribution relative to the best natural estimator; b) characterizes the rate of inferring all symmetric properties compared with the best estimator over any label-invariant distribution collection; c) serves as the limit of profile compression, for which we derive optimal near-linear-time block and sequential algorithms. To further our understanding of profile entropy, we investigate its attributes, provide algorithms for approximating its value, and determine its magnitude for numerous structural distribution families.

To further our understanding of profile entropy, we investigate its attributes, provide algorithms for approximating its value, and determine its magnitude for numerous structural distribution families.

paragraphs: A sample's profile records how frequently its symbols occur while leaving aside their identities. The paper studies profile entropy for samples from discrete distributions and shows that it connects three problems: estimating distributions, inferring symmetric properties, and compressing profiles. This places the pattern of observed frequencies at the center of the analysis.

For distribution estimation, profile entropy determines the speed of estimation relative to the best natural estimator. For symmetric properties, it characterizes inference rates relative to the best estimator over any label-invariant collection of distributions. These comparisons are central to the claims: the results describe performance against specified reference estimators and distribution collections.

Profile entropy also sets the limit for compressing profiles. The authors develop optimal block and sequential compression algorithms with near-linear running time. They further investigate the quantity's properties, give algorithms to approximate it, and determine its scale for several structured distribution families. Together, these results make profile entropy both a unifying theoretical measure and a quantity that can be studied computationally.
summary.tldr: Profile entropy links distribution estimation, symmetric-property inference, and optimal compression of observed frequency patterns.

title: Profile Entropy: A Fundamental Measure for the Learnability and Compressibility of Distributions

abstract: We investigate finite stochastic partial monitoring, which is a general model for sequential learning with limited feedback. While Thompson sampling is one of the most promising algorithms on a variety of online decision-making problems, its properties for stochastic partial monitoring have not been theoretically investigated, and the existing algorithm relies on a heuristic approximation of the posterior distribution. To mitigate these problems, we present a novel Thompson-sampling-based algorithm, which enables us to exactly sample the target parameter from the posterior distribution. Besides, we prove that the new algorithm achieves the logarithmic problem-dependent expected pseudo-regret $\mathsf{O}(\log T)$ for a linearized variant of the problem with local observability. This result is the first regret bound of Thompson sampling for partial monitoring, which also becomes the first logarithmic regret bound of Thompson sampling for linear bandits.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decision-making when feedback reveals only limited information about the consequences of an action. Finite stochastic partial monitoring provides a general framework for this situation. Although Thompson sampling had worked well in several online decision problems, its behavior in this framework lacked a theoretical analysis, and an existing implementation used a heuristic approximation to the posterior distribution.

The authors introduce a Thompson-sampling-based algorithm that can draw the target parameter exactly from its posterior. This addresses the sampling approximation directly. They also analyze a linearized version of the problem under local observability, a condition on how the available feedback supports distinguishing relevant decisions.

Under those conditions, the algorithm achieves problem-dependent expected pseudo-regret growing only logarithmically with the number of rounds. This means its expected cumulative decision disadvantage has a slowly growing bound, with constants that depend on the problem. The result supplies the first Thompson sampling regret bound for partial monitoring and also the first logarithmic bound for linear bandits. The stated guarantee is tied to the analyzed variant and observability condition.
summary.tldr: A new Thompson sampling algorithm enables exact posterior sampling and achieves logarithmic expected pseudo-regret for a locally observable, linearized partial-monitoring problem.

title: Analysis and Design of Thompson Sampling for Stochastic Partial Monitoring

abstract: Deep clustering integrates embedding and clustering together to obtain the optimal nonlinear embedding space, which is more effective in real-world scenarios compared with conventional clustering methods. However, the robustness of the clustering network is prone to being attenuated especially when it encounters an adversarial attack. A small perturbation in the embedding space will lead to diverse clustering results since the labels are absent. In this paper, we propose a robust deep clustering method based on adversarial learning. Specifically, we first attempt to define adversarial samples in the embedding space for the clustering network. Meanwhile, we devise an adversarial attack strategy to explore samples that easily fool the clustering layers but do not impact the performance of the deep embedding. We then provide a simple yet efficient defense algorithm to improve the robustness of the clustering network. Experimental results on two popular datasets show that the proposed adversarial learning method can significantly enhance the robustness and further improve the overall clustering performance. Particularly, the proposed method is generally applicable to multiple existing clustering frameworks to boost their robustness. The source code is available at https://github.com/xdxuyang/ALRDC.

paragraphs: Deep clustering learns a representation of data and a way to divide that representation into groups together. The paper examines a vulnerability in this arrangement: small changes within the learned representation can cause substantially different cluster assignments. Without labels to anchor those assignments, the clustering component can be susceptible to adversarial manipulation.

The authors define adversarial examples directly in the embedding space, where the network represents its inputs. They then devise an attack that seeks examples capable of misleading the clustering layers while preserving the performance of the embedding component. This separates disruption of the grouping decision from damage to the representation itself and provides a focused way to investigate clustering robustness.

The paper also introduces a defense based on adversarial learning. On two datasets, the reported experiments show substantial improvements in robustness alongside better overall clustering performance. The method can be applied to multiple existing clustering frameworks, making its contribution broader than a single clustering architecture. These findings support adversarial training as a practical way to strengthen the grouping stage of deep clustering.
summary.tldr: The paper develops embedding-space attacks and an adversarial defense that improve the robustness and performance of multiple deep clustering frameworks.

title: Adversarial Learning for Robust Deep Clustering

abstract: Neural implicit shape representations are an emerging paradigm that offers many potential benefits over conventional discrete representations, including memory efficiency at a high spatial resolution. Generalizing across shapes with such neural implicit representations amounts to learning priors over the respective function space and enables geometry reconstruction from partial or noisy observations. Existing generalization methods rely on conditioning a neural network on a low-dimensional latent code that is either regressed by an encoder or jointly optimized in the auto-decoder framework. Here, we formalize learning of a shape space as a meta-learning problem and leverage gradient-based meta-learning algorithms to solve this task. We demonstrate that this approach performs on par with auto-decoder based approaches while being an order of magnitude faster at test-time inference. We further demonstrate that the proposed gradient-based method outperforms encoder-decoder based methods that leverage pooling-based set encoders.

paragraphs: Neural implicit representations describe shapes through learned functions, offering potential memory benefits at high spatial resolution. To generalize across shapes, a model must learn prior knowledge about the space of those functions. Such knowledge enables reconstruction from observations that may be incomplete or noisy.

Existing approaches represent each shape using a low-dimensional latent code, obtained either through an encoder or through optimization in an auto-decoder framework. MetaSDF instead formulates learning the shape space as a meta-learning problem and applies gradient-based meta-learning. The central change is how shared knowledge across shapes is learned and used for adaptation.

The authors report performance comparable to auto-decoder approaches while making test-time inference an order of magnitude faster. They also report better performance than encoder-decoder methods using pooling-based set encoders. These comparisons show that the proposed formulation can combine effective shape reconstruction with faster inference in the evaluated setting. The result makes learning across a space of shape functions a practical alternative to the latent-code approaches considered in the paper.
summary.tldr: MetaSDF uses gradient-based meta-learning for shape representations, matching auto-decoder performance with roughly tenfold faster test-time inference.

title: MetaSDF: Meta-Learning Signed Distance Functions

abstract: Efficient exploration is one of the main challenges in reinforcement learning (RL). Most existing sample-efficient algorithms assume the existence of a single reward function during exploration. In many practical scenarios, however, there is not a single underlying reward function to guide the exploration, for instance, when an agent needs to learn many skills simultaneously, or multiple conflicting objectives need to be balanced. To address these challenges, we propose the \textit{task-agnostic RL} framework: In the exploration phase, the agent first collects trajectories by exploring the MDP without the guidance of a reward function. After exploration, it aims at finding near-optimal policies for $N$ tasks, given the collected trajectories augmented with \textit{sampled rewards} for each task. We present an efficient task-agnostic RL algorithm, \textsc{UCBZero}, that finds $\epsilon$-optimal policies for $N$ arbitrary tasks after at most $\tilde O(\log(N)H^5SA/\epsilon^2)$ exploration episodes. We also provide an $\Omega(\log (N)H^2SA/\epsilon^2)$ lower bound, showing that the $\log$ dependency on $N$ is unavoidable. Furthermore, we provide an $N$-independent sample complexity bound of \textsc{UCBZero} in the statistically easier setting when the ground truth reward functions are known.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often assumes a reward function is available to guide exploration. That assumption is less suitable when one set of experience must support many skills or competing objectives. This paper defines task-agnostic reinforcement learning: an agent explores without reward guidance, then uses the collected trajectories and sampled task rewards to learn policies for multiple tasks.

The proposed UCBZero algorithm finds policies within a specified tolerance of optimality for N arbitrary tasks. Its exploration bound grows logarithmically with N, alongside dependence on the horizon, numbers of states and actions, and required accuracy. A lower bound also contains a logarithmic dependence on N, showing that this dependence cannot generally be eliminated in the sampled-reward setting.

The paper separately studies the easier case where the true reward functions are known after exploration. There, UCBZero has a sample-complexity bound independent of the number of tasks. These results clarify how reusable exploration can support many later objectives and how the cost changes depending on whether rewards are known or must be learned from samples.
summary.tldr: UCBZero explores without rewards and supports many later tasks, with logarithmic task-count dependence that is unavoidable when rewards are sampled.

title: Task-agnostic Exploration in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: For a certain scaling of the initialization of stochastic gradient descent (SGD), wide neural networks (NN) have been shown to be well approximated by reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) methods. Recent empirical work showed that, for some classification tasks, RKHS methods can replace NNs without a large loss in performance. On the other hand, two-layers NNs are known to encode richer smoothness classes than RKHS and we know of special examples for which SGD-trained NN provably outperform RKHS. This is true even in the wide network limit, for a different scaling of the initialization. How can we reconcile the above claims? For which tasks do NNs outperform RKHS? If covariates are nearly isotropic, RKHS methods suffer from the curse of dimensionality, while NNs can overcome it by learning the best low-dimensional representation. Here we show that this curse of dimensionality becomes milder if the covariates display the same low-dimensional structure as the target function, and we precisely characterize this tradeoff. Building on these results, we present the spiked covariates model that can capture in a unified framework both behaviors observed in earlier works. We hypothesize that such a latent low-dimensional structure is present in image classification. We numerically test this hypothesis by showing that specific perturbations of the training distribution degrade the performances of RKHS methods much more significantly than NNs.

paragraphs: Wide neural networks can behave like kernel methods under one scaling of initialization, yet neural networks can outperform them under another. This paper investigates how these observations fit together. It focuses on the relationship between the structure of the input variables and the low-dimensional structure of the function being learned.

When inputs are nearly isotropic, kernel methods face a curse of dimensionality, while neural networks can learn a useful low-dimensional representation. The authors show that this disadvantage becomes milder when the input distribution already shares the target function's low-dimensional structure. They characterize the tradeoff and introduce a spiked covariates model that captures both patterns within one framework.

The authors hypothesize that a similar latent structure exists in image classification. Numerical tests show that specific perturbations of the training distribution hurt kernel methods much more than neural networks. These experiments support the hypothesis without establishing it universally. The work explains why comparing the methods requires attention to input geometry as well as the target function.
summary.tldr: The advantage of neural networks over kernel methods depends partly on whether inputs already share the target function's low-dimensional structure.

title: When Do Neural Networks Outperform Kernel Methods?

abstract: This paper presents new algorithms to solve the feature-sparsity constrained PCA problem (FSPCA), which performs feature selection and PCA simultaneously. Existing optimization methods for FSPCA require data distribution assumptions and are lack of global convergence guarantee. Though the general FSPCA problem is NP-hard, we show that, for a low-rank covariance, FSPCA can be solved globally (Algorithm 1). Then, we propose another strategy (Algorithm 2) to solve FSPCA for the general covariance by iteratively building a carefully designed proxy. We prove (data-dependent) approximation bound and convergence guarantees for the new algorithms. For the spectrum of covariance with exponential/Zipf's distribution, we provide exponential/posynomial approximation bound. Experimental results show the promising performance and efficiency of the new algorithms compared with the state-of-the-arts on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Feature-sparse principal component analysis combines feature selection with dimensionality reduction. It seeks a principal subspace while restricting which original features are used. The paper addresses the difficulty of optimizing this combined objective: the general problem is NP-hard, and the existing methods described in the abstract rely on distributional assumptions and lack global convergence guarantees.

The authors separate a tractable special case from the general setting. For low-rank covariance, their first algorithm can solve the problem globally. For general covariance, a second algorithm iteratively builds a carefully designed proxy problem. The global solution claim for low-rank covariance therefore does not automatically extend to arbitrary covariance matrices.

The analysis supplies data-dependent approximation bounds and convergence guarantees. It also provides particular approximation bounds when the covariance spectrum follows exponential or Zipf distributions. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show promising performance and efficiency relative to existing methods. The work contributes both algorithms and a more explicit account of how attainable solution quality depends on the covariance structure.
summary.tldr: New feature-sparse PCA algorithms provide a global solution for low-rank covariance and approximation guarantees for more general cases.

title: Learning Feature Sparse Principal Subspace

abstract: This paper presents an algorithm to reconstruct temporally consistent 3D meshes of deformable object instances from videos in the wild. Without requiring annotations of 3D mesh, 2D keypoints, or camera pose for each video frame, we pose video-based reconstruction as a self-supervised online adaptation problem applied to any incoming test video. We first learn a category-specific 3D reconstruction model from a collection of single-view images of the same category that jointly predicts the shape, texture, and camera pose of an image. Then, at inference time, we adapt the model to a test video over time using self-supervised regularization terms that exploit temporal consistency of an object instance to enforce that all reconstructed meshes share a common texture map, a base shape, as well as parts. We demonstrate that our algorithm recovers temporally consistent and reliable 3D structures from videos of non-rigid objects including those of animals captured in the wild -- an extremely challenging task rarely addressed before.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a moving, deformable object from video requires more than producing a plausible 3D shape in each frame. The shapes should also remain consistent representations of the same object over time. This paper treats that requirement as an online adaptation problem, using the incoming test video itself to refine a reconstruction model.

The method first learns a category-specific model from single-view images belonging to the same category. That model jointly predicts shape, texture, and camera pose. During inference, self-supervised regularization adapts it over time so that reconstructed meshes share a texture map, a base shape, and parts. These shared elements connect the framewise reconstructions.

The video adaptation does not require per-frame annotations of 3D meshes, 2D keypoints, or camera pose. The authors demonstrate temporally consistent and reliable reconstructions for non-rigid objects, including animals filmed in the wild. The contribution is using an object's continuity through a video as supervision for adaptation, while starting from a learned model of its category.
summary.tldr: A category-specific reconstruction model adapts to test videos using temporal consistency to produce coherent 3D meshes of deformable objects.

title: Online Adaptation for Consistent Mesh Reconstruction in the Wild

abstract: We propose PLLay, a novel topological layer for general deep learning models based on persistence landscapes, in which we can efficiently exploit the underlying topological features of the input data structure. In this work, we show differentiability with respect to layer inputs, for a general persistent homology with arbitrary filtration. Thus, our proposed layer can be placed anywhere in the network and feed critical information on the topological features of input data into subsequent layers to improve the learnability of the networks toward a given task. A task-optimal structure of PLLay is learned during training via backpropagation, without requiring any input featurization or data preprocessing. We provide a novel adaptation for the DTM function-based filtration, and show that the proposed layer is robust against noise and outliers through a stability analysis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by classification experiments on various datasets.
originalAbstract: We propose PLLay, a novel topological layer for general deep learning models based on persistence landscapes, in which we can efficiently exploit the underlying topological features of the input data structure. In this work, we show differentiability with respect to layer inputs, for a general persistent homology with arbitrary filtration. Thus, our proposed layer can be placed anywhere in the network and feed critical information on the topological features of input data into subsequent layers to improve the learnability of the networks toward a given task. A task-optimal structure of PLLay is learned during training via backpropagation, without requiring any input featurization or data preprocessing. We provide a novel adaptation for the DTM function-based filtration, and show that the proposed layer is robust against noise and outliers through a stability analysis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by classification experiments on various datasets.

paragraphs: Topological features describe structural properties of data that can be useful for learning. This paper introduces PLLay, a neural-network layer based on persistence landscapes, to make such information available within general deep learning models. The aim is to let later layers use topological structure as part of solving the task.

The authors show differentiability with respect to layer inputs for general persistent homology with arbitrary filtration. This supports placing PLLay at any position in a network and learning its task-specific structure through backpropagation. The approach does not require a separate input featurization or preprocessing stage, bringing the topological representation into the trainable model itself.

The paper also develops an adaptation using a distance-to-measure function-based filtration and provides a stability analysis supporting robustness to noise and outliers. Classification experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. Together, these contributions address both integration and reliability: topological information can participate in end-to-end training, while the stability results explain resistance to disruptions in the data.
summary.tldr: PLLay integrates trainable persistence-landscape features into neural networks, with differentiability and stability results supporting end-to-end use.

title: PLLay: Efficient Topological Layer based on Persistent Landscapes

abstract: Previous research in fair classification mostly focuses on a single decision model. In reality, there usually exist multiple decision models within a system and all of which may contain a certain amount of discrimination. Such realistic scenarios introduce new challenges to fair classification: since discrimination may be transmitted from upstream models to downstream models, building decision models separately without taking upstream models into consideration cannot guarantee to achieve fairness. In this paper, we propose an approach that learns multiple classifiers and achieves fairness for all of them simultaneously, by treating each decision model as a soft intervention and inferring the post-intervention distributions to formulate the loss function as well as the fairness constraints. We adopt surrogate functions to smooth the loss function and constraints, and theoretically show that the excess risk of the proposed loss function can be bounded in a form that is the same as that for traditional surrogated loss functions. Experiments using both synthetic and real-world datasets show the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Fairness becomes harder when a system contains several decision models. Discrimination in an earlier model can carry forward into later models, so developing each classifier separately cannot guarantee fairness across the system. This paper addresses that interaction by learning multiple classifiers together, with the aim of achieving fairness for all of them simultaneously.

The approach treats each decision model as a soft intervention: a change to how decisions are generated within the system. It then infers the distributions resulting from those interventions and uses them to define both the learning objective and the fairness constraints. This connects the training of individual classifiers to the consequences of decisions elsewhere in the system.

To make the loss and constraints smooth, the authors use surrogate functions. They prove that the resulting excess risk can be bounded in the same mathematical form used for traditional surrogate losses. This supplies theoretical support for their loss formulation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets also support the approach’s effectiveness, complementing the theoretical result with empirical evidence.
summary.tldr: The paper jointly learns multiple classifiers using soft interventions to address discrimination that can propagate between decision models.

title: Fair Multiple Decision Making Through Soft Interventions

abstract: Contrastive learning applied to self-supervised representation learning has seen a resurgence in recent years, leading to state of the art performance in the unsupervised training of deep image models. Modern batch contrastive approaches subsume or significantly outperform traditional contrastive losses such as triplet, max-margin and the N-pairs loss. In this work, we extend the self-supervised batch contrastive approach to the fully-supervised setting, allowing us to effectively leverage label information. Clusters of points belonging to the same class are pulled together in embedding space, while simultaneously pushing apart clusters of samples from different classes. We analyze two possible versions of the supervised contrastive (SupCon) loss, identifying the best-performing formulation of the loss. On ResNet-200, we achieve top-1 accuracy of 81.4% on the ImageNet dataset, which is 0.8% above the best number reported for this architecture. We show consistent outperformance over cross-entropy on other datasets and two ResNet variants. The loss shows benefits for robustness to natural corruptions, and is more stable to hyperparameter settings such as optimizers and data augmentations. In reduced data settings, it outperforms cross-entropy significantly. Our loss function is simple to implement and reference TensorFlow code is released at https://t.ly/supcon.

paragraphs: Supervised Contrastive Learning adapts batch contrastive learning to use class labels directly. Its objective draws representations of examples from the same class together and separates representations from different classes. This makes class relationships shape the embedding space during training, extending an approach developed for self-supervised representation learning.

The paper examines two versions of the supervised contrastive loss and identifies the stronger formulation. On ImageNet with ResNet-200, it reports 81.4% top-1 accuracy, exceeding the best previously reported result for that architecture by 0.8 percentage points. It also reports consistent improvements over cross-entropy on other datasets and two ResNet variants.

The loss improves robustness to natural corruptions, is more stable across optimizer and augmentation settings, and substantially outperforms cross-entropy in reduced-data experiments. These findings support label-informed contrastive training as a useful alternative objective for supervised image learning. The contribution combines a simple-to-implement loss with evidence that organizing representations by class can improve several aspects of model behavior.
summary.tldr: Supervised contrastive learning uses labels to organize embeddings by class, improving reported accuracy, corruption robustness, and training stability.

title: Supervised Contrastive Learning

abstract: We revisit the problem of counting the number of distinct elements $\dist$ in a data stream $D$, over a domain $[u]$. We propose an $(\epsilon,\delta)$-differentially private algorithm that approximates $\dist$ within a factor of $(1\pm\gamma)$, and with additive error of $O(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}/\epsilon)$, using space $O(\ln(\ln(u)/\gamma)/\gamma^2)$. We improve on the prior work at least quadratically and up to exponentially, in terms of both space and additive error. Our additive error guarantee is optimal up to a factor of $O(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)})$, and the space bound is optimal up to a factor of $O\left(\min\left\{\ln\left(\frac{\ln(u)}{\gamma}\right), \frac{1}{\gamma^2}\right\}\right)$. We assume the existence of an ideal uniform random hash function, and ignore the space required to store it. We later relax this requirement by assuming pseudorandom functions and appealing to a computational variant of differential privacy, SIM-CDP. Our algorithm is built on top of the celebrated Flajolet-Martin (FM) sketch. We show that FM-sketch is differentially private as is, as long as there are $\approx \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}/(\epsilon\gamma)$ distinct elements in the data set. Along the way, we prove a structural result showing that the maximum of $k$ i.i.d. random variables is statistically close (in the sense of $\epsilon$-differential privacy) to the maximum of $(k+1)$ i.i.d. samples from the same distribution, as long as $k=\Omega\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}\right)$. Finally, experiments show that our algorithms introduces error within an order of magnitude of the non-private analogues for streams with thousands of distinct elements, even while providing strong privacy guarantee ($\eps\leq 1$).

paragraphs: Counting distinct elements in a stream requires balancing memory use, approximation error, and privacy. This paper builds a differentially private counting algorithm on the Flajolet-Martin sketch. A central result is that the sketch itself satisfies differential privacy once the number of distinct elements exceeds a threshold determined by the privacy and accuracy parameters.

The algorithm provides a multiplicative approximation together with additive error proportional to the square root of log(1/delta), divided by epsilon. The authors establish improvements over prior work ranging from quadratic to exponential in space and additive error, with near-optimality guarantees up to stated factors. A supporting structural result compares maxima of k and k+1 independent, identically distributed samples.

The initial analysis assumes an ideal uniform random hash function and excludes its storage cost. The authors later replace that assumption with pseudorandom functions and a computational privacy notion, SIM-CDP. Experiments with thousands of distinct elements show error within an order of magnitude of non-private counterparts, even for epsilon at most one. The privacy result therefore depends on explicit counting and hashing conditions.
summary.tldr: Under stated hashing and distinct-count conditions, the Flajolet-Martin sketch itself provides differential privacy and supports space-efficient private counting.

title: The Flajolet-Martin Sketch Itself Preserves Differential Privacy: Private Counting with Minimal Space

abstract: We consider the problem of online learning and its application to solving minimax games. For the online learning problem, Follow the Perturbed Leader (FTPL) is a widely studied algorithm which enjoys the optimal $O(T^{1/2})$ \emph{worst case} regret guarantee for both convex and nonconvex losses. In this work, we show that when the sequence of loss functions is \emph{predictable}, a simple modification of FTPL which incorporates optimism can achieve better regret guarantees, while retaining the optimal worst-case regret guarantee for unpredictable sequences. A key challenge in obtaining these tighter regret bounds is the stochasticity and optimism in the algorithm, which requires different analysis techniques than those commonly used in the analysis of FTPL. The key ingredient we utilize in our analysis is the dual view of perturbation as regularization. While our algorithm has several applications, we consider the specific application of minimax games. For solving smooth convex-concave games, our algorithm only requires access to a linear optimization oracle. For Lipschitz and smooth nonconvex-nonconcave games, our algorithm requires access to an optimization oracle which computes the perturbed best response. In both these settings, our algorithm solves the game up to an accuracy of $O(T^{-1/2})$ using $T$ calls to the optimization oracle. An important feature of our algorithm is that it is highly parallelizable and requires only $O(T^{1/2})$ iterations, with each iteration making $O(T^{1/2})$ parallel calls to the optimization oracle.

The contribution therefore combines improved treatment of predictable losses with a parallelizable game-solving procedure. Its computational claims depend on access to the appropriate oracle for each class of games.
summary.tldr: Optimistic Follow the Perturbed Leader exploits predictable losses while preserving worst-case regret and supporting parallel algorithms for smooth minimax games.

title: Follow the Perturbed Leader: Optimism and Fast Parallel Algorithms for Smooth Minimax Games

abstract: In statistical learning and analysis from shared data, which is increasingly widely adopted in platforms such as federated learning and meta-learning, there are two major concerns: privacy and robustness. Each participating individual should be able to contribute without the fear of leaking one's sensitive information. At the same time, the system should be robust in the presence of malicious participants inserting corrupted data. Recent algorithmic advances in learning from shared data focus on either one of these threats, leaving the system vulnerable to the other. We bridge this gap for the canonical problem of estimating the mean from i.i.d.~samples. We introduce PRIME, which is the first efficient algorithm that achieves both privacy and robustness for a wide range of distributions. We further complement this result with a novel exponential time algorithm that improves the sample complexity of PRIME, achieving a near-optimal guarantee and matching that of a known lower bound for (non-robust) private mean estimation. This proves that there is no extra statistical cost to simultaneously guaranteeing privacy and robustness.

paragraphs: Learning from shared data raises two distinct concerns: protecting individual contributors’ information and resisting maliciously corrupted data. Addressing only one can leave the other unresolved. This paper studies both requirements together for the basic statistical task of estimating a mean from independently and identically distributed samples.

The authors introduce PRIME, which they describe as the first efficient algorithm to provide both privacy and robustness across a broad range of distributions. This establishes a computationally efficient route to joint protection, rather than requiring practitioners to choose between the two goals in the studied mean-estimation setting.

A second algorithm improves the sample requirement but takes exponential time. Its near-optimal statistical guarantee matches a known lower bound for private mean estimation without robustness. This shows that simultaneously obtaining privacy and robustness need not impose an extra statistical cost in the setting covered by the result. The distinction between the algorithms matters: the strongest sample guarantee belongs to the exponential-time method, while PRIME supplies the efficient approach. The paper separates what is statistically achievable from what its efficient algorithm achieves.
summary.tldr: PRIME efficiently combines private and robust mean estimation, while an exponential-time method shows near-optimal sample guarantees without extra statistical cost for robustness.

title: Robust and differentially private mean estimation

abstract: Generating fluent and relevant language to describe visual content is critical for the video captioning task. Many existing methods generate captions using sequence models that predict words in a left-to-right order. In this paper, we investigate a graph-structured model for caption generation by explicitly modeling the hierarchical structure in the sentences to further improve the fluency and relevance of sentences. To this end, we propose a novel video captioning method that generates a sentence by first constructing a multi-modal dependency tree and then traversing the constructed tree, where the syntactic structure and semantic relationship in the sentence are represented by the tree topology. To take full advantage of the information from both vision and language, both the visual and textual representation features are encoded into each tree node. Different from existing dependency parsing methods that generate uni-modal dependency trees for language understanding, our method construct s multi-modal dependency trees for language generation of images and videos. We also propose a tree-structured reinforcement learning algorithm to effectively optimize the captioning model where a novel reward is designed by evaluating the semantic consistency between the generated sub-tree and the ground-truth tree. Extensive experiments on several video captioning datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Video captioning requires a sentence that is both fluent and relevant to what appears in the video. Many approaches generate one word after another from left to right. This paper instead makes sentence hierarchy explicit, using a graph-structured generation process to represent relationships that a purely sequential output order does not directly expose.

The method first constructs a multimodal dependency tree and then traverses it to produce the sentence. The tree’s topology represents syntactic structure and semantic relationships, while each node contains both visual and textual features. This adapts dependency-tree ideas from understanding language to generating language grounded in images and videos.

Training uses a tree-structured reinforcement learning algorithm with a reward that evaluates semantic consistency between a generated subtree and the ground-truth tree. This supplies feedback about the developing hierarchical structure. Experiments on several video-captioning datasets demonstrate the method’s effectiveness, supporting explicit sentence structure as a useful component of visually grounded caption generation.
summary.tldr: Generating captions through multimodal dependency trees makes sentence structure and visual grounding explicit during generation and training.

title: Multi-modal Dependency Tree for Video Captioning

abstract: Large Transformer models yield impressive results on many tasks, but are expensive to train, or even fine-tune, and so slow at decoding that their use and study becomes out of reach. We address this problem by leveraging sparsity. We study sparse variants for all layers in the Transformer and propose Scaling Transformers, a family of next generation Transformer models that use sparse layers to scale efficiently and perform unbatched decoding much faster than the standard Transformer as we scale up the model size. Surprisingly, the sparse layers are enough to obtain the same perplexity as the standard Transformer with the same number of parameters. We also integrate with prior sparsity approaches to attention and enable fast inference on long sequences even with limited memory. This results in performance competitive to the state-of-the-art on long text summarization.

paragraphs: Large Transformers can deliver strong results, but their training, fine-tuning, and decoding costs make them difficult to use and study. This paper investigates sparsity throughout the architecture, studying sparse alternatives for every layer. The resulting model family, called Scaling Transformers, aims to make increasing model size computationally more manageable.

The authors report that the sparse layers achieve the same perplexity as a standard Transformer with the same parameter count. They also find much faster unbatched decoding as model size grows. Together, these findings support the possibility of retaining the reported language-modeling quality while reducing a practical cost of generating outputs with larger models.

The approach is additionally combined with earlier methods for sparse attention, enabling fast inference on long sequences under limited memory. On long-text summarization, the resulting system achieves performance competitive with the state of the art. The paper therefore connects layer-wide sparsity to two related uses: more efficient scaling of Transformer models and practical processing of long inputs.
summary.tldr: Scaling Transformers use sparse layers to match reported dense-model perplexity at equal parameter count while accelerating unbatched decoding.

title: Sparse is Enough in Scaling Transformers

abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers information from a teacher network to a student. Most approaches focus on training the student after the teacher is already available. This paper instead asks how to train a teacher whose learned representations will be easier for students to use.

During teacher optimization, the method jointly trains student branches to encourage representations that support knowledge transfer. The main intervention therefore happens while the teacher is being learned. The subsequent distillation procedure remains straightforward, allowing most existing distillation methods to adopt the technique and potentially improve student accuracy and convergence speed.

Experiments show strong accuracy across several established distillation techniques and different teacher–student combinations. The reported benefits also extend to cases where the architectures differ and the eventual student models are unknown during teacher training. This distinction matters: the jointly trained branches help shape the teacher, but the useful transfer is not restricted to a known final student architecture. The paper presents teacher preparation as a broadly compatible component of the distillation process.
summary.tldr: Jointly training student branches with a teacher produces representations that improve later knowledge distillation.

title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation

abstract: Significant effort has been placed on developing decision support tools to improve patient care. However, drivers of real-world clinical decisions in complex medical scenarios are not yet well-understood, resulting in substantial gaps between these tools and practical applications. In light of this, we highlight that more attention on understanding clinical decision-making is required both to elucidate current clinical practices and to enable effective human-machine interactions. This is imperative in high-stakes scenarios with scarce available resources. Using organ transplantation as a case study, we formalize the desiderata of methods for understanding clinical decision-making. We show that most existing machine learning methods are insufficient to meet these requirements and propose iTransplant, a novel data-driven framework to learn the factors affecting decisions on organ offers in an instance-wise fashion directly from clinical data, as a possible solution. Through experiments on real-world liver transplantation data from OPTN, we demonstrate the use of iTransplant to: (1) discover which criteria are most important to clinicians for organ offer acceptance; (2) identify patient-specific organ preferences of clinicians allowing automatic patient stratification; and (3) explore variations in transplantation practices between different transplant centers. Finally, we emphasize that the insights gained by iTransplant can be used to inform the development of future decision support tools.

paragraphs: Decision support tools can be difficult to connect to clinical practice when the factors driving clinicians' decisions are poorly understood. This paper studies that gap through organ transplantation, where decisions are complex and resources are scarce. It first specifies requirements for methods intended to explain clinical decision-making.

The authors argue that most existing machine-learning methods do not satisfy those requirements and propose iTransplant as a possible solution. The framework learns factors associated with organ-offer decisions directly from clinical data, producing explanations for individual cases. This focus allows the analysis to reflect patient-specific preferences instead of treating every acceptance decision as governed by the same priorities.

Experiments with real-world OPTN liver transplantation data demonstrate three uses: identifying important acceptance criteria, grouping patients through clinicians' organ preferences, and examining differences between transplant centers. These findings describe observed decision practices and their variation. The authors position that understanding as information that can guide future decision support tools and improve how those tools fit into human decision-making.
summary.tldr: iTransplant learns case-specific factors in organ-offer decisions to characterize clinical preferences and inform future decision support.

title: Closing the loop in medical decision support by understanding clinical decision-making: A case study on organ transplantation

abstract: We study the theoretical convergence properties of random-search methods when optimizing non-convex objective functions without having access to derivatives. We prove that standard random-search methods that do not rely on second-order information converge to a second-order stationary point. However, they suffer from an exponential complexity in terms of the input dimension of the problem. In order to address this issue, we propose a novel variant of random search that exploits negative curvature by only relying on function evaluations. We prove that this approach converges to a second-order stationary point at a much faster rate than vanilla methods: namely, the complexity in terms of the number of function evaluations is only linear in the problem dimension. We test our algorithm empirically and find good agreements with our theoretical results.

paragraphs: Random-search methods optimize functions by evaluating candidate points without requiring derivatives. For nonconvex objectives, understanding where such methods converge involves more than checking whether the gradient is small. This paper studies convergence to second-order stationary points, which also account for curvature and provide a stronger target than first-order stationarity.

The authors prove that standard random-search methods can reach such points even without explicitly using second-order information. However, their complexity grows exponentially with the number of input dimensions. That result separates the possibility of convergence from its computational practicality: a method may eventually reach the desired type of point while requiring an unfavorable number of evaluations.

To address this dependence, the paper introduces a random-search variant that exploits negative curvature using only function evaluations. Its evaluation complexity depends linearly on dimension, a substantial improvement over the exponential dependence of the standard methods analyzed. Empirical tests agree well with the theoretical findings. The contribution shows how curvature-sensitive search can improve dimension scaling even when derivative information is unavailable.
summary.tldr: A derivative-free random-search method exploits negative curvature to achieve second-order convergence with linear rather than exponential dependence on dimension.

title: On the Second-order Convergence Properties of Random Search Methods

abstract: Mutual information (MI) maximization provides an appealing formalism for learning representations of data. In the context of reinforcement learning (RL), such representations can accelerate learning by discarding irrelevant and redundant information, while retaining the information necessary for control. Much prior work on these methods has addressed the practical difficulties of estimating MI from samples of high-dimensional observations, while comparatively less is understood about which MI objectives yield representations that are sufficient for RL from a theoretical perspective. In this paper, we formalize the sufficiency of a state representation for learning and representing the optimal policy, and study several popular MI based objectives through this lens. Surprisingly, we find that two of these objectives can yield insufficient representations given mild and common assumptions on the structure of the MDP. We corroborate our theoretical results with empirical experiments on a simulated game environment with visual observations.

paragraphs: A useful reinforcement learning representation should discard irrelevant information while preserving what an agent needs to choose optimal actions. Mutual-information maximization offers a formal way to learn representations, but optimizing an information objective does not automatically settle whether the resulting representation supports control. This paper investigates that theoretical question.

The authors formalize sufficiency in terms of a representation's ability to support both learning and expressing the optimal policy. They then examine several popular mutual-information objectives using that definition. Two of the objectives can produce insufficient representations under assumptions about the decision process that the authors describe as mild and common.

Experiments in a simulated game with visual observations corroborate the theoretical results. The finding concerns what an objective encourages a representation to retain, beyond the practical difficulty of estimating mutual information from high-dimensional samples. It shows that some popular objectives can lose information needed for optimal control, giving a concrete reason to evaluate representation objectives against policy sufficiency as well as information-based criteria.
summary.tldr: Two popular mutual-information objectives can learn representations that fail to preserve enough information for optimal control.

title: Which Mutual-Information Representation Learning Objectives are Sufficient for Control?

abstract: As annotations of data can be scarce in large-scale practical problems, leveraging unlabelled examples is one of the most important aspects of machine learning. This is the aim of semi-supervised learning. To benefit from the access to unlabelled data, it is natural to diffuse smoothly knowledge of labelled data to unlabelled one. This induces to the use of Laplacian regularization. Yet, current implementations of Laplacian regularization suffer from several drawbacks, notably the well-known curse of dimensionality. In this paper, we design a new class of algorithms overcoming this issue, unveiling a large body of spectral filtering methods. Additionally, we provide a statistical analysis showing that our estimators exhibit desirable behaviors. They are implemented through (reproducing) kernel methods, for which we provide realistic computational guidelines in order to make our method usable with large amounts of data.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning aims to benefit from abundant unlabeled examples when annotations are scarce. One natural strategy is to extend information from labeled observations smoothly across the data. Laplacian regularization expresses this idea, but existing implementations face difficulties, including the curse of dimensionality.

This paper develops a new class of algorithms intended to overcome that dimensionality problem. The approach reveals a broad family of spectral filtering methods within the proposed treatment of Laplacian regularization. It therefore offers a collection of related algorithmic choices for using unlabeled data, organized around a shared mathematical framework.

The authors provide statistical analysis establishing desirable behavior of their estimators and implement them through reproducing kernel methods. They also give computational guidance aimed at making the approach usable with large datasets. The contribution combines a response to the stated dimensionality drawback with analysis and implementation considerations, connecting the statistical motivation for smooth information transfer to methods designed for practical amounts of data.
summary.tldr: A new family of Laplacian-regularized methods addresses dimensionality difficulties in semi-supervised learning, with statistical analysis and kernel-based implementation guidance.

title: Overcoming the curse of dimensionality with Laplacian regularization in semi-supervised learning

abstract: Multi-agent behavior modeling aims to understand the interactions that occur between agents. We present a multi-agent dataset from behavioral neuroscience, the Caltech Mouse Social Interactions (CalMS21) Dataset. Our dataset consists of trajectory data of social interactions, recorded from videos of freely behaving mice in a standard resident-intruder assay. To help accelerate behavioral studies, the CalMS21 dataset provides benchmarks to evaluate the performance of automated behavior classification methods in three settings: (1) for training on large behavioral datasets all annotated by a single annotator, (2) for style transfer to learn inter-annotator differences in behavior definitions, and (3) for learning of new behaviors of interest given limited training data. The dataset consists of 6 million frames of unlabeled tracked poses of interacting mice, as well as over 1 million frames with tracked poses and corresponding frame-level behavior annotations. The challenge of our dataset is to be able to classify behaviors accurately using both labeled and unlabeled tracking data, as well as being able to generalize to new settings.
