paragraphs: CalMS21 supports automated analysis of social interactions between mice. Its data consist of movement trajectories tracked from videos of freely behaving animals in a standard resident-intruder assay. The broader aim is to accelerate behavioral neuroscience studies by providing a shared resource for evaluating methods that classify interactions.

The benchmark separates three learning settings. One uses a large dataset labeled by a single annotator. Another tests adaptation to differences in how annotators define behaviors. The third asks methods to learn new behaviors from limited examples. Together, these settings address both learning an established labeling scheme and adapting when the definitions or available examples change.

The collection contains six million frames of unlabeled tracked poses and more than one million frames with poses and frame-level behavior labels. This combination makes the use of labeled and unlabeled tracking data a central challenge. Success also requires generalization to new settings, so the benchmark goes beyond classification under one fixed source of annotations and one fixed set of behaviors.
summary.tldr: CalMS21 benchmarks mouse interaction classification, adaptation across annotators, and learning new behaviors from limited labeled examples.

title: The Multi-Agent Behavior Dataset: Mouse Dyadic Social Interactions

abstract: Partially monotone regression is a regression analysis in which the target values are monotonically increasing with respect to a subset of input features. The TensorFlow Lattice library is one of the standard machine learning libraries for partially monotone regression. It consists of several neural network layers, and its core component is the lattice layer. One of the problems of the lattice layer is that it requires the projected gradient descent algorithm with many constraints to train it. Another problem is that it cannot receive a high-dimensional input vector due to the memory consumption. We propose a novel neural network layer, the hierarchical lattice layer (HLL), as an extension of the lattice layer so that we can use a standard stochastic gradient descent algorithm to train HLL while satisfying monotonicity constraints and so that it can receive a high-dimensional input vector. Our experiments demonstrate that HLL did not sacrifice its prediction performance on real datasets compared with the lattice layer.

paragraphs: Partially monotone regression requires predictions to increase monotonically with respect to selected input features. This makes the direction of those feature effects a constraint on the model. The paper focuses on lattice layers, a core component of TensorFlow Lattice, and asks how to preserve these constraints while making training and input handling more practical.

Conventional lattice layers present two problems highlighted in the abstract. Training requires projected gradient descent with many constraints, and memory consumption prevents the layer from accepting high-dimensional input vectors. The proposed hierarchical lattice layer extends the original construction to address both issues. It supports standard stochastic gradient descent while satisfying monotonicity constraints and can receive high-dimensional inputs.

Experiments on real datasets show that these changes did not sacrifice predictive performance relative to the lattice layer. The reported contribution is therefore a more usable way to build partially monotone neural networks: the required directional behavior is maintained while the training procedure and dimensionality restrictions are improved.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical lattice layers preserve monotonicity while supporting standard stochastic training and high-dimensional inputs without reported predictive losses.

title: Hierarchical Lattice Layer for Partially Monotone Neural Networks

abstract: Complex systems are often decomposed into modular subsystems for engineering tractability. Although various equation based white-box modeling techniques make use of such structure, learning based methods have yet to incorporate these ideas broadly. We present a modular simulation framework for modeling homogeneous multibody dynamical systems, which combines ideas from graph neural networks and neural differential equations. We learn to model the individual dynamical subsystem as a neural ODE module. Full simulation of the composite system is orchestrated via spatio-temporal message passing between these modules. An arbitrary number of modules can be combined to simulate systems of a wide variety of coupling topologies. We evaluate our framework on a variety of systems and show that message passing allows coordination between multiple modules over time for accurate predictions and in certain cases, enables zero-shot generalization to new system configurations. Furthermore, we show that our models can be transferred to new system configurations with lower data requirement and training effort, compared to those trained from scratch.

paragraphs: Complex physical systems can often be understood as interacting subsystems. This paper brings that modular viewpoint to learned simulation of homogeneous multibody systems. Rather than learning only a single complete-system model, the framework learns an individual dynamical subsystem as a reusable neural ordinary differential equation module.

To simulate a complete system, the modules exchange messages across space and time. This combines the interaction structure of graph neural networks with continuous-time learned dynamics. An arbitrary number of modules can be assembled with different coupling patterns, allowing the same framework to represent a variety of system configurations.

Experiments show that message passing coordinates the modules over time and supports accurate predictions. In some cases, the learned modules generalize to new configurations without additional training. When adaptation is needed, transferring the models requires less data and training effort than learning from scratch. These findings support modularity as a useful design principle for learned simulation, while keeping the zero-shot claim specific to the cases where it was observed.
summary.tldr: Reusable neural dynamics modules communicate through message passing to simulate coupled systems and reduce the effort needed to adapt to new configurations.

title: Learning Modular Simulations for Homogeneous Systems

abstract: We say an algorithm is batch size-invariant if changes to the batch size can largely be compensated for by changes to other hyperparameters. Stochastic gradient descent is well-known to have this property at small batch sizes, via the learning rate. However, some policy optimization algorithms (such as PPO) do not have this property, because of how they control the size of policy updates. In this work we show how to make these algorithms batch size-invariant. Our key insight is to decouple the proximal policy (used for controlling policy updates) from the behavior policy (used for off-policy corrections). Our experiments help explain why these algorithms work, and additionally show how they can make more efficient use of stale data.
originalAbstract: We say an algorithm is batch size-invariant if changes to the batch size can largely be compensated for by changes to other hyperparameters. However, some policy optimization algorithms (such as PPO) do not have this property, because of how they control the size of policy updates. Our key insight is to decouple the proximal policy (used for controlling policy updates) from the behavior policy (used for off-policy corrections). Our experiments help explain why these algorithms work, and additionally show how they can make more efficient use of stale data.

paragraphs: Changing how many examples an algorithm processes together can change its learning behavior. The paper calls an algorithm batch size-invariant when adjustments to other hyperparameters can largely compensate for that change. Ordinary stochastic gradient descent has this property at small batch sizes through learning-rate adjustments, but some policy optimization algorithms, including PPO, do not.

The authors trace the difficulty to how these algorithms restrict policy updates. Their solution separates two reference policies with different jobs. The proximal policy controls the size of an update, while the behavior policy accounts for the policy that generated the training data through off-policy corrections. Decoupling these roles makes it possible to adjust batch size without tying both mechanisms to the same reference.

The paper shows how this modification makes the affected algorithms batch size-invariant in the stated sense. Experiments also help explain their behavior and demonstrate more efficient use of stale data. The practical significance is greater flexibility in training configuration and data reuse, with invariance meaning approximate compensation rather than identical behavior under every batch size.
summary.tldr: Separating the policies used for update control and data correction makes policy optimization more adaptable to batch-size changes and stale data.

title: Batch size-invariance for policy optimization

abstract: We present a rotated hyperbolic wrapped normal distribution (RoWN), a simple yet effective alteration of a hyperbolic wrapped normal distribution (HWN). The HWN expands the domain of probabilistic modeling from Euclidean to hyperbolic space, where a tree can be embedded with arbitrary low distortion in theory. In this work, we analyze the geometric properties of the diagonal HWN, a standard choice of distribution in probabilistic modeling. The analysis shows that the distribution is inappropriate to represent the data points at the same hierarchy level through their angular distance with the same norm in the Poincar\'e disk model. We then empirically verify the presence of limitations of HWN, and show how RoWN, the proposed distribution, can alleviate the limitations on various hierarchical datasets, including noisy synthetic binary tree, WordNet, and Atari 2600 Breakout. The code is available at https://github.com/ml-postech/RoWN.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to represent uncertainty around data organized into hierarchies. Hyperbolic space is attractive for this purpose because, in theory, trees can be embedded there with arbitrarily little distortion. The hyperbolic wrapped normal distribution brings probabilistic modeling into that space, but the authors show that a commonly used diagonal version has an important geometric mismatch.

The mismatch concerns points at the same level of a hierarchy. In the Poincaré disk representation, the arrangement under study gives these points equal norms and expresses their differences through angular distance. The authors analyze why the diagonal distribution is unsuitable for representing this arrangement. They introduce a rotated version, RoWN, as a simple modification intended to address that problem.

Experiments verify limitations of the original distribution and show that RoWN can alleviate them on a noisy synthetic binary tree, WordNet, and Atari 2600 Breakout. The contribution connects a specific geometric weakness to a targeted distributional change: choosing hyperbolic space alone does not settle how uncertainty should be represented within it.
summary.tldr: RoWN rotates a hyperbolic probability distribution to alleviate a geometric mismatch in representing hierarchical data.

title: A Rotated Hyperbolic Wrapped Normal Distribution for Hierarchical Representation Learning

abstract: Elimination algorithms for bandit identification, which prune the plausible correct answers sequentially until only one remains, are computationally convenient since they reduce the problem size over time. However, existing elimination strategies are often not fully adaptive (they update their sampling rule infrequently) and are not easy to extend to combinatorial settings, where the set of answers is exponentially large in the problem dimension. On the other hand, most existing fully-adaptive strategies to tackle general identification problems are computationally demanding since they repeatedly test the correctness of every answer, without ever reducing the problem size. We show that adaptive methods can be modified to use elimination in both their stopping and sampling rules, hence obtaining the best of these two worlds: the algorithms (1) remain fully adaptive, (2) suffer a sample complexity that is never worse of their non-elimination counterpart, and (3) provably eliminate certain wrong answers early. We confirm these benefits experimentally, where elimination improves significantly the computational complexity of adaptive methods on common tasks like best-arm identification in linear bandits.

paragraphs: Bandit identification algorithms gather observations until they can select an answer with a required confidence. Elimination methods discard implausible answers along the way, reducing subsequent computation. However, existing versions often update their sampling choices infrequently and can be difficult to extend to problems with exponentially many possible answers.

Fully adaptive methods can respond more continuously to the evidence, but many repeatedly check every answer without shrinking the problem. This paper shows how to incorporate elimination into both the sampling rule and the stopping rule of adaptive methods. The resulting algorithms retain adaptivity while using discarded answers to reduce the work that remains.

The authors prove that the modified methods have sample complexity no worse than their corresponding non-elimination versions and eliminate certain incorrect answers early. These are separate benefits: they preserve observation efficiency while creating opportunities to save computation. Experiments confirm substantial computational improvements on common tasks, including best-arm identification in linear bandits. The contribution connects adaptive data collection with progressive simplification of the identification problem.
summary.tldr: Adding elimination to adaptive bandit identification preserves sample efficiency while reducing computation and removing some wrong answers early.

title: On Elimination Strategies for Bandit Fixed-Confidence Identification

abstract: There is growing interest in concept-based models (CBMs) that combine high-performance and interpretability by acquiring and reasoning with a vocabulary of high-level concepts. A key requirement is that the concepts be interpretable. Existing CBMs tackle this desideratum using a variety of heuristics based on unclear notions of interpretability, and fail to acquire concepts with the intended semantics. We address this by providing a clear definition of interpretability in terms of alignment between the model’s representation and an underlying data generation process, and introduce GlanceNets, a new CBM that exploits techniques from disentangled representation learning and open-set recognition to achieve alignment, thus improving the interpretability of the learned concepts. We show that GlanceNets, paired with concept-level supervision, achieve better alignment than state-of-the-art approaches while preventing spurious information from unintendedly leaking into the learned concepts.

paragraphs: Concept-based models make predictions through a vocabulary of high-level concepts, with the aim of making their reasoning understandable. That goal depends on each learned concept actually carrying its intended meaning. The authors argue that existing heuristic approaches lack a clear account of interpretability and can learn representations whose semantics do not match the concepts they are supposed to express.

The paper defines interpretability through alignment between the model’s representation and an underlying process that generates the data. GlanceNets pursue this alignment by combining techniques from disentangled representation learning and open-set recognition. This gives concept learning an explicit target: correspondence with the relevant factors of data generation.

With concept-level supervision, GlanceNets achieve better alignment than the compared state-of-the-art approaches while preventing unintended spurious information from leaking into learned concepts. This matters because a concept representation can otherwise carry information beyond its stated meaning. The findings connect interpretability to the content of the representation, with concept supervision forming part of the demonstrated setup.
summary.tldr: GlanceNets use concept supervision, disentangled representations, and open-set recognition to improve semantic alignment and prevent unintended information leakage.

title: GlanceNets: Interpretable, Leak-proof Concept-based Models

abstract: We consider approximate dynamic programming in $\gamma$-discounted Markov decision processes and apply it to approximate planning with linear value-function approximation. Our first contribution is a new variant of Approximate Policy Iteration (API), called Confident Approximate Policy Iteration (CAPI), which computes a deterministic stationary policy with an optimal error bound scaling linearly with the product of the effective horizon $H$ and the worst-case approximation error $\epsilon$ of the action-value functions of stationary policies. This improvement over API (whose error scales with $H^2$) comes at the price of an $H$-fold increase in memory cost. Unlike Scherrer and Lesner [2012], who recommended computing a non-stationary policy to achieve a similar improvement (with the same memory overhead), we are able to stick to stationary policies. This allows for our second contribution, the application of CAPI to planning with local access to a simulator and $d$-dimensional linear function approximation. As such, we design a planning algorithm that applies CAPI to obtain a sequence of policies with successively refined accuracies on a dynamically evolving set of states. The algorithm outputs an $\tilde O(\sqrt{d}H\epsilon)$-optimal policy after issuing $\tilde O(dH^4/\epsilon^2)$ queries to the simulator, simultaneously achieving the optimal accuracy bound and the best known query complexity bound, while earlier algorithms in the literature achieve only one of them. This query complexity is shown to be tight in all parameters except $H$. These improvements come at the expense of a mild (polynomial) increase in memory and computational costs of both the algorithm and its output policy.

paragraphs: Approximate planning must account for errors in estimated action values. In discounted Markov decision processes, ordinary Approximate Policy Iteration has an error bound that scales with H² times the worst-case approximation error ε, where H is the effective horizon. Confident Approximate Policy Iteration reduces this dependence to Hε while retaining a deterministic stationary policy.

The improvement requires H times as much memory. The authors then apply CAPI to planning with local simulator access and d-dimensional linear value-function approximation, refining policies over a changing collection of states.

It combines an optimal accuracy bound with the best known query bound, which earlier algorithms achieved separately. The query bound is tight except in its dependence on H. These gains entail polynomial increases in memory and computation, including costs associated with the output policy.
summary.tldr: CAPI improves planning accuracy while retaining stationary policies and combines strong simulator-query bounds with increased memory and computation.

title: Confident Approximate Policy Iteration for Efficient Local Planning in $q^\pi$-realizable MDPs

abstract: This paper introduces an interpretable contextual bandit algorithm using Tsetlin Machines, which solves complex pattern recognition tasks using propositional (Boolean) logic. The proposed bandit learning algorithm relies on straightforward bit manipulation, thus simplifying computation and interpretation. We then present a mechanism for performing Thompson sampling with Tsetlin Machine, given its non-parametric nature. Our empirical analysis shows that Tsetlin Machine as a base contextual bandit learner outperforms other popular base learners on eight out of nine datasets. We further analyze the interpretability of our learner, investigating how arms are selected based on propositional expressions that model the context.

paragraphs: A contextual bandit chooses among available actions using information about the current context. This paper introduces a learner based on Tsetlin Machines, which represent patterns using propositional Boolean logic. The aim is to make action selection interpretable while keeping the underlying computation straightforward through bit manipulation.

The authors develop a mechanism for Thompson sampling with this non-parametric learner. This supplies the action-selection procedure needed to use a Tsetlin Machine in the bandit setting. Because the learned patterns take the form of propositional expressions, the model also provides a concrete way to examine how contextual conditions influence the choice of an arm.

In the empirical comparison, the Tsetlin Machine base learner outperforms other popular base learners on eight of nine datasets. The paper separately investigates interpretability by analyzing the expressions behind arm selection. Together, these results support Boolean-rule learning as a competitive basis for contextual bandits in the evaluated settings, with decisions that can be inspected through the same logical structure used to make them.
summary.tldr: A Boolean-logic contextual bandit learner supports interpretable action selection and outperforms compared base learners on eight of nine datasets.

title: Tsetlin Machine for Solving Contextual Bandit Problems

abstract: The Off-Policy Evaluation (OPE) problem consists in evaluating the performance of new policies from the data collected by another one. OPE is crucial when evaluating a new policy online is too expensive or risky. Many of the state-of-the-art OPE estimators are based on the Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS) technique, which provides an unbiased estimator when the full support assumption holds, i.e., when the logging policy assigns a non-zero probability to each action. However, there are several scenarios where this assumption does not hold in practice, i.e., there is deficient support, and the IPS estimator is biased in the general case.In this paper, we consider two alternative estimators for the deficient support OPE problem. We first show how to adapt an estimator that was originally proposed for a different domain to the deficient support setting.Then, we propose another estimator, which is a novel contribution of this paper.These estimators exploit additional information about the actions, which we call side information, in order to make reliable estimates on the unsupported actions. Under alternative assumptions that do not require full support, we show that the considered estimators are unbiased.We also provide a theoretical analysis of the concentration when relaxing all the assumptions. Finally, we provide an experimental evaluation showing how the considered estimators are better suited for the deficient support setting compared to the baselines.

Many of the state-of-the-art OPE estimators are based on the Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS) technique, which provides an unbiased estimator when the full support assumption holds, i.e., when the logging policy assigns a non-zero probability to each action. However, there are several scenarios where this assumption does not hold in practice, i.e., there is deficient support, and the IPS estimator is biased in the general case.In this paper, we consider two alternative estimators for the deficient support OPE problem. We first show how to adapt an estimator that was originally proposed for a different domain to the deficient support setting.Then, we propose another estimator, which is a novel contribution of this paper.These estimators exploit additional information about the actions, which we call side information, in order to make reliable estimates on the unsupported actions. Under alternative assumptions that do not require full support, we show that the considered estimators are unbiased.We also provide a theoretical analysis of the concentration when relaxing all the assumptions. Finally, we provide an experimental evaluation showing how the considered estimators are better suited for the deficient support setting compared to the baselines.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a new decision policy would perform using data collected by another policy. This is useful when direct testing is costly or risky. A common technique, inverse propensity scoring, is unbiased under full support: the data-collecting policy must give every action a nonzero probability. When some actions are never selected, that guarantee generally fails.

The paper considers two estimators for this deficient-support setting. One adapts an estimator developed for another domain; the other is newly proposed. Both use additional information about actions to help estimate outcomes for actions unsupported by the logged data. The extra information supplies a basis for inference where direct observations are unavailable.

The authors prove unbiasedness under alternative assumptions that do not require full support. They also analyze concentration when relaxing the assumptions and compare the estimators experimentally with baselines. The reported results favor the proposed approaches in deficient-support settings. Their contribution is a conditional route to reliable evaluation using side information, with the assumptions explicitly replacing the usual coverage requirement.
summary.tldr: Two estimators use action side information to support off-policy evaluation without full action coverage, with unbiasedness under alternative assumptions.

title: Off-Policy Evaluation with Deficient Support Using Side Information

abstract: The alignment of adjacent frames is considered an essential operation in video super-resolution (VSR). Advanced VSR models, including the latest VSR Transformers, are generally equipped with well-designed alignment modules. However, the progress of the self-attention mechanism may violate this common sense. In this paper, we rethink the role of alignment in VSR Transformers and make several counter-intuitive observations. Our experiments show that: (i) VSR Transformers can directly utilize multi-frame information from unaligned videos, and (ii) existing alignment methods are sometimes harmful to VSR Transformers. These observations indicate that we can further improve the performance of VSR Transformers simply by removing the alignment module and adopting a larger attention window. Nevertheless, such designs will dramatically increase the computational burden, and cannot deal with large motions. Therefore, we propose a new and efficient alignment method called patch alignment, which aligns image patches instead of pixels. VSR Transformers equipped with patch alignment could demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks. Our work provides valuable insights on how multi-frame information is used in VSR and how to select alignment methods for different networks/datasets. Codes and models will be released at https://github.com/XPixelGroup/RethinkVSRAlignment.

title: Rethinking Alignment in Video Super-Resolution Transformers

abstract: We study the smooth minimax optimization problem $\min_{\bf x}\max_{\bf y} f({\bf x},{\bf y})$, where $f$ is $\ell$-smooth, strongly-concave in ${\bf y}$ but possibly nonconvex in ${\bf x}$. Most of existing works focus on finding the first-order stationary point of the function $f({\bf x},{\bf y})$ or its primal function $P({\bf x})\triangleq \max_{\bf y} f({\bf x},{\bf y})$, but few of them focus on achieving the second-order stationary point, which is essential to nonconvex problems. In this paper, we propose a novel approach for minimax optimization, called Minimax Cubic Newton (MCN), which could find an ${\mathcal O}\left(\varepsilon,\kappa^{1.5}\sqrt{\rho\varepsilon}\right)$-second-order stationary point of $P({\bf x})$ with calling ${\mathcal O}\left(\kappa^{1.5}\sqrt{\rho}\varepsilon^{-1.5}\right)$ times of second-order oracles and $\tilde{\mathcal O}\left(\kappa^{2}\sqrt{\rho}\varepsilon^{-1.5}\right)$ times of first-order oracles, where $\kappa$ is the condition number and $\rho$ is the Lipschitz continuous constant for the Hessian of $f({\bf x},{\bf y})$. In addition, we propose an inexact variant of MCN for high-dimensional problems to avoid calling the expensive second-order oracles. Instead, our method solves the cubic sub-problem inexactly via gradient descent and matrix Chebyshev expansion. This strategy still obtains the desired approximate second-order stationary point with high probability but only requires $\tilde{\mathcal O}\left(\kappa^{1.5}\ell\varepsilon^{-2}\right)$ Hessian-vector oracle calls and $\tilde{\mathcal O}\left(\kappa^{2}\sqrt{\rho}\varepsilon^{-1.5}\right)$ first-order oracle calls. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that considers the non-asymptotic convergence behavior of finding second-order stationary points for minimax problems without the convex-concave assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper studies minimax problems where one variable is minimized while another is maximized. The objective is smooth and strongly concave in the maximizing variable, but it may be nonconvex in the minimizing variable. The target is the primal objective: the value obtained after maximizing over the second variable.

The authors propose Minimax Cubic Newton, or MCN, to find approximate second-order stationary points of that primal objective. These points satisfy conditions involving both gradients and curvature, giving a stronger local criterion than first-order stationarity alone. The analysis provides explicit finite-accuracy bounds on the required first-order and second-order oracle calls, with dependence on accuracy, conditioning, and Hessian smoothness.

For high-dimensional problems, an inexact variant avoids expensive full second-order oracle calls. It approximately solves cubic subproblems using gradient descent and matrix Chebyshev expansion, relying instead on Hessian-vector products. This version reaches the desired approximate stationarity with high probability. The contribution is a non-asymptotic convergence analysis beyond convex-concave minimax problems, while retaining the stated strong concavity assumption on the maximizing variable.
summary.tldr: Minimax Cubic Newton provides finite-accuracy guarantees for second-order stationarity in smooth nonconvex, strongly concave minimax problems.

title: Finding Second-Order Stationary Points in Nonconvex-Strongly-Concave Minimax Optimization

abstract: Sparse training is a popular technique to reduce the overhead of training large models. Although previous work has shown promising results for nonstructured sparse models, it is still unclear whether a sparse model with structural constraints can be trained from scratch to high accuracy. In this work, we study the dynamic sparse training for a class of sparse models with shuffled block structures. Compared to nonstructured models, such fine-grained structured models are more hardware-friendly and can effectively accelerate the training process. We propose an algorithm that keeps adapting the sparse model while maintaining the active parameters in shuffled blocks. We conduct experiments on a variety of networks and datasets and obtain positive results. In particular, on ImageNet, we achieve dense accuracy for ResNet50 and ResNet18 at 0.5 sparsity. On CIFAR10/100, we show that dense accuracy can be recovered at 0.6 sparsity for various models. At higher sparsity, our algorithm can still match the accuracy of nonstructured sparse training in most cases, while reducing the training time by up to 5x due to the fine-grained block structures in the models.

paragraphs: Sparse training reduces the number of active model parameters, but the arrangement of those parameters matters for computational efficiency. Unstructured sparsity can deliver good accuracy while being less convenient for hardware. This paper asks whether models with structural constraints can be trained from scratch without giving up the accuracy benefits of sparse learning.

The proposed algorithm dynamically adapts the sparse model while keeping active parameters arranged in shuffled blocks. These fine-grained structures are more hardware-friendly than unstructured patterns. The method therefore treats the organization of active parameters as part of training, seeking both accurate models and structures that can accelerate computation.

On ImageNet, the method matches dense-model accuracy for ResNet50 and ResNet18 at 0.5 sparsity. On CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, various models recover dense accuracy at 0.6 sparsity. At higher sparsity, it matches unstructured sparse training accuracy in most cases, with training-time reductions of up to fivefold. These results show that the studied structural constraints can retain strong accuracy while making sparsity computationally useful.
summary.tldr: Dynamically maintaining shuffled blocks of active parameters enables sparse training that combines strong accuracy with speedups of up to fivefold.

title: Exposing and Exploiting Fine-Grained Block Structures for Fast and Accurate Sparse Training

abstract: We present the largest and most comprehensive empirical study of pre-trained visual representations (PVRs) or visual ‘foundation models’ for Embodied AI. First, we curate CortexBench, consisting of 17 different tasks spanning locomotion, navigation, dexterous, and mobile manipulation. Next, we systematically evaluate existing PVRs and find that none are universally dominant. To study the effect of pre-training data size and diversity, we combine over 4,000 hours of egocentric videos from 7 different sources (over 4.3M images) and ImageNet to train different-sized vision transformers using Masked Auto-Encoding (MAE) on slices of this data. Contrary to inferences from prior work, we find that scaling dataset size and diversity does not improve performance universally (but does so on average). Our largest model, named VC-1, outperforms all prior PVRs on average but does not universally dominate either. Next, we show that task- or domain-specific adaptation of VC-1 leads to substantial gains, with VC-1 (adapted) achieving competitive or superior performance than the best known results on all of the benchmarks in CortexBench. Finally, we present real-world hardware experiments, in which VC-1 and VC-1 (adapted) outperform the strongest pre-existing PVR. Overall, this paper presents no new techniques but a rigorous systematic evaluation, a broad set of findings about PVRs (that in some cases, refute those made in narrow domains in prior work), and open-sourced code and models (that required over 10,000 GPU-hours to train) for the benefit of the research community.

The authors assemble CortexBench, covering 17 tasks across locomotion, navigation, dexterous manipulation, and mobile manipulation. Existing representations show different strengths across these tasks, with no single model consistently winning everywhere. This broad comparison tests how far shared visual representations can serve diverse embodied behaviors.

To examine scaling, the authors train vision transformers with masked autoencoding using ImageNet and slices of a collection exceeding 4,000 hours of egocentric video from seven sources. Hardware experiments also favor VC-1 and its adapted version over the strongest pre-existing representation. The contribution is systematic evaluation and released resources, with findings that distinguish broad average progress from the additional value of adaptation.
summary.tldr: A broad embodied-AI evaluation finds average benefits from visual pretraining scale and substantial further gains from task or domain adaptation.

title: Where are we in the search for an Artificial Visual Cortex for Embodied Intelligence?

abstract: A major challenge in designing efficient statistical supervised learning algorithms is finding representations that perform well not only on available training samples but also on unseen data. While the study of representation learning has spurred much interest, most existing such approaches are heuristic; and very little is known about theoretical generalization guarantees. For example, the information bottleneck method seeks a good generalization by finding a minimal description of the input that is maximally informative about the label variable, where minimality and informativeness are both measured by Shannon’s mutual information. In this paper, we establish a compressibility framework that allows us to derive upper bounds on the generalization error of a representation learning algorithm in terms of the ``Minimum Description Length'' (MDL) of the labels or the latent variables (representations). Rather than the mutual information between the encoder’s input and the representation, which is often believed to reflect the algorithm’s generalization capability in the related literature but in fact, falls short of doing so, our new bounds involve the "multi-letter" relative entropy between the distribution of the representations (or labels) of the training and test sets and a fixed prior. In particular, these new bounds reflect the structure of the encoder and are not vacuous for deterministic algorithms. Our compressibility approach, which is information-theoretic in nature, builds upon that of Blum-Langford for PAC-MDL bounds and introduces two essential ingredients: block-coding and lossy-compression. The latter allows our approach to subsume the so-called geometrical compressibility as a special case. To the best knowledge of the authors, the established generalization bounds are the first of their kind for Information Bottleneck type encoders and representation learning. Finally, we partly exploit the theoretical results by introducing a new data-dependent prior. Numerical simulations illustrate the advantages of well-chosen such priors over classical priors used in IB.

paragraphs: Representation learning seeks features that remain useful beyond the training examples. The authors derive upper bounds on generalization error using Minimum Description Length, providing a formal connection between a representation's description and its ability to support learning on unseen data.

summary.tldr: A compression-based framework bounds representation-learning generalization error and yields informative guarantees even for deterministic encoders.

title: Minimum Description Length and Generalization Guarantees for Representation Learning

abstract: Curiosity has established itself as a powerful exploration strategy in deep reinforcement learning. Notably, leveraging expected future novelty as intrinsic motivation has been shown to efficiently generate exploratory trajectories, as well as a robust dynamics model. We consider the challenge of extracting goal-conditioned behavior from the products of such unsupervised exploration techniques, without any additional environment interaction. We find that conventional goal-conditioned reinforcement learning approaches for extracting a value function and policy fall short in this difficult offline setting. By analyzing the geometry of optimal goal-conditioned value functions, we relate this issue to a specific class of estimation artifacts in learned values. In order to mitigate their occurrence, we propose to combine model-based planning over learned value landscapes with a graph-based value aggregation scheme. We show how this combination can correct both local and global artifacts, obtaining significant improvements in zero-shot goal-reaching performance across diverse simulated environments.

This paper asks how to turn those products into goal-directed behavior without collecting any additional interactions. The task is to reach specified goals using information gathered during exploration that was not organized around those goals.

The authors find that conventional approaches for learning goal-conditioned values and policies struggle in this offline setting. By examining the geometry of optimal goal-conditioned value functions, they connect the problem to particular artifacts in learned value estimates. Such artifacts matter because planning and action selection depend on the shape of those estimates, not merely on having a dynamics model.

Their method combines model-based planning over learned value landscapes with graph-based aggregation of values. The combination can correct both local and global estimation artifacts, addressing problems at different scales. Across diverse simulated environments, it significantly improves zero-shot goal-reaching performance. The result shows a way to make curiosity-generated data more useful for later goals while preserving the requirement of no further environment interaction.
summary.tldr: Combining model-based planning with graph-based value aggregation improves offline goal reaching from curiosity-driven exploration.

title: Goal-conditioned Offline Planning from Curious Exploration

abstract: Event cameras have emerged as a promising vision sensor in recent years due to their unparalleled temporal resolution and dynamic range. While registration of 2D RGB images to 3D point clouds is a long-standing problem in computer vision, no prior work studies 2D-3D registration for event cameras. To this end, we propose E2PNet, the first learning-based method for event-to-point cloud registration.The core of E2PNet is a novel feature representation network called Event-Points-to-Tensor (EP2T), which encodes event data into a 2D grid-shaped feature tensor. This grid-shaped feature enables matured RGB-based frameworks to be easily used for event-to-point cloud registration, without changing hyper-parameters and the training procedure. EP2T treats the event input as spatio-temporal point clouds. Unlike standard 3D learning architectures that treat all dimensions of point clouds equally, the novel sampling and information aggregation modules in EP2T are designed to handle the inhomogeneity of the spatial and temporal dimensions. Experiments on the MVSEC and VECtor datasets demonstrate the superiority of E2PNet over hand-crafted and other learning-based methods. Compared to RGB-based registration, E2PNet is more robust to extreme illumination or fast motion due to the use of event data. Beyond 2D-3D registration, we also show the potential of EP2T for other vision tasks such as flow estimation, event-to-image reconstruction and object recognition. The source code can be found at: https://github.com/Xmu-qcj/E2PNet.

Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and dynamic range, making them attractive under difficult viewing conditions. The paper introduces a learning-based approach to this registration problem, extending a task traditionally studied with ordinary two-dimensional RGB images to a different kind of visual input.

Specialized sampling and aggregation account for the different roles of space and time. summary.tldr: E2PNet converts event streams into spatial feature grids to align them with 3D point clouds, improving robustness in difficult viewing conditions.

title: E2PNet: Event to Point Cloud Registration with Spatio-Temporal Representation Learning

abstract: Learnt deep neural networks for image super-resolution fail easily if the assumed degradation model in training mismatches that of the real degradation source at the inference stage. Instead of attempting to exhaust all degradation variants in simulation, which is unwieldy and impractical, we propose a novel adversarial neural degradation (AND) model that can, when trained in conjunction with a deep restoration neural network under a minmax criterion, generate a wide range of highly nonlinear complex degradation effects without any explicit supervision. The AND model has a unique advantage over the current state of the art in that it can generalize much better to unseen degradation variants and hence deliver significantly improved restoration performance on real-world images.

paragraphs: Image super-resolution models learn to restore detail from degraded images, but their performance can depend heavily on how their training images were damaged. When the degradation encountered during use differs from the training assumption, restoration can fail. This paper addresses that mismatch without trying to manually enumerate every possible degradation.

The proposed adversarial neural degradation model, AND, learns alongside a restoration network under a minmax training objective. The two networks have opposing roles: the degradation model produces challenging damaged images, while the restoration model learns to recover them. This joint training can produce a broad range of complex, nonlinear degradation effects without explicit supervision of the degradation process.

The paper reports better generalization to previously unseen degradation variants and substantially improved restoration of real-world images compared with the current state of the art. The contribution is a learned way to broaden the restoration challenges encountered during training. Its stated benefit is improved robustness to degradation mismatch, rather than a requirement to specify all possible real-world damage in advance.
summary.tldr: AND jointly trains a degradation network and a restoration network to improve super-resolution on unseen and real-world degradations.

title: AND: Adversarial Neural Degradation for Learning Blind Image Super-Resolution

abstract: Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) and Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control are foundational and extensively researched problems in optimal control. We investigate LQR and LQG problems with semi-adversarial perturbations and time-varying adversarial bandit loss functions. The best-known sublinear regret algorithm~\cite{gradu2020non} has a $T^{\frac{3}{4}}$ time horizon dependence, and its authors posed an open question about whether a tight rate of $\sqrt{T}$ could be achieved. We answer in the affirmative, giving an algorithm for bandit LQR and LQG which attains optimal regret, up to logarithmic factors. A central component of our method is a new scheme for bandit convex optimization with memory, which is of independent interest.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear quadratic control when the environment includes semi-adversarial perturbations and losses that can change adversarially over time. Feedback is bandit-style, so the controller does not receive the entire loss function. The goal is to keep regret, the accumulated shortfall relative to the problem's comparator, small as the interaction horizon grows.

The authors give an algorithm for both Linear Quadratic Regulator and Linear Quadratic Gaussian problems whose regret grows at the square-root rate in the time horizon, up to logarithmic factors. This improves the previously best-known horizon dependence of T to the three-quarter power and resolves the stated open question about achieving the tighter rate.

A central ingredient is a new method for bandit convex optimization with memory. Memory matters because control decisions influence subsequent system behavior, linking present choices to later losses. The result establishes optimal regret up to logarithmic factors for the studied control setting. It also contributes an optimization method that the authors identify as independently useful beyond its role in the control algorithm.
summary.tldr: A new bandit control algorithm achieves square-root regret up to logarithmic factors for the studied LQR and LQG problems.

title: Optimal Rates for Bandit Nonstochastic Control

abstract: Images contain rich relational knowledge that can help machines understand the world. Existing methods on visual knowledge extraction often rely on the pre-defined format (e.g., sub-verb-obj tuples) or vocabulary (e.g., relation types), restricting the expressiveness of the extracted knowledge. In this work, we take a first exploration to a new paradigm of open visual knowledge extraction. To achieve this, we present OpenVik which consists of an open relational region detector to detect regions potentially containing relational knowledge and a visual knowledge generator that generates format-free knowledge by prompting the large multimodality model with the detected region of interest. We also explore two data enhancement techniques for diversifying the generated format-free visual knowledge. Extensive knowledge quality evaluations highlight the correctness and uniqueness of the extracted open visual knowledge by OpenVik. Moreover, integrating our extracted knowledge across various visual reasoning applications shows consistent improvements, indicating the real-world applicability of OpenVik.

This paper explores open visual knowledge extraction, where the output is not confined to such formats. Its OpenVik system combines region detection with generation from a large multimodality model.

The first component finds image regions likely to contain relational knowledge. The second uses a detected region of interest to prompt the multimodality model, which generates format-free knowledge about it. This connects the generation process to image areas selected for their relational content. The authors also investigate two data enhancement techniques intended to diversify the generated knowledge.

Quality evaluations highlight the correctness and uniqueness of OpenVik's extracted knowledge. The authors additionally integrate that knowledge into multiple visual reasoning applications and report consistent improvements. These results support the usefulness of more expressive visual knowledge beyond its quality as standalone output. The work presents an initial exploration of this extraction paradigm and evidence that its outputs can benefit downstream reasoning.
summary.tldr: OpenVik extracts format-free relational knowledge by prompting a multimodality model with selected image regions.

title: Open Visual Knowledge Extraction via Relation-Oriented Multimodality Model Prompting

abstract: Certifiable, adaptive uncertainty estimates for unknown quantities are an essential ingredient of sequential decision-making algorithms. Standard approaches rely on problem-dependent concentration results and are limited to a specific combination of parameterization, noise family, and estimator. In this paper, we revisit the likelihood-based inference principle and propose to use \emph{likelihood ratios} to construct \emph{any-time valid} confidence sequences without requiring specialized treatment in each application scenario. Our method is especially suitable for problems with well-specified likelihoods, and the resulting sets always maintain the prescribed coverage in a model-agnostic manner. The size of the sets depends on a choice of estimator sequence in the likelihood ratio. We discuss how to provably choose the best sequence of estimators and shed light on connections to online convex optimization with algorithms such as Follow-the-Regularized-Leader. To counteract the initially large bias of the estimators, we propose a reweighting scheme that also opens up deployment in non-parametric settings such as RKHS function classes. We provide a \emph{non-asymptotic} analysis of the likelihood ratio confidence sets size for generalized linear models, using insights from convex duality and online learning. We showcase the practical strength of our method on generalized linear bandit problems, survival analysis, and bandits with various additive noise distributions.

paragraphs: Sequential decisions require uncertainty estimates that remain trustworthy as new observations arrive. Standard confidence constructions often depend on specialized arguments for a particular model, noise distribution, and estimator. This paper proposes likelihood-ratio confidence sequences as a more general approach, with validity that holds across observation times.

The method is especially suited to settings with well-specified likelihoods. Its confidence sets maintain the prescribed coverage, while their size depends on the estimator sequence used in the likelihood ratio. The authors investigate principled choices of that sequence and connect the problem to online convex optimization, including Follow-the-Regularized-Leader. This distinguishes the validity of the uncertainty statement from how informative its resulting set is.

A reweighting scheme addresses large initial estimator bias and enables use with nonparametric function classes such as reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. The paper also gives finite-sample size analysis for generalized linear models. Applications to generalized linear bandits, survival analysis, and bandits with different additive noise distributions demonstrate the method’s practical range.
summary.tldr: Likelihood-ratio confidence sequences provide anytime-valid uncertainty estimates, with estimator selection and reweighting helping control their size.

title: Likelihood Ratio Confidence Sets for Sequential Decision Making

abstract: Abstaining classifiers have the option to abstain from making predictions on inputs that they are unsure about. These classifiers are becoming increasingly popular in high-stakes decision-making problems, as they can withhold uncertain predictions to improve their reliability and safety. When evaluating black-box abstaining classifier(s), however, we lack a principled approach that accounts for what the classifier would have predicted on its abstentions. These missing predictions matter when they can eventually be utilized, either directly or as a backup option in a failure mode. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach and perspective to the problem of evaluating and comparing abstaining classifiers by treating abstentions as missing data. Our evaluation approach is centered around defining the counterfactual score of an abstaining classifier, defined as the expected performance of the classifier had it not been allowed to abstain. We specify the conditions under which the counterfactual score is identifiable: if the abstentions are stochastic, and if the evaluation data is independent of the training data (ensuring that the predictions are missing at random), then the score is identifiable. Note that, if abstentions are deterministic, then the score is unidentifiable because the classifier can perform arbitrarily poorly on its abstentions. Leveraging tools from observational causal inference, we then develop nonparametric and doubly robust methods to efficiently estimate this quantity under identification. Our approach is examined in both simulated and real data experiments.

paragraphs: A classifier that abstains can withhold predictions when it is uncertain. Evaluating only its visible predictions leaves another question unanswered: how well would it have performed if it had been required to predict every time? This matters when withheld predictions might later be used directly or as a fallback.

The paper treats abstentions as missing data and defines a counterfactual score: expected performance without the option to abstain. It gives conditions under which that score can be identified. Stochastic abstentions together with evaluation data independent of training data provide the stated missing-at-random setting. With deterministic abstention, the score is unidentifiable because performance on the withheld cases can be arbitrarily poor.

Under identification, the authors use observational causal-inference tools to develop nonparametric and doubly robust estimators. They examine the approach with simulated and real data. The contribution is a principled way to compare the underlying predictive performance of abstaining systems, with explicit conditions governing when the available observations can support that comparison.
summary.tldr: The paper defines and estimates how abstaining classifiers would perform without abstention, while specifying when that score is identifiable.

title: Counterfactually Comparing Abstaining Classifiers

abstract: Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) aims to address the challenge of distribution shift between the dataset and the learned policy, where the value of out-of-distribution (OOD) data may be erroneously estimated due to overgeneralization. It has been observed that a considerable portion of the benefits derived from the conservative terms designed by existing offline RL approaches originates from their impact on the learned representation. This observation prompts us to scrutinize the learning dynamics of offline RL, formalize the process of generalization, and delve into the prevalent overgeneralization issue in offline RL. We then investigate the potential to rein the generalization from the representation perspective to enhance offline RL. Finally, we present Representation Distinction (RD), an innovative plug-in method for improving offline RL algorithm performance by explicitly differentiating between the representations of in-sample and OOD state-action pairs generated by the learning policy. Considering scenarios in which the learning policy mirrors the behavioral policy and similar samples may be erroneously distinguished, we suggest a dynamic adjustment mechanism for RD based on an OOD data generator to prevent data representation collapse and further enhance policy performance. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying RD to specially-designed backbone algorithms and widely-used offline RL algorithms. The proposed RD method significantly improves their performance across various continuous control tasks on D4RL datasets, surpassing several state-of-the-art offline RL algorithms.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains from a fixed dataset, but the learned policy may choose actions unlike those represented in that data. Excessive generalization can then produce incorrect value estimates. This paper examines the problem through learned representations, motivated by the observation that much of the benefit of existing conservative penalties comes from how they change those representations.

The authors study learning dynamics and formalize generalization before proposing Representation Distinction, a plug-in method. RD explicitly separates representations of dataset state-action pairs from out-of-distribution pairs produced by the learning policy. The aim is to control how broadly information transfers in the representation, addressing the source of erroneous value estimates.

The method also includes dynamic adjustment using an out-of-distribution data generator. This addresses cases where the learned policy resembles the behavior policy, making rigid separation liable to distinguish similar samples incorrectly. The authors report that RD improves specially designed and widely used offline learning algorithms on D4RL continuous control tasks, surpassing several state-of-the-art approaches in those evaluations.
summary.tldr: Representation Distinction improves offline reinforcement learning by adaptively separating representations of dataset examples and out-of-distribution policy choices.

title: Reining Generalization in Offline Reinforcement Learning via Representation Distinction

abstract: Online learning to rank (OLTR) is a sequential decision-making problem where a learning agent selects an ordered list of items and receives feedback through user clicks. Although potential attacks against OLTR algorithms may cause serious losses in real-world applications, there is limited knowledge about adversarial attacks on OLTR. This paper studies attack strategies against multiple variants of OLTR. Our first result provides an attack strategy against the UCB algorithm on classical stochastic bandits with binary feedback, which solves the key issues caused by bounded and discrete feedback that previous works cannot handle. Building on this result, we design attack algorithms against UCB-based OLTR algorithms in position-based and cascade models. Finally, we propose a general attack strategy against any algorithm under the general click model. Each attack algorithm manipulates the learning agent into choosing the target attack item $T-o(T)$ times, incurring a cumulative cost of $o(T)$. Experiments on synthetic and real data further validate the effectiveness of our proposed attack algorithms.

paragraphs: Online learning to rank repeatedly presents an ordered list of items and learns from user clicks. This paper investigates how an attacker can steer that learning process toward a chosen item. The central question is whether a relatively small cumulative attack cost can produce a persistent distortion in what the system selects.

The analysis begins with a UCB algorithm for stochastic bandits with binary feedback. This setting creates difficulties because feedback is both bounded and discrete. After addressing those difficulties, the authors construct attacks on UCB-based ranking algorithms under position-based and cascade click models. They also introduce a general strategy against any algorithm within the general click model studied.

Each proposed attack makes the learner choose the target item T minus o(T) times while paying a cumulative cost of o(T). In plain language, as the interaction horizon grows, the target is selected on an overwhelming fraction of rounds while average attack cost vanishes. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the attacks’ effectiveness. The results expose a strong vulnerability within the analyzed feedback settings.
summary.tldr: The paper develops attacks that steer online ranking learners toward a target item on nearly all rounds at sublinear cumulative cost.

title: Adversarial Attacks on Online Learning to Rank with Click Feedback

abstract: Due to the limited availability of data, existing few-shot learning methods trained from scratch fail to achieve satisfactory performance. In contrast, large-scale pre-trained models such as CLIP demonstrate remarkable few-shot and zero-shot capabilities. To enhance the performance of pre-trained models for downstream tasks, fine-tuning the model on downstream data is frequently necessary. However, fine-tuning the pre-trained model leads to a decrease in its generalizability in the presence of distribution shift, while the limited number of samples in few-shot learning makes the model highly susceptible to overfitting. Consequently, existing methods for fine-tuning few-shot learning primarily focus on fine-tuning the model's classification head or introducing additional structure. In this paper, we introduce a fine-tuning approach termed Feature Discrimination Alignment (FD-Align). Our method aims to bolster the model's generalizability by preserving the consistency of spurious features across the fine-tuning process. Extensive experimental results validate the efficacy of our approach for both ID and OOD tasks. Once fine-tuned, the model can seamlessly integrate with existing methods, leading to performance improvements. Our code can be found in https://github.com/skingorz/FD-Align.

paragraphs: Large pretrained models can perform well with very little downstream data, but adapting them introduces a tension. Fine-tuning may improve task performance while weakening generalization under distribution shift. With only a few training examples, the model is also especially susceptible to overfitting, making it difficult to preserve the benefits of pretraining.

FD-Align introduces a fine-tuning approach centered on maintaining consistency in spurious features across adaptation. Its stated goal is to strengthen generalizability by constraining how these features change during fine-tuning. This differs in emphasis from approaches that concentrate on adjusting the classification head or adding extra structure to the pretrained model.

The authors report extensive experiments supporting the method on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks. They also find that the resulting fine-tuned model can be combined with existing methods for further performance improvements. The findings support feature consistency as a useful consideration when adapting pretrained models from few examples, particularly when performance must carry beyond the distribution used for adaptation.
summary.tldr: FD-Align preserves spurious-feature consistency during few-shot fine-tuning to improve generalization on in-distribution and shifted tasks.

title: FD-Align: Feature Discrimination Alignment for Fine-tuning Pre-Trained Models in Few-Shot Learning

abstract: Recently, multivariate time series (MTS) forecasting techniques have seen rapid development and widespread applications across various fields. Transformer-based and GNN-based methods have shown promising potential due to their strong ability to model interaction of time and variables. However, by conducting a comprehensive analysis of the real-world data, we observe that the temporal fluctuations and heterogeneity between variables are not well handled by existing methods. To address the above issues, we propose CrossGNN, a linear complexity GNN model to refine the cross-scale and cross-variable interaction for MTS. To deal with the unexpected noise in time dimension, an adaptive multi-scale identifier (AMSI) is leveraged to construct multi-scale time series with reduced noise. A Cross-Scale GNN is proposed to extract the scales with clearer trend and weaker noise. Cross-Variable GNN is proposed to utilize the homogeneity and heterogeneity between different variables. By simultaneously focusing on edges with higher saliency scores and constraining those edges with lower scores, the time and space complexity (i.e., $O(L)$) of CrossGNN can be linear with the input sequence length $L$. Extensive experimental results on 8 real-world MTS datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of CrossGNN compared with state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Forecasting several time-varying variables together requires understanding both patterns over time and relationships between variables. The authors’ analysis of real-world data identifies two difficulties that existing methods handle poorly: temporal fluctuations and differences among variables. CrossGNN addresses both by refining which interactions its graph neural networks emphasize.

An adaptive multi-scale identifier first constructs versions of the time series at multiple scales with reduced noise. A cross-scale graph network then extracts scales showing clearer trends and weaker noise. A separate cross-variable graph network models both similarities and differences among variables, allowing the forecasting system to use these distinct kinds of relationships together.

The model emphasizes edges with higher saliency scores while constraining lower-scoring edges. This design allows time and space complexity to scale linearly with input sequence length. Experiments on eight real-world multivariate time-series datasets demonstrate effectiveness compared with state-of-the-art methods. The approach connects noise handling and interaction selection: its forecasting representation depends on choosing informative temporal scales and variable relationships while controlling the cost of processing longer sequences.
summary.tldr: CrossGNN refines interactions across time scales and variables to forecast noisy multivariate series with linear complexity in sequence length.

title: CrossGNN: Confronting Noisy Multivariate Time Series Via Cross Interaction Refinement

abstract: We consider the problem of guaranteeing maximin-share ($\MMS$) when allocating a set of indivisible items to a set of agents with fractionally subadditive ($\XOS$) valuations. For $\XOS$ valuations, it has been previously shown that for some instances no allocation can guarantee a fraction better than $1/2$ of maximin-share to all the agents. Also, a deterministic allocation exists that guarantees $0.219225$ of the maximin-share of each agent. Our results involve both deterministic and randomized allocations. On the deterministic side, we improve the best approximation guarantee for fractionally subadditive valuations to $3/13 = 0.230769$. We develop new ideas on allocating large items in our allocation algorithm which might be of independent interest. Furthermore, we investigate randomized algorithms and the Best-of-both-worlds fairness guarantees. We propose a randomized allocation that is $1/4$-$\MMS$ ex-ante and $1/8$-$\MMS$ ex-post for $\XOS$ valuations. Moreover, we prove an upper bound of $3/4$ on the ex-ante guarantee for this class of valuations.

paragraphs: Allocating indivisible items fairly is difficult because items cannot be split to balance everyone’s value precisely. This paper studies guarantees relative to each agent’s maximin share for fractionally subadditive, or XOS, valuations. In this setting, some instances prevent any allocation from giving every agent more than half of their maximin share.

For deterministic allocations, the authors improve the known guaranteed fraction from 0.219225 to 3/13, approximately 0.230769. Their allocation algorithm introduces new ways of handling large items. This strengthens the worst-case fairness guarantee for the stated valuation class, rather than claiming that every instance can achieve each agent’s full maximin share.

The randomized result combines two kinds of protection: an expected guarantee before the random allocation is drawn and a minimum guarantee for the allocation actually realized. The proposed scheme provides one-quarter of maximin share ex ante and one-eighth ex post. The paper also establishes an upper bound of three-quarters on the ex-ante guarantee for XOS valuations. Together, the results distinguish improvements available through randomization from limits on what such guarantees can promise.
summary.tldr: The paper improves deterministic maximin-share fairness for XOS valuations and gives randomized guarantees both in expectation and after allocation.

title: Randomized and Deterministic Maximin-share Approximations for Fractionally Subadditive Valuations

abstract: Utilizing auxiliary outlier datasets to regularize the machine learning model has demonstrated promise for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection and safe prediction. Due to the labor intensity in data collection and cleaning, automating outlier data generation has been a long-desired alternative. Despite the appeal, generating photo-realistic outliers in the high dimensional pixel space has been an open challenge for the field. To tackle the problem, this paper proposes a new framework Dream-OOD, which enables imagining photo-realistic outliers by way of diffusion models, provided with only the in-distribution (ID) data and classes. Specifically, Dream-OOD learns a text-conditioned latent space based on ID data, and then samples outliers in the low-likelihood region via the latent, which can be decoded into images by the diffusion model. Different from prior works [16, 95], Dream-OOD enables visualizing and understanding the imagined outliers, directly in the pixel space. We conduct comprehensive quantitative and qualitative studies to understand the efficacy of Dream-OOD, and show that training with the samples generated by Dream-OOD can significantly benefit OOD detection performance.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks a model to recognize inputs that differ from the data it was trained to handle. Auxiliary outlier examples can help train this ability, but collecting and cleaning them takes work. Dream-OOD addresses this problem by generating photorealistic outlier images using the supplied in-distribution data and class information.

The framework learns a text-conditioned latent space from the in-distribution data. It samples from low-likelihood regions of that space, then uses a diffusion model to decode those samples into images. This organizes outlier generation around a learned representation of the familiar data, with unusual latent samples providing the material for generated outliers.

Producing actual images makes the imagined outliers available for visual inspection and interpretation. The authors use both quantitative and qualitative studies to investigate the framework, and report that training with its generated samples can significantly improve out-of-distribution detection. The stated finding supports generated outliers as useful training material in the evaluated setting, while the visual outputs make their content more directly understandable.
summary.tldr: Dream-OOD uses diffusion models to generate inspectable outlier images that can improve out-of-distribution detection.

title: Dream the Impossible: Outlier Imagination with Diffusion Models

abstract: Several studies have compared the in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) performance of models in computer vision and NLP. They report a frequent positive correlation and some surprisingly never even observe an inverse correlation indicative of a necessary trade-off. The possibility of inverse patterns is important to determine whether ID performance can serve as a proxy for OOD generalization capabilities.This paper shows that inverse correlations between ID and OOD performance do happen with multiple real-world datasets, not only in artificial worst-case settings. We explain theoretically how these cases arise and how past studies missed them because of improper methodologies that examined a biased selection of models.Our observations lead to recommendations that contradict those found in much of the current literature.- High OOD performance sometimes requires trading off ID performance.- Focusing on ID performance alone may not lead to optimal OOD performance. It may produce diminishing (eventually negative) returns in OOD performance.- In these cases, studies on OOD generalization that use ID performance for model selection (a common recommended practice) will necessarily miss the best-performing models, making these studies blind to a whole range of phenomena.

paragraphs: A common model-selection strategy assumes that better performance on familiar data predicts better performance after a distribution shift. This paper examines when that assumption breaks down. It shows inverse relationships between in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance across multiple real-world datasets, extending the issue beyond constructed worst-case examples.

The authors provide a theoretical explanation for how these inverse relationships arise. They also argue that earlier studies missed them because their methods examined biased selections of models. Which models enter a comparison can therefore change the apparent relationship between performance on familiar data and performance under a shift.

The implication is conditional but consequential: in some settings, improving shifted-data performance requires giving up some familiar-data performance. Continued optimization of the latter can yield diminishing and eventually negative returns for the former. In those cases, selecting models only by in-distribution performance necessarily excludes the best out-of-distribution choices. The findings challenge the reliability of that selection rule without claiming that the relationship is always negative.
summary.tldr: Real-world datasets can exhibit inverse ID–OOD performance relationships, making selection by ID performance alone miss the best OOD models.

title: ID and OOD Performance Are Sometimes Inversely Correlated on Real-world Datasets

abstract: A recent development in Bayesian optimization is the use of local optimization strategies, which can deliver strong empirical performance on high-dimensional problems compared to traditional global strategies. The "folk wisdom" in the literature is that the focus on local optimization sidesteps the curse of dimensionality; however, little is known concretely about the expected behavior or convergence of Bayesian local optimization routines. We first study the behavior of the local approach, and find that the statistics of individual local solutions of Gaussian process sample paths are surprisingly good compared to what we would expect to recover from global methods. We then present the first rigorous analysis of such a Bayesian local optimization algorithm recently proposed by Müller et al. (2021), and derive convergence rates in both the noisy and noiseless settings.

paragraphs: Local Bayesian optimization has shown strong empirical performance on high-dimensional problems compared with traditional global strategies. A common explanation is that focusing locally avoids the curse of dimensionality. This paper examines that intuition more carefully by studying both the quality of local solutions and the convergence behavior of a particular local optimization algorithm.

First, the authors analyze individual local solutions of functions drawn from a Gaussian process. They find that these solutions have surprisingly favorable statistics compared with what one would expect global methods to recover. This provides evidence relevant to why a local search strategy can work well, even when it does not pursue a global search directly.

The paper then gives the first rigorous analysis of a previously proposed Bayesian local optimization algorithm and derives convergence rates with both noisy and noiseless observations. These are guarantees for the analyzed procedure and settings. Together, the results replace part of the informal explanation for local optimization’s success with concrete statements about solution behavior and convergence.
summary.tldr: The paper studies why local Bayesian optimization performs well and establishes convergence rates for a specific algorithm with and without observation noise.

title: The Behavior and Convergence of Local Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Despite the recent advancements in offline reinforcement learning via supervised learning (RvS) and the success of the decision transformer (DT) architecture in various domains, DTs have fallen short in several challenging benchmarks. The root cause of this underperformance lies in their inability to seamlessly connect segments of suboptimal trajectories. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel approach to enhance RvS methods by integrating intermediate targets. We introduce the Waypoint Transformer (WT), using an architecture that builds upon the DT framework and conditioned on automatically-generated waypoints. The results show a significant increase in the final return compared to existing RvS methods, with performance on par or greater than existing state-of-the-art temporal difference learning-based methods. Additionally, the performance and stability improvements are largest in the most challenging environments and data configurations, including AntMaze Large Play/Diverse and Kitchen Mixed/Partial.
