paragraphs: Waypoint Transformer addresses a difficulty in offline reinforcement learning through supervised learning: useful behavior may require connecting pieces of trajectories that are individually suboptimal. The authors identify this inability to combine trajectory segments as a source of Decision Transformer underperformance on challenging benchmarks. Their approach adds intermediate targets to help guide behavior.

The model builds on the Decision Transformer architecture and conditions its decisions on automatically generated waypoints. These waypoints provide targets along the way to the final objective, giving the model additional structure for choosing actions. The contribution is a way to enhance supervised-learning approaches to reinforcement learning by incorporating intermediate guidance into the policy's conditioning.

Results show significantly higher final returns than existing reinforcement-learning-via-supervised-learning methods. Performance matches or exceeds state-of-the-art temporal-difference methods in the reported comparisons. The largest improvements in performance and stability occur in the most challenging environments and data configurations, including AntMaze Large Play/Diverse and Kitchen Mixed/Partial. These findings support intermediate targets as a useful response to the trajectory-connection problem identified by the authors.
summary.tldr: Waypoint Transformer uses automatically generated intermediate targets to improve offline reinforcement learning, especially in challenging trajectory-combination settings.

title: Waypoint Transformer: Reinforcement Learning via Supervised Learning with Intermediate Targets

abstract: This paper scales object-level reconstruction to complex scenes, advancing interactive scene reconstruction. We introduce two datasets, OmniSim and InterReal, featuring 28 scenes with multiple interactive objects. To tackle the challenge of inaccurate interactive motion recovery in complex scenes, we propose LiveScene, a scene-level language-embedded interactive radiance field that efficiently reconstructs and controls multiple objects. By decomposing the interactive scene into local deformable fields, LiveScene enables separate reconstruction of individual object motions, reducing memory consumption. Additionally, our interaction-aware language embedding localizes individual interactive objects, allowing for arbitrary control using natural language. Our approach demonstrates significant superiority in novel view synthesis, interactive scene control, and language grounding performance through extensive experiments. Project page: https://livescenes.github.io.

paragraphs: Reconstructing an interactive scene requires capturing how multiple objects move, as well as how the scene looks. Scaling from individual objects to complex scenes makes accurate motion recovery difficult. This paper introduces LiveScene to reconstruct and control several interactive objects within one scene, alongside the OmniSim and InterReal datasets containing 28 scenes.

LiveScene represents the scene using local deformable fields. This decomposition lets the system reconstruct individual object motions separately and reduces memory consumption. It also incorporates language embeddings designed around interaction, so that natural-language references can localize particular interactive objects and support their control within the reconstructed scene.

Experiments report significant improvements in rendering unseen viewpoints, controlling interactive scenes, and grounding language in scene objects. These outcomes address connected aspects of the same representation: appearance, motion, and the ability to identify what a language instruction refers to. The contribution is a scene-level framework that combines those capabilities while retaining separate representations of individual objects' motion.
summary.tldr: LiveScene combines local deformable fields and interaction-aware language embeddings to reconstruct, render, and control multiple objects in complex scenes.

title: LiveScene: Language Embedding Interactive Radiance Fields for Physical Scene Control and Rendering

abstract: Even for simple arithmetic tasks like integer addition, it is challenging for Transformers to generalize to longer sequences than those encountered during training. To tackle this problem, we propose *position coupling*, a simple yet effective method that directly embeds the structure of the tasks into the positional encoding of a (decoder-only) Transformer. Taking a departure from the vanilla absolute position mechanism assigning unique position IDs to each of the tokens, we assign the same position IDs to two or more "relevant" tokens; for integer addition tasks, we regard digits of the same significance as in the same position. On the empirical side, we show that with the proposed position coupling, our models trained on 1 to 30-digit additions can generalize up to *200-digit* additions (6.67x of the trained length). On the theoretical side, we prove that a 1-layer Transformer with coupled positions can solve the addition task involving exponentially many digits, whereas any 1-layer Transformer without positional information cannot entirely solve it. We also demonstrate that position coupling can be applied to other algorithmic tasks such as Nx2 multiplication and a two-dimensional task. Our codebase is available at [github.com/HanseulJo/position-coupling](https://github.com/HanseulJo/position-coupling).

paragraphs: Transformers can struggle with arithmetic sequences longer than those seen during training, even for integer addition. Position coupling addresses this by putting task structure directly into positional encodings. Instead of assigning every token a distinct position ID, the method gives shared IDs to tokens that play related roles.

For addition, digits with the same significance receive the same position ID. This explicitly represents an arithmetic relationship within the input's positional information. In experiments, models trained on additions involving 1 to 30 digits generalize to 200-digit additions, reaching 6.67 times the maximum training length.

The paper also proves that a one-layer Transformer with coupled positions can solve addition involving exponentially many digits, whereas a one-layer Transformer without positional information cannot solve the task completely. This theoretical comparison specifically concerns the absence of positional information. Additional demonstrations cover N-by-2 multiplication and a two-dimensional task. Together, the results show how task-informed position assignments can support length generalization, with both empirical evidence and an expressivity result for the stated architecture.
summary.tldr: Position coupling assigns shared position IDs to structurally related tokens, enabling addition models trained on up to 30 digits to generalize to 200 digits.

title: Position Coupling: Improving Length Generalization of Arithmetic Transformers Using Task Structure

abstract: Machine unlearning (MU) has emerged to enhance the privacy and trustworthiness of deep neural networks. Approximate MU is a practical method for large-scale models. Our investigation into approximate MU starts with identifying the steepest descent direction, minimizing the output Kullback-Leibler divergence to exact MU inside a parameters' neighborhood. This probed direction decomposes into three components: weighted forgetting gradient ascent, fine-tuning retaining gradient descent, and a weight saliency matrix. Such decomposition derived from Euclidean metric encompasses most existing gradient-based MU methods. Nevertheless, adhering to Euclidean space may result in sub-optimal iterative trajectories due to the overlooked geometric structure of the output probability space. We suggest embedding the unlearning update into a manifold rendered by the remaining geometry, incorporating second-order Hessian from the remaining data. It helps prevent effective unlearning from interfering with the retained performance. However, computing the second-order Hessian for large-scale models is intractable. To efficiently leverage the benefits of Hessian modulation, we propose a fast-slow parameter update strategy to implicitly approximate the up-to-date salient unlearning direction.Free from specific modal constraints, our approach is adaptable across computer vision unlearning tasks, including classification and generation. Extensive experiments validate our efficacy and efficiency. Notably, our method successfully performs class-forgetting on ImageNet using DiT and forgets a class on CIFAR-10 using DDPM in just 50 steps, compared to thousands of steps required by previous methods. Code is available at [Unified-Unlearning-w-Remain-Geometry](https://github.com/K1nght/Unified-Unlearning-w-Remain-Geometry).

paragraphs: Approximate machine unlearning aims to remove learned information efficiently from large models. The paper begins by identifying a local update direction that minimizes output Kullback-Leibler divergence from exact unlearning. This direction decomposes into forgetting gradient ascent, retaining gradient descent, and a weight-saliency matrix, connecting many existing gradient-based methods.

The authors argue that Euclidean updates can overlook the geometry of output probabilities and produce suboptimal trajectories. They instead incorporate geometry from the remaining data through second-order Hessian information, aiming to protect retained performance during unlearning. Because explicitly computing this information is intractable for large models, they propose fast-slow parameter updates that implicitly approximate the desired direction.

Experiments cover computer vision classification and generation and support the method's efficiency and effectiveness. The authors report class forgetting on ImageNet with DiT and class forgetting on CIFAR-10 with DDPM in 50 steps, compared with thousands for previous methods. The approach combines a unifying account of existing updates with an efficient approximation to geometry-aware unlearning.
summary.tldr: The method uses geometry from retained data and fast-slow updates to make approximate unlearning efficient while helping preserve retained performance.

title: Unified Gradient-Based Machine Unlearning with Remain Geometry Enhancement

abstract: Multimodal contrastive learning (MCL) has recently demonstrated significant success across various tasks. However, the existing MCL treats all negative samples equally and ignores the potential semantic association with positive samples, which limits the model's ability to achieve fine-grained alignment. In multi-view scenarios, MCL tends to prioritize shared information while neglecting modality-specific unique information across different views, leading to feature suppression and suboptimal performance in downstream tasks. To address these limitations, we propose a novel contrastive framework name *QUEST: Quadruple Multimodal Contrastive Learning with Constraints and Self-Penalization*. In the QUEST framework, we propose quaternion contrastive objectives and orthogonal constraints to extract sufficient unique information. Meanwhile, a shared information-guided penalization is introduced to ensure that shared information does not excessively influence the optimization of unique information. Our method leverages quaternion vector spaces to simultaneously optimize shared and unique information. Experiments on multiple datasets show that our method achieves superior performance in multimodal contrastive learning benchmarks. On public benchmark, our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, and on synthetic shortcut datasets, we outperform existing baseline methods by an average of 97.95\% on the CLIP model.

paragraphs: Multimodal contrastive learning aligns information from different modalities, but the paper identifies two weaknesses in existing approaches. Treating all negative examples alike overlooks possible semantic relationships with positive examples. In addition, emphasizing information shared across views can suppress information unique to a modality, reducing the usefulness of learned features.

QUEST uses quaternion vector spaces to optimize shared and unique information together. Its contrastive objectives and orthogonality constraints are designed to extract sufficient unique information. A further penalty guided by shared information prevents the shared component from exerting excessive influence over the optimization of unique features.

The central aim is to preserve what different views have in common while also learning what each contributes individually. Experiments across multiple datasets report superior multimodal contrastive-learning performance, including state-of-the-art results on a public benchmark. On synthetic shortcut datasets using CLIP, the authors report an average improvement of 97.95% over existing baselines. That large reported gain belongs specifically to the synthetic shortcut setting described in the abstract.
summary.tldr: QUEST jointly learns shared and modality-specific information using quaternion objectives, constraints, and penalization, improving the evaluated contrastive-learning results.

title: QUEST: Quadruple Multimodal Contrastive Learning with Constraints and Self-Penalization

abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated great success in text-to-video (T2V) generation. However, existing methods may face challenges when handling complex (long) video generation scenarios that involve multiple objects or dynamic changes in object numbers. To address these limitations, we propose VideoTetris, a novel framework that enables compositional T2V generation. Specifically, we propose spatio-temporal compositional diffusion to precisely follow complex textual semantics by manipulating and composing the attention maps of denoising networks spatially and temporally. Moreover, we propose a new dynamic-aware data processing pipeline and a consistency regularization method to enhance the consistency of auto-regressive video generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our VideoTetris achieves impressive qualitative and quantitative results in compositional T2V generation. Code is available at: https://github.com/YangLing0818/VideoTetris

paragraphs: Text-to-video diffusion models can struggle with complex scenes containing several objects or changing numbers of objects over time. Longer videos make this harder because the generated sequence must follow evolving textual instructions while remaining coherent. VideoTetris addresses these challenges through compositional control over video generation.

Its central mechanism manipulates and combines attention maps within denoising networks across both space and time. This gives the generation process a way to organize different parts of the textual description according to where and when they should influence the video. The framework also adds a data-processing pipeline that accounts for dynamics and a consistency regularizer for autoregressive generation.

The experiments report strong qualitative and quantitative results for compositional text-to-video generation. The components address related but distinct needs: attention composition supports complex textual semantics, while the processing pipeline and regularizer improve consistency as generation proceeds. Together, they offer a framework for handling videos whose content changes over time, including scenes where object composition is more complicated than a single persistent subject.
summary.tldr: VideoTetris composes attention across space and time to generate complex videos while improving consistency during autoregressive generation.

title: VideoTetris: Towards Compositional Text-to-Video Generation

abstract: Mean-field Langevin dynamics (MLFD) is a class of interacting particle methods that tackle convex optimization over probability measures on a manifold, which are scalable, versatile, and enjoy computational guarantees. However, some important problems -- such as risk minimization for infinite width two-layer neural networks, or sparse deconvolution -- are originally defined over the set of signed, rather than probability, measures. In this paper, we investigate how to extend the MFLD framework to convex optimization problems over signed measures.Among two known reductions from signed to probability measures -- the lifting and the bilevel approaches -- we show that the bilevel reduction leads to stronger guarantees and faster rates (at the price of a higher per-iteration complexity).In particular, we investigate the convergence rate of MFLD applied to the bilevel reduction in the low-noise regime and obtain two results. First, this dynamics is amenable to an annealing schedule, adapted from [Suzuki et al., 2023], that results in polynomial convergence rates to a fixed multiplicative accuracy. Second, we investigate the problem of learning a single neuron with the bilevel approach and obtain local exponential convergence rates that depend polynomially on the dimension and noise level (to compare with the exponential dependence that would result from prior analyses).

paragraphs: Mean-field Langevin dynamics uses interacting particles to solve convex optimization problems over probability measures. Some important applications instead require signed measures, which can assign negative as well as positive weights. The paper studies how to extend this optimization framework to that setting, including problems associated with infinite-width two-layer networks and sparse deconvolution.

The authors compare two existing ways to translate signed-measure problems into probability-measure problems: lifting and bilevel reduction. They show that the bilevel approach provides stronger guarantees and faster convergence rates, with higher computational complexity per iteration. This is an explicit tradeoff between the progress guaranteed across iterations and the work required for each one.

For the low-noise regime, an annealing schedule yields polynomial convergence rates to a fixed multiplicative accuracy. In the specific problem of learning one neuron, the authors also obtain local exponential convergence with polynomial dependence on dimension and noise level, improving the exponential dependence from earlier analyses. These results concern distinct guarantees: the single-neuron result is local, while the annealing result targets a specified multiplicative accuracy.
summary.tldr: A bilevel reduction extends mean-field Langevin optimization to signed measures with stronger convergence guarantees at greater per-iteration cost.

title: Mean-Field Langevin Dynamics for Signed Measures via a Bilevel Approach

abstract: Robust reinforcement learning is essential for deploying reinforcement learning algorithms in real-world scenarios where environmental uncertainty predominates.Traditional robust reinforcement learning often depends on rectangularity assumptions, where adverse probability measures of outcome states are assumed to be independent across different states and actions. This assumption, rarely fulfilled in practice, leads to overly conservative policies. To address this problem, we introduce a new time-constrained robust MDP (TC-RMDP) formulation that considers multifactorial, correlated, and time-dependent disturbances, thus more accurately reflecting real-world dynamics. This formulation goes beyond the conventional rectangularity paradigm, offering new perspectives and expanding the analytical framework for robust RL.We propose three distinct algorithms, each using varying levels of environmental information, and evaluate them extensively on continuous control benchmarks. Our results demonstrate that these algorithms yield an efficient tradeoff between performance and robustness, outperforming traditional deep robust RL methods in time-constrained environments while preserving robustness in classical benchmarks.This study revisits the prevailing assumptions in robust RL and opens new avenues for developing more practical and realistic RL applications.

paragraphs: Robust reinforcement learning seeks policies that work despite environmental uncertainty. Traditional formulations often assume that adverse transition distributions can vary independently across states and actions, a property called rectangularity. The paper argues that this assumption is rarely realistic and can lead to policies that are overly conservative.

Time-Constrained Robust MDPs provide a formulation that allows disturbances to involve multiple factors, remain correlated, and change over time. This expands the uncertainty model beyond independent adverse choices at each state and action. The authors develop three algorithms that use different amounts of environmental information, connecting the formulation to several levels of knowledge about the system.

Evaluations on continuous-control benchmarks show a favorable tradeoff between performance and robustness. The algorithms outperform traditional deep robust reinforcement learning methods in time-constrained environments while preserving robustness on classical benchmarks. The result supports modeling the structure of disturbances more explicitly: accounting for how uncertainty is related across conditions and time can reduce excessive conservatism without discarding robustness in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Time-Constrained Robust MDPs model correlated, time-dependent disturbances and improve the performance–robustness tradeoff in evaluated control tasks.

title: Time-Constrained Robust MDPs

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently emerged as powerful tools for addressing complex optimization problems. It has been theoretically demonstrated that GNNs can universally approximate the solution mapping functions of linear programming (LP) problems. However, these theoretical results typically require GNNs to have large parameter sizes. Conversely, empirical experiments have shown that relatively small GNNs can solve LPs effectively, revealing a significant discrepancy between theoretical predictions and practical observations. In this work, we aim to bridge this gap by providing a theoretical foundation for the effectiveness of small-size GNNs. We prove that polylogarithmic-depth, constant-width GNNs are sufficient to solve packing and covering LPs, two widely used classes of LPs. Our proof leverages the capability of GNNs to simulate a variant of the gradient descent algorithm on a carefully selected potential function. Additionally, we introduce a new GNN architecture, termed GD-Net. Experimental results demonstrate that GD-Net significantly outperforms conventional GNN structures while using fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Earlier theory shows that graph neural networks can approximate solution mappings for linear programs, but those results typically call for large networks. Experiments suggest that smaller networks can work well. This paper addresses that mismatch by identifying classes of linear programs for which compact networks have a theoretical justification.

The main result proves that constant-width graph neural networks with polylogarithmic depth are sufficient to solve packing and covering linear programs. The construction relies on the network's ability to simulate a variant of gradient descent applied to a carefully chosen potential function. This connects network computation to a specific optimization procedure and establishes sufficiency for those two classes.

The authors also introduce an architecture called GD-Net. Experiments show that it significantly outperforms conventional graph neural network structures while using fewer parameters. Together, the proof and architecture provide theoretical and empirical support for compact models in this setting. The theorem concerns packing and covering problems, so its significance lies in explaining small-network capability for these widely used classes without requiring a universal claim about every linear program.
summary.tldr: The paper proves compact GNNs suffice for packing and covering linear programs and introduces GD-Net, which improves reported performance with fewer parameters.

title: On the Power of Small-size Graph Neural Networks for Linear Programming

abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning framework that trains accurate global models while preserving clients' privacy-sensitive data. However, most FL approaches assume that clients possess labeled data, which is often not the case in practice. Federated Semi-Supervised Learning (FSSL) addresses this label deficiency problem, targeting situations where only the server has a small amount of labeled data while clients do not. However, a significant performance gap exists between Centralized Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) and FSSL. This gap arises from confirmation bias, which is more pronounced in FSSL due to multiple local training epochs and the separation of labeled and unlabeled data. We propose $(FL)^2$, a robust training method for unlabeled clients using sharpness-aware consistency regularization. We show that regularizing the original pseudo-labeling loss is suboptimal, and hence we carefully select unlabeled samples for regularization. We further introduce client-specific adaptive thresholding and learning status-aware aggregation to adjust the training process based on the learning progress of each client. Our experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves performance and bridges the gap with SSL, particularly in scenarios with scarce labeled data.
originalAbstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning framework that trains accurate global models while preserving clients' privacy-sensitive data. However, most FL approaches assume that clients possess labeled data, which is often not the case in practice. Federated Semi-Supervised Learning (FSSL) addresses this label deficiency problem, targeting situations where only the server has a small amount of labeled data while clients do not. However, a significant performance gap exists between Centralized Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) and FSSL. This gap arises from confirmation bias, which is more pronounced in FSSL due to multiple local training epochs and the separation of labeled and unlabeled data. We propose $(FL)^2$, a robust training method for unlabeled clients using sharpness-aware consistency regularization. We show that regularizing the original pseudo-labeling loss is suboptimal, and hence we carefully select unlabeled samples for regularization. We further introduce client-specific adaptive thresholding and learning status-aware aggregation to adjust the training process based on the learning progress of each client. Our experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly improves performance and bridges the gap with SSL, particularly in scenarios with scarce labeled data.

paragraphs: This paper considers federated learning where clients have unlabeled data and only the server has a small labeled collection. Such a setup can perform substantially worse than centralized semi-supervised learning. The authors attribute the gap to confirmation bias: training reinforces incorrect model-generated labels, with repeated local training and the separation of labeled and unlabeled data making the problem more pronounced.

Their method, (FL)², introduces sharpness-aware consistency regularization for client training. The authors find that applying regularization to the original pseudo-labeling loss is suboptimal, so they carefully select which unlabeled samples receive it. This selection makes the regularization strategy a targeted part of learning from uncertain labels.

The framework also adapts thresholds separately for each client and adjusts aggregation according to clients’ learning progress. These mechanisms let training respond to differences in how clients are learning. On three benchmark datasets, the method substantially improves performance and bridges the gap with centralized semi-supervised learning, particularly when labeled examples are scarce. The result supports coordinating sample selection, local adaptation, and aggregation when supervision is concentrated at the server.
summary.tldr: (FL)² improves federated learning with unlabeled clients through selective regularization and training adjustments based on client progress.

title: (FL)$^2$: Overcoming Few Labels in Federated Semi-Supervised Learning

abstract: Recent breakthroughs in vision-language models (VLMs) emphasize the necessity of benchmarking human preferences in real-world multimodal interactions. To address this gap, we launched WildVision-Arena (WV-Arena), an online platform that collects human preferences to evaluate VLMs. We curated WV-Bench by selecting 500 high-quality samples from 8,000 user submissions in WV-Arena. WV-Bench uses GPT-4 as the judge to compare each VLM with Claude-3-Sonnet, achieving a Spearman correlation of 0.94 with the WV-Arena Elo. This significantly outperforms other benchmarks like MMVet, MMMU, and MMStar.Our comprehensive analysis of 20K real-world interactions reveals important insights into the failure cases of top-performing VLMs. For example, we find that although GPT-4V surpasses many other models like Reka-Flash, Opus, and Yi-VL-Plus in simple visual recognition and reasoning tasks, it still faces challenges with subtle contextual cues, spatial reasoning, visual imagination, and expert domain knowledge. Additionally, current VLMs exhibit issues with hallucinations and safety when intentionally provoked. We are releasing our chat and feedback data to further advance research in the field of VLMs.

paragraphs: WildVision evaluates vision-language models through human preferences in real-world multimodal interactions. Its online arena collects user judgments, while a smaller benchmark draws 500 selected examples from 8,000 submissions. The goal is to make benchmark evaluation more closely reflect the preferences observed when people actually interact with these models.

Its rankings achieve a Spearman correlation of 0.94 with the arena's Elo rankings, exceeding the reported alignment of MMVet, MMMU, and MMStar. The study additionally finds hallucination and safety problems under intentional provocation. Together, the preference benchmark and failure analysis provide complementary views of model performance.
summary.tldr: WildVision builds a human-preference arena and aligned benchmark while documenting vision-language model failures in real-world interactions.

title: WildVision: Evaluating Vision-Language Models in the Wild with Human Preferences

abstract: The Stackelberg prediction game (SPG) is a popular model for characterizing strategic interactions between a learner and an adversarial data provider. Although optimization problems in SPGs are often NP-hard, a notable special case involving the least squares loss (SPG-LS) has gained significant research attention recently, (Bishop et al. 2020; Wang et al. 2021; Wang et al. 2022). The latest state-of-the-art method for solving the SPG-LS problem is the spherically constrained least squares reformulation (SCLS) method proposed in the work of Wang et al. (2022). However, the lack of theoretical analysis on the error of the SCLS method limits its large-scale applications. In this paper, we investigate the estimation error between the learner obtained by the SCLS method and the actual learner. Specifically, we reframe the estimation error of the SCLS method as a Primary Optimization ($\textbf{PO}$) problem and utilize the Convex Gaussian min-max theorem (CGMT) to transform the $\textbf{PO}$ problem into an Auxiliary Optimization ($\textbf{AO}$) problem. Subsequently, we provide a theoretical error analysis for the SCLS method based on this simplified $\textbf{AO}$ problem. This analysis not only strengthens the theoretical framework of the SCLS method but also confirms the reliability of the learner produced by it. We further conduct experiments to validate our theorems, and the results are in excellent agreement with our theoretical predictions.

summary.tldr: The paper derives and experimentally validates an estimation-error analysis for the SCLS method used in least-squares Stackelberg prediction games.

title: Error Analysis of Spherically Constrained Least Squares Reformulation in Solving the Stackelberg Prediction Game

abstract: Many of the recent advances in computer vision and language models can be attributed to the success of transfer learning via the pre-training of large foundation models. However, a theoretical framework which explains this empirical success is incomplete and remains an active area of research. Flatness of the loss surface and neural collapse have recently emerged as useful pre-training metrics which shed light on the implicit biases underlying pre-training. In this paper, we explore the geometric complexity of a model's learned representations as a fundamental mechanism that relates these two concepts. We show through experiments and theory that mechanisms which affect the geometric complexity of the pre-trained network also influence the neural collapse. Furthermore, we show how this effect of the geometric complexity generalizes to the neural collapse of new classes as well, thus encouraging better performance on downstream tasks, particularly in the few-shot setting.

paragraphs: This paper seeks a better explanation for why pretraining helps models learn downstream tasks. Two properties of pretrained models have attracted attention: the flatness of the loss surface and neural collapse in learned representations. The authors investigate geometric complexity as a mechanism connecting these properties, shifting attention toward the structure of the representations themselves.

Using theory and experiments, they show that mechanisms affecting a pretrained network's geometric complexity also influence neural collapse. This links changes in representation geometry to a property used to understand pretraining's implicit biases. The work therefore treats geometric complexity as an explanatory connection between existing observations, rather than considering flatness and neural collapse independently.

The authors further show that this influence extends to neural collapse for new classes. That extension matters for transfer learning because downstream tasks involve learning beyond the original pretraining classes. The paper connects the effect to better downstream performance, particularly when only a few examples are available. Its findings contribute a geometric account of transfer behavior without presenting a complete theory of every factor behind pretraining's success.
summary.tldr: Theory and experiments connect representation complexity to neural collapse, including for new classes, helping explain few-shot transfer performance.

title: The Impact of Geometric Complexity on Neural Collapse in Transfer Learning

abstract: This paper introduces a boosted conformal procedure designed to tailor conformalized prediction intervals toward specific desired properties, such as enhanced conditional coverage or reduced interval length. We employ machine learning techniques, notably gradient boosting, to systematically improve upon a predefined conformity score function. This process is guided by carefully constructed loss functions that measure the deviation of prediction intervals from the targeted properties. The procedure operates post-training, relying solely on model predictions and without modifying the trained model (e.g., the deep network). Systematic experiments demonstrate that starting from conventional conformal methods, our boosted procedure achieves substantial improvements in reducing interval length and decreasing deviation from target conditional coverage.

The procedure operates post-training, relying solely on model predictions and without modifying the trained model (e.g., the deep network). paragraphs: Prediction intervals express uncertainty by returning a range of possible outcomes. Their usefulness depends on properties such as their width and how coverage behaves under different conditions. This paper introduces a procedure for adapting conformal prediction intervals toward selected goals, including shorter intervals or closer agreement with a target level of conditional coverage.

The method starts with an existing conformity score, the scoring function used to construct conformal intervals. It then applies machine learning techniques, particularly gradient boosting, to improve that function. Carefully designed losses measure how far the resulting intervals deviate from the desired properties, giving the improvement process a specific objective.

The procedure runs after the predictive model has been trained and uses its predictions without changing the model itself. Experiments starting from conventional conformal methods report substantial reductions in interval length and in deviation from target conditional coverage. These findings support adjusting the uncertainty procedure as a practical way to improve interval behavior around an already trained predictor; they do not assert exact conditional coverage.
summary.tldr: Gradient boosting refines conformal scoring functions after model training to produce shorter intervals or improve alignment with target conditional coverage.

title: Boosted Conformal Prediction Intervals

abstract: Instruction data is crucial for improving the capability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to align with human-level performance. Recent research LIMA demonstrates that alignment is essentially a process where the model adapts instructions' interaction style or format to solve various tasks, leveraging pre-trained knowledge and skills. Therefore, for instructional data, the most important aspect is the task it represents, rather than the specific semantics and knowledge information. The latent representations of instructions play roles for some instruction-related tasks like data selection and demonstrations retrieval. However, they are always derived from text embeddings, encompass overall semantic information that influences the representation of task categories. In this work, we introduce a new concept, instruction embedding, and construct Instruction Embedding Benchmark (IEB) for its training and evaluation. Then, we propose a baseline Prompt-based Instruction Embedding (PIE) method to make the representations more attention on tasks. The evaluation of PIE, alongside other embedding methods on IEB with two designed tasks, demonstrates its superior performance in accurately identifying task categories. Moreover, the application of instruction embeddings in four downstream tasks showcases its effectiveness and suitability for instruction-related tasks.

paragraphs: Representations of instructions are useful for selecting training data and retrieving demonstrations. Ordinary text embeddings capture broad semantic content, which can interfere with identifying the kind of task an instruction requests. This paper emphasizes task identity as the relevant organizing principle for such instruction-related uses.

The authors introduce instruction embeddings and create the Instruction Embedding Benchmark for training and evaluation. They also propose Prompt-based Instruction Embedding, or PIE, as a baseline designed to make representations focus more strongly on tasks. The distinction is between representing the overall content of an instruction and representing the operation it asks a model to perform.

PIE is compared with other embedding methods on two tasks in the new benchmark and performs better at identifying task categories. Applications across four downstream tasks also support the usefulness of instruction embeddings. The results connect the proposed representation goal to practical uses: when selecting or retrieving instructions, accurately capturing task type can provide information that broad semantic similarity does not adequately isolate.
summary.tldr: Instruction embeddings focus on requested task types, with PIE improving task identification and supporting four downstream applications.

title: Instruction Embedding: Latent Representations of Instructions Towards Task Identification

abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a prominent approach for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) by minimizing a combined loss function that incorporates both boundary loss and PDE residual loss. Despite their remarkable empirical performance in various scientific computing tasks, PINNs often fail to generate reasonable solutions, and such pathological behaviors remain difficult to explain and resolve. In this paper, we identify that PINNs can be adversely trained when gradients of each loss function exhibit a significant imbalance in their magnitudes and present a negative inner product value. To address these issues, we propose a novel optimization framework, *Dual Cone Gradient Descent* (DCGD), which adjusts the direction of the updated gradient to ensure it falls within a dual cone region. This region is defined as a set of vectors where the inner products with both the gradients of the PDE residual loss and the boundary loss are non-negative. Theoretically, we analyze the convergence properties of DCGD algorithms in a non-convex setting. On a variety of benchmark equations, we demonstrate that DCGD outperforms other optimization algorithms in terms of various evaluation metrics. In particular, DCGD achieves superior predictive accuracy and enhances the stability of training for failure modes of PINNs and complex PDEs, compared to existing optimally tuned models. Moreover, DCGD can be further improved by combining it with popular strategies for PINNs, including learning rate annealing and the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK).

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks solve differential equations by minimizing losses for both the equation residual and its boundary conditions. These objectives can produce problematic training signals. The paper identifies a harmful situation in which their gradients differ greatly in magnitude and have a negative inner product, meaning their directions conflict.

Dual Cone Gradient Descent adjusts the gradient used for an update so that it lies in a region having nonnegative inner products with both component gradients. This geometric constraint addresses how the two objectives interact, rather than relying only on the combined loss value. The authors also analyze the convergence properties of the resulting algorithms in a nonconvex setting.

It can also be combined with learning-rate annealing and Neural Tangent Kernel strategies for further improvement. The findings connect a specific gradient conflict to a practical optimization intervention.
summary.tldr: DCGD adjusts conflicting physics and boundary-loss gradients, improving the accuracy and training stability of physics-informed neural networks on benchmark equations.

title: Dual Cone Gradient Descent for Training Physics-Informed Neural Networks

abstract: Deep learning based neural decoding from stereotactic electroencephalography (sEEG) would likely benefit from scaling up both dataset and model size. To achieve this, combining data across multiple subjects is crucial. However, in sEEG cohorts, each subject has a variable number of electrodes placed at distinct locations in their brain, solely based on clinical needs. Such heterogeneity in electrode number/placement poses a significant challenge for data integration, since there is no clear correspondence of the neural activity recorded at distinct sites between individuals. Here we introduce seegnificant: a training framework and architecture that can be used to decode behavior across subjects using sEEG data. We tokenize the neural activity within electrodes using convolutions and extract long-term temporal dependencies between tokens using self-attention in the time dimension. The 3D location of each electrode is then mixed with the tokens, followed by another self-attention in the electrode dimension to extract effective spatiotemporal neural representations. Subject-specific heads are then used for downstream decoding tasks. Using this approach, we construct a multi-subject model trained on the combined data from 21 subjects performing a behavioral task. We demonstrate that our model is able to decode the trial-wise response time of the subjects during the behavioral task solely from neural data. We also show that the neural representations learned by pretraining our model across individuals can be transferred in a few-shot manner to new subjects. This work introduces a scalable approach towards sEEG data integration for multi-subject model training, paving the way for cross-subject generalization for sEEG decoding.

paragraphs: Pooling stereotactic EEG data across people could support larger training datasets, but electrode recordings do not line up neatly between individuals. Each person has a different number of electrodes at locations chosen for clinical needs. The paper introduces seegnificant, a framework designed to learn across this variability rather than require a direct correspondence between recording sites.

The model then incorporates each electrode's 3D location and applies attention across electrodes to learn spatial and temporal representations. Representations learned through multi-person pretraining also transfer to new subjects with few examples. These findings demonstrate cross-subject decoding and transfer in the evaluated task, supporting the framework as a scalable approach to integrating heterogeneous sEEG recordings.
summary.tldr: Seegnificant combines electrode activity and location to decode behavior across subjects and transfer learned representations to new people with few examples.

title: Neural decoding from stereotactic EEG: accounting for electrode variability across subjects

abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) is an emerging uncertainty quantification framework that allows us to construct a prediction set to cover the true label with a pre-specified marginal or conditional probability.Although the valid coverage guarantee has been extensively studied for classification problems, CP often produces large prediction sets which may not be practically useful.This issue is exacerbated for the setting of class-conditional coverage on imbalanced classification tasks with many and/or imbalanced classes.This paper proposes the Rank Calibrated Class-conditional CP (RC3P) algorithm to reduce the prediction set sizes to achieve class-conditional coverage, where the valid coverage holds for each class.In contrast to the standard class-conditional CP (CCP) method that uniformly thresholds the class-wise conformity score for each class, the augmented label rank calibration step allows RC3P to selectively iterate this class-wise thresholding subroutine only for a subset of classes whose class-wise top-$k$ error is small.We prove that agnostic to the classifier and data distribution, RC3P achieves class-wise coverage. We also show that RC3P reduces the size of prediction sets compared to the CCP method. Comprehensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that RC3P achieves class-wise coverage and $26.25\\%$ $\downarrow$ reduction in prediction set sizes on average.

We also show that RC3P reduces the size of prediction sets compared to the CCP method. Comprehensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that RC3P achieves class-wise coverage and $26.25\\%$ $\downarrow$ reduction in prediction set sizes on average.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction expresses uncertainty by returning a set of possible labels with a specified coverage probability. A useful set should contain the correct label while remaining small enough to inform a decision. Achieving coverage separately for each class can produce especially large sets when there are many classes or substantial class imbalance.

The proposed RC3P algorithm adds label-rank calibration to class-conditional conformal prediction. Standard class-conditional calibration applies class-wise score thresholding uniformly across classes. RC3P selectively applies that subroutine to a subset of classes with small class-wise top-k error. This uses information about how labels rank in the classifier's predictions to make the calibration more selective.

The authors prove class-wise coverage without tying the result to a particular classifier or data distribution, and show smaller prediction sets than the standard class-conditional method. Experiments across real-world datasets report an average set-size reduction of 26.25% while achieving class-wise coverage. The contribution is more compact uncertainty reporting while retaining a coverage target for each class.
summary.tldr: RC3P uses label-rank calibration to reduce prediction-set sizes while providing class-wise coverage guarantees.

title: Conformal Prediction for Class-wise Coverage via Augmented Label Rank Calibration

abstract: Randomized smoothing is a popular certified defense against adversarial attacks. In its essence, we need to solve a problem of statistical estimation which is usually very time-consuming since we need to perform numerous (usually $10^5$) forward passes of the classifier for every point to be certified. In this paper, we review the statistical estimation problems for randomized smoothing to find out if the computational burden is necessary. In particular, we consider the (standard) task of adversarial robustness where we need to decide if a point is robust at a certain radius or not using as few samples as possible while maintaining statistical guarantees. We present estimation procedures employing confidence sequences enjoying the same statistical guarantees as the standard methods, with the optimal sample complexities for the estimation task and empirically demonstrate their good performance. Additionally, we provide a randomized version of Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals resulting in strictly stronger certificates.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing provides statistical certificates of resistance to adversarial perturbations, but certification can require many classifier evaluations for each input. The paper notes that roughly 100,000 forward passes are commonly used. It asks whether that computational burden is necessary for the specific decision of certifying robustness at a chosen radius.

The authors develop estimation procedures based on confidence sequences. These procedures aim to use as few samples as possible while retaining the statistical guarantees of standard methods. Their analysis establishes optimal sample complexities for the estimation task, and empirical evaluations show good performance. This targets the statistical work inside certification rather than changing the classifier’s learned predictions.

The paper also introduces a randomized version of Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals that produces strictly stronger certificates. Together, the contributions address both the sampling cost of deciding robustness and the strength of the resulting certificate. The optimality statement concerns the specified estimation problem, while the empirical findings support the procedures’ practical effectiveness.
summary.tldr: Confidence-sequence estimators reduce randomized-smoothing certification work with optimal sample complexity, while randomized confidence intervals strengthen certificates.

title: Treatment of Statistical Estimation Problems in Randomized Smoothing for Adversarial Robustness

abstract: Developing intelligent pediatric consultation systems offers promising prospects for improving diagnostic efficiency, especially in China, where healthcare resources are scarce. Despite recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) for Chinese medicine, their performance is sub-optimal in pediatric applications due to inadequate instruction data and vulnerable training procedures.To address the above issues, this paper builds PedCorpus, a high-quality dataset of over 300,000 multi-task instructions from pediatric textbooks, guidelines, and knowledge graph resources to fulfil diverse diagnostic demands. Upon well-designed PedCorpus, we propose PediatricsGPT, the first Chinese pediatric LLM assistant built on a systematic and robust training pipeline.In the continuous pre-training phase, we introduce a hybrid instruction pre-training mechanism to mitigate the internal-injected knowledge inconsistency of LLMs for medical domain adaptation. Immediately, the full-parameter Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is utilized to incorporate the general medical knowledge schema into the models. After that, we devise a direct following preference optimization to enhance the generation of pediatrician-like humanistic responses. In the parameter-efficient secondary SFT phase,a mixture of universal-specific experts strategy is presented to resolve the competency conflict between medical generalist and pediatric expertise mastery. Extensive results based on the metrics, GPT-4, and doctor evaluations on distinct downstream tasks show that PediatricsGPT consistently outperforms previous Chinese medical LLMs. The project and data will be released at https://github.com/ydk122024/PediatricsGPT.

After that, we devise a direct following preference optimization to enhance the generation of pediatrician-like humanistic responses. In the parameter-efficient secondary SFT phase,a mixture of universal-specific experts strategy is presented to resolve the competency conflict between medical generalist and pediatric expertise mastery. Extensive results based on the metrics, GPT-4, and doctor evaluations on distinct downstream tasks show that PediatricsGPT consistently outperforms previous Chinese medical LLMs. The project and data will be released at https://github.com/ydk122024/PediatricsGPT.

paragraphs: PediatricsGPT addresses weaknesses in Chinese medical language models on pediatric tasks. The authors identify insufficient instruction data and fragile training procedures as contributing problems. They build PedCorpus, a dataset of more than 300,000 multitask instructions drawn from pediatric textbooks, guidelines, and knowledge graph resources, and use it to support a dedicated pediatric assistant.

The training pipeline has several stages with distinct purposes. Hybrid instruction pretraining addresses inconsistency between existing and newly introduced medical knowledge. Full-parameter supervised fine-tuning incorporates a general medical knowledge structure, followed by preference optimization aimed at more humanistic, pediatrician-like responses. A second, parameter-efficient fine-tuning stage uses universal and specialized experts to address conflict between general medical competence and pediatric expertise.

Evaluations using metrics, GPT-4, and doctors across different downstream tasks report consistent improvements over previous Chinese medical language models. The work combines a domain-specific instruction resource with a training sequence designed around knowledge adaptation, response style, and specialization. Its stated findings concern performance in those evaluations of the pediatric assistant.
summary.tldr: PediatricsGPT combines a large Chinese pediatric instruction dataset with staged training to improve pediatric task performance in the reported evaluations.

title: PediatricsGPT: Large Language Models as Chinese Medical Assistants for Pediatric Applications

abstract: In ill-posed imaging inverse problems, there can exist many hypotheses that fit both the observed measurements and prior knowledge of the true image. Rather than returning just one hypothesis of that image, posterior samplers aim to explore the full solution space by generating many probable hypotheses, which can later be used to quantify uncertainty or construct recoveries that appropriately navigate the perception/distortion trade-off. In this work, we propose a fast and accurate posterior-sampling conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) that, through a novel form of regularization, aims for correctness in the posterior mean as well as the trace and K principal components of the posterior covariance matrix. Numerical experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms competitors in a wide range of ill-posed imaging inverse problems.

paragraphs: An ill-posed imaging inverse problem can admit many images that agree with the observed measurements and prior knowledge. A posterior sampler generates multiple plausible reconstructions to explore that ambiguity. These samples can support uncertainty estimates or help balance perceptual quality against reconstruction distortion, making the distribution of outputs important beyond any single recovered image.

The paper proposes pcaGAN, a fast conditional generative adversarial network designed for posterior sampling. Its new regularization targets the posterior mean together with the trace and K principal components of the posterior covariance. In plain language, the training objective aims to match the average reconstruction, the total amount of variation, and key directions in which plausible reconstructions differ.

This connects the generator’s training to both its central prediction and the structure of its uncertainty. Numerical experiments report that the method outperforms competitors across a wide range of ill-posed imaging inverse problems. The stated aim of the regularization is correctness in these posterior statistics, giving a concrete statistical target for improving generated sets of candidate images.
summary.tldr: pcaGAN regularizes the mean and covariance structure of generated reconstructions to improve posterior sampling for ambiguous imaging problems.

title: pcaGAN: Improving Posterior-Sampling cGANs via Principal Component Regularization

abstract: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) have emerged as a transformative approach for aligning visual and textual understanding. They typically require extremely high computational resources (e.g., thousands of GPUs) for training to achieve cross-modal alignment at multi-granularity levels. We argue that a key source of this inefficiency lies in the vision encoders they widely equip with, e.g., CLIP and SAM, which lack the alignment with language at multi-granularity levels. To address this issue, in this paper, we leverage hyperbolic space, which inherently models hierarchical levels and thus provides a principled framework for bridging the granularity gap between visual and textual modalities at an arbitrary granularity level. Concretely, we propose an efficient training paradigm for MLLMs, dubbed as \blg, which can optimize visual representations to align with their textual counterparts at an arbitrary granularity level through dynamic hyperbolic radius adjustment in hyperbolic space. \alg employs learnable matrices with M\"{o}bius multiplication operations, implemented via three effective configurations: diagonal scaling matrices, block-diagonal matrices, and banded matrices, providing a flexible yet efficient parametrization strategy. Comprehensive experiments across multiple MLLM benchmarks demonstrate that \alg consistently improves both existing pre-training and fine-tuning MLLMs clearly with less than 1\% additional parameters.

paragraphs: HyperET addresses the cost of aligning visual and textual representations in multimodal language models. The authors argue that commonly used vision encoders lack alignment with language across different levels of detail. This granularity gap creates work for later training stages that must connect visual information with corresponding textual concepts.

The proposed training approach uses hyperbolic space because its geometry naturally represents hierarchical levels. Dynamic adjustment of the hyperbolic radius aligns visual representations with text at different granularities. Learnable matrices act through Möbius multiplication, with diagonal, block-diagonal, and banded configurations offering alternative compact parameterizations.

Across multiple multimodal benchmarks, experiments report consistent improvements to existing models in pre-training and fine-tuning settings while adding less than 1% to the parameter count. The result supports geometric alignment as a relatively small addition that can improve multimodal learning. The reported parameter overhead quantifies the size of the added mechanism; the broader efficiency motivation is to make cross-modal alignment easier by explicitly representing relationships among levels of detail.
summary.tldr: HyperET aligns visual and textual representations at multiple granularities in hyperbolic space, improving benchmarks with less than 1% additional parameters.

title: HyperET: Efficient Training in Hyperbolic Space for Multi-modal Large Language Models

abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving methods aim to directly map raw sensor inputs to future driving actions such as planned trajectories, bypassing traditional modular pipelines. While these approaches have shown promise, they often operate under a one-shot paradigm that relies heavily on the current scene context, potentially underestimating the importance of scene dynamics and their temporal evolution. This limitation restricts the model’s ability to make informed and adaptive decisions in complex driving scenarios. We propose a new perspective: the future trajectory of an autonomous vehicle is closely intertwined with the evolving dynamics of its environment, and conversely, the vehicle’s own future states can influence how the surrounding scene unfolds. Motivated by this bidirectional relationship, we introduce **SeerDrive**, a novel end-to-end framework that jointly models future scene evolution and trajectory planning in a closed-loop manner. Our method first predicts future bird’s-eye view (BEV) representations to anticipate the dynamics of the surrounding scene, then leverages this foresight to generate future-context-aware trajectories. Two key components enable this: (1) future-aware planning, which injects predicted BEV features into the trajectory planner, and (2) iterative scene modeling and vehicle planning, which refines both future scene prediction and trajectory generation through collaborative optimization. Extensive experiments on the NAVSIM and nuScenes benchmarks show that SeerDrive significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: End-to-end driving systems map sensor inputs directly to planned actions, but one-shot planning can rely too heavily on the scene as it currently appears. SeerDrive starts from the relationship between a vehicle’s future motion and its changing surroundings: scene evolution informs the plan, and the vehicle’s future states can influence how the scene develops.

The framework predicts future bird’s-eye-view representations of the surroundings and supplies those predicted features to the trajectory planner. It then iteratively refines both scene predictions and vehicle plans through collaborative optimization. This creates a feedback process in which the two predictions are developed together instead of treating future scene information as a fixed input.

Experiments on NAVSIM and nuScenes show significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods. The results support using anticipated scene dynamics within trajectory generation and refining the two jointly. The contribution is a framework for future-aware planning, with benchmark evidence that accounting for this bidirectional relationship improves end-to-end driving performance.
summary.tldr: SeerDrive jointly refines future scene predictions and driving trajectories, significantly improving performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes.

title: Future-Aware End-to-End Driving: Bidirectional Modeling of Trajectory Planning and Scene Evolution

abstract: Music-driven 3D dance generation has attracted increasing attention in recent years, with promising applications in choreography, virtual reality, and creative content creation. Previous research has generated promising realistic dance movement from audio signals. However, traditional methods underutilize genre conditioning, often treating it as auxiliary modifiers rather than core semantic drivers. This oversight compromises music-motion synchronization and disrupts dance genre continuity, particularly during complex rhythmic transitions, thereby leading to visually unsatisfactory effects. To address the challenge, we propose MEGADance, a novel architecture for music-driven 3D dance generation. By decoupling choreographic consistency into dance generality and genre specificity, MEGADance demonstrates significant dance quality and strong genre controllability. It consists of two stages: (1) High-Fidelity Dance Quantization Stage (HFDQ), which encodes dance motions into a latent representation by Finite Scalar Quantization (FSQ) and reconstructs them with kinematic-dynamic constraints, and (2) Genre-Aware Dance Generation Stage (GADG), which maps music into the latent representation by synergistic utilization of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism with Mamba-Transformer hybrid backbone. Extensive experiments on the FineDance and AIST++ dataset demonstrate the state-of-the-art performance of MEGADance both qualitatively and quantitatively. Code will be released upon acceptance.

paragraphs: Music-driven dance generation must coordinate movement with rhythm while maintaining a coherent dance style. The paper argues that treating genre as a secondary adjustment underuses information that should guide choreography. This can weaken synchronization and disrupt genre continuity, especially when the music passes through complex rhythmic transitions.

MEGADance separates properties shared across dance from properties specific to a genre. Its first stage encodes motion into a latent representation using Finite Scalar Quantization, then reconstructs it under kinematic and dynamic constraints. This stage establishes a representation that the second stage can use to generate dance from music.

The generation stage combines a mixture-of-experts mechanism with a Mamba–Transformer hybrid backbone to map music into that representation. Genre conditioning is therefore built into the generation architecture. Experiments on FineDance and AIST++ report state-of-the-art qualitative and quantitative performance, alongside strong control over genre. The findings support organizing the model around both general movement structure and genre-specific information, with the two-stage design connecting motion representation to music-conditioned choreography.
summary.tldr: MEGADance combines quantized motion representations and genre-aware experts to generate music-driven 3D dance with strong genre control.

title: MEGADance: Mixture-of-Experts Architecture for Genre-Aware 3D Dance Generation

abstract: In off-policy policy evaluation (OPE) tasks within reinforcement learning, Temporal Difference Learning(TD) and Fitted Q-Iteration (FQI) have traditionally been viewed as differing in the number of updates toward the target value function: TD makes one update, FQI makes an infinite number, and Partial Fitted Q-Iteration (PFQI) performs a finite number. We show that this view is not accurate, and provide a new mathematical perspective under linear value function approximation that unifies these methods as a single iterative method solving same linear system, but using different matrix splitting schemes and preconditioners. We show that increasing the number of updates under the same target value function, i.e., the target network technique, is a transition from using a constant preconditioner to using a data-feature adaptive preconditioner. This elucidates, for the first time, why TD convergence does not necessarily imply FQI convergence, and establishes tight convergence connections among TD, PFQI, and FQI. Our framework enables sharper theoretical results than previous work and characterization of the convergence conditions for each algorithm, without relying on assumptions about the features (e.g., linear independence). We also provide an encoder-decoder perspective to better understand TD’s convergence conditions, and prove, for the first time, that when a large learning rate doesn’t work, trying a smaller one may help(for batch TD). Our framework also leads to the discovery of new crucial conditions on features for convergence, and shows how common assumptions about features influence convergence, e.g., the assumption of linearly independent features can be dropped without compromising the convergence guarantees of stochastic TD in the on-policy setting. This paper is also the first to introduce matrix splitting into the convergence analysis of these algorithms.

paragraphs: Temporal Difference learning, Partial Fitted Q-Iteration, and Fitted Q-Iteration are often distinguished by how many updates they perform toward a fixed target. This paper argues that this explanation misses an important mathematical difference. For off-policy evaluation with linear value approximations, the methods solve the same linear system through different matrix decompositions and preconditioners, which shape how the iterative solution progresses.

Under this view, performing more updates with a fixed target changes the preconditioner from a constant one toward one adapted to the data and features. This explains why convergence of Temporal Difference learning does not automatically imply convergence of Fitted Q-Iteration. The framework establishes precise relationships and conditions for convergence across the three methods.

The analysis also clarifies the role of learning rates and feature assumptions. For batch Temporal Difference learning, it proves that a smaller learning rate may help when a larger one fails. Separately, it shows that linear independence of features is unnecessary for certain on-policy stochastic convergence guarantees. These results refine when familiar algorithms can be expected to converge.
summary.tldr: A shared linear-system perspective explains convergence differences among TD, PFQI, and FQI through their matrix splittings and preconditioners.

title: A Unifying View of Linear Function Approximation in Off-Policy RL Through Matrix Splitting and Preconditioning

abstract: Many online learning applications adopt the stochastic bandit problem with a linear reward model, where the unknown parameter exhibits a succinct structure. We study minimax regret lower bounds which allow to know whether more efficient algorithms can be proposed. We introduce a general definition of succinctness and propose a novel framework for constructing minimax regret lower bounds based on an information-regret trade-off. When applied to entry-sparse vectors, our framework sharpens a recent lower bound by (Hao et al, NeurIPS 2020). We further apply our framework to derive novel results. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first lower bounds for the group-sparse and low-rank matrix settings.

When applied to entry-sparse vectors, our framework sharpens a recent lower bound by (Hao et al, NeurIPS 2020). We further apply our framework to derive novel results. paragraphs: Stochastic bandit problems describe learning through repeated choices whose rewards are initially uncertain. This paper considers linear reward models in which the unknown parameter has a compact underlying structure. The central question is how much regret any learning algorithm must incur: how much reward it must lose, in the worst case, while discovering which choices are better.

The authors introduce a general definition of this structural compactness, called succinctness, and a framework for proving minimax regret lower bounds. Its organizing principle is an information–regret trade-off. Actions provide information about the unknown parameter, but acquiring that information can also cost reward. Lower bounds formalize the unavoidable cost of this learning process.

For vectors with only a few nonzero entries, the framework strengthens an existing lower bound. It also produces bounds for group-sparse parameters and low-rank matrices, which the authors describe as the first for those settings to their knowledge. These results help assess whether improved regret guarantees remain possible, rather than supplying a new bandit algorithm.
summary.tldr: A general information–regret framework establishes stronger or new limits on learning in bandits with compact parameter structures.

title: A Novel General Framework for Sharp Lower Bounds in Succinct Stochastic Bandits

abstract: We introduce PartCrafter, the first structured 3D generative model that jointly synthesizes multiple semantically meaningful and geometrically distinct 3D meshes from a single RGB image. Unlike existing methods that either produce monolithic 3D shapes or follow two-stage pipelines, i.e. first segmenting an image and then reconstructing each segment, PartCrafter adopts a unified, compositional generation architecture that does not rely on pre-segmented inputs. Conditioned on a single image, it simultaneously denoises multiple 3D parts, enabling end-to-end part-aware generation of both individual objects and complex multi-object scenes. PartCrafter builds upon a pretrained 3D mesh diffusion transformer (DiT) trained on whole objects, inheriting the pretrained weights, encoder, and decoder, and introduces two key innovations: (1) A compositional latent space, where each 3D part is represented by a set of disentangled latent tokens; (2) A hierarchical attention mechanism that enables structured information flow both within individual parts and across all parts, ensuring global coherence while preserving part-level detail during generation. To support part-level supervision, we curate a new dataset by mining part-level annotations from large-scale 3D object datasets. Experiments show that PartCrafter outperforms existing approaches in generating decomposable 3D meshes, including parts that are not directly visible in input images, demonstrating the strength of part-aware generative priors for 3D understanding and synthesis. Code and training data are released.

paragraphs: PartCrafter generates multiple meaningful three-dimensional mesh parts from a single RGB image. It handles individual objects and multi-object scenes within one generation architecture, without requiring the image to be segmented first. The result is a structured collection of geometrically distinct parts, making decomposition part of the generation process itself.

The model builds on a pretrained whole-object mesh diffusion transformer, reusing its weights, encoder, and decoder. Each part receives its own set of disentangled latent tokens, and all parts are denoised simultaneously. Hierarchical attention connects information within each part and across the collection. This structure supports detailed individual components while coordinating their contribution to a coherent overall result.

The authors curate part-level supervision by mining annotations from large 3D object datasets. Experiments report better generation of decomposable meshes than existing approaches, including parts that are not directly visible in the input image. These findings support the value of learned part-aware generative priors for producing structured 3D content from limited visual evidence. Code and training data are released.
summary.tldr: PartCrafter jointly generates distinct, coordinated 3D mesh parts from one image, including parts hidden from view.

title: PartCrafter: Structured 3D Mesh Generation via Compositional Latent Diffusion Transformers

abstract: Human Activity Recognition (HAR) with wearable sensors is challenged by limited interpretability, which significantly impacts cross-dataset generalization. To address this challenge, we propose Motion-Primitive Transformer (MoPFormer), a novel self-supervised framework that enhances interpretability by tokenizing inertial measurement unit signals into semantically meaningful motion primitives and leverages a Transformer architecture to learn rich temporal representations. MoPFormer comprises two stages. The first stage is to partition multi-channel sensor streams into short segments and quantize them into discrete ``motion primitive'' codewords, while the second stage enriches those tokenized sequences through a context-aware embedding module and then processes them with a Transformer encoder. The proposed MoPFormer can be pre-trained using a masked motion-modeling objective that reconstructs missing primitives, enabling it to develop robust representations across diverse sensor configurations. Experiments on six HAR benchmarks demonstrate that MoPFormer not only outperforms state-of-the-art methods but also successfully generalizes across multiple datasets. More importantly, the learned motion primitives significantly enhance both interpretability and cross-dataset performance by capturing fundamental movement patterns that remain consistent across similar activities, regardless of dataset origin.

paragraphs: Recognizing activities from wearable sensors requires interpreting changing signals and transferring that understanding across datasets. MoPFormer tackles these challenges by representing inertial sensor data as meaningful motion primitives. These discrete units make fundamental movement patterns a central part of both the model’s representation and its interpretability.

The framework first divides multichannel sensor streams into short segments and quantizes them into motion-primitive codewords. A context-aware embedding module enriches the resulting token sequence before a Transformer encoder processes it. Self-supervised pretraining uses masked motion modeling: the model reconstructs missing primitives to learn temporal representations across diverse sensor configurations.
