The authors attribute enhanced interpretability and cross-dataset performance to primitives that capture movement patterns shared by similar activities across dataset origins. The findings support treating sensor streams as sequences of reusable movement units, with the Transformer learning how those units fit together over time.
summary.tldr: MoPFormer turns wearable sensor signals into motion-primitive tokens, improving interpretability and cross-dataset activity recognition.

title: MoPFormer: Motion-Primitive Transformer for Wearable-Sensor Activity Recognition

abstract: Dataset condensation aims to synthesize compact yet informative datasets that retain the training efficacy of full-scale data, offering substantial gains in efficiency. Recent studies reveal that the condensation process can be vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where malicious triggers are injected into the condensation dataset, manipulating model behavior during inference. While prior approaches have made progress in balancing attack success rate and clean test accuracy, they often fall short in preserving stealthiness, especially in concealing the visual artifacts of condensed data or the perturbations introduced during inference. To address this challenge, we introduce \textsc{Sneakdoor}, which enhances stealthiness without compromising attack effectiveness. \textsc{Sneakdoor} exploits the inherent vulnerability of class decision boundaries and incorporates a generative module that constructs input-aware triggers aligned with local feature geometry, thereby minimizing detectability. This joint design enables the attack to remain imperceptible to both human inspection and statistical detection. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that \textsc{Sneakdoor} achieves a compelling balance among attack success rate, clean test accuracy, and stealthiness, substantially improving the invisibility of both the synthetic data and triggered samples while maintaining high attack efficacy. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/XJTU-AI-Lab/SneakDoor}.

paragraphs: Dataset condensation creates a small synthetic training set intended to retain the usefulness of a much larger dataset. This paper examines backdoor attacks against condensation based on distribution matching. Such attacks aim to make a trained model behave maliciously on triggered inputs while preserving its performance on ordinary inputs.

SNEAKDOOR focuses on stealth in both the condensed training images and the triggered inference samples. Its design exploits vulnerabilities around class decision boundaries and uses a generative module to produce input-dependent triggers aligned with local feature geometry. The purpose of this coordination is to reduce conspicuous changes while retaining the influence needed to induce the backdoor behavior.

Across multiple datasets, the authors report a favorable balance between attack success, clean test accuracy, and stealth. They describe reduced visibility of synthetic-data artifacts and triggered-sample perturbations, including concealment from human inspection and statistical detection in the studied setting. The security significance is that preserving ordinary accuracy alone does not capture the problem: a condensed dataset can retain useful training behavior while also carrying a difficult-to-notice mechanism for manipulating later predictions.
summary.tldr: SNEAKDOOR demonstrates stealthier backdoors in condensed datasets while maintaining strong attack success and ordinary test accuracy.

title: SNEAKDOOR: Stealthy Backdoor Attacks against Distribution Matching-based Dataset Condensation

abstract: Quantum computing is an emerging field recognized for the significant speedup it offers over classical computing through quantum algorithms. However, designing and implementing quantum algorithms pose challenges due to the complex nature of quantum mechanics and the necessity for precise control over quantum states. Despite the significant advancements in AI, there has been a lack of datasets specifically tailored for this purpose. In this work, we introduce QCircuitBench, the first benchmark dataset designed to evaluate AI's capability in designing and implementing quantum algorithms in the form of quantum circuit codes. abstract: Data deviations in electronic health records (EHR) refer to discrepancies between recorded entries and a patient’s actual physiological state, indicating a decline in EHR data fidelity. Such deviations can result from pre-analytical variability, documentation errors, or unvalidated data sources. Effectively detecting data deviations is clinically valuable for identifying erroneous records, excluding them from downstream clinical workflows, and informing corrective actions. Despite its importance and practical relevance, this problem remains largely underexplored in existing research. To bridge this gap, we propose a bi-level knowledge distillation approach centered on a task-agnostic formulation of EHR data fidelity as an intrinsic measure of data reliability. Our approach performs layered knowledge distillation in two levels: from a computation-intensive, task-specific data Shapley oracle to a neural oracle for individual tasks, and then to a unified EHR data fidelity predictor. This design enables the integration of task-specific insights into a holistic assessment of a patient’s EHR data fidelity from a multi-task perspective. By tracking the outputs of this learned predictor, we detect potential data deviations in EHR data. Experiments on both real-world EHR data from National University Hospital in Singapore and the public MIMIC-III dataset consistently validate the effectiveness of our approach in detecting data deviations in EHR data. Case studies further demonstrate its practical value in identifying clinically meaningful data deviations.

title: Detecting Data Deviations in Electronic Health Records

abstract: Brain disorders have been consistently associated with abnormalities in specific brain regions or neural circuits. Identifying key brain regional activities and functional connectivity patterns is essential for discovering more precise neurobiological biomarkers. However, previous studies have primarily emphasized alterations in functional connectivity while overlooking abnormal neuronal population activity within brain regions. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel Local-Global Coupling Spiking Graph Transformer (LGC-SGT) that jointly models both inter-regional connectivity differences and deviations in neuronal population firing rates within brain regions, enabling a dual-perspective neuropathological analysis. The global pathway leverages spike-based computation in LGC-SGT to model biologically plausible aberrant neural firing dynamics, while the local pathway adaptively captures abnormal graph-based representations of brain connectivity learned by local plasticity in the liquid state machine module. Furthermore, we design a shortcut-enhanced output strategy in LGC-SGT with the hybrid loss function to suppress outlier interference caused by inter-individual and inter-center variability, enabling a more robust decision boundary. Extensive experiments on three brain disorder datasets demonstrate that our model consistently outperforms state-of-the-art graph methods in brain disorder diagnosis. Moreover, it facilitates the extraction of interpretable neurobiological biomarkers by jointly analyzing regional neural activity and functional connectivity, offering a more comprehensive framework for brain disorder understanding and diagnosis.

title: Local-Global Coupling Spiking Graph Transformer for Brain Disorders Diagnosis from Two Perspectives

abstract: Inverse problems, where the goal is to recover an unknown signal from noisy or incomplete measurements, are central to applications in medical imaging, remote sensing, and computational biology. Diffusion models have recently emerged as powerful priors for solving such problems. However, existing methods either rely on projection-based techniques that enforce measurement consistency through heuristic updates, or they approximate the likelihood $p(\boldsymbol{y} \mid \boldsymbol{x})$, often resulting in artifacts and instability under complex or high-noise conditions. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework called coupled data and measurement space diffusion posterior sampling (C-DPS), which eliminates the need for constraint tuning or likelihood approximation. C-DPS introduces a forward stochastic process in the measurement space $\{\boldsymbol{y}_t\}$, evolving in parallel with the data-space diffusion $\{\boldsymbol{x}_t\}$, which enables the derivation of a closed-form posterior $p(\boldsymbol{x}_{t-1} \mid \boldsymbol{x}_t, \boldsymbol{y}_{t-1})$. This coupling allows for accurate and recursive sampling based on a well-defined posterior distribution. Empirical results demonstrate that C-DPS consistently outperforms existing baselines, both qualitatively and quantitatively, across multiple inverse problem benchmarks.

paragraphs: Inverse problems recover an unknown signal from measurements that may be noisy or incomplete. Diffusion models can supply prior information about plausible signals, but connecting that prior to the measurements is difficult. Existing approaches described in the paper use heuristic consistency updates or approximate likelihoods, which can produce artifacts and instability in challenging conditions.

C-DPS introduces a stochastic process for the measurements that evolves alongside the diffusion process for the signal. Coupling these two processes allows the authors to derive a closed-form posterior for the preceding signal state, conditioned on the current signal state and the preceding measurement state. Sampling can then proceed recursively using this defined distribution, without the constraint tuning or likelihood approximation targeted by the method.

Across multiple inverse-problem benchmarks, the authors report consistent qualitative and quantitative improvements over existing baselines. The approach matters because it changes how measurement information enters diffusion sampling: the measurements become part of the evolving probabilistic construction. The reported results support this coupling as a way to improve reconstruction.
summary.tldr: C-DPS couples signal and measurement diffusion to derive recursive posterior sampling without constraint tuning or likelihood approximation.

title: Coupled Data and Measurement Space Dynamics for Enhanced Diffusion Posterior Sampling

abstract: Deep neural networks, particularly neural operators, provide an efficient alternative to costly simulations in surrogate modeling. However, their performance is often constrained by the need for large-scale labeled datasets, which are costly and challenging to acquire in many scientific domains. Semi-supervised learning reduces label reliance by leveraging unlabeled data yet remains vulnerable to noisy pseudo-labels that mislead training and undermine robustness. To address these challenges, we propose a novel framework, Uncertainty-Informed Meta Pseudo Labeling (UMPL). The core mechenism is to refine pseudo-label quality through uncertainty-informed feedback signals. Specifically, the teacher model generates pseudo labels via epistemic uncertainty, while the student model learns from these labels and provides feedback based on aleatoric uncertainty. This interplay forms a meta-learning loop where enhanced generalization and improved pseudo-label quality reinforce each other, enabling the student model to achieve more stable uncertainty estimation and leading to more robust training. Notably, This framework is model-agnostic and can be seamlessly integrated into various neural architectures, facilitating effective exploitation of unlabeled data to enhance generalization in distribution shifts and out-of-distribution scenarios. Extensive evaluations of four models across seven tasks covering steady state and transient prediction problems demonstrate that UMPL consistently outperforms the best existing semi-supervised regression methods. When using only 10% of the fully supervised training data, UMPL achieves a 14.18% improvement, highlighting its strong effectiveness under limited supervision. Our codes are available at https://github.com/small-dumpling/UMPL.

title: Uncertainty-Informed Meta Pseudo Labeling for Surrogate Modeling with Limited Labeled Data

abstract: Generative models of graphs based on discrete Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) offer a principled approach to molecular generation by systematically removing structural noise through iterative atom and bond adjustments. However, existing formulations are fundamentally limited by their inability to adapt the graph size (that is, the number of atoms) during the diffusion process, severely restricting their effectiveness in conditional generation scenarios such as property-driven molecular design, where the targeted property often correlates with the molecular size. In this paper, we reformulate the noising and denoising processes to support monotonic insertion and deletion of nodes. The resulting model, which we call GrIDDD, dynamically grows or shrinks the chemical graph during generation. GrIDDD matches or exceeds the performance of existing graph diffusion models on molecular property targeting despite being trained on a more difficult problem. Furthermore, when applied to molecular optimization, GrIDDD exhibits competitive performance compared to specialized optimization models. This work paves the way for size-adaptive molecular generation with graph diffusion.

paragraphs: Graph diffusion models generate molecules by progressively adjusting atoms and bonds as structural noise is removed. Existing formulations keep the number of atoms fixed during that process. This is restrictive when generation targets a molecular property that correlates with size, because achieving the target may call for a larger or smaller molecule.

The paper introduces GrIDDD by reformulating both noising and denoising to support monotonic node insertion and deletion. The resulting process can grow or shrink a chemical graph during generation. This expands the decisions made by the model: molecular size can change as the structure develops, instead of remaining fixed while only atom and bond assignments are adjusted.

For molecular property targeting, GrIDDD matches or exceeds existing graph diffusion models despite learning the more difficult size-adaptive task. It also performs competitively against specialized models when applied to molecular optimization. The findings show that allowing graph size to change can be compatible with strong generation performance, providing a practical direction for diffusion-based molecular design where size is part of the problem.
summary.tldr: GrIDDD lets molecular diffusion models grow or shrink graphs during generation while maintaining competitive property-targeting and optimization performance.

title: Graph Diffusion that can Insert and Delete

abstract: We provide an algorithm with regret $O(C d \log \log T)$ for contextual pricing with $C$ corrupted rounds, improving over the previous bound of $O(d^3 C \log^2(T))$ of Krishnamurthy et al. The result is based on a reduction that calls the uncorrupted algorithm as a black-box, unlike the previous approach that modifies the inner workings of the uncorrupted algorithm. As a result, it leads to a conceptually simpler algorithm. Finally, we provide a lower bound ruling out a $O(C + d\log \log T)$ algorithm. This shows that robustifying contextual pricing is harder than robustifying contextual search with $\epsilon$-ball losses, for which it is possible to design algorithms where corruptions add only an extra additive term $C$ to the regret.

paragraphs: The paper studies contextual pricing when some rounds are corrupted, so the learning algorithm must remain effective despite unreliable information. Its main result is an algorithm with regret O(C d log log T), where C is the number of corrupted rounds. This improves the previous bound of O(d³ C log² T), reducing the dependence on both dimension and the time horizon.

The construction uses an algorithm for the uncorrupted problem as a black box. Rather than changing that algorithm’s internal operations, a reduction builds robustness around it. This yields a conceptually simpler design and makes the connection between the clean and corrupted versions of contextual pricing explicit.

A lower bound rules out regret of O(C + d log log T). Consequently, corruption cannot generally be handled with only the additive C penalty represented by that proposed bound. This distinguishes pricing from contextual search with epsilon-ball losses, where such an additive corruption term is achievable. The paper therefore provides both an improved method and a boundary on a particularly attractive form of robustness.
summary.tldr: A black-box reduction improves regret for corrupted contextual pricing, while a lower bound rules out a purely additive corruption penalty of the proposed form.

title: Robust Contextual Pricing

abstract: Generalist models have achieved remarkable success in both language and vision-language tasks, showcasing the potential of unified modeling. However, effectively integrating fine-grained perception tasks like detection and segmentation into these models remains a significant challenge. This is primarily because these tasks often rely heavily on task-specific designs and architectures that can complicate the modeling process. To address this challenge, we present UFO, a framework that unifies fine-grained visual perception tasks through an open-ended language interface. By transforming all perception targets into the language space, UFO unifies object-level detection, pixel-level segmentation, and image-level vision-language tasks into a single model. Additionally, we introduce a novel embedding retrieval approach that relies solely on the language interface to support segmentation tasks. Our framework bridges the gap between fine-grained perception and vision-language tasks, significantly simplifying architectural design and training strategies while achieving comparable or superior performance to methods with intricate task-specific designs. After multi-task training on five standard visual perception datasets, UFO outperforms the previous state-of-the-art generalist models by 12.3 mAP on COCO instance segmentation and 3.3 mIoU on ADE20K semantic segmentation. Furthermore, our method seamlessly integrates with existing MLLMs, effectively combining fine-grained perception capabilities with their advanced language abilities, thereby achieving superior performance on the challenging reasoning segmentation. Code and models are available at https://github.com/nnnth/UFO.

title: UFO: A Unified Approach to Fine-grained Visual Perception via Open-ended Language Interface

abstract: Predicting human mobility is inherently challenging due to complex long-range dependencies and multi-scale periodic behaviors. To address this, we introduce RHYTHM (Reasoning with Hierarchical Temporal Tokenization for Human Mobility), a unified framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) as general-purpose spatio-temporal predictors and trajectory reasoners. Methodologically, RHYTHM employs temporal tokenization to partition each trajectory into daily segments and encode them as discrete tokens with hierarchical attention that captures both daily and weekly dependencies, thereby quadratically reducing the sequence length while preserving cyclical information. Additionally, we enrich token representations by adding pre-computed prompt embeddings for trajectory segments and prediction targets via a frozen LLM, and feeding these combined embeddings back into the LLM backbone to capture complex interdependencies. Computationally, RHYTHM keeps the pretrained LLM backbone frozen, yielding faster training and lower memory usage. We evaluate our model against state-of-the-art methods using three real-world datasets. Notably, RHYTHM achieves a 2.4% improvement in overall accuracy, a 5.0% increase on weekends, and a 24.6% reduction in training time. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/he-h/rhythm.

abstract: Firms' algorithm development practices are often homogeneous Whether firms train algorithms on similar data or rely on similar pre-trained models, the result is correlated predictions. In the context of personalized pricing, correlated algorithms can be viewed as a means to collude among competing firms, but whether or not this conduct is legal depends on the mechanisms of achieving collusion. We investigate the precise mechanisms through a formal game-theoretic model. Indeed, we find that (1) higher correlation diminishes consumer welfare and (2) as consumers become more price sensitive, firms are increasingly incentivized to compromise on the accuracy of their predictions in exchange for coordination. We demonstrate our theoretical results in a stylized empirical study where two firms compete using personalized pricing algorithms. Our results demonstrate a new mechanism for achieving collusion through correlation, which allows us to analyze its legal implications. Correlation through algorithms is a new frontier of anti-competitive behavior that is largely unconsidered by US antitrust law.

paragraphs: Competing firms may build pricing algorithms using similar training data or pretrained models, causing their predictions to be correlated. This paper asks how that correlation can affect competition when firms personalize prices. It develops a formal game-theoretic model to identify the mechanism linking similar predictions to coordinated outcomes.

Within the model, greater correlation reduces consumer welfare. The analysis also finds that as consumers become more sensitive to prices, firms have stronger incentives to sacrifice predictive accuracy in exchange for coordination. This makes the relationship between prediction quality and competitive behavior consequential: a firm can have an incentive to prefer predictions that align with a competitor's, even at some cost to accuracy.

A stylized empirical study involving two competing firms demonstrates the theoretical results. The authors use the identified mechanism to discuss legal implications, arguing that algorithmic correlation represents an underconsidered area of US antitrust law. The findings concern a specific route to reduced competition through correlated algorithms, with the formal model and empirical illustration providing the supporting evidence.
summary.tldr: A game-theoretic model shows how correlated personalized-pricing algorithms can reduce consumer welfare and incentivize firms to trade accuracy for coordination.

title: Homogeneous Algorithms Can Reduce Competition in Personalized Pricing

abstract: Hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) pose significant safety concerns that impede their broader deployment. Recent research in hallucination detection has demonstrated that LLMs' internal representations contain truthfulness hints, which can be harnessed for detector training. However, the performance of these detectors is heavily dependent on the internal representations of predetermined tokens, fluctuating considerably when working on free-form generations with varying lengths and sparse distributions of hallucinated entities. To address this, we propose HaMI, a novel approach that enables robust detection of hallucinations through adaptive selection and learning of critical tokens that are most indicative of hallucinations. We achieve this robustness by an innovative formulation of the Hallucination detection task as Multiple Instance (HaMI) learning over token-level representations within a sequence, thereby facilitating a joint optimisation of token selection and hallucination detection on generation sequences of diverse forms. Comprehensive experimental results on four hallucination benchmarks show that HaMI significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: A language model’s internal representations can contain clues about whether its generated text is truthful. Detectors that read those clues from predetermined tokens, however, can perform inconsistently when responses vary in length or contain only a few hallucinated entities. The useful evidence may be concentrated in different parts of each answer.

HaMI addresses this problem by learning which tokens matter for detection. It treats the token representations within a generated sequence as a multiple-instance learning problem, jointly optimizing token selection and the hallucination judgment. This allows the detector to adapt its focus to each sequence instead of relying on a fixed choice of tokens.

Across four hallucination benchmarks, the authors report that HaMI significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches. The result supports adaptive selection as a way to make better use of truthfulness signals already present inside the model. Its central contribution is connecting the search for informative token representations directly to detector training, particularly for free-form responses with unevenly distributed hallucination evidence.
summary.tldr: HaMI jointly learns which token representations to inspect and how to detect hallucinations, improving robustness across varied generated responses.

title: Robust Hallucination Detection in LLMs via Adaptive Token Selection

abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have garnered considerable attention for their ability to tackle complex tasks through the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) approach. However, their tendency toward overthinking results in unnecessarily lengthy reasoning chains, dramatically increasing the inference costs. To mitigate this issue, we introduce VeriThinker, a novel approach for CoT compression. Unlike conventional methods that fine-tune LRMs directly on the original reasoning task using synthetic concise CoT data, we innovatively fine-tune the model solely through an auxiliary verification task. By training LRMs to accurately verify the correctness of CoT solutions, the LRMs inherently become more discerning about the necessity of subsequent self-reflection steps, thereby effectively suppressing overthinking. Extensive experiments validate that VeriThinker substantially reduces reasoning chain lengths while maintaining or even slightly improving accuracy. When applied to DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, our approach reduces reasoning tokens on MATH500 from 3790 to 2125 while improving accuracy by 0.8% (94.0% to 94.8%), and on AIME25, tokens decrease from 14321 to 10287 with a 2.1% accuracy gain (38.7% to 40.8%). Additionally, our experiments demonstrate that VeriThinker can also be zero-shot generalized to speculative reasoning.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can spend many tokens on unnecessary reflection, raising inference costs. VeriThinker aims to shorten these reasoning chains by fine-tuning solely on an auxiliary verification task. The model learns to judge the correctness of chain-of-thought solutions, rather than being trained directly on concise solutions to the original task.

The proposed mechanism is that better verification helps a model recognize whether further reflection is necessary. Experiments show substantially shorter reasoning while maintaining or slightly improving accuracy. This makes verification training relevant to efficiency as well as correctness: learning to assess a solution can reduce the amount of additional reasoning the model produces.

For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on MATH500, reasoning tokens fall from 3,790 to 2,125 while accuracy rises from 94.0% to 94.8%. On AIME25, tokens decrease from 14,321 to 10,287 and accuracy increases from 38.7% to 40.8%. The authors also report zero-shot transfer to speculative reasoning. These results support verification as an indirect route to compressing reasoning in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: VeriThinker trains models to verify solutions, reducing reasoning length while preserving or slightly improving accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: VeriThinker: Learning to Verify Makes Reasoning Model Efficient

abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models built on pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) require extensive post-training, resulting in high computational overhead that limits scalability and deployment. Existing sparsification strategies—such as Mixture-of-Depths, layer skipping, and early exit—fall short by neglecting the semantic coupling across vision-language-action modalities, and focusing narrowly on intra-LLM computation while overlooking end-to-end coherence from perception to control. To address these challenges, we propose **CogVLA**, a Cognition-Aligned Vision-Language-Action framework that leverages instruction-driven routing and sparsification to improve both efficiency and performance. CogVLA draws inspiration from human multimodal coordination and introduces a 3-stage progressive architecture. 1) **Encoder-FiLM based Aggregation Routing (EFA-Routing)** injects instruction information into the vision encoder to selectively aggregate and compress dual-stream visual tokens, forming a instruction-aware latent representation. 2) Building upon this compact visual encoding, **LLM-FiLM based Pruning Routing (LFP-Routing)** introduces action intent into the language model by pruning instruction-irrelevant visually grounded tokens, thereby achieving token-level sparsity. 3) To ensure that compressed perception inputs can still support accurate and coherent action generation, we introduce **V‑L‑A Coupled Attention (CAtten)**, which combines causal vision-language attention with bidirectional action parallel decoding. Extensive experiments on the LIBERO benchmark and real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that CogVLA achieves state-of-the-art performance with success rates of 97.4\% and 70.0\%, respectively, while reducing training costs by 2.5$\times$ and decreasing inference latency by 2.8$\times$ compared to OpenVLA.

paragraphs: CogVLA addresses the computational expense of adapting vision-language models to control robots. Its central idea is to let the instruction guide which visual information survives each stage of processing. This matters because reducing computation within the language model alone can overlook the connections between seeing a scene, understanding a request, and producing an appropriate action.

The framework has three stages. First, it injects instruction information into the vision encoder to combine and compress two streams of visual tokens. Second, it introduces action intent into the language model and removes visually grounded tokens that are irrelevant to the instruction. Third, a coupled attention mechanism connects vision and language processing with parallel action decoding, helping the compressed representation support coherent actions.

Compared with OpenVLA, they report 2.5× lower training costs and 2.8× lower inference latency. These findings support coordinating compression across the entire perception-to-control process.
summary.tldr: CogVLA uses instructions to compress visual processing and coordinate action generation, improving reported robotic performance while reducing training cost and latency.

title: CogVLA: Cognition-Aligned Vision-Language-Action Models via Instruction-Driven Routing & Sparsification

abstract: We study the problem of Offline Safe Reinforcement Learning (OSRL), where the goal is to learn a reward-maximizing policy from fixed data under a cumulative cost constraint. We propose a novel OSRL approach that frames the problem as a minimax objective and solves it by combining offline RL with online optimization algorithms. We prove the approximate optimality of this approach when integrated with an approximate offline RL oracle and no-regret online optimization. We also present a practical approximation that can be combined with any offline RL algorithm, eliminating the need for offline policy evaluation. Empirical results on the DSRL benchmark demonstrate that our method reliably enforces safety constraints under stringent cost budgets, while achieving high rewards. The code is available at https://github.com/yassineCh/O3SRL.

We propose a novel OSRL approach that frames the problem as a minimax objective and solves it by combining offline RL with online optimization algorithms. We prove the approximate optimality of this approach when integrated with an approximate offline RL oracle and no-regret online optimization. We also present a practical approximation that can be combined with any offline RL algorithm, eliminating the need for offline policy evaluation. paragraphs: Offline safe reinforcement learning aims to learn a high-reward policy from a fixed dataset while respecting a cumulative cost budget. The challenge is to optimize performance and enforce that constraint using the available data. This paper proposes a method that combines offline reinforcement learning with online optimization inside the learning procedure.

The authors express the problem as a minimax objective and solve it by combining the two types of algorithms. They prove approximate optimality when the approach uses an approximate offline reinforcement-learning oracle and no-regret online optimization. The guarantee is therefore tied to those components. The use of online optimization concerns the optimization process, while the policy-learning problem remains based on fixed data.

A practical approximation can be paired with any offline reinforcement-learning algorithm and removes the need for offline policy evaluation. On the DSRL benchmark, the method reliably satisfies safety constraints under stringent cost budgets while obtaining high rewards. The contribution links a theoretically supported formulation with a practical route for adding cost-constrained learning to existing offline methods.
summary.tldr: This method combines offline reinforcement learning and online optimization to learn high-reward policies under cumulative cost constraints.

title: Online Optimization for Offline Safe Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In real-world environments, a well-designed model must be capable of handling dynamically evolving distributions, where both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) samples appear unpredictably and individually, making real-time adaptation particularly challenging. While open-set test-time adaptation has demonstrated effectiveness in adjusting to distribution shifts, existing methods often rely on batch processing and struggle to manage single-sample data stream in open-set environments. To address this limitation, we propose Open-IRT, a novel open-set Intermediate-Representation-based Test-time adaptation framework tailored for single-image test-time adaptation with vision-language models. Open-IRT comprises two key modules designed for dynamic, single-sample adaptation in open-set scenarios. The first is Polarity-aware Prompt-based OOD Filter module, which fully constructs the ID-OOD distribution, considering both the absolute semantic alignment and relative semantic polarity. The second module, Intermediate Domain-based Test-time Adaptation module, constructs an intermediate domain and indirectly decomposes the ID-OOD distributional discrepancy to refine the separation boundary during the test-time. Extensive experiments on a range of domain adaptation benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of Open-IRT. Compared to previous state-of-the-art methods, it achieves significant improvements on representative benchmarks, such as CIFAR-100C and SVHN — with gains of +8.45\% in accuracy, -10.80\% in FPR95, and +11.04\% in AUROC.

paragraphs: A deployed image model may receive familiar and unfamiliar inputs one at a time while its environment changes. Open-set test-time adaptation must handle those shifts while separating in-distribution inputs from out-of-distribution ones. The paper targets the single-image setting, where adaptation methods that depend on batches are difficult to apply.

Its Open-IRT framework uses a vision-language model and two connected modules. A prompt-based out-of-distribution filter considers both absolute semantic alignment and relative semantic polarity when characterizing familiar and unfamiliar inputs. A second module constructs an intermediate domain, using it to break down the distributional discrepancy indirectly and refine the separation boundary during testing.

The intermediate representation supplies a way to adjust that boundary under the constraints of single-sample arrival. Across domain-adaptation benchmarks, the authors report improvements over previous state-of-the-art methods. For representative benchmarks including CIFAR-100C and SVHN, the abstract lists gains of 8.45% in accuracy and 11.04% in AUROC, alongside a 10.80% reduction in FPR95. These findings support both improved recognition and stronger separation of unfamiliar inputs in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Open-IRT uses semantic filtering and an intermediate domain to adapt vision-language models to individual images in open-set streams.

title: OOD-Barrier: Build a Middle-Barrier for Open-Set Single-Image Test Time Adaptation via Vision Language Models

abstract: In recent years, data poisoning attacks have been increasingly designed to appear harmless and even beneficial, often with the intention of verifying dataset ownership or safeguarding private data from unauthorized use. However, these developments have the potential to cause misunderstandings and conflicts, as data poisoning has traditionally been regarded as a security threat to machine learning systems. To address this issue, it is imperative for harmless poisoning generators to claim ownership of their generated datasets, enabling users to identify potential poisoning to prevent misuse. In this paper, we propose the deployment of watermarking schemes as a solution to this challenge. We introduce two provable and practical watermarking approaches for data poisoning: post-poisoning watermarking and poisoning-concurrent watermarking. Our analyses demonstrate that when the watermarking length is $\Theta(\sqrt{d}/\epsilon_w)$ for post-poisoning watermarking, and falls within the range of $\Theta(1/\epsilon_w^2)$ to $O(\sqrt{d}/\epsilon_p)$ for poisoning-concurrent watermarking, the watermarked poisoning dataset provably ensures both watermarking detectability and poisoning utility, certifying the practicality of watermarking under data poisoning attacks. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on several attacks, models, and datasets.

paragraphs: Some data-poisoning methods are intended to support ownership verification or protect private data from unauthorized use. Their resemblance to harmful poisoning can nevertheless create confusion and conflict. This paper proposes watermarking generated poisoned datasets so that ownership can be claimed and users can identify potential poisoning.

The authors develop two approaches: adding a watermark after poisoning and incorporating watermarking during the poisoning process. Their analysis gives watermark-length conditions under which detectability and poisoning utility are both guaranteed. For post-poisoning watermarking, the stated length scales as Θ(√d/ε_w); for concurrent watermarking, the stated range extends from Θ(1/ε_w²) to O(√d/ε_p).

These are conditional guarantees tied to the specified scaling requirements. They establish that making the watermark detectable can coexist with preserving the poisoning's intended effect. Experiments across several attacks, models, and datasets validate the theoretical findings. The contribution is an attribution mechanism for poisoned data, with theory and experiments addressing whether attribution remains possible without removing the utility that motivated the data modification.
summary.tldr: Two watermarking schemes provide conditional guarantees that poisoned datasets remain attributable while preserving poisoning utility.

title: Provable Watermarking for Data Poisoning Attacks

abstract: We propose a new framework for learning the world dynamics of feature-rich environments in model-based reinforcement learning. The main idea is formalized as a new, factored state-transition representation that supports efficient online-learning of the relevant features. We construct the transition models through predicting how the actions change the world. We introduce an online sparse coding learning technique for feature selection in high-dimensional spaces. We derive theoretical guarantees for our framework and empirically demonstrate its practicality in both simulated and real robotics domains.
originalAbstract: We propose a new framework for learning the world dynamics of feature-rich environments in model-based reinforcement learning. The main idea is formalized as a new, factored state-transition representation that supports efficient online-learning of the relevant features. We construct the transition models through predicting how the actions change the world. We introduce an online sparse coding learning technique for feature selection in high-dimensional spaces. We derive theoretical guarantees for our framework and empirically demonstrate its practicality in both simulated and real robotics domains.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning learns how an environment changes under actions. In environments described by many features, part of that challenge is identifying which features are relevant to the dynamics. This paper proposes a framework that learns the transition model and selects useful features online.

The central representation is a new factored state-transition model. The authors construct it by predicting how actions change the world, and design the representation to support efficient online learning of relevant features. An online sparse-coding technique performs feature selection in the high-dimensional space, connecting the choice of model inputs to the process of learning action effects.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees for the framework and demonstrates its practicality in both simulated and real robotics domains. The contribution lies in integrating representation, feature selection, and dynamics learning into one online approach. Its stated findings support learning useful transition models in feature-rich settings; the abstract's empirical claim concerns practicality rather than a specified improvement in reward or a numerical speedup.
summary.tldr: A factored transition model and online sparse coding jointly learn action effects and select relevant features for model-based reinforcement learning.

title: Online Feature Selection for Model-based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Natural gradient ascent (NGA) is a popular optimization method that uses a positive definite metric tensor. In many applications the metric tensor is only guaranteed to be positive semidefinite (e.g., when using the Fisher information matrix as the metric tensor), in which case NGA is not applicable. In our first contribution, we derive generalized natural gradient ascent (GeNGA), a generalization of NGA which allows for positive semidefinite non-smooth metric tensors. In our second contribution we show that, in standard settings, GeNGA and NGA can both be divergent. We then establish sufficient conditions to ensure that both achieve various forms of convergence. In our third contribution we show how several reinforcement learning methods that use NGA without positive definite metric tensors can be adapted to properly use GeNGA.

In many applications the metric tensor is only guaranteed to be positive semidefinite (e.g., when using the Fisher information matrix as the metric tensor), in which case NGA is not applicable. In our first contribution, we derive generalized natural gradient ascent (GeNGA), a generalization of NGA which allows for positive semidefinite non-smooth metric tensors. In our second contribution we show that, in standard settings, GeNGA and NGA can both be divergent. We then establish sufficient conditions to ensure that both achieve various forms of convergence. In our third contribution we show how several reinforcement learning methods that use NGA without positive definite metric tensors can be adapted to properly use GeNGA.

paragraphs: Natural gradient ascent uses a metric tensor to shape optimization updates. Its usual formulation requires that metric to be positive definite. In applications, including those using the Fisher information matrix, the metric may only be positive semidefinite, leaving the standard method inapplicable in the form considered here.

The paper introduces generalized natural gradient ascent, or GeNGA, to accommodate positive semidefinite metrics that may also be nonsmooth. This extends the range of geometries the optimization method can handle. The authors then examine convergence rather than assuming that a natural-gradient construction automatically produces stable progress.

Their analysis shows that both ordinary natural gradient ascent and GeNGA can diverge in standard settings. They also establish sufficient conditions for several forms of convergence, separating the method’s definition from the conditions needed for successful optimization. Finally, they show how reinforcement learning methods that use natural gradients without positive definite metrics can be adapted to GeNGA. The result is both a broader algorithm and a more qualified understanding of its behavior.
summary.tldr: GeNGA extends natural gradient ascent to semidefinite, nonsmooth metrics and establishes both divergence examples and sufficient convergence conditions.

title: GeNGA: A Generalization of Natural Gradient Ascent with Positive and Negative Convergence Results

abstract: We use Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) networks to learn representations of video sequences. Our model uses an encoder LSTM to map an input sequence into a fixed length representation. This representation is decoded using single or multiple decoder LSTMs to perform different tasks, such as reconstructing the input sequence, or predicting the future sequence. We experiment with two kinds of input sequences – patches of image pixels and high-level representations (“percepts") of video frames extracted using a pretrained convolutional net. We explore different design choices such as whether the decoder LSTMs should condition on the generated output. We analyze the outputs of the model qualitatively to see how well the model can extrapolate the learned video representation into the future and into the past. We further evaluate the representations by finetuning them for a supervised learning problem – human action recognition on the UCF-101 and HMDB-51 datasets. We show that the representations help improve classification accuracy, especially when there are only few training examples. Even models pretrained on unrelated datasets (300 hours of YouTube videos) can help action recognition performance.

paragraphs: The paper learns video representations by asking a sequence model to reconstruct observed frames or predict future ones. An encoder LSTM compresses an input sequence into a fixed-length representation. One or more decoder LSTMs then use that representation for these tasks, providing a way to learn from video without action labels.

Experiments use both image-pixel patches and higher-level frame representations extracted by a pretrained convolutional network. The authors examine design choices, including whether a decoder should condition on its generated outputs. Qualitative analysis explores how the learned representation supports extending a sequence into the future or reconstructing information about the past.

To test usefulness for recognition, the representations are fine-tuned on human-action classification using UCF-101 and HMDB-51. They improve classification accuracy, particularly when training examples are scarce. Pretraining on an unrelated collection of 300 hours of YouTube video can also help. These results indicate that the sequence-learning tasks can produce transferable representations in the evaluated settings, including when labeled action data are limited.
summary.tldr: LSTM reconstruction and prediction learn transferable video representations that improve action recognition, especially with limited labeled examples.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Video Representations using LSTMs

abstract: One-hot CNN (convolutional neural network) has been shown to be effective for text categorization (Johnson & Zhang, 2015). We view it as a special case of a general framework which jointly trains a linear model with a non-linear feature generator consisting of ‘text region embedding + pooling’. Under this framework, we explore a more sophisticated region embedding method using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). LSTM can embed text regions of variable (and possibly large) sizes, whereas the region size needs to be fixed in a CNN. We seek effective and efficient use of LSTM for this purpose in the supervised and semi-supervised settings. The best results were obtained by combining region embeddings in the form of LSTM and convolution layers trained on unlabeled data. The results indicate that on this task, embeddings of text regions, which can convey complex concepts, are more useful than embeddings of single words in isolation. We report performances exceeding the previous best results on four benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: This paper treats text classification as jointly learning a linear classifier and a nonlinear feature generator. The feature generator embeds regions of text and then pools their representations. Within this framework, the authors investigate LSTMs as a way to represent regions whose lengths can vary and may be large.

The variable-length capability distinguishes the proposed LSTM region embeddings from the fixed region sizes used in convolutional networks. The work explores effective and efficient use in both supervised and semi-supervised learning. Its best results combine LSTM-based and convolution-based region embeddings trained on unlabeled data, bringing the two forms of representation together.

The reported performance exceeds previous best results on four benchmark datasets. The findings indicate that, for this classification task, embeddings of text regions are more useful than embeddings of individual words considered separately. Regions can convey complex concepts, making the unit of representation central to the paper's argument. The empirical conclusion concerns the evaluated text-categorization setting and supports learning features over larger stretches of text.
summary.tldr: Combining LSTM and convolutional text-region embeddings learned from unlabeled data improved classification across four benchmarks.

title: Supervised and Semi-Supervised Text Categorization using LSTM for Region Embeddings

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a new set of reinforcement learning (RL) tasks in Minecraft (a flexible 3D world). We then use these tasks to systematically compare and contrast existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) architectures with our new memory-based DRL architectures. These tasks are designed to emphasize, in a controllable manner, issues that pose challenges for RL methods including partial observability (due to first-person visual observations), delayed rewards, high-dimensional visual observations, and the need to use active perception in a correct manner so as to perform well in the tasks. While these tasks are conceptually simple to describe, by virtue of having all of these challenges simultaneously they are difficult for current DRL architectures. Additionally, we evaluate the generalization performance of the architectures on environments not used during training. The experimental results show that our new architectures generalize to unseen environments better than existing DRL architectures.

We then use these tasks to systematically compare and contrast existing deep reinforcement learning (DRL) architectures with our new memory-based DRL architectures. These tasks are designed to emphasize, in a controllable manner, issues that pose challenges for RL methods including partial observability (due to first-person visual observations), delayed rewards, high-dimensional visual observations, and the need to use active perception in a correct manner so as to perform well in the tasks. While these tasks are conceptually simple to describe, by virtue of having all of these challenges simultaneously they are difficult for current DRL architectures. Additionally, we evaluate the generalization performance of the architectures on environments not used during training. The experimental results show that our new architectures generalize to unseen environments better than existing DRL architectures.

paragraphs: The paper introduces reinforcement-learning tasks in Minecraft to examine several difficulties together. Agents receive first-person visual observations, encounter delayed rewards, and must deal with high-dimensional input. They also need to use active perception appropriately, making the acquisition of useful observations part of successful behavior.

The tasks expose these challenges in a controllable way, allowing systematic comparisons between existing deep reinforcement-learning architectures and new architectures that use memory. Although the tasks are simple to describe, their combination of partial observability, visual complexity, delayed feedback, and perception requirements makes them difficult for the architectures studied.

The evaluation also tests performance in environments excluded from training. The authors report that their new memory-based architectures generalize better to these unseen environments than existing architectures. This finding concerns transfer within the evaluated tasks, alongside performance under the combined learning challenges. The contribution includes both a task collection for examining these capabilities and architectural evidence that memory-based designs can improve generalization in that setting.
summary.tldr: Controlled Minecraft tasks show improved generalization from new memory-based reinforcement-learning architectures in the evaluated environments.

title: Control of Memory, Active Perception, and Action in Minecraft

abstract: Structured Prediction Energy Networks (SPENs) are a simple, yet expressive family of structured prediction models (Belanger and McCallum, 2016). An energy function over candidate structured outputs is given by a deep network, and predictions are formed by gradient-based optimization. This paper presents end-to-end learning for SPENs, where the energy function is discriminatively trained by back-propagating through gradient-based prediction. In our experience, the approach is substantially more accurate than the structured SVM method of Belanger and McCallum (2016), as it allows us to use more sophisticated non-convex energies. We provide a collection of techniques for improving the speed, accuracy, and memory requirements of end-to-end SPENs, and demonstrate the power of our method on 7-Scenes image denoising and CoNLL-2005 semantic role labeling tasks. In both, inexact minimization of non-convex SPEN energies is superior to baseline methods that use simplistic energy functions that can be minimized exactly.

paragraphs: Structured Prediction Energy Networks assign an energy to each candidate structured output using a deep network. Prediction then searches for a low-energy output through gradient-based optimization. This paper develops end-to-end training that back-propagates through that prediction process, allowing the energy function to learn from the procedure used to produce predictions.

The authors report substantially better accuracy than the earlier structured SVM training method in their experience. They attribute this benefit to the ability to use more sophisticated non-convex energy functions. They also provide techniques to improve speed, accuracy, and memory requirements, addressing the practical costs of training through an optimization procedure.

The method is demonstrated on 7-Scenes image denoising and CoNLL-2005 semantic role labeling. In both tasks, approximate minimization of the richer non-convex energies outperforms baselines whose simpler energies can be minimized exactly. The findings show that, in these experiments, the expressive quality of the energy function matters enough to outweigh the advantage of exact optimization for a simpler model.
summary.tldr: Training through prediction optimization lets structured energy networks use richer energies that outperform simpler, exactly optimized baselines on two tasks.

title: End-to-End Learning for Structured Prediction Energy Networks

abstract: Many real-world problems, such as network packet routing and urban traffic control, are naturally modeled as multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL) problems. However, existing multi-agent RL methods typically scale poorly in the problem size. Therefore, a key challenge is to translate the success of deep learning on single-agent RL to the multi-agent setting. A major stumbling block is that independent Q-learning, the most popular multi-agent RL method, introduces nonstationarity that makes it incompatible with the experience replay memory on which deep Q-learning relies. This paper proposes two methods that address this problem: 1) using a multi-agent variant of importance sampling to naturally decay obsolete data and 2) conditioning each agent’s value function on a fingerprint that disambiguates the age of the data sampled from the replay memory. Results on a challenging decentralised variant of StarCraft unit micromanagement confirm that these methods enable the successful combination of experience replay with multi-agent RL.

paragraphs: Experience replay lets a reinforcement-learning agent train on stored interactions. In a multi-agent setting, those interactions can become misleading as other agents change their behavior during learning. The paper identifies this nonstationarity as a major obstacle to combining independent Q-learning with the replay memory used in deep Q-learning.

The authors propose two ways to make stored experience usable. One adapts importance sampling to the multi-agent setting so that obsolete data naturally receive less influence. The other conditions each agent's value function on a fingerprint that helps distinguish the age of replayed data. These approaches address different aspects of the problem: how strongly an old sample should count and how its context should be interpreted.

Experiments use a challenging decentralized version of StarCraft unit micromanagement. The results confirm that the proposed methods enable experience replay to work successfully with multi-agent reinforcement learning in that setting. The contribution is a targeted response to changing training conditions, supporting the transfer of a central deep reinforcement-learning technique to environments with multiple simultaneously learning agents.
summary.tldr: Importance weighting and age-disambiguating fingerprints make experience replay usable for independently learning agents in a decentralized StarCraft task.

title: Stabilising Experience Replay for Deep Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We develop and study multicalibration as a new measure of fairness in machine learning that aims to mitigate inadvertent or malicious discrimination that is introduced at training time (even from ground truth data). Multicalibration guarantees meaningful (calibrated) predictions for every subpopulation that can be identified within a specified class of computations. The specified class can be quite rich; in particular, it can contain many overlapping subgroups of a protected group. We demonstrate that in many settings this strong notion of protection from discrimination is provably attainable and aligned with the goal of obtaining accurate predictions. Along the way, we present algorithms for learning a multicalibrated predictor, study the computational complexity of this task, and illustrate tight connections to the agnostic learning model.

paragraphs: A predictor can appear reliable at a broad population level while giving less meaningful predictions to smaller subpopulations. This paper introduces multicalibration as a fairness criterion intended to address discrimination introduced during training, including discrimination present in the ground-truth data. The requirement applies calibrated predictions across a specified collection of identifiable subpopulations.

The collection is defined by a class of computations that can identify groups. It can be rich enough to include many overlapping subgroups within a protected group, extending the requirement beyond a single coarse partition. The scope of the guarantee is therefore explicit: it covers every subpopulation identifiable within that chosen computational class.

The authors show that this protection is provably achievable in many settings and can align with accurate prediction. They provide learning algorithms, investigate the computational difficulty of constructing multicalibrated predictors, and establish close connections with agnostic learning. The contribution combines a more detailed group-level reliability target with analysis of when and how a learner can achieve it.
summary.tldr: Multicalibration requires calibrated predictions across computationally identifiable, potentially overlapping subgroups and is provably achievable in many settings.

title: Multicalibration: Calibration for the (Computationally-Identifiable) Masses

abstract: We establish a data-dependent notion of algorithmic stability for Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), and employ it to develop novel generalization bounds. This is in contrast to previous distribution-free algorithmic stability results for SGD which depend on the worst-case constants. By virtue of the data-dependent argument, our bounds provide new insights into learning with SGD on convex and non-convex problems. In the convex case, we show that the bound on the generalization error depends on the risk at the initialization point. In the non-convex case, we prove that the expected curvature of the objective function around the initialization point has crucial influence on the generalization error. In both cases, our results suggest a simple data-driven strategy to stabilize SGD by pre-screening its initialization. As a corollary, our results allow us to show optimistic generalization bounds that exhibit fast convergence rates for SGD subject to a vanishing empirical risk and low noise of stochastic gradient.

paragraphs: Algorithmic stability links how sensitive training is to its data with how well the learned model generalizes. Previous stability analyses of stochastic gradient descent used distribution-free, worst-case quantities. This paper develops a data-dependent notion of stability, allowing the resulting generalization bounds to reflect properties of the learning problem more directly.

The analysis highlights initialization in two different settings. For convex objectives, the bound on generalization error depends on the risk at the starting point. For nonconvex objectives, the expected curvature near that point has an important influence. These results connect generalization to where optimization begins, as well as to properties of the objective encountered there.

Both findings suggest screening candidate initializations using data as a way to stabilize SGD. The paper also derives optimistic bounds with fast convergence rates when empirical risk vanishes and stochastic gradient noise is low. Those conditions are essential to that favorable conclusion; the work does not assert that every SGD run automatically receives the same fast generalization rate.
summary.tldr: Data-dependent stability bounds connect SGD generalization to initialization and yield fast rates under vanishing empirical risk and low gradient noise.

title: Data-Dependent Stability of Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: This paper provides a simple procedure to fit generative networks to target distributions, with the goal of a small Wasserstein distance (or other optimal transport costs). The approach is based on two principles: (a) if the source randomness of the network is a continuous distribution (the "semi-discrete" setting), then the Wasserstein distance is realized by a deterministic optimal transport mapping; (b) given an optimal transport mapping between a generator network and a target distribution, the Wasserstein distance may be decreased via a regression between the generated data and the mapped target points. The procedure here therefore alternates these two steps, forming an optimal transport and regressing against it, gradually adjusting the generator network towards the target distribution. Mathematically, this approach is shown to minimize the Wasserstein distance to both the empirical target distribution, and also its underlying population counterpart. Empirically, good performance is demonstrated on the training and testing sets of the MNIST and Thin-8 data. The paper closes with a discussion of the unsuitability of the Wasserstein distance for certain tasks, as has been identified in prior work (Arora et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2017).

paragraphs: This paper trains a generative network by repeatedly finding where its outputs should move and then teaching the network to make that move. The objective is to bring the generated distribution closer to a target distribution, measured through Wasserstein distance or another optimal transport cost. This gives the training procedure an explicit distribution-matching goal.

The approach uses a semi-discrete setting in which the network's input randomness has a continuous distribution. In this setting, the relevant Wasserstein distance is realized by a deterministic optimal transport mapping. Once that mapping is available, regression between generated examples and their assigned target points may decrease the distance. Training alternates between constructing the transport mapping and updating the generator through regression.

The mathematical analysis establishes minimization of the distance to both the observed target distribution and its underlying population distribution. Experiments report good training and testing performance on MNIST and Thin-8. The paper also discusses situations where Wasserstein distance is unsuitable, distinguishing successful optimization of this objective from its appropriateness for a particular task.
summary.tldr: Alternating optimal transport mappings with regression provides a gradual way to train generators to minimize Wasserstein distance.

title: A Gradual, Semi-Discrete Approach to Generative Network Training via Explicit Wasserstein Minimization

abstract: Recent work (Cohen & Welling, 2016) has shown that generalizations of convolutions, based on group theory, provide powerful inductive biases for learning. In these generalizations, filters are not only translated but can also be rotated, flipped, etc. However, coming up with exact models of how to rotate a 3x3 filter on a square pixel-grid is difficult. In this paper, we learn how to transform filters for use in the group convolution, focussing on roto-translation. For this, we learn a filter basis and all rotated versions of that filter basis. Filters are then encoded by a set of rotation invariant coefficients. To rotate a filter, we switch the basis. We demonstrate we can produce feature maps with low sensitivity to input rotations, while achieving high performance on MNIST and CIFAR-10.

In this paper, we learn how to transform filters for use in the group convolution, focussing on roto-translation. For this, we learn a filter basis and all rotated versions of that filter basis. paragraphs: Group convolutions extend ordinary convolution by transforming filters through operations such as rotations and flips as well as translations. These transformations provide useful structure for learning, but defining exact rotations of a small filter on a square pixel grid is difficult. This paper focuses on learning filter transformations for rotations and translations.

The method learns a filter basis together with rotated versions of that basis. Each filter is represented by coefficients that stay unchanged under rotation. Rotating the filter then means switching to the corresponding basis while retaining those coefficients. This creates a learned form of weight sharing across orientations and places the transformation structure inside the filter representation.

The authors demonstrate feature maps with low sensitivity to input rotations and high performance on MNIST and CIFAR-10. Low sensitivity is the stated result, rather than exact invariance to every possible rotation. The approach matters because it provides a practical way to learn how filters transform when a precise hand-designed rotation rule is awkward on the underlying pixel grid.
summary.tldr: Learning rotated filter bases enables generalized weight sharing and produces rotation-insensitive features with high performance on MNIST and CIFAR-10.

title: Learning to Convolve: A Generalized Weight-Tying Approach

abstract: We study the Short-and-Sparse (SaS) deconvolution problem of recovering a short signal a0 and a sparse signal x0 from their convolution. We propose a method based on nonconvex optimization, which under certain conditions recovers the target short and sparse signals, up to a signed shift symmetry which is intrinsic to this model. This symmetry plays a central role in shaping the optimization landscape for deconvolution. We give a regional analysis, which characterizes this landscape geometrically, on a union of subspaces. Our geometric characterization holds when the length-p0 short signal a0 has shift coherence {\textmu}, and x0 follows a random sparsity model with sparsity rate $\theta$ $\in$ [c1/p0, c2/(p0\sqrt{\mu}+\sqrt{p0})] / (log^2(p0)) . Based on this geometry, we give a provable method that successfully solves SaS deconvolution with high probability.

paragraphs: Short-and-sparse deconvolution tries to recover two signals from their convolution: one short signal and one sparse signal. The paper proposes a nonconvex optimization method for this recovery problem. A central feature is signed-shift symmetry, an intrinsic ambiguity that means the target signals are recovered only up to the corresponding sign and shift transformations.

The authors study how this symmetry shapes the optimization landscape. Their analysis characterizes the landscape regionally over a union of subspaces. The characterization depends on the short signal's length and shift coherence, together with a random sparsity model for the sparse signal. Its sparsity rate must lie within a specified range determined by those quantities.

Using this geometric analysis, the authors give a method that solves the recovery problem with high probability under the stated conditions. The result shows how understanding symmetry and local geometric structure can support a provable method for a nonconvex problem. Its recovery guarantee remains conditional on the signal and sparsity assumptions and retains the model's unavoidable signed-shift ambiguity.
summary.tldr: A geometric analysis yields high-probability short-and-sparse deconvolution under specified signal conditions, up to intrinsic signed-shift ambiguity.

title: Geometry and Symmetry in Short-and-Sparse Deconvolution

abstract: Planning in Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) inherently gathers the information necessary to act optimally under uncertainties. The framework can be extended to model pure information gathering tasks by considering belief-based rewards. This allows us to use reward shaping to guide POMDP planning to informative beliefs by using a weighted combination of the original reward and the expected information gain as the objective. In this work we propose a novel online algorithm, Information Particle Filter Tree (IPFT), to solve problems with belief-dependent rewards on continuous domains. It simulates particle-based belief trajectories in a Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) approach to construct a search tree in the belief space. The evaluation shows that the consideration of information gain greatly improves the performance in problems where information gathering is an essential part of the optimal policy.

The framework can be extended to model pure information gathering tasks by considering belief-based rewards. paragraphs: An agent acting under partial observability must choose actions using beliefs about an uncertain state. Sometimes an action is valuable because it reveals information, even if its immediate task reward is small. This paper studies planning with rewards that depend directly on beliefs, including combinations of ordinary reward and expected information gain.

Information Particle Filter Tree, or IPFT, is an online planning algorithm for continuous-domain problems with these belief-dependent rewards. It simulates trajectories of particle-based beliefs and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to build a search tree in belief space. The approach therefore evaluates how actions change both the task situation and the agent’s uncertainty about it.

The evaluation finds that including information gain substantially improves performance when gathering information is an essential part of an optimal policy. The contribution is a practical planning procedure for that reward formulation, rather than a claim that information gain always improves decision-making. Its usefulness is demonstrated specifically in problems where better-informed beliefs support better subsequent actions.
summary.tldr: IPFT plans through particle-based beliefs so continuous-domain agents can explicitly value informative actions.

title: Information Particle Filter Tree: An Online Algorithm for POMDPs with Belief-Based Rewards on Continuous Domains

abstract: This paper formalizes the binarization operations over neural networks from a learning perspective. In contrast to classical hand crafted rules (\eg hard thresholding) to binarize full-precision neurons, we propose to learn a mapping from full-precision neurons to the target binary ones. Each individual weight entry will not be binarized independently. Instead, they are taken as a whole to accomplish the binarization, just as they work together in generating convolution features. To help the training of the binarization mapping, the full-precision neurons after taking sign operations is regarded as some auxiliary supervision signal, which is noisy but still has valuable guidance. An unbiased estimator is therefore introduced to mitigate the influence of the supervision noise. Experimental results on benchmark datasets indicate that the proposed binarization technique attains consistent improvements over baselines.

Each individual weight entry will not be binarized independently. Instead, they are taken as a whole to accomplish the binarization, just as they work together in generating convolution features. To help the training of the binarization mapping, the full-precision neurons after taking sign operations is regarded as some auxiliary supervision signal, which is noisy but still has valuable guidance. paragraphs: Converting full-precision neural network values to binary ones is often governed by a fixed rule such as hard thresholding. This paper instead treats binarization as something to learn. It proposes a mapping from full-precision neurons to binary neurons, making the conversion itself part of the learning problem rather than prescribing each binary decision in advance.

The mapping considers weight entries together instead of binarizing each entry independently. This reflects the fact that the weights jointly generate convolutional features. To help train the mapping, the method uses sign-transformed full-precision neurons as an auxiliary supervision signal. The authors treat this signal as informative but noisy and introduce an unbiased estimator to mitigate the noise's influence.

Benchmark experiments show consistent improvements over the compared baselines. These findings support learning a coordinated binarization mapping with help from imperfect supervision. The contribution combines two ideas: respecting the collective role of weights when making binary choices and explicitly accounting for noise in the signal used to guide those choices.
summary.tldr: A learned joint binarization mapping uses noise-corrected auxiliary supervision to improve binary neural networks over evaluated baselines.

title: Training Binary Neural Networks through Learning with Noisy Supervision

abstract: Learning long-range behaviors on complex high-dimensional agents is a fundamental problem in robot learning. For such tasks, we argue that transferring learned information from a morphologically simpler agent can massively improve the sample efficiency of a more complex one. To this end, we propose a hierarchical decoupling of policies into two parts: an independently learned low-level policy and a transferable high-level policy. To remedy poor transfer performance due to mismatch in morphologies, we contribute two key ideas. First, we show that incentivizing a complex agent’s low-level to imitate a simpler agent’s low-level significantly improves zero-shot high-level transfer. Second, we show that KL-regularized training of the high level stabilizes learning and prevents mode-collapse. Finally, on a suite of publicly released navigation and manipulation environments, we demonstrate the applicability of hierarchical transfer on long-range tasks across morphologies. Our code and videos can be found at https://sites.google.com/berkeley.edu/morphology-transfer.
