paragraphs: Learning long-range behavior can be expensive for agents with complex bodies and many control dimensions. This paper investigates transferring knowledge from a simpler body to a more complex one. It separates control into an independently learned low-level policy and a high-level policy designed to transfer between agents with different morphologies.

Differences between bodies can make direct high-level transfer work poorly. The authors address this by encouraging the complex agent’s low-level controller to imitate the simpler agent’s low-level behavior. They show that this significantly improves zero-shot high-level transfer. A second component applies KL-regularized training to the high-level policy, which stabilizes learning and prevents mode collapse in the studied setting.

Experiments on navigation and manipulation environments demonstrate hierarchical transfer for long-range tasks across morphologies. The approach matters because it identifies an adaptation point below the transferred policy: improving compatibility between low-level behaviors can make high-level knowledge more reusable. The findings support the authors’ proposal that learning with a simpler agent can improve the sample efficiency of a more complex agent.
summary.tldr: Low-level imitation and regularized high-level learning improve the transfer of long-range control policies between agents with different bodies.

title: Hierarchically Decoupled Imitation For Morphological Transfer

abstract: Graph generation techniques are increasingly being adopted for drug discovery. Previous graph generation approaches have utilized relatively small molecular building blocks such as atoms or simple cycles, limiting their effectiveness to smaller molecules. Indeed, as we demonstrate, their performance degrades significantly for larger molecules. In this paper, we propose a new hierarchical graph encoder-decoder that employs significantly larger and more flexible graph motifs as basic building blocks. Our encoder produces a multi-resolution representation for each molecule in a fine-to-coarse fashion, from atoms to connected motifs. Each level integrates the encoding of constituents below with the graph at that level. Our autoregressive coarse-to-fine decoder adds one motif at a time, interleaving the decision of selecting a new motif with the process of resolving its attachments to the emerging molecule. We evaluate our model on multiple molecule generation tasks, including polymers, and show that our model significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Generating molecular graphs from individual atoms or small cycles can become less effective as molecules grow larger. The authors demonstrate substantial performance degradation for earlier approaches in that setting. Their response is to use larger, more flexible structural motifs as building blocks, making molecular generation operate at several levels of detail.

The encoder builds a fine-to-coarse representation, starting with atoms and progressing to connected motifs. At each level, it combines information from the smaller constituents with the graph structure at that level. The decoder reverses this direction: it constructs a molecule one motif at a time, alternating between choosing a motif and deciding how to attach it.

This hierarchy connects detailed molecular information with decisions about larger pieces of structure. The authors evaluate the model on several molecule-generation tasks, including polymers, and report significant improvements over previous state-of-the-art baselines. The findings support using richer building blocks for the evaluated generation problems, particularly in the context of the difficulties they identify with larger molecules.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical molecular generator builds graphs from larger structural motifs and significantly improves results on evaluated tasks, including polymers.

title: Hierarchical Generation of Molecular Graphs using Structural Motifs

abstract: The construction in the recent paper by Du et al. [2019] implies that searching for a near-optimal action in a bandit sometimes requires examining essentially all the actions, even if the learner is given linear features in R^d that approximate the rewards with a small uniform error. We use the Kiefer-Wolfowitz theorem to prove a positive result that by checking only a few actions, a learner can always find an action that is suboptimal with an error of at most O($\epsilon$$\sqrt{}$d) where $\epsilon$ is the approximation error of the features. Thus, features are useful when the approximation error is small relative to the dimensionality of the features. The idea is applied to stochastic bandits and reinforcement learning with a generative model where the learner has access to d-dimensional linear features that approximate the action-value functions for all policies to an accuracy of $\epsilon$. For linear bandits, we prove a bound on the regret of order d$\sqrt{}$(n log(k)) + $\epsilon$n$\sqrt{}$d log(n) with k the number of actions and n the horizon. For RL we show that approximate policy iteration can learn a policy that is optimal up to an additive error of order $\epsilon$$\sqrt{}$d/(1 − $\gamma$)^2 and using about d/($\epsilon$^2(1 − $\gamma$)^4) samples from the generative model. These bounds are independent of the finer details of the features. We also investigate how the structure of the feature set impacts the tradeoff between sample complexity and estimation error.

The authors prove a complementary result: checking only a few actions can always find one whose suboptimality is at most O(epsilon times the square root of d), where d is feature dimension.

This guarantee explains why approximation quality must be assessed together with dimensionality. The authors extend the idea to stochastic bandits, proving a regret bound that combines a learning term with an accumulated feature-approximation term. The bounds do not depend on finer details of the features, although the paper also investigates how feature structure changes the tradeoff between sampling and estimation error.

For reinforcement learning, the result assumes access to a generative model and features that approximate every policy's action-value function within epsilon. Approximate policy iteration then achieves additive error of order epsilon times square root of d divided by (1 − gamma) squared, with a stated sample bound. The assumptions make clear which kind of representation quality supports the guarantee.
summary.tldr: Approximately linear features can support efficient action selection and reinforcement learning, with guarantees that explicitly trade approximation error against feature dimension.

title: Learning with Good Feature Representations in Bandits and in RL with a Generative Model

abstract: We investigate the challenge of multi-output learning, where the goal is to learn a vector-valued function based on a supervised data set. This includes a range of important problems in Machine Learning including multi-target regression, multi-class classification and multi-label classification. We begin our analysis by introducing the self-bounding Lipschitz condition for multi-output loss functions, which interpolates continuously between a classical Lipschitz condition and a multi-dimensional analogue of a smoothness condition. We then show that the self-bounding Lipschitz condition gives rise to optimistic bounds for multi-output learning, which attain the minimax optimal rate up to logarithmic factors. The proof exploits local Rademacher complexity combined with a powerful minoration inequality due to Srebro, Sridharan and Tewari. As an application we derive a state-of-the-art generalisation bound for multi-class gradient boosting.

paragraphs: Multi-output learning predicts a vector rather than a single scalar. This framework includes predicting several numerical targets, selecting among multiple classes, and assigning multiple labels. The paper develops generalization theory for these problems, aiming to describe how accurately learned predictors can perform beyond their supervised training data.

The central tool is a self-bounding Lipschitz condition on the loss function. It connects the classical Lipschitz condition to a multidimensional smoothness condition through a continuous range of possibilities. Under this condition, the authors derive optimistic learning bounds that achieve minimax-optimal rates up to logarithmic factors. The guarantee is therefore tied to a specified property of the loss.

The proof combines local Rademacher complexity with a minoration inequality. As a concrete application, the authors obtain a state-of-the-art generalization bound for multiclass gradient boosting. The contribution supplies a shared analytical condition for several multi-output settings and shows that it can produce strong guarantees for an established learning method.
summary.tldr: A self-bounding loss condition yields nearly minimax-optimal generalization bounds for multi-output learning and a strong multiclass boosting guarantee.

title: Optimistic Bounds for Multi-output Learning

abstract: Machine learning algorithms are known to be susceptible to data poisoning attacks, where an adversary manipulates the training data to degrade performance of the resulting classifier. In this work, we present a unifying view of randomized smoothing over arbitrary functions, and we leverage this novel characterization to propose a new strategy for building classifiers that are pointwise-certifiably robust to general data poisoning attacks. As a specific instantiation, we utilize our framework to build linear classifiers that are robust to a strong variant of label flipping, where each test example is targeted independently. In other words, for each test point, our classifier includes a certification that its prediction would be the same had some number of training labels been changed adversarially. Randomized smoothing has previously been used to guarantee—with high probability—test-time robustness to adversarial manipulation of the input to a classifier; we derive a variant which provides a deterministic, analytical bound, sidestepping the probabilistic certificates that traditionally result from the sampling subprocedure. Further, we obtain these certified bounds with minimal additional runtime complexity over standard classification and no assumptions on the train or test distributions. We generalize our results to the multi-class case, providing the first multi-class classification algorithm that is certifiably robust to label-flipping attacks.

paragraphs: Training-data poisoning changes the data used to build a classifier rather than only altering an input at prediction time. This paper develops a general view of randomized smoothing over arbitrary functions and uses it to construct classifiers with pointwise certificates against poisoning. Each certificate concerns the stability of a particular test prediction.

The concrete application builds linear classifiers resistant to label flipping. For each test example, the certificate guarantees that its prediction would remain unchanged if some number of training labels had been adversarially modified. The attack model permits a different targeted attack for each test point. This is a prediction-invariance guarantee, rather than a statement that the unchanged prediction must be correct.

They report minimal additional runtime complexity relative to standard classification and require no assumptions about training or test distributions. They also extend the results to multiple classes, presenting what they identify as the first multiclass classification algorithm with certified robustness to label-flipping attacks.
summary.tldr: A smoothing framework provides deterministic, per-prediction certificates that linear classifiers withstand a bounded number of adversarial training-label changes.

title: Certified Robustness to Label-Flipping Attacks via Randomized Smoothing

abstract: In this paper, we study a family of non-convex and possibly non-smooth inf-projection minimization problems, where the target objective function is equal to minimization of a joint function over another variable. This problem include difference of convex (DC) functions and a family of bi-convex functions as special cases. We develop stochastic algorithms and establish their first-order convergence for finding a (nearly) stationary solution of the target non-convex function under different conditions of the component functions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that comprehensively studies stochastic optimization of non-convex inf-projection minimization problems with provable convergence guarantee. Our algorithms enable efficient stochastic optimization of a family of non-decomposable DC functions and a family of bi-convex functions. To demonstrate the power of the proposed algorithms we consider an important application in variance-based regularization. Experiments verify the effectiveness of our inf-projection based formulation and the proposed stochastic algorithm in comparison with previous stochastic algorithms based on the min-max formulation for achieving the same effect.

paragraphs: An inf-projection objective is defined by minimizing a joint function over an additional variable. The outer optimization then works with the value left after that minimization. This paper studies such objectives when they are non-convex and potentially non-smooth, covering difference-of-convex functions and a family of bi-convex functions as special cases.

The authors develop stochastic algorithms and establish first-order convergence toward a nearly stationary solution. The guarantees depend on different conditions imposed on the component functions. A nearly stationary point is the stated target, so the results do not amount to a general global-minimum guarantee. The framework enables efficient stochastic optimization for covered non-decomposable difference-of-convex and bi-convex problems.

Variance-based regularization provides the application used to demonstrate the approach. Experiments compare the inf-projection formulation and its stochastic algorithm with earlier stochastic methods that use a min-max formulation for the same effect. The reported effectiveness shows why changing the mathematical formulation can be useful: it brings the application within a class for which the paper develops both algorithms and convergence analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper develops stochastic methods with conditional convergence guarantees for non-convex inf-projection objectives and applies them to variance-based regularization.

title: Stochastic Optimization for Non-convex Inf-Projection Problems

abstract: Least-Mean-Squares (\textsc{LMS}) solvers comprise a class of fundamental optimization problems such as linear regression, and regularized regressions such as Ridge, LASSO, and Elastic-Net. Data summarization techniques for big data generate summaries called coresets and sketches to speed up model learning under streaming and distributed settings. For example, \citep{nips2019} design a fast and accurate Caratheodory set on input data to boost the performance of existing \textsc{LMS} solvers. In retrospect, we explore classical Householder transformation as a candidate for sketching and accurately solving LMS problems. We find it to be a simpler, memory-efficient, and faster alternative that always existed to the above strong baseline. We also present a scalable algorithm based on the construction of distributed Householder sketches to solve \textsc{LMS} problem across multiple worker nodes. We perform thorough empirical analysis with large synthetic and real datasets to evaluate the performance of Householder sketch and compare with \citep{nips2019}. Our results show Householder sketch speeds up existing \textsc{LMS} solvers in the scikit-learn library up to $100$x-$400$x. Also, it is $10$x-$100$x faster than the above baseline with similar numerical stability. The distributed algorithm demonstrates linear scalability with a near-negligible communication overhead.

paragraphs: Least-mean-squares problems include linear regression and regularized variants such as Ridge, LASSO, and Elastic-Net. Large datasets can make these problems expensive to solve, motivating compact data summaries called sketches or coresets. This paper revisits the classical Householder transformation as a way to construct sketches that accelerate existing solvers while retaining numerical accuracy.

The authors compare Householder sketches with an existing Caratheodory-set approach and find them simpler, more memory efficient, and faster. They also develop a distributed algorithm that constructs Householder sketches across worker nodes. This extends the same summarization idea to settings where computation is spread over multiple machines.

Experiments on large synthetic and real datasets report speedups of up to 100 to 400 times for existing scikit-learn solvers. Compared with the cited sketching baseline, the method is 10 to 100 times faster with similar numerical stability. The distributed implementation demonstrates linear scalability and nearly negligible communication overhead, supporting the practical value of this classical transformation for modern large-data regression.
summary.tldr: Householder sketches substantially accelerate existing regression solvers and support scalable distributed computation with similar numerical stability to the compared baseline.

title: Householder Sketch for Accurate and Accelerated Least-Mean-Squares Solvers

abstract: Deep generative models have been demonstrated as state-of-the-art density estimators. Yet, recent work has found that they often assign a higher likelihood to data from outside the training distribution. This seemingly paradoxical behavior has caused concerns over the quality of the attained density estimates. In the context of hierarchical variational autoencoders, we provide evidence to explain this behavior by out-of-distribution data having in-distribution low-level features. We argue that this is both expected and desirable behavior. With this insight in hand, we develop a fast, scalable and fully unsupervised likelihood-ratio score for OOD detection that requires data to be in-distribution across all feature-levels. We benchmark the method on a vast set of data and model combinations and achieve state-of-the-art results on out-of-distribution detection.

paragraphs: A generative model can assign higher likelihood to unfamiliar data than to data resembling its training set. This appears troubling if likelihood is treated as a direct measure of familiarity. The paper examines this behavior in hierarchical variational autoencoders, whose representations contain features at multiple levels.

The authors provide evidence that unfamiliar examples can nevertheless have familiar low-level features. Those features help explain why the model assigns high likelihood even when the example is outside the training distribution overall. They argue that recognizing such shared structure is expected and desirable, so the observed behavior need not mean that the density estimate itself is poor.

Using this explanation, the authors develop an unsupervised likelihood-ratio score for detecting out-of-distribution inputs. The score requires consistency with the training distribution across all feature levels rather than relying on overall likelihood alone. They describe the method as fast and scalable and report state-of-the-art detection results across many data and model combinations. The finding distinguishes modeling shared features from deciding whether an entire input is familiar.
summary.tldr: Familiar low-level features explain some high likelihoods on unfamiliar inputs, motivating a multilevel likelihood-ratio detector.

title: Hierarchical VAEs Know What They Don’t Know

abstract: Tensor decomposition is a powerful framework for multiway data analysis. Despite the success of existing approaches, they ignore the sparse nature of the tensor data in many real-world applications, explicitly or implicitly assuming dense tensors. To address this model misspecification and to exploit the sparse tensor structures, we propose Nonparametric dEcomposition of Sparse Tensors (\ours), which can capture both the sparse structure properties and complex relationships between the tensor nodes to enhance the embedding estimation. Specifically, we first use completely random measures to construct tensor-valued random processes. We prove that the entry growth is much slower than that of the corresponding tensor size, which implies sparsity. Given finite observations (\ie projections), we then propose two nonparametric decomposition models that couple Dirichlet processes and Gaussian processes to jointly sample the sparse entry indices and the entry values (the latter as a nonlinear mapping of the embeddings), so as to encode both the structure properties and nonlinear relationships of the tensor nodes into the embeddings. Finally, we use the stick-breaking construction and random Fourier features to develop a scalable, stochastic variational learning algorithm. We show the advantage of our approach in sparse tensor generation, and entry index and value prediction in several real-world applications.

paragraphs: Tensors organize data across multiple dimensions, and decomposition learns representations of the entities participating in those dimensions. Many real datasets are sparse, yet decomposition methods can explicitly or implicitly assume density. This paper makes sparsity part of the probabilistic model so that the pattern of observed entries can help shape the learned representations.

The construction begins with completely random measures defining tensor-valued random processes. The authors prove that the number of entries grows much more slowly than the corresponding tensor size, establishing sparsity. For finite observations, two decomposition models combine Dirichlet processes and Gaussian processes to generate entry locations and values jointly. Values depend nonlinearly on the embeddings, allowing structural and value information to inform them together.

For scalable learning, the paper combines stick-breaking constructions and random Fourier features in a stochastic variational algorithm. Experiments show advantages in generating sparse tensors and predicting entry indices and values in several real-world applications. The approach therefore treats sparse structure as information to model alongside nonlinear relationships between entities.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric tensor model jointly learns sparse entry patterns and nonlinear values to improve entity embeddings and prediction.

title: Nonparametric Decomposition of Sparse Tensors

abstract: Comparison of data representations is a complex multi-aspect problem. We propose a method for comparing two data representations. We introduce the Representation Topology Divergence (RTD) score measuring the dissimilarity in multi-scale topology between two point clouds of equal size with a one-to-one correspondence between points. The two data point clouds can lie in different ambient spaces. The RTD score is one of the few topological data analysis based practical methods applicable to real machine learning datasets. Experiments show the agreement of RTD with the intuitive assessment of data representation similarity. The proposed RTD score is sensitive to the data representation’s fine topological structure. We use the RTD score to gain insights on neural networks representations in computer vision and NLP domains for various problems: training dynamics analysis, data distribution shift, transfer learning, ensemble learning, disentanglement assessment.

Experiments show the agreement of RTD with the intuitive assessment of data representation similarity. The proposed RTD score is sensitive to the data representation’s fine topological structure. paragraphs: Two models can represent the same examples in different spaces, making direct comparison challenging. This paper introduces Representation Topology Divergence, or RTD, to compare the multiscale topology of two representations. It treats each representation as a point cloud and measures differences in their structural organization across scales.

The method requires equal-sized point clouds with a one-to-one correspondence between points. This matches the setting where each example has one representation in each space. The ambient spaces themselves can differ, so the comparison does not require both representations to occupy the same surrounding coordinate space.

Experiments show agreement between RTD and intuitive judgments of representation similarity, as well as sensitivity to fine topological structure. The authors use it to investigate training dynamics, distribution shift, transfer learning, ensembles, and disentanglement in vision and natural language processing. Its contribution is a practical topological perspective on representation comparison across these problems. RTD measures a particular structural aspect of similarity, consistent with the paper’s recognition that comparing representations is a problem with multiple aspects.
summary.tldr: RTD compares the multiscale topology of corresponding data representations, even when they occupy different ambient spaces.

title: Representation Topology Divergence: A Method for Comparing Neural Network Representations.

abstract: Adaptive defenses, which optimize at test time, promise to improve adversarial robustness. We categorize such adaptive test-time defenses, explain their potential benefits and drawbacks, and evaluate a representative variety of the latest adaptive defenses for image classification. Unfortunately, none significantly improve upon static defenses when subjected to our careful case study evaluation. Some even weaken the underlying static model while simultaneously increasing inference computation. While these results are disappointing, we still believe that adaptive test-time defenses are a promising avenue of research and, as such, we provide recommendations for their thorough evaluation. We extend the checklist of Carlini et al. (2019) by providing concrete steps specific to adaptive defenses.

paragraphs: Adaptive test-time defenses perform optimization when processing inputs, with the aim of improving resistance to adversarial manipulation. This paper examines whether that additional adaptation delivers stronger image classification defenses. It first categorizes these approaches and discusses the potential advantages and drawbacks of adapting during inference.

The authors then conduct careful case studies of a representative selection of recent adaptive defenses. None of the evaluated methods significantly improves on static defenses under their evaluation. Some reduce the robustness of the underlying static model while also requiring more computation at inference, so the additional optimization does not reliably translate into a security benefit in these cases.

The authors nevertheless regard adaptation at test time as a promising research direction. They contribute concrete recommendations for evaluating such methods, extending an existing adversarial-defense checklist with steps specific to adaptation. The paper’s message is grounded in the evaluated defenses: their results call for stronger assessment of claimed robustness gains while leaving open the development of more effective adaptive methods.
summary.tldr: Case studies find no significant robustness gains from the evaluated adaptive test-time defenses and motivate more targeted evaluation practices.

title: Evaluating the Adversarial Robustness of Adaptive Test-time Defenses

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) agents are often sensitive to visual changes that were unseen in their training environments. To address this problem, we leverage the sequential nature of RL to learn robust representations that encode only task-relevant information from observations based on the unsupervised multi-view setting. Specif- ically, we introduce a novel contrastive version of the Multi-View Information Bottleneck (MIB) objective for temporal data. We train RL agents from pixels with this auxiliary objective to learn robust representations that can compress away task-irrelevant information and are predictive of task-relevant dynamics. This approach enables us to train high-performance policies that are robust to visual distractions and can generalize well to unseen environments. We demonstrate that our approach can achieve SOTA performance on a di- verse set of visual control tasks in the DeepMind Control Suite when the background is replaced with natural videos. In addition, we show that our approach outperforms well-established base- lines for generalization to unseen environments on the Procgen benchmark. Our code is open- sourced and available at https://github. com/BU-DEPEND-Lab/DRIBO.

We train RL agents from pixels with this auxiliary objective to learn robust representations that can compress away task-irrelevant information and are predictive of task-relevant dynamics. paragraphs: An agent learning from pixels can become sensitive to visual details that change outside its training environment. DRIBO addresses this by teaching the agent to represent information relevant to its task while compressing away distractions. The approach uses the sequential character of reinforcement learning to connect useful representations with task-relevant dynamics.

The authors introduce a contrastive version of the multi-view information bottleneck objective for temporal data. This becomes an auxiliary training objective alongside reinforcement learning. Its purpose is to encourage representations that retain predictive information about the task while reducing irrelevant visual information, using an unsupervised multi-view setting.

The paper demonstrates strong performance under two forms of visual variation. On DeepMind Control Suite tasks with backgrounds replaced by natural videos, DRIBO can achieve state-of-the-art performance. On Procgen, it outperforms established baselines when generalizing to unseen environments. These findings support the use of temporally informed representation learning for policies that must function despite distracting or unfamiliar visuals, within the control and generalization settings evaluated.
summary.tldr: DRIBO adds a temporal multi-view information bottleneck objective to help pixel-based reinforcement learning resist distractions and generalize to unseen environments.

title: DRIBO: Robust Deep Reinforcement Learning via Multi-View Information Bottleneck

abstract: Weight norm $\|w\|$ and margin $\gamma$ participate in learning theory via the normalized margin $\gamma/\|w\|$. Since standard neural net optimizers do not control normalized margin, it is hard to test whether this quantity causally relates to generalization. This paper designs a series of experimental studies that explicitly control normalized margin and thereby tackle two central questions. First: does normalized margin always have a causal effect on generalization? The paper finds that no—networks can be produced where normalized margin has seemingly no relationship with generalization, counter to the theory of Bartlett et al. (2017). Second: does normalized margin ever have a causal effect on generalization? The paper finds that yes—in a standard training setup, test performance closely tracks normalized margin. The paper suggests a Gaussian process model as a promising explanation for this behavior.

paragraphs: Learning theory uses normalized margin, the margin divided by the weight norm, to study generalization. Ordinary neural-network optimizers do not directly control this quantity, which makes its causal role difficult to investigate. This paper designs experiments that explicitly manipulate normalized margin to examine when it influences performance on unseen data.

The first question is whether normalized margin always has a causal effect. The authors find that it does not: they can produce networks in which normalized margin appears unrelated to generalization. This finding challenges the theoretical account discussed in the paper and shows why a universal interpretation of the quantity would be too strong.

The second question is whether normalized margin can have a causal effect at all. In a standard training setup, test performance closely tracks it, giving a positive answer in that setting. The authors suggest a Gaussian process model as a promising explanation. Together, the experiments identify a context-dependent relationship: normalized margin can be informative and influential without serving as a universal account of generalization.
summary.tldr: Experiments controlling normalized margin find that it can influence generalization in standard training but does not do so universally.

title: Investigating Generalization by Controlling Normalized Margin

abstract: In this work, we study the use of the Bellman equation as a surrogate objective for value prediction accuracy. While the Bellman equation is uniquely solved by the true value function over all state-action pairs, we find that the Bellman error (the difference between both sides of the equation) is a poor proxy for the accuracy of the value function. In particular, we show that (1) due to cancellations from both sides of the Bellman equation, the magnitude of the Bellman error is only weakly related to the distance to the true value function, even when considering all state-action pairs, and (2) in the finite data regime, the Bellman equation can be satisfied exactly by infinitely many suboptimal solutions. This means that the Bellman error can be minimized without improving the accuracy of the value function. We demonstrate these phenomena through a series of propositions, illustrative toy examples, and empirical analysis in standard benchmark domains.

paragraphs: The Bellman equation is fundamental to value prediction in reinforcement learning: over all state-action pairs, its unique solution is the true value function. This paper asks whether the size of a prediction’s Bellman error is therefore a reliable measure of value accuracy. It shows that the connection is much weaker than that reasoning suggests.

The first issue is cancellation between the two sides of the equation. Such cancellation can make the residual poorly reflect distance from the true value function, even when every state-action pair is considered. The second issue arises with finite data: infinitely many suboptimal value functions can satisfy the observed Bellman equations exactly.

Consequently, reducing Bellman error need not improve value prediction accuracy. The authors support these findings with propositions, small illustrative examples, and empirical analysis on standard benchmarks. The distinction is between uniquely solving the full equation and using its residual as a practical optimization target. The former property does not make the latter a dependable measure of prediction quality.
summary.tldr: Bellman error can shrink without improving value accuracy because of residual cancellations and non-unique solutions with finite data.

title: Why Should I Trust You, Bellman? The Bellman Error is a Poor Replacement for Value Error

abstract: A major challenge in studying robustness in deep learning is defining the set of “meaningless” perturbations to which a given Neural Network (NN) should be invariant. Most work on robustness implicitly uses a human as the reference model to define such perturbations. Our work offers a new view on robustness by using another reference NN to define the set of perturbations a given NN should be invariant to, thus generalizing the reliance on a reference “human NN” to any NN. This makes measuring robustness equivalent to measuring the extent to which two NNs share invariances. We propose a measure called \stir, which faithfully captures the extent to which two NNs share invariances. \stir re-purposes existing representation similarity measures to make them suitable for measuring shared invariances. Using our measure, we are able to gain insights about how shared invariances vary with changes in weight initialization, architecture, loss functions, and training dataset. Our implementation is available at: \url{https://github.com/nvedant07/STIR}.

paragraphs: A robustness measurement needs a definition of which input changes should leave a model unaffected. Such definitions commonly rely on human judgments about what counts as a meaningless change. This paper proposes using another neural network as the reference, making robustness a question about how much two networks agree on what can change without mattering.

The resulting measure, STIR, captures shared invariances between networks. An invariance describes a change to which a network is insensitive. STIR adapts existing measures of representation similarity so they can assess this property. Its focus is therefore on agreement about tolerated changes, giving the choice of reference network an explicit role in the assessment.

The authors use STIR to study how shared invariances vary with weight initialization, architecture, loss function, and training dataset. This supplies a framework for investigating which design and training choices influence representational robustness relative to another model. The contribution broadens the reference used to define robustness and provides a measurement tool for examining the resulting relationships between networks.
summary.tldr: STIR measures representational robustness through the input invariances shared by a network and a chosen reference network.

title: Measuring Representational Robustness of Neural Networks Through Shared Invariances

abstract: Hidden Networks (Ramanujan et al., 2020) showed the possibility of finding accurate subnetworks within a randomly weighted neural network by training a connectivity mask, referred to as supermask. We show that the supermask stops improving even though gradients are not zero, thus underutilizing backpropagated information. To address this we propose a method that extends Hidden Networks by training an overlay of multiple hierarchical supermasks{—}a multicoated supermask. This method shows that using multiple supermasks for a single task achieves higher accuracy without additional training cost. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show that Multicoated Supermasks enhance the tradeoff between accuracy and model size. A ResNet-101 using a 7-coated supermask outperforms its Hidden Networks counterpart by 4%, matching the accuracy of a dense ResNet-50 while being an order of magnitude smaller.

paragraphs: Hidden Networks find useful subnetworks inside a randomly weighted neural network by learning which connections to retain. The learned connectivity pattern is called a supermask. This paper identifies a training problem: the supermask can stop improving even when gradients remain nonzero, leaving available learning information underused.

The proposed solution overlays multiple hierarchical supermasks for the same task, producing a multicoated supermask. This extends the connectivity representation available to the method. The authors report that using several masks increases accuracy without additional training cost, addressing the observed stagnation while retaining the hidden-network approach.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet show a better balance between accuracy and model size. In the highlighted result, a ResNet-101 with seven coats outperforms its Hidden Networks counterpart by a reported 4%. It also matches the accuracy of a dense ResNet-50 while being an order of magnitude smaller. These findings show that a richer mask structure can improve the usefulness of subnetworks found within random weights.
summary.tldr: Layering hierarchical supermasks improves the reported accuracy–size tradeoff of subnetworks selected from randomly weighted networks.

title: Multicoated Supermasks Enhance Hidden Networks

abstract: Studying the dynamics of open quantum systems can enable breakthroughs both in fundamental physics and applications to quantum engineering and quantum computation. Since the density matrix $\rho$, which is the fundamental description for the dynamics of such systems, is high-dimensional, customized deep generative neural networks have been instrumental in modeling $\rho$. However, the complex-valued nature and normalization constraints of $\rho$, as well as its complicated dynamics, prohibit a seamless connection between open quantum systems and the recent advances in deep generative modeling. Here we lift that limitation by utilizing a reformulation of open quantum system dynamics to a partial differential equation (PDE) for a corresponding probability distribution $Q$, the Husimi Q function. Thus, we model the Q function seamlessly with off-the-shelf deep generative models such as normalizing flows. Additionally, we develop novel methods for learning normalizing flow evolution governed by high-dimensional PDEs based on the Euler method and the application of the time-dependent variational principle. We name the resulting approach Q-Flow and demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of Q-Flow on open quantum system simulations, including the dissipative harmonic oscillator and the dissipative bosonic model. Q-Flow is superior to conventional PDE solvers and state-of-the-art physics-informed neural network solvers, especially in high-dimensional systems.

paragraphs: Open quantum systems are commonly described using a density matrix, whose high dimensionality, complex values, normalization constraints, and dynamics complicate generative modeling. Q-Flow changes the representation of the problem so that standard deep generative models can be used more directly to study its evolution.

The contribution combines a probabilistic reformulation of quantum dynamics with techniques for evolving a generative model, connecting tools for probability distributions to a demanding class of physical simulations.
summary.tldr: Q-Flow represents open quantum dynamics through probability distributions modeled by normalizing flows, improving the reported high-dimensional simulations.

title: Q-Flow: Generative Modeling for Differential Equations of Open Quantum Dynamics with Normalizing Flows

abstract: Nearly all practical neural models for classification are trained using the cross-entropy loss. Yet this ubiquitous choice is supported by little theoretical or empirical evidence. Recent work (Hui & Belkin, 2020) suggests that training using the (rescaled) square loss is often superior in terms of the classification accuracy. In this paper we propose the "squentropy" loss, which is the sum of two terms: the cross-entropy loss and the average square loss over the incorrect classes. We provide an extensive set of experiment on multi-class classification problems showing that the squentropy loss outperforms both the pure cross-entropy and rescaled square losses in terms of the classification accuracy. We also demonstrate that it provides significantly better model calibration than either of these alternative losses and, furthermore, has less variance with respect to the random initialization. Additionally, in contrast to the square loss, squentropy loss can frequently be trained using exactly the same optimization parameters, including the learning rate, as the standard cross-entropy loss, making it a true ”plug-and-play” replacement. Finally, unlike the rescaled square loss, multiclass squentropy contains no parameters that need to be adjusted.

paragraphs: The loss function tells a classifier how to evaluate its mistakes during training. Cross-entropy is the usual choice, but this paper investigates whether combining it with a square-loss component improves results. The proposed loss, called squentropy, adds cross-entropy to the average square loss over the incorrect classes.

This construction retains the familiar classification objective while also penalizing scores assigned to wrong classes through the additional term. In extensive multiclass experiments, squentropy achieves better classification accuracy than either cross-entropy alone or a rescaled square loss. The authors also report better calibration, meaning that confidence estimates better reflect prediction correctness, and lower variation across random initializations.

The practical appeal is that multiclass squentropy introduces no extra parameters requiring adjustment. It can also frequently use the same optimization settings, including learning rate, as cross-entropy. That makes it a potentially convenient replacement within an existing training setup. The evidence supports improvements across the reported experiments, while the ability to reuse training settings is explicitly frequent rather than guaranteed for every model.
summary.tldr: Squentropy combines cross-entropy with a penalty on incorrect classes, improving accuracy, calibration, and initialization stability in reported experiments.

title: Cut your Losses with Squentropy

abstract: Score-based generative models (SGMs) learn a family of noise-conditional score functions corresponding to the data density perturbed with increasingly large amounts of noise. These perturbed data densities are linked together by the Fokker-Planck equation (FPE), a partial differential equation (PDE) governing the spatial-temporal evolution of a density undergoing a diffusion process. In this work, we derive a corresponding equation called the score FPE that characterizes the noise-conditional scores of the perturbed data densities (i.e., their gradients). Surprisingly, despite the impressive empirical performance, we observe that scores learned through denoising score matching (DSM) fail to fulfill the underlying score FPE, which is an inherent self-consistency property of the ground truth score. We prove that satisfying the score FPE is desirable as it improves the likelihood and the degree of conservativity. Hence, we propose to regularize the DSM objective to enforce satisfaction of the score FPE, and we show the effectiveness of this approach across various datasets.

paragraphs: Score-based generative models learn functions describing data distributions at different noise levels. These distributions are connected by the Fokker-Planck equation, which describes how a density evolves during diffusion. The paper asks whether the learned score functions respect the corresponding relationship across noise levels.

The authors derive a score version of the Fokker-Planck equation. It expresses a self-consistency property that the true scores satisfy. They observe that scores learned through denoising score matching can fail to satisfy this equation despite strong empirical performance. This identifies a mathematical relationship that the usual training objective does not reliably enforce.

The paper proves that satisfying the score equation improves likelihood and the degree of conservativity, a property concerning consistency with a gradient field. It then adds a regularization term to denoising score matching to encourage that consistency. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution ties an additional training constraint directly to the diffusion process underlying the model, giving the regularizer a theoretical motivation alongside empirical support.
summary.tldr: FP-Diffusion improves score-based models by regularizing their learned scores to satisfy the diffusion process's underlying consistency equation.

title: FP-Diffusion: Improving Score-based Diffusion Models by Enforcing the Underlying Score Fokker-Planck Equation

abstract: Unsupervised denoising is a crucial challenge in real-world imaging applications. Unsupervised deep-learning methods have demonstrated impressive performance on benchmarks based on synthetic noise. However, no metrics exist to evaluate these methods in an unsupervised fashion. This is highly problematic for the many practical applications where ground-truth clean images are not available. In this work, we propose two novel metrics: the unsupervised mean squared error (MSE) and the unsupervised peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), which are computed using only noisy data. We provide a theoretical analysis of these metrics, showing that they are asymptotically consistent estimators of the supervised MSE and PSNR. Controlled numerical experiments with synthetic noise confirm that they provide accurate approximations in practice. We validate our approach on real-world data from two imaging modalities: videos in raw format and transmission electron microscopy. Our results demonstrate that the proposed metrics enable unsupervised evaluation of denoising methods based exclusively on noisy data.

paragraphs: Denoising methods can be trained without clean reference images, yet evaluating them often still depends on having those references. This creates a practical mismatch: strong performance on synthetic-noise benchmarks does not supply a way to assess a method where only noisy observations exist. The paper addresses this evaluation problem directly.

The authors introduce unsupervised versions of mean squared error and peak signal-to-noise ratio that use noisy data alone. Their theoretical analysis establishes asymptotic consistency: the proposed quantities approach their supervised counterparts in the relevant large-sample limit. This supports their use as estimators of familiar quality measures, rather than treating them as unrelated proxies.

Controlled experiments with synthetic noise show accurate approximations in practice. The authors also validate the approach on raw-format video and transmission electron microscopy data, covering two real imaging modalities. The stated result is that denoising methods can be evaluated using exclusively noisy observations. The asymptotic guarantee and empirical checks play complementary roles: one establishes limiting behavior, while the other demonstrates usefulness in the examined finite-data settings.
summary.tldr: Two noisy-data-only metrics estimate conventional denoising quality measures, with asymptotic guarantees and validation on synthetic and real imaging data.

title: Evaluating Unsupervised Denoising Requires Unsupervised Metrics

abstract: We introduce a multi-fidelity estimator of covariance matrices that employs the log-Euclidean geometry of the symmetric positive-definite manifold. The estimator fuses samples from a hierarchy of data sources of differing fidelities and costs for variance reduction while guaranteeing definiteness, in contrast with previous approaches. The new estimator makes covariance estimation tractable in applications where simulation or data collection is expensive; to that end, we develop an optimal sample allocation scheme that minimizes the mean-squared error of the estimator given a fixed budget. Guaranteed definiteness is crucial to metric learning, data assimilation, and other downstream tasks. Evaluations of our approach using data from physical applications (heat conduction, fluid dynamics) demonstrate more accurate metric learning and speedups of more than one order of magnitude compared to benchmarks.

paragraphs: Estimating covariance matrices can be expensive when each sample requires a costly simulation or measurement. This paper combines data sources with different costs and levels of fidelity, using their shared information to reduce estimation variance. Its central concern is to gain that efficiency while preserving positive definiteness, a structural property needed by downstream methods.

The proposed estimator works with the log-Euclidean geometry of symmetric positive-definite matrices. This geometric formulation guarantees definiteness when combining information across the hierarchy of sources, addressing a weakness of previous approaches. The authors also develop an optimal allocation of samples across sources to minimize mean squared error under a fixed budget.

Evaluations use physical application data from heat conduction and fluid dynamics. The reported outcomes include more accurate metric learning and speedups exceeding an order of magnitude relative to the benchmarks. These findings connect the estimator’s mathematical structure to practical value: cheaper sources can help reduce sampling costs while the resulting covariance estimate retains a property crucial for metric learning, data assimilation, and related tasks.
summary.tldr: A geometry-aware covariance estimator combines sources of different costs while guaranteeing positive definiteness and optimally allocating a fixed sampling budget.

title: Multi-Fidelity Covariance Estimation in the Log-Euclidean Geometry

abstract: We study monotone variational inequalities that can arise as optimality conditions for constrained convex optimization or convex-concave minimax problems and propose a novel algorithm that uses only one gradient/operator evaluation and one projection onto the constraint set per iteration. The algorithm, which we call fOGDA-VI, achieves a $o(\frac{1}{k})$ rate of convergence in terms of the restricted gap function as well as the natural residual for the last iterate. Moreover, we provide a convergence guarantee for the sequence of iterates to a solution of the variational inequality. These are the best theoretical convergence results for numerical methods for (only) monotone variational inequalities reported in the literature. To empirically validate our algorithm we investigate a two-player matrix game with mixed strategies of the two players. Concluding, we show promising results regarding the application of fOGDA-VI to the training of generative adversarial nets.

paragraphs: The paper studies monotone variational inequalities, a mathematical framework that can describe solutions to constrained convex optimization and convex-concave minimax problems. These problems include situations where competing objectives must reach an equilibrium. The authors propose fOGDA-VI, an algorithm that requires just one gradient or operator evaluation and one projection back onto the permitted set at each iteration.

Its main contribution is a convergence guarantee for the last iterate: the actual current solution estimate, rather than an average of previous estimates. Two measures of solution error, the restricted gap and natural residual, decrease at a rate of o(1/k). The paper also proves that the sequence of estimates converges to a solution.

Together, these results combine inexpensive iterations with strong theoretical progress guarantees under monotonicity. The authors describe them as the strongest reported guarantees for this setting. They evaluate the method on a two-player matrix game and report promising results for training generative adversarial networks; that application is presented as empirical evidence rather than an extension of the stated theoretical guarantees.
summary.tldr: fOGDA-VI combines inexpensive updates with strong last-iterate convergence guarantees for monotone variational inequalities.

title: A Fast Optimistic Method for Monotone Variational Inequalities

abstract: This paper proposes a payoff perturbation technique for the Mirror Descent (MD) algorithm in games where the gradient of the payoff functions is monotone in the strategy profile space, potentially containing additive noise. The optimistic family of learning algorithms, exemplified by optimistic MD, successfully achieves last-iterate convergence in scenarios devoid of noise, leading the dynamics to a Nash equilibrium. A recent re-emerging trend underscores the promise of the perturbation approach, where payoff functions are perturbed based on the distance from an anchoring, or slingshot, strategy. In response, we propose Adaptively Perturbed MD (APMD), which adjusts the magnitude of the perturbation by repeatedly updating the slingshot strategy at a predefined interval. This innovation empowers us to find a Nash equilibrium of the underlying game with guaranteed rates. Empirical demonstrations affirm that our algorithm exhibits significantly accelerated convergence.

paragraphs: Learning in a game involves changing strategies in response to payoffs while other players also change theirs. This paper considers games whose payoff gradients are monotone over the strategy space, with the possibility of additive noise. The aim is to find a Nash equilibrium. The abstract contrasts this setting with noiseless cases where optimistic mirror descent achieves convergence of the latest strategy iterate.

The proposed method modifies mirror descent by perturbing payoffs according to distance from an anchor strategy, called the slingshot strategy. Adaptively Perturbed Mirror Descent repeatedly updates that anchor at a predefined interval. Updating the reference strategy adjusts the magnitude of the perturbation as learning proceeds.

The authors establish guaranteed rates for finding an equilibrium in the studied setting and report significantly faster convergence in empirical demonstrations. The contribution is an adaptive use of payoff perturbations within mirror descent, with both theoretical and experimental support. The equilibrium guarantees are tied to the paper’s monotone-game setting rather than stated for arbitrary strategic interactions.
summary.tldr: Updating an anchor strategy lets perturbed mirror descent find equilibria at guaranteed rates in the studied monotone games.

title: Adaptively Perturbed Mirror Descent for Learning in Games

abstract: Many recent prompting strategies for large language models (LLMs) query the model multiple times sequentially – first to produce intermediate results and then the final answer. However, using these methods, both decoder and model are unaware of potential follow-up prompts, leading to disconnected and undesirably wordy intermediate responses. In this work, we address this issue by proposing prompt sketching, a new prompting paradigm in which an LLM does not only respond by completing a prompt, but by predicting values for multiple variables in a template. This way, sketching grants users more control over the generation process, e.g., by providing a reasoning framework via intermediate instructions, leading to better overall results. The key idea enabling sketching with existing, autoregressive models is to adapt the decoding procedure to also score follow-up instructions during text generation, thus optimizing overall template likelihood in inference. Our experiments show that in a zero-shot setting, prompt sketching outperforms existing, sequential prompting schemes such as direct asking or chain-of-thought on 7 out of 8 LLM benchmarking tasks, including state tracking, arithmetic reasoning, and general question answering. To facilitate future use, we release a number of generic, yet effective sketches applicable to many tasks, and an open source library called dclib, powering our sketch-aware decoders as part of https://github.com/eth-sri/lmql.

paragraphs: Many prompting workflows ask a language model for intermediate results before requesting a final answer. When generating each intermediate response, the model and decoder do not account for later prompts. The paper identifies this disconnect as a cause of unnecessarily wordy and poorly connected intermediate text.

Prompt sketching instead asks the model to fill multiple variables within a template. Instructions between those variables can provide a reasoning framework and give users more control over generation. To make this work with existing autoregressive models, the authors modify decoding so that it also scores follow-up instructions, optimizing the likelihood of the overall template during inference.

In zero-shot experiments, prompt sketching outperforms existing prompting schemes, including direct asking and chain-of-thought, on seven of eight evaluated tasks. These include state tracking, arithmetic reasoning, and general question answering. The result supports considering later instructions while generating earlier template values. The authors also release reusable sketches and an open-source library implementing the sketch-aware decoders.
summary.tldr: Prompt sketching makes decoding account for follow-up instructions while filling a template, outperforming compared prompting schemes on seven of eight tasks.

title: Prompt Sketching for Large Language Models

abstract: The growing richness of large-scale datasets has been crucial in driving the rapid advancement and wide adoption of machine learning technologies. The massive collection and usage of data, however, pose an increasing risk for people’s private and sensitive information due to either inadvertent mishandling or malicious exploitation. Besides legislative solutions, many technical approaches have been proposed towards data privacy protection. However, they bear various limitations such as leading to degraded data availability and utility, or relying on heuristics and lacking solid theoretical bases. To overcome these limitations, we propose a formal information-theoretic definition for this utility-preserving privacy protection problem, and design a data-driven learnable data transformation framework that is capable of selectively suppressing sensitive attributes from target datasets while preserving the other useful attributes, regardless of whether or not they are known in advance or explicitly annotated for preservation. We provide rigorous theoretical analyses on the operational bounds for our framework, and carry out comprehensive experimental evaluations using datasets of a variety of modalities, including facial images, voice audio clips, and human activity motion sensor signals. Results demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our method under various configurations on a multitude of tasks. Our source code is available at this URL.
originalAbstract: The growing richness of large-scale datasets has been crucial in driving the rapid advancement and wide adoption of machine learning technologies. The massive collection and usage of data, however, pose an increasing risk for people’s private and sensitive information due to either inadvertent mishandling or malicious exploitation. Besides legislative solutions, many technical approaches have been proposed towards data privacy protection. However, they bear various limitations such as leading to degraded data availability and utility, or relying on heuristics and lacking solid theoretical bases. To overcome these limitations, we propose a formal information-theoretic definition for this utility-preserving privacy protection problem, and design a data-driven learnable data transformation framework that is capable of selectively suppressing sensitive attributes from target datasets while preserving the other useful attributes, regardless of whether or not they are known in advance or explicitly annotated for preservation. We provide rigorous theoretical analyses on the operational bounds for our framework, and carry out comprehensive experimental evaluations using datasets of a variety of modalities, including facial images, voice audio clips, and human activity motion sensor signals. Results demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our method under various configurations on a multitude of tasks. Our source code is available at this URL.

paragraphs: Rich datasets can support useful machine learning while also exposing sensitive information about people. Removing sensitive information can damage other useful properties, and heuristic transformations may provide little theoretical guidance about that tradeoff. MaSS formulates the problem in information-theoretic terms and develops a learned transformation designed to suppress selected sensitive attributes.

The framework aims to retain other useful attributes even when those attributes were not specified or explicitly labeled for preservation. This matters because a dataset’s future uses need not be fully known when privacy protection is applied. The objective is selective suppression: reducing designated sensitive information while keeping the transformed data useful more broadly.

The authors analyze the framework’s operational bounds and evaluate it across facial images, voice recordings, and human-activity motion sensor signals. They report effectiveness and generalizability across multiple tasks and configurations. The work combines a formal account of the suppression-and-utility problem with evidence across different data types, supporting a learned approach to preserving utility beyond a predefined list of retained attributes.
summary.tldr: MaSS learns to suppress selected sensitive attributes while preserving useful information, including attributes not explicitly designated for retention.

title: MaSS: Multi-attribute Selective Suppression for Utility-preserving Data Transformation from an Information-theoretic Perspective

abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion models achieve state-of-the-art results in image synthesis and editing. However, leveraging such pre-trained models for video editing is considered a major challenge. Many existing works attempt to enforce temporal consistency in the edited video through explicit correspondence mechanisms, either in pixel space or between deep features. These methods, however, struggle with strong nonrigid motion. In this paper, we introduce a fundamentally different approach, which is based on the observation that spatiotemporal slices of natural videos exhibit similar characteristics to natural images. Thus, the same T2I diffusion model that is normally used only as a prior on video frames, can also serve as a strong prior for enhancing temporal consistency by applying it on spatiotemporal slices. Based on this observation, we present Slicedit, a method for text-based video editing that utilizes a pre-trained T2I diffusion model to process both spatial and spatiotemporal slices. Our method generates videos that retain the structure and motion of the original video while adhering to the target text. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate Slicedit’s ability to edit a wide range of real-world videos, confirming its clear advantages compared to existing baselines.

paragraphs: Editing video with a pretrained image diffusion model requires maintaining consistency as the scene changes over time. Many methods explicitly match pixels or features between frames, but strong nonrigid motion makes those correspondences difficult. Slicedit approaches the problem using the visual structure found in slices through space and time.

A text-to-image model can therefore act as a prior on those slices as well as on ordinary video frames. Slicedit processes both spatial and spatiotemporal slices, using the same kind of image model to support appearance editing and temporal consistency.

The method produces text-guided edits while retaining the original video’s structure and motion. Extensive experiments across real-world videos show advantages over existing baselines in the reported evaluations. The contribution demonstrates a way to reuse pretrained image-generation capabilities across a video’s time dimension, making the representation of the video itself central to preserving consistency during editing.
summary.tldr: Slicedit applies an image diffusion model to video frames and spatiotemporal slices to produce text-guided edits with consistent motion.

title: Slicedit: Zero-Shot Video Editing With Text-to-Image Diffusion Models Using Spatio-Temporal Slices

abstract: We introduce MOMENT, a family of open-source foundation models for general-purpose time series analysis. Pre-training large models on time series data is challenging due to (1) the absence of a large and cohesive public time series repository, and (2) diverse time series characteristics which make multi-dataset training onerous. Additionally, (3) experimental benchmarks to evaluate these models, especially in scenarios with limited resources, time, and supervision, are still in their nascent stages. To address these challenges, we compile a large and diverse collection of public time series, called the Time series Pile, and systematically tackle time series-specific challenges to unlock large-scale multi-dataset pre-training. Finally, we build on recent work to design a benchmark to evaluate time series foundation models on diverse tasks and datasets in limited supervision settings. Experiments on this benchmark demonstrate the effectiveness of our pre-trained models with minimal data and task-specific fine-tuning. Finally, we present several interesting empirical observations about large pre-trained time series models. Pre-trained models (AutonLab/MOMENT-1-large) and Time Series Pile (AutonLab/Timeseries-PILE) are available on Huggingface.

paragraphs: MOMENT is a family of open models intended for general-purpose time-series analysis. The paper addresses the infrastructure and learning challenges behind that goal: public datasets are fragmented, time series have diverse characteristics, and evaluation for settings with little supervision is still developing. These obstacles affect both pretraining and assessment.

The authors compile public datasets into a large, varied collection called the Time Series Pile. They also systematically address time-series-specific difficulties in training across datasets. Alongside the models and data collection, they develop a benchmark covering different tasks and datasets under limited supervision.

Experiments on that benchmark show that the pretrained models are effective with little data and limited task-specific fine-tuning. The contribution therefore combines reusable models with the data and evaluation framework needed to study them. This makes the paper relevant to whether shared pretraining can support varied time-series applications without requiring substantial labeled data or extensive adaptation for each individual task.
summary.tldr: MOMENT provides open time-series foundation models, a diverse pretraining collection, and evidence of effectiveness under limited supervision.

title: MOMENT: A Family of Open Time-series Foundation Models

abstract: Estimating the ratio of two probability densities from finitely many samples, is a central task in machine learning and statistics. In this work, we show that a large class of kernel methods for density ratio estimation suffers from error saturation, which prevents algorithms from achieving fast error convergence rates on highly regular learning problems. To resolve saturation, we introduce iterated regularization in density ratio estimation to achieve fast error rates. Our methods outperform its non-iteratively regularized versions on benchmarks for density ratio estimation as well as on large-scale evaluations for importance-weighted ensembling of deep unsupervised domain adaptation models.

paragraphs: Density-ratio estimation uses samples to estimate how two probability distributions differ at a given point. This paper identifies a limitation in a broad class of kernel-based estimators: their error convergence can saturate. On highly regular problems, that saturation prevents the methods from achieving the faster error rates the problem structure could otherwise support.

The proposed remedy is iterated regularization. The authors introduce it into density-ratio estimation to overcome the saturation effect and obtain fast error rates. The contribution therefore concerns how an estimator benefits from favorable problem structure, rather than only whether it can produce a usable ratio estimate.

Experiments compare the proposed methods with their counterparts using non-iterative regularization. The iterated versions perform better on density-ratio benchmarks and in large-scale evaluations of importance-weighted ensembles of deep unsupervised domain adaptation models. These evaluations connect the estimation result to a downstream use of density ratios. Together, the findings support repeated regularization as a way to address a specific convergence bottleneck with practical consequences.
summary.tldr: Iterated regularization overcomes error-rate saturation in kernel density-ratio estimation and improves the reported estimation and domain-adaptation results.

title: Overcoming Saturation in Density Ratio Estimation by Iterated Regularization

abstract: Variational inference (VI) is a popular approach in Bayesian inference, that looks for the best approximation of the posterior distribution within a parametric family, minimizing a loss that is (typically) the reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. Despite its empirical success, the theoretical properties of VI have only recently received attention, and is restricted to the Gaussian case. This research paper aims to contribute to the theoretical study of VI in the non-Gaussian case by investigating the setting of Mixture of Gaussians with fixed covariance. In this view, VI over this specific family can be casted as the minimization of a Mollified relative entropy, i.e. the KL between the convolution (with respect to a Gaussian kernel) of an atomic measure supported on Diracs, where the support of the atomic measure correspond to the localization of the Gaussian components, and the target distribution. Hence, solving variational inference is equivalent to optimizing the positions of the Diracs (the particles), which can be done through gradient descent and takes the form of an interacting particle system. We study two sources of error in variational inference in this context. The first is an optimization result that is a descent lemma establishing that the algorithm decreases the objective at each iteration. The second is an approximation error that upper bounds the mollified relative entropy between an optimal finite mixture and the target distribution.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a Bayesian posterior by choosing a distribution from a manageable family. This paper studies mixtures of Gaussians with fixed covariance, extending theoretical analysis beyond a single Gaussian approximation. Holding covariance fixed focuses the optimization on where the Gaussian components are located.

The authors express the mixture as point masses smoothed by a Gaussian kernel. Its discrepancy from the target is measured by a mollified relative entropy, a Kullback-Leibler divergence involving that smoothed distribution. Optimizing the mixture then becomes a problem of moving particles representing component locations. Gradient descent on those positions takes the form of an interacting particle system.

The analysis separates optimization error from approximation error. A descent lemma establishes that each algorithm iteration decreases the objective. A second result upper-bounds the discrepancy between an optimal finite mixture and the target distribution. These address different questions: whether the algorithm makes progress and how closely the chosen mixture family can represent the target. Neither statement alone amounts to exact recovery of an arbitrary posterior.
summary.tldr: The paper gives objective-descent and approximation-error guarantees for variational inference with fixed-covariance Gaussian mixtures.

title: Theoretical Guarantees for Variational Inference with Fixed-Variance Mixture of Gaussians

abstract: Many machine learning problems can be seen as approximating a target distribution using a particle distribution by minimizing their statistical discrepancy. Wasserstein Gradient Flow can move particles along a path that minimizes the $f$-divergence between the target and particle distributions. To move particles, we need to calculate the corresponding velocity fields derived from a density ratio function between these two distributions. Previous works estimated such density ratio functions and then differentiated the estimated ratios. These approaches may suffer from overfitting, leading to a less accurate estimate of the velocity fields. Inspired by non-parametric curve fitting, we directly estimate these velocity fields using interpolation techniques. We prove that our estimators are consistent under mild conditions. We validate their effectiveness using novel applications on domain adaptation and missing data imputation. The code for reproducing our results can be found at https://github.com/anewgithubname/gradest2.

paragraphs: Many learning problems involve moving a collection of particles so that its distribution better matches a target distribution. Wasserstein gradient flow provides a way to move those particles while reducing an f-divergence, a measure of statistical discrepancy. Implementing that movement requires a velocity field specifying how the particles should change.

Earlier approaches estimate a density ratio between the particle and target distributions, then differentiate the estimate to obtain velocities. The paper identifies a possible weakness in this sequence: overfitting the ratio can make the resulting velocity estimates inaccurate. Drawing inspiration from nonparametric curve fitting, the authors instead estimate the velocity fields directly through interpolation.

The authors prove consistency of their estimators under mild conditions and demonstrate their effectiveness in domain adaptation and missing-data imputation. The theoretical claim is conditional on those conditions, while the applications establish empirical usefulness in the tested settings. The contribution targets the quantity needed to move particles directly, addressing a source of error in the intermediate ratio-estimation approach.
summary.tldr: Directly interpolating particle velocity fields offers a consistent, condition-dependent alternative to differentiating estimated density ratios.

title: Minimizing $f$-Divergences by Interpolating Velocity Fields

abstract: This work targets a novel text-driven whole-body motion generation task, which takes a given textual description as input and aims at generating high-quality, diverse, and coherent facial expressions, hand gestures, and body motions simultaneously. Previous works on text-driven motion generation tasks mainly have two limitations: they ignore the key role of fine-grained hand and face controlling in vivid whole-body motion generation, and lack a good alignment between text and motion. To address such limitations, we propose a Text-aligned whOle-body Motion generATiOn framework, named HumanTOMATO, which is the first attempt to our knowledge towards applicable holistic motion generation in this research area. To tackle this challenging task, our solution includes two key designs: (1) a Holistic Hierarchical VQ-VAE (aka H${}^{2}$VQ) and a Hierarchical-GPT for fine-grained body and hand motion reconstruction and generation with two structured codebooks; and (2) a pre-trained text-motion-alignment model to help generated motion align with the input textual description explicitly. Comprehensive experiments verify that our model has significant advantages in both the quality of generated motions and their alignment with text.
