paragraphs: HumanTOMATO tackles generating coordinated facial expressions, hand gestures, and body movement from a text description. The task aims for motions that are diverse, high quality, and coherent across the whole body. The paper identifies two shortcomings in earlier work: insufficient attention to fine hand and face control, and weak alignment between generated movement and the text.

The framework includes a hierarchical motion representation and generator. A Holistic Hierarchical VQ-VAE and a Hierarchical-GPT use two structured codebooks for detailed body and hand motion reconstruction and generation. This design provides an organized representation for those motion components, addressing the need for detail within a broader whole-body generation task.

A separate pretrained text-motion alignment model explicitly helps the generated movement match the description. The approach therefore addresses both how motion is represented and how its meaning connects to language. The reported experiments show significant advantages in motion quality and text alignment. These findings support the combined design for producing expressive whole-body movement that follows the supplied description.
summary.tldr: HumanTOMATO combines hierarchical motion modeling with explicit text-motion alignment to improve text-driven whole-body generation.

title: HumanTOMATO: Text-aligned Whole-body Motion Generation

abstract: Although neural networks have demonstrated significant success in various reinforcement-learning tasks, even the highest-performing deep models often fail to generalize. As an alternative, object-oriented approaches offer a promising path towards better efficiency and generalization; however, they typically address narrow problem classes and require extensive domain knowledge. To overcome these limitations, we introduce QORA, an algorithm that constructs models expressive enough to solve a variety of domains, including those with stochastic transition functions, directly from a domain-agnostic object-based state representation. We also provide a novel benchmark suite to evaluate learners’ generalization capabilities. In our test domains, QORA achieves 100% predictive accuracy using almost four orders of magnitude fewer observations than a neural-network baseline, demonstrates zero-shot transfer to modified environments, and adapts rapidly when applied to tasks involving previously unseen object interactions. Finally, we give examples of QORA’s learned rules, showing them to be easily interpretable.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning models can perform well in one environment yet struggle when that environment changes. Object-oriented methods offer a possible route to better transfer, but often require substantial domain knowledge or cover narrow settings. QORA learns an interpretable object-relational model directly from a domain-agnostic representation of states as objects.

The algorithm constructs models expressive enough to cover varied domains, including environments with stochastic transitions. The authors also introduce a benchmark suite for evaluating generalization. Their approach makes relationships and interactions among objects central to the learned model, and examples of its learned rules demonstrate that those rules are readily interpretable.

In the tested domains, QORA reaches 100% predictive accuracy with almost four orders of magnitude fewer observations than a neural-network baseline. It transfers to modified environments without additional training and adapts rapidly to tasks containing previously unseen object interactions. These are distinct capabilities: immediate transfer for the tested modifications and rapid learning for new interactions. The findings support the value of object-relational modeling within the evaluated domains.
summary.tldr: QORA learns interpretable object-relational models that achieve data-efficient prediction, zero-shot transfer, and rapid adaptation in its test domains.

title: QORA: Zero-Shot Transfer via Interpretable Object-Relational Model Learning

abstract: Imitation learning has emerged as a promising approach for addressing sequential decision-making problems, with the assumption that expert demonstrations are optimal. However, in real-world scenarios, most demonstrations are often imperfect, leading to challenges in the effectiveness of imitation learning. While existing research has focused on optimizing with imperfect demonstrations, the training typically requires a certain proportion of optimal demonstrations to guarantee performance. To tackle these problems, we propose to purify the potential noises in imperfect demonstrations first, and subsequently conduct imitation learning from these purified demonstrations. Motivated by the success of diffusion model, we introduce a two-step purification via diffusion process. In the first step, we apply a forward diffusion process to smooth potential noises in imperfect demonstrations by introducing additional noise. Subsequently, a reverse generative process is utilized to recover the optimal demonstration from the diffused ones. We provide theoretical evidence supporting our approach, demonstrating that the distance between the purified and optimal demonstration can be bounded. Empirical results on MuJoCo and RoboSuite demonstrate the effectiveness of our method from different aspects.

paragraphs: Imitation learning trains a decision-making system from demonstrations, but real demonstrations often contain imperfect behavior. The paper describes a difficulty with approaches that learn directly from such data: their performance guarantees typically depend on having some proportion of optimal examples. It investigates improving the demonstrations before using them for imitation learning.

The proposed purification procedure has two diffusion stages. A forward process adds noise, with the aim of smoothing the noise already present in imperfect demonstrations. A reverse generative process then reconstructs demonstrations from those diffused versions, seeking to recover optimal behavior. Imitation learning takes place after this purification step, so demonstration quality becomes an explicit target of the pipeline.

The theoretical analysis bounds the distance between purified and optimal demonstrations. That provides evidence for the approach without implying that purification always reconstructs an exactly optimal example. Experiments in MuJoCo and RoboSuite support its effectiveness from multiple perspectives. Together, the results motivate treating demonstration cleanup as a component of learning sequential behavior from imperfect examples.
summary.tldr: A diffusion-based purification step improves imperfect demonstrations before imitation learning, supported by a distance bound and experiments in MuJoCo and RoboSuite.

title: Imitation Learning from Purified Demonstrations

abstract: Commonly used image tokenizers produce a 2D grid of spatially arranged tokens. In contrast, so-called 1D image tokenizers represent images as highly compressed one-dimensional sequences of as few as 32 discrete tokens. We find that the high degree of compression achieved by a 1D tokenizer with vector quantization enables image editing and generative capabilities through heuristic manipulation of tokens, demonstrating that even very crude manipulations – such as copying and replacing tokens between latent representations of images – enable fine-grained image editing by transferring appearance and semantic attributes. Motivated by the expressivity of the 1D tokenizer’s latent space, we construct an image generation pipeline leveraging gradient-based test-time optimization of tokens with plug-and-play loss functions such as reconstruction or CLIP similarity. Our approach is demonstrated for inpainting and text-guided image editing use cases, and can generate diverse and realistic samples without requiring training of any generative model.

paragraphs: Image tokenizers often represent an image as a spatial grid of tokens. This paper studies highly compressed one-dimensional representations containing as few as 32 discrete tokens. It finds that the latent space of a tokenizer using vector quantization supports useful image manipulations, even through simple operations on these compact token sequences.

Copying and replacing tokens between image representations can transfer appearance and semantic attributes, enabling fine-grained editing. Building on that observation, the authors construct a generation pipeline that optimizes tokens at test time using gradients. Interchangeable objectives, including reconstruction and CLIP similarity, guide the optimization toward a desired output.

The approach is demonstrated for inpainting and text-guided image editing, producing diverse and realistic samples without training a generative model. The key distinction is that generation uses the expressive representation already provided by the tokenizer, together with token manipulation or test-time optimization. The findings show that a compressed image representation can support more than storage and reconstruction: it can also provide a workable space for controlled synthesis.
summary.tldr: A highly compressed image tokenizer supports editing and generation through token manipulation and test-time optimization without generative-model training.

title: Highly Compressed Tokenizer Can Generate Without Training

abstract: In traditional reinforcement learning (RL), the learner aims to solve a single objective optimization problem: find the policy that maximizes expected reward. However, in many real-world settings, it is important to optimize over multiple objectives simultaneously. For example, when we are interested in fairness, states might have feature annotations corresponding to multiple (intersecting) demographic groups to whom reward accrues, and our goal might be to maximize the reward of the group receiving the minimal reward. In this work, we consider a multi-objective optimization problem in which each objective is defined by a state-based reweighting of a single scalar reward function. This generalizes the problem of maximizing the reward of the minimum reward group. We provide oracle-efficient algorithms to solve these multi-objective RL problems even when the number of objectives is very large — for tabular MDPs, as well as for large MDPs when the group functions have additional structure. The contribution of this paper is that we are able to solve this class of multi-objective RL problems with a possibly exponentially large class of constraints over intersecting groups in both tabular and large state space MDPs in an oracle-efficient manner. Finally, we experimentally validate our theoretical results and demonstrate applications on a preferential attachment graph MDP.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning policy can maximize total reward while distributing its benefits unevenly across groups. This paper studies objectives that account for multiple, potentially overlapping groups. One motivating example is maximizing the reward received by the least-rewarded group, which makes the distribution of benefits part of the policy-learning problem.

The authors consider a broader formulation in which each objective reweights a single reward function according to the current state. They provide oracle-efficient algorithms that can handle very large collections of these objectives, including possibly exponentially many constraints over intersecting groups. Oracle efficiency describes the algorithms' use of specified subproblem-solving capabilities, rather than an unrestricted claim about every possible implementation.

The results cover tabular Markov decision processes and large state spaces when the group functions have additional structure. That structural qualification is central to the large-state-space result. Experiments validate the theoretical findings and illustrate applications on a preferential attachment graph environment. The contribution makes a large family of overlapping fairness objectives algorithmically tractable under the stated formulation and conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper provides oracle-efficient reinforcement-learning algorithms for possibly exponentially many intersecting-group objectives, with structural conditions for large state spaces.

title: Intersectional Fairness in Reinforcement Learning with Large State and Constraint Spaces

abstract: Deciphering protein folding and unfolding pathways under tension is essential for deepening our understanding of fundamental biological mechanisms. Such insights hold the promise of developing treatments for a range of debilitating and fatal conditions, including muscular disorders like Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy and neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s disease. Single molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS) is a powerful technique for investigating forces involved in protein domains folding and unfolding. However, SMFS trials often involve multiple protein molecules, necessitating filtering to isolate measurements from single-molecule trials. Currently, manual visual inspection is the primary method for classifying single-molecule data; a process that is both time-consuming and requires significant expertise. Here, we both apply state-of-the-art machine learning models and present a novel deep learning model tailored to SMFS data. The proposed model employs a dual-branch fusion strategy; one branch integrates the physics of protein molecules, and the other operates independently of physical constraints. This model automates the isolation of single-molecule measurements, significantly enhancing data processing efficiency. To train and validate our approach, we developed a physics-based Monte Carlo engine to simulate force spectroscopy datasets, including trials involving single molecules, multiple molecules, and no molecules. Our model achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming five baseline methods on both simulated and experimental datasets. It attains nearly 100% accuracy across all simulated datasets and an average accuracy of $79.6 \pm 5.2$% on experimental datasets, using only $\sim$30 training samples, surpassing baseline methods by 11.4%. Notably, even without expert annotations on experimental data, the model achieves an average accuracy of $72.0 \pm 5.9$% when pre-trained on corresponding simulated datasets. With our deep learning approach, the time required to extract meaningful statistics from single-molecule SMFS trials is reduced from a day to under an hour. This work results in SMFS experimental datasets from four important protein molecules crucial to many biological pathways. To support further research, we have made our datasets publicly available and provided a Python-based toolbox (https://github.com/SalapakaLab-SIMBioSys/SMFS-Identification).

title: A Physics-Augmented Deep Learning Framework for Classifying Single Molecule Force Spectroscopy Data

abstract: Current approaches for training Process Reward Models (PRMs) often involve deconposing responses into multiple reasoning steps using rule-based techniques, such as using predefined placeholder tokens or setting the reasoning step’s length to a fixed size. These approaches overlook the fact that certain words don’t usually indicate true decision points. To address this, we propose AdaptiveStep, a method that divides reasoning steps based on the model’s confidence in predicting the next word, offering more information on decision-making at each step, improving downstream tasks like reward model training. Moreover, our method requires no manual annotation. Experiments with AdaptiveStep-trained PRMs in mathematical reasoning and code generation show that the outcome PRM achieves state-of-the-art Best-of-N performance, surpassing greedy search strategy with token-level value-guided decoding, while also reducing construction costs by over 30% compared to existing open-source PRMs. We also provide a thorough analysis and case study on its performance, transferability, and generalization capabilities. We provide our code on https://github.com/Lux0926/ASPRM.

paragraphs: Process reward models evaluate intermediate reasoning steps, so their training depends on where a response is divided. Existing approaches often use fixed lengths or predefined markers. These boundaries can separate text without identifying a meaningful decision. AdaptiveStep instead uses the model’s confidence in predicting the next word to determine reasoning steps, aiming to make each segment more informative about the model’s decision-making.

This changes how training material is organized before the reward model learns from it. The method requires no manual annotation, making confidence a practical signal for automatically constructing step boundaries. Its central contribution is therefore a way to connect the segmentation of reasoning with the behavior of the model producing it.

In mathematical reasoning and code generation experiments, reward models trained with AdaptiveStep achieved state-of-the-art Best-of-N performance, which involves selecting among multiple candidate responses. They also surpassed the evaluated greedy search strategy using token-level value guidance. Construction costs fell by over 30% relative to existing open-source process reward models. These results support confidence-based segmentation as a useful component of reward-model training.
summary.tldr: AdaptiveStep uses next-word confidence to divide reasoning into steps, improving process reward models while lowering construction costs.

title: AdaptiveStep: Automatically Dividing Reasoning Step through Model Confidence

abstract: The accurate interpretation of Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals is pivotal for diagnosing cardiovascular diseases. Integrating ECG signals with accompanying textual reports further holds immense potential to enhance clinical diagnostics by combining physiological data and qualitative insights. However, this integration faces significant challenges due to inherent modality disparities and the scarcity of labeled data for robust cross-modal learning. To address these obstacles, we propose D-BETA, a novel framework that pre-trains ECG and text data using a contrastive masked auto-encoder architecture, uniquely combining generative and boosted discriminative capabilities for robust cross-modal representations. This is accomplished through masked modality modeling, specialized loss functions, and an improved negative sampling strategy tailored for cross-modal alignment. Extensive experiments on five public datasets across diverse downstream tasks demonstrate that D-BETA significantly outperforms existing methods, achieving an average AUC improvement of 15% in linear probing with only one percent of training data and 2% in zero-shot performance without requiring training data over state-of-the-art models. These results highlight the effectiveness of D-BETA, underscoring its potential to advance automated clinical diagnostics through multi-modal representations.

paragraphs: ECG signals describe physiological activity, while accompanying reports provide textual interpretations. Learning from both could strengthen automated ECG interpretation, but the two kinds of data differ substantially and labeled examples can be scarce. D-BETA addresses this problem by pretraining representations that connect ECG signals with text.

The framework combines a masked auto-encoder with contrastive learning. Masked modality modeling supplies a generative learning task, while the discriminative components help distinguish and align information across the two modalities. Specialized losses and an improved negative sampling strategy support this alignment. The combination aims to make the learned representations useful for downstream decisions as well as for the pretraining tasks.

Experiments cover five public datasets and several downstream tasks. The authors report an average AUC improvement of 15% in linear probing using only one percent of training data, and a 2% improvement in zero-shot performance over state-of-the-art models. These findings support the usefulness of joint ECG-text representations when downstream supervision is scarce or absent, while the clinical application remains a stated potential.
summary.tldr: D-BETA combines masked reconstruction and contrastive learning to improve ECG-text representations for low-data and zero-shot tasks.

title: Boosting Masked ECG-Text Auto-Encoders as Discriminative Learners

abstract: Non-autoregressive Transformers (NATs) have garnered significant attention due to their efficient decoding compared to autoregressive methods. However, existing conditional dependency modeling schemes based on masked language modeling introduce a training-inference gap in NATs. For instance, while NATs sample target words during training to enhance input, this condition cannot be met during inference, and simply annealing the sampling rate to zero during training leads to model performance degradation. We demonstrate that this training-inference gap prevents NATs from fully realizing their potential. To address this, we propose an adaptive end-to-end quantization alignment training framework, which introduces a semantic consistency space to adaptively align NAT training, eliminating the need for target information and thereby bridging the training-inference gap.Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms most existing fully NAT models, delivering performance on par with Autoregressive Transformer (AT) while being 17.0 times more efficient in inference.

paragraphs: Non-autoregressive translation models offer efficient decoding, but their training can give them information unavailable when translating new text. In the approaches examined here, training sometimes supplies sampled words from the correct translation. At inference, those target words are unknown. The paper identifies this mismatch as an obstacle to realizing the models’ full translation performance.

Simply reducing the frequency of supplied target words to zero during training does not solve the problem cleanly: the authors report that this degrades performance. They instead propose adaptive end-to-end quantization alignment, which introduces a space designed to maintain semantic consistency. Training is adaptively aligned in that space without requiring target information as an input aid, bringing training conditions closer to actual use.

In the reported experiments, the framework outperforms most existing fully non-autoregressive models. It also reaches performance comparable to an autoregressive Transformer while delivering 17.0 times greater inference efficiency. The result suggests that addressing the information mismatch can preserve the decoding advantages of non-autoregressive translation while substantially improving its quality.
summary.tldr: AEQA-NAT aligns translation training with inference conditions, achieving autoregressive-comparable performance with substantially more efficient inference in the reported experiments.

title: AEQA-NAT : Adaptive End-to-end Quantization Alignment Training Framework for Non-autoregressive Machine Translation

abstract: The general-utility Markov decision processes (GUMDPs) framework generalizes the MDPs framework by considering objective functions that depend on the frequency of visitation of state-action pairs induced by a given policy. In this work, we contribute with the first analysis on the impact of the number of trials, i.e., the number of randomly sampled trajectories, in infinite-horizon GUMDPs. We show that, as opposed to standard MDPs, the number of trials plays a key-role in infinite-horizon GUMDPs and the expected performance of a given policy depends, in general, on the number of trials. We consider both discounted and average GUMDPs, where the objective function depends, respectively, on discounted and average frequencies of visitation of state-action pairs. First, we study policy evaluation under discounted GUMDPs, proving lower and upper bounds on the mismatch between the finite and infinite trials formulations for GUMDPs. Second, we address average GUMDPs, studying how different classes of GUMDPs impact the mismatch between the finite and infinite trials formulations. Third, we provide a set of empirical results to support our claims, highlighting how the number of trajectories and the structure of the underlying GUMDP influence policy evaluation.

paragraphs: General-utility Markov decision processes evaluate policies through objectives that depend on how frequently state-action pairs are visited. This paper asks how policy evaluation changes when those frequencies come from a finite number of sampled trajectories. Even though each trajectory has an infinite horizon, the number of independently sampled trials can still matter.

The authors show that a policy’s expected performance generally depends on the number of trials, unlike in standard Markov decision processes. They analyze both discounted visitation frequencies and average visitation frequencies. This distinction separates two ways of summarizing behavior over time, each of which can interact differently with the general-utility objective.

For discounted problems, the paper proves upper and lower bounds on the mismatch between finite-trial and infinite-trial formulations. For average problems, it studies how different classes of general-utility processes affect that mismatch. Empirical results support the analysis and show how trajectory count and problem structure influence evaluation. The findings make trial count part of the policy-evaluation formulation itself.
summary.tldr: In infinite-horizon general-utility decision processes, a policy’s expected evaluation can depend on how many trajectories are sampled.

title: The Number of Trials Matters in Infinite-Horizon General-Utility Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Latent diffusion models have emerged as the leading approach for generating high-quality images and videos, utilizing compressed latent representations to reduce the computational burden of the diffusion process. While recent advancements have primarily focused on scaling diffusion backbones and improving autoencoder reconstruction quality, the interaction between these components has received comparatively less attention. In this work, we perform a spectral analysis of modern autoencoders and identify inordinate high-frequency components in their latent spaces, which are especially pronounced in the autoencoders with a large bottleneck channel size. We hypothesize that this high-frequency component interferes with the coarse-to-fine nature of the diffusion synthesis process and hinders the generation quality. To mitigate the issue, we propose scale equivariance: a simple regularization strategy that aligns latent and RGB spaces across frequencies by enforcing scale equivariance in the decoder. It requires minimal code changes and only up to $20$K autoencoder fine-tuning steps, yet significantly improves generation quality, reducing FID by 19% for image generation on ImageNet-1K 256x256 and FVD by at least 44% for video generation on Kinetics-700 17x256x256. The source code is available at https://github.com/snap-research/diffusability.

paragraphs: Latent diffusion generates images and videos in a compressed representation supplied by an autoencoder. This paper examines whether that representation is well suited to the diffusion process. Spectral analysis reveals unusually strong high-frequency components in modern autoencoder latent spaces, particularly when the compressed representation has a large number of channels.

The authors hypothesize that these components interfere with diffusion’s coarse-to-fine synthesis process. They propose a scale-equivariance regularizer for the decoder to align the frequency behavior of latent representations and RGB outputs. The method targets the interaction between the autoencoder and diffusion model, extending attention beyond reconstruction quality or the size of the diffusion backbone.

The change requires minimal code modifications and up to 20,000 autoencoder fine-tuning steps. Reported results include a 19% reduction in FID for ImageNet-1K image generation at 256-by-256 resolution and at least a 44% reduction in FVD for Kinetics-700 video generation. These improvements support the usefulness of the regularizer, while the proposed interference mechanism is presented as a hypothesis.
summary.tldr: A scale-equivariance regularizer makes autoencoder latents more suitable for diffusion, improving reported image and video generation quality with limited fine-tuning.

title: Improving the Diffusability of Autoencoders

abstract: Tree-search-based reasoning methods have significantly enhanced the reasoning capability of large language models (LLMs) by facilitating the exploration of multiple intermediate reasoning steps, i.e., thoughts. However, these methods suffer from substantial inference latency, as they have to generate numerous reasoning thoughts, severely limiting LLM applicability. To address this challenge, we propose a novel Speculative Search (SpecSearch) framework that significantly accelerates LLM reasoning by optimizing thought generation. Specifically, SpecSearch utilizes a small model to strategically collaborate with a large model at both thought and token levels, efficiently generating high-quality reasoning thoughts. The major pillar of SpecSearch is a novel quality-preserving rejection mechanism, which effectively filters out thoughts whose quality falls below that of the large model’s outputs. Moreover, we show that SpecSearch preserves comparable reasoning quality to the large model. Experiments on both the Qwen and Llama models demonstrate that SpecSearch significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, achieving up to 2.12$\times$ speedup with comparable reasoning quality.

paragraphs: Tree-based reasoning lets a language model explore multiple intermediate thoughts before settling on an answer. That exploration can improve reasoning, but generating many candidate thoughts also adds substantial inference delay. SpecSearch targets this generation cost, which can make otherwise useful search-based reasoning difficult to deploy.

The framework coordinates a small model with a large model at two scales: complete reasoning thoughts and individual tokens. Its central component is a rejection mechanism designed to preserve quality by filtering thoughts that fall below the quality of the large model's outputs. The collaboration therefore depends on screening proposed reasoning, alongside making generation faster.

The authors show that SpecSearch maintains reasoning quality comparable to the large model. Experiments with Qwen and Llama report improvements over state-of-the-art approaches, including speedups of up to 2.12 times with comparable reasoning quality. That figure is the reported maximum, rather than a uniform gain. The result suggests that coordinating generation across model sizes can reduce the latency cost of exploring multiple reasoning paths.
summary.tldr: SpecSearch coordinates small and large models to accelerate reasoning search by up to 2.12 times while maintaining comparable reasoning quality.

title: Accelerating Large Language Model Reasoning via Speculative Search

abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have significantly propelled the development of large multi-modal models (LMMs), highlighting the potential for general and intelligent assistants. However, most LMMs model visual and textual modalities separately, leading to recent efforts to develop native LMMs using a single transformer. Despite the promise, these native models are resource-intensive and often exhibit performance gaps compared to their compositional counterparts. To alleviate this issue, we propose a simple yet efficient method to construct a baseline for the native and end-to-end large multi-modal model in a single transformer. First, we propose a new early-fusion LMM that can fuse multi-modal inputs in the early stage and respond to visual instructions in an auto-regressive manner. Second, we devise an efficient training recipe for the proposed model, which harnesses the prior knowledge of the pre-trained models, addressing both the performance limitations and the challenge of resource consumption. The proposed model demonstrates superior performance compared to other LMMs using one transformer and significantly narrows the performance gap with compositional LMMs.

paragraphs: Many large multimodal models process visual and textual information with separate components. Native multimodal models instead seek to handle both within a single Transformer, but the paper identifies two obstacles: substantial resource requirements and performance gaps relative to compositional models. HaploVL presents a baseline intended to make this unified approach more effective and efficient.

The model uses early fusion, bringing multimodal inputs together near the beginning of processing. It then produces responses to visual instructions autoregressively, generating the response sequentially. A second contribution is the training recipe, which draws on knowledge from pretrained models. This recipe is designed to address both the difficulty of achieving strong performance and the resources required to train a unified model.

The reported results exceed those of other evaluated single-Transformer multimodal models and substantially narrow the gap with compositional alternatives. The claim is a reduction of that gap, rather than complete elimination. The work provides a concrete baseline for studying how early integration and pretrained knowledge can strengthen end-to-end multimodal understanding in one Transformer.
summary.tldr: HaploVL combines early multimodal fusion with an efficient training recipe to strengthen a single-Transformer vision-language model.

title: HaploVL: A Single-Transformer Baseline for Multi-Modal Understanding

abstract: Existing context-based offline meta-reinforcement learning (COMRL) methods primarily focus on task representation learning and given-context adaptation performance. They often assume that the adaptation context is collected using task-specific behavior policies or through multiple rounds of collection. However, in real applications, the context should be collected by a policy in a one-shot manner to ensure efficiency and safety. We find that intrinsic context ambiguity across multiple tasks and out-of-distribution (OOD) issues due to distribution shift significantly affect the performance of one-shot adaptation, which has been largely overlooked in most COMRL research. To address this problem, we propose using heteroscedastic uncertainty in representation learning to identify ambiguous and OOD contexts, and train an uncertainty-aware context collecting policy for effective one-shot online adaptation. The proposed method can be integrated into various COMRL frameworks, including classifier-based, reconstrution-based and contrastive learning-based approaches. Empirical evaluations on benchmark tasks show that our method can improve one-shot adaptation performance by up to 36% and zero-shot adaptation performance by up to 34% compared to existing baseline COMRL methods.

paragraphs: An agent adapting to a new task needs observations that reveal what that task requires. Existing context-based offline meta-reinforcement learning methods often assume those observations come from task-specific behavior or repeated collection. CERTAIN examines the more demanding situation in which a policy must gather useful context in a single attempt, motivated by efficiency and safety.

The authors identify two obstacles: context can be ambiguous across tasks, and newly collected observations can differ from the training distribution. Their method uses heteroscedastic uncertainty, meaning uncertainty that varies with the context, to identify both problems. It then trains a context-collection policy that accounts for this uncertainty when gathering information for adaptation.

CERTAIN can be incorporated into classification, reconstruction, and contrastive learning approaches to task representation. Benchmark evaluations report improvements of up to 36% for one-shot adaptation and up to 34% for zero-shot adaptation over existing methods. These are maximum reported gains, supporting the value of learning how to collect informative context alongside learning how to interpret it.
summary.tldr: CERTAIN uses context-dependent uncertainty to improve information collection and adaptation when an agent gets only one opportunity to gather context.

title: CERTAIN: Context Uncertainty-aware One-Shot Adaptation for Context-based Offline Meta Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Learning mesh-based operators from data can match training objectives while implicitly violating algebraic consistency constraints that classical discretizations satisfy by construction. Such violations can introduce near-kernel directions, degrade conditioning as resolution increases, and distort the low-frequency spectral structure on which downstream solvers and diagnostics rely. This work introduces a low-overhead compatibility certificate for learned operator pairs, together with a closed-form projection that maps a learned pair to its Frobenius-nearest chain-compatible operator. The certificate provides an explicit distance-to-compatibility and yields perturbation bounds for the discrete operator. These bounds imply stability guarantees for elliptic solves and for low-frequency spectral counts, provided a spectral gap separates the kernel from the rest of the spectrum and boundary treatments are well posed. Experiments on standard elliptic problems show that defect-aware training prevents condition-number blow-up at higher resolutions, improves robustness under mesh and topological distribution shifts, and maintains predictive accuracy relative to unconstrained learning. Overall, these results support the use of deployment-neutral, computable algebraic consistency checks to detect and control failure modes that are not revealed by loss values alone.

paragraphs: A learned numerical operator can fit training data while breaking algebraic relationships that traditional mesh discretizations preserve automatically. Such violations can make numerical problems harder to solve and distort low-frequency behavior. This paper introduces a computationally inexpensive certificate for checking compatibility between learned operator pairs.

The certificate measures distance from the required algebraic structure. A closed-form projection also produces the nearest compatible operator in Frobenius distance, giving both a diagnostic and a correction mechanism. The authors derive perturbation bounds that connect compatibility defects to changes in the discrete operator. Guarantees for elliptic solves and low-frequency spectral counts require a gap separating the kernel from the remaining spectrum and well-posed boundary treatments.

Experiments on standard elliptic problems show that training with awareness of these defects prevents condition numbers from blowing up at higher resolutions. It also improves robustness when meshes or topology change, while maintaining predictive accuracy relative to unconstrained learning. The contribution makes structural consistency directly measurable, exposing numerical failure modes that a favorable training loss alone may not reveal.
summary.tldr: A compatibility certificate and nearest-compatible projection help detect and control structural defects in learned mesh operators.

title: Certificates for Complex-Compatible Learned Cochain Laplacians

abstract: While humans perceive the world through diverse modalities that operate synergistically to support a holistic understanding of their surroundings, existing omnivideo models still face substantial challenges on audio-visual understanding tasks. In this paper, we propose OmniVideo-R1, a novel reinforced framework that improves mixed-modality reasoning. OmniVideo-R1 empowers models to "think with omnimodal cues" by two key strategies: (1) query-intensive grounding based on self-supervised learning paradigms; and (2) modality-attentive fusion built upon contrastive learning paradigms. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that OmniVideo-R1 consistently outperforms strong baselines, highlighting its effectiveness and robust generalization capabilities.

paragraphs: Understanding audio and video together requires a model to connect evidence across modalities in a way that serves the question being asked. The paper identifies persistent difficulty with this combined reasoning in existing omnivideo models. OmniVideo-R1 is a reinforced framework intended to improve how models reason using multiple kinds of perceptual cues.

The framework has two central strategies. Query-intensive grounding uses a self-supervised learning approach to connect reasoning with the query. Modality-attentive fusion uses a contrastive learning approach to combine modalities. These components address related parts of the problem: grounding processing in the question and bringing audio-visual information together to support the reasoning task.

Experiments across multiple benchmarks show consistent improvements over strong baselines, which the authors present as evidence of effectiveness and robust generalization. The stated contribution is therefore both a framework for mixed-modality reasoning and empirical support for its combination of grounding and fusion. Its emphasis is on making multimodal cues useful together for answering a query, rather than merely providing a model with several input streams.
summary.tldr: OmniVideo-R1 improves audio-visual reasoning by combining query-focused grounding with modality-attentive fusion.

title: OmniVideo-R1: Reinforcing Audio-visual Reasoning with Query Intention and Modality Attention

abstract: Existing proxy-based hashing methods optimize samples toward independently learned proxies using isolated similarity constraints. Although efficient, this design overlooks the fact that proxies are learned jointly but lack explicit relational or competitive interactions during optimization. Consequently, proxy responses to a sample are often accumulated rather than contrasted, leading to weakly defined decision regions and limited discriminative structure in the Hamming space. In contrast, our method organizes multiple proxies into sample-specific relational structures, enabling proxies to interact and compete when responding to each sample. Through structure-guided learning, these interactions explicitly contrast positive and negative proxy responses, thereby shaping clearer and more discriminative decision boundaries. Extensive experiments on standard cross-modal benchmarks demonstrate that this structured discrimination consistently improves retrieval accuracy and embedding separability. The source code is available at https://github.com/QinLab-WFU/DDSPH.

paragraphs: Cross-modal retrieval uses representations that make related items from different modalities searchable together. Proxy-based hashing learns these representations with reference points called proxies. The paper identifies a weakness in methods that constrain similarity to each proxy separately: although the proxies are trained jointly, their responses do not explicitly compete or express relationships during optimization.

The proposed method organizes several proxies into a relational structure specific to each sample. Structure-guided learning then contrasts positive and negative proxy responses, instead of simply accumulating their effects. This interaction is intended to define clearer decision regions in the Hamming space where the learned binary representations are compared, giving retrieval a more discriminative organization.

Experiments on standard cross-modal benchmarks show consistent improvements in retrieval accuracy and separation between embeddings. These findings support the paper’s central claim that the relationships among proxies are useful training information. The contribution concerns how reference points interact around a sample: explicitly contrasting their responses improves the structure of the representation used to distinguish relevant from irrelevant retrieval results.
summary.tldr: Making hashing proxies interact and compete for each sample produces clearer representation boundaries and improves cross-modal retrieval.

title: Deep Discriminative Structure Proxy Hashing for Cross-modal Retrieval

abstract: Modeling graphs demands a careful balance between long-range propagation of information across nodes and the controlled dissipation of noisy or redundant signals to ensure stable learning and generalization. This challenge is exacerbated in dynamic graphs, where structural and temporal information interact, leading to uncontrolled information accumulation and amplifying noise, thereby affecting generalization. We introduce LAMP, a dynamic graph model for snapshot-based dynamic graphs that incorporates adaptive, learned dissipation within a principled dynamical systems framework. Our architecture combines impulsive neural ODEs with an antisymmetric parameterization to model conservative information flow, alongside data-driven dissipative dynamics that regulate information retention over space and time. This formulation yields stable yet expressive representations and enables effective long-range dependency modeling while avoiding pathological information buildup. We provide a theoretical analysis establishing stability guarantees and characterizing the representational power. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, particularly on tasks requiring extended-range dependency modeling.

Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, particularly on tasks requiring extended-range dependency modeling.

paragraphs: Information in a graph must travel far enough to connect related nodes, while noisy or repetitive signals need to fade. When a graph changes over time, these demands interact: information accumulated across connections and successive snapshots can become excessive. This paper introduces LAMP, a model that learns how much information to retain and dissipate in snapshot-based dynamic graphs.

LAMP describes information processing through a dynamical systems framework. It combines impulsive neural ordinary differential equations with an antisymmetric parameterization that supports conservative information flow. Alongside that component, learned dissipative dynamics regulate retention across both space and time. The architecture therefore combines mechanisms for carrying information over long distances with mechanisms for controlling its accumulation.

The authors provide theoretical stability guarantees and analyze the model’s representational power. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance, particularly for tasks requiring extended-range dependencies. The stated contribution is a way to make memory retention adaptive while preserving stable, expressive graph representations, addressing information buildup as part of the model’s dynamics.
summary.tldr: LAMP learns how to retain and dissipate information in changing graphs, supporting stable representations and long-range dependencies.

title: Adaptive Memory Retention in Dynamic Graphs

abstract: Existing multimodal retrieval systems excel at semantic matching but implicitly assume that query-image relevance can be measured in isolation. This paradigm overlooks the rich dependencies inherent in realistic visual streams, where information is distributed across temporal sequences rather than confined to single snapshots. To bridge this gap, we introduce DeepImageSearch, a novel agentic paradigm that reformulates image retrieval as an autonomous exploration task. Models must plan and perform multi-step reasoning over raw visual histories to locate targets based on implicit contextual cues. We construct DISBench, a challenging benchmark built on interconnected visual data. To address the scalability challenge of creating context-dependent queries, we propose a human-model collaborative pipeline that employs vision-language models to mine latent spatiotemporal associations, effectively offloading intensive context discovery before human verification. Furthermore, we build a robust baseline using a modular agent framework equipped with fine-grained tools and a dual-memory system for long-horizon navigation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DISBench poses significant challenges to state-of-the-art models, highlighting the necessity of incorporating agentic reasoning into next-generation retrieval systems.

paragraphs: An image’s relevance can depend on what happened elsewhere in a visual history. A system that compares a query with each image independently may miss that context. DeepImageSearch reframes retrieval as an exploration task in which an agent plans several steps and reasons over visual sequences to identify a target from implicit contextual clues.

The authors introduce DISBench to evaluate this capability using interconnected visual data. Creating suitable queries requires finding relationships across space and time, so their construction pipeline combines model assistance with human checking. Vision-language models discover candidate associations, reducing the context-discovery work that humans must perform before verifying the resulting material.

The paper also provides a modular agent baseline with fine-grained tools and a dual-memory system designed for extended navigation. Experiments find that DISBench remains challenging for state-of-the-art models. These results highlight a retrieval capability that isolated semantic matching does not adequately assess: following contextual relationships across a visual history to determine which image actually satisfies the request.
summary.tldr: DeepImageSearch evaluates image retrieval that requires agents to explore visual histories and reason about context spanning multiple images.

title: DeepImageSearch: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Context-Aware Image Retrieval in Visual Histories

abstract: This paper proposes a power-enhanced panel Granger causality test (PE-PGCT) for assessing the Granger non-causality in heterogeneous and potentially high-dimensional panel data. Building on any existing panel Granger non-causality test, we show, both theoretically and empirically, that the proposed PE-PGCT boosts its power substantially. The power gains are particularly significant in situations of high-dimensional panels when the cross-sectional dimension exceeds the time dimension, as well as under sparse alternatives when the signals are sparsely distributed across panel units. We establish rigorous theoretical guarantees on the asymptotic behavior of the proposed power enhancement component, demonstrating attractive power enhancement properties that it induces negligible size distortion under the null hypothesis while delivering significant power gain under the alternatives. The empirical performances are illustrated via extensive simulation studies, as well as a real-world application.

paragraphs: The paper improves tests of Granger non-causality for panel data, where multiple units are observed over time and their behavior may differ. Its focus is statistical power: the ability of a test to detect departures from non-causality when such signals are present. This becomes challenging in large panels, particularly when meaningful signals occur in only a few units.

The proposed PE-PGCT adds a power-enhancement component to an existing panel Granger non-causality test. The authors establish asymptotic guarantees showing that this component produces negligible distortion of the test's size under the null while increasing power under alternatives. In practical terms, the enhancement aims to improve detection without materially changing the false-positive behavior in the theoretical limit.

Theoretical and empirical findings show especially substantial gains when there are more panel units than time observations, and when signals are sparse across units. Extensive simulations and a real-world application illustrate performance. The contribution is an enhancement usable with existing panel tests, with benefits concentrated in statistically difficult high-dimensional and sparse settings.
summary.tldr: PE-PGCT enhances existing panel Granger tests, especially for high-dimensional or sparse signals, with asymptotically negligible null size distortion.

title: Power-Boosted Granger-Causal Discovery for Large Heterogeneous Panel Data

abstract: We argue that high-quality motion data can steer tracking policies toward better optimization trajectories early in training. In this work, we introduce LIMMT (Less Is More for Motion Tracking). To our knowledge, this is the first data-centric study for physics-based humanoid motion tracking. We go beyond simply removing erroneous clips. We define motion data quality through three dimensions: physics feasibility, diversity, and complexity. We show that training with under 3% of AMASS yields better tracking performance than training with the full dataset. Extensive experiments and analyses validate the effectiveness of our framework.

paragraphs: LIMMT examines how the choice of motion training data affects physics-based humanoid motion tracking. The authors argue that high-quality examples can guide a tracking policy toward better optimization trajectories early in training. This shifts attention toward the composition of the training set and how those examples influence the learning process.

Their definition of quality goes beyond identifying and deleting erroneous clips. It includes three dimensions: physical feasibility, diversity, and complexity. These dimensions distinguish whether motions are compatible with physics, how varied the selected motions are, and how complex they are. The framework treats data selection as a substantive part of learning a capable tracking policy.

The central reported finding is that training on less than 3% of AMASS produces better tracking performance than training on the complete dataset. Additional experiments and analyses support the framework's effectiveness. This result shows that, in the evaluated setting, a carefully chosen small training collection can be more useful than the full available motion dataset.
summary.tldr: LIMMT improves humanoid motion tracking by selecting training data for physical feasibility, diversity, and complexity, using less than 3% of AMASS.

title: LIMMT: Less Is More for Motion Tracking

abstract: Probabilistic super-resolution of high-dimensional spatial fields using diffusion models is often computationally prohibitive due to the cost of operating directly in pixel space. We propose PODiff, a structured conditional generative framework that performs diffusion in a fixed, variance-ordered Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) coefficient space, exploiting the orthogonality of POD modes to impose an interpretable, variance-ordered latent geometry. This design enables efficient ensemble generation, preserves dominant spatial structure, and yields spatially interpretable, well-calibrated uncertainty at substantially lower computational cost. We evaluate PODiff on sea surface temperature downscaling over the West Australian coast and on a controlled advection–diffusion benchmark. PODiff achieves reconstruction accuracy comparable to pixel-space and learned-latent diffusion while using a substantially smaller structured latent space, requiring significantly less memory, and producing more reliable uncertainty estimates than deterministic and Monte Carlo Dropout baselines.

paragraphs: Probabilistic super-resolution needs to reconstruct fine spatial detail while representing uncertainty, but pixel-space diffusion can be expensive for scientific fields. PODiff moves generation into a structured low-dimensional coefficient space. That space is defined by Proper Orthogonal Decomposition rather than a learned, unconstrained latent encoder.

The orthogonal modes are ordered by explained variance, giving the latent representation an interpretable relationship to dominant spatial structure. Conditional diffusion operates on these coefficients to generate ensembles efficiently. This design aims to preserve large-scale patterns while making uncertainty spatially meaningful and reducing memory requirements.

Tests on sea-surface-temperature downscaling near Western Australia and an advection–diffusion benchmark match the reconstruction accuracy of pixel-space and learned-latent diffusion. PODiff uses less memory and gives more reliable uncertainty than deterministic and Monte Carlo Dropout baselines. The contribution is an efficient structured alternative, with evidence scoped to those scientific reconstruction problems.
summary.tldr: PODiff performs scientific super-resolution in orthogonal, variance-ordered coefficients, preserving accuracy with lower cost and useful uncertainty estimates.

title: PODiff: Latent Diffusion in Proper Orthogonal Decomposition Space for Scientific Super-Resolution

abstract: Modeling recognition between T-cell receptors (TCRs) and peptide-MHC (pMHC) complexes is a fundamental challenge in computational immunology, constrained by sparse paired interaction data relative to abundant unpaired sequences. We introduce DecoderTCR, a masked language model framework that addresses this through two contributions: (1) a compositional continual pre-training curriculum that learns component representations from marginal data before refining cross-chain dependencies, and (2) Iterative Entropy-Guided Refinement (IEGR), a non-autoregressive decoding algorithm that resolves high-confidence positions first to provide context for uncertain regions. On held-out benchmarks, DecoderTCR achieves 0.96 AUROC for zero-shot pMHC binding prediction and 0.76 AUROC for epitope-specific TCR recognition, approaching supervised baselines without epitope-specific training. Learned representations recover structural contacts without coordinate supervision, and generated sequences exhibit realistic recombination statistics. Experimental validation across two rounds of wet-lab screening reveals a prediction-generation gap that can be narrowed via a lab-in-the-loop paradigm for TCR design.

paragraphs: Predicting recognition between T-cell receptors and peptide-MHC complexes is difficult because paired interaction examples are scarce, even though unpaired sequences are abundant. DecoderTCR uses a masked language model to exploit that imbalance. Its training curriculum first learns representations of separate components from unpaired data, then refines dependencies across chains.

Those decisions supply context for more uncertain regions. summary.tldr: DecoderTCR learns from abundant unpaired sequences and generates through confidence-guided refinement, while laboratory tests reveal a prediction–generation gap.

title: DecoderTCR: Compositional Pretraining and Entropy-Guided Decoding for TCR-pMHC Interactions

abstract: Collaborative perception enhances environment understanding through multi-agent information sharing, but its performance in real-world scenarios is constrained by heterogeneous sensor modalities and model architectures. Recent protocol-based two-stage methods alleviate this problem by mapping heterogeneous features into a shared protocol space; however, independently trained modality-specific converters often generate modality-specific pseudo-protocol distributions, leading to semantic inconsistency and error accumulation, which is particularly pronounced in scenarios with large modality discrepancies. To address this issue, we propose CauseCollab, a causal unified and modality-agnostic network. CauseCollab formulates representation learning in the protocol space from a causal perspective, explicitly disentangling semantic factors from modality-specific statistical confounders via causal metric learning. Meanwhile, CauseCollab adopts context-guided Unified Converter for heterogeneous modalities to ensure cross-modal semantic consistency. In addition, integrating new modalities only requires training adapters with minimal parameters. Extensive experiments on the OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets demonstrate that CauseCollab achieves state-of-the-art performance, with more significant gains in scenarios involving large modality gaps.

paragraphs: Collaborative perception lets multiple agents combine what they observe, but their sensors and models may produce incompatible features. Mapping every feature type into a shared representation seems helpful. However, independently trained converters can retain modality-specific patterns, so features that supposedly share a format still disagree in meaning. These mismatches can accumulate during fusion.

CauseCollab approaches this problem by separating semantic information from statistical factors associated with the sensing modality. Its causal metric learning formulation aims to disentangle those factors within the shared protocol space. A context-guided unified converter then handles heterogeneous modalities while promoting agreement in their semantic representations. Adding a new modality requires training an adapter with relatively few parameters.

Experiments on OPV2V and DAIR-V2X report state-of-the-art performance, with larger gains when modalities differ substantially. This pattern supports the motivation for explicitly addressing modality-related inconsistency. The practical contribution is a shared conversion framework that targets the meaning of exchanged features while keeping the adaptation required for new modalities small.
summary.tldr: CauseCollab improves collaborative perception by separating shared semantic content from modality-specific effects in exchanged features.

title: CauseCollab: Causal Unified and Modality-Agnostic Network for Heterogeneous Collaborative Perception

abstract: Short-term precipitation nowcasting is inherently under-constrained due to limited historical observation windows: identical observations can lead to multiple plausible future trajectories, especially for extreme events. Existing generative methods rely solely on visual features and lack explicit constraints on precipitation motion semantics, resulting in ambiguous dynamics, blurred details, and unstable predictions. We propose LangPrecip, the first language-guided precipitation nowcasting framework, and contribute LangPrecip-160K, a large-scale radar-text paired dataset with 160K annotated sequences. LangPrecip addresses the under-constrained challenge by leveraging natural-language motion descriptions as explicit semantic constraints to reduce motion ambiguity and introducing a dual-path wavelet consistency unfolding decoder that enforces physical data fidelity during latent-to-pixel reconstruction. By reformulating nowcasting as semantically constrained trajectory generation under the Rectified Flow paradigm with model-based decoder optimization, LangPrecip produces sharper and more physically consistent forecasts. Experiments on Swedish and MRMS benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements over state-of-the-art vision-only methods, achieving over 60% and 19% relative gains in heavy-rainfall CSI at 80-minute lead time with enhanced spatial detail preservation. Dataset is available at https://github.com/UESTC-LXD/LangPrecip.

paragraphs: A short sequence of rainfall observations can support several plausible futures, particularly during extreme events. LangPrecip addresses this ambiguity by adding natural-language descriptions of precipitation motion to radar-based forecasting. The paper also introduces LangPrecip-160K, a dataset containing 160,000 annotated radar-and-text sequences to support this multimodal approach.

The framework treats forecasting as trajectory generation constrained by motion semantics, using Rectified Flow. Language descriptions narrow the motion possibilities the model must consider. A dual-path decoder combines wavelet consistency with an unfolding approach to reconstruction, enforcing physical data fidelity when converting latent representations into pixel-level forecasts. The semantic and reconstruction components target different sources of forecast ambiguity and lost detail.

On the Swedish and MRMS benchmarks, the authors report relative heavy-rainfall CSI gains exceeding 60% and 19%, respectively, at an 80-minute lead time against state-of-the-art vision-only methods. They also report sharper spatial detail and more physically consistent predictions. These results support combining explicit motion descriptions with constrained reconstruction for the evaluated precipitation-nowcasting tasks.
summary.tldr: LangPrecip combines radar observations, language descriptions of motion, and a consistency-focused decoder to improve short-term rainfall forecasts.

title: LangPrecip: Language-Aware Multimodal Precipitation Nowcasting

abstract: Understanding and decoding brain activity into visual representations is a fundamental challenge at the intersection of neuroscience and artificial intelligence. While electroencephalogram (EEG) visual decoding has shown promise due to its non-invasive and low-cost nature, existing methods suffer from Hierarchical Neural Encoding Neglect (HNEN), a critical limitation in which flat neural representations fail to model the brain’s hierarchical visual processing. Inspired by the hierarchical organization of visual cortex, we propose ViEEG, a neuro-inspired framework that addresses HNEN. ViEEG decomposes each visual stimulus into three biologically aligned components, namely contour, foreground object, and contextual scene, which serve as anchors for a three-stream EEG encoder. These EEG features are progressively integrated via cross-attention routing, simulating cortical information flow from low-level to high-level vision. We further adopt hierarchical contrastive learning for EEG-CLIP representation alignment, enabling zero-shot object recognition. Extensive experiments on THINGS-EEG dataset demonstrate that ViEEG significantly outperforms previous methods by a large margin in both subject-dependent and subject-independent settings. Results on THINGS-MEG dataset further confirm ViEEG’s generalization to different neural modalities. ViEEG not only advances the performance frontier but also sets a new paradigm for EEG brain visual decoding. Our code is available at https://github.com/LauMason/ViEEG.

paragraphs: ViEEG decodes visual information from EEG recordings using a representation inspired by hierarchical processing in the visual cortex. The paper argues that flat neural representations overlook this organization. It therefore separates visual stimuli into contour, foreground object, and contextual scene components, which anchor three corresponding streams of an EEG encoder.

The contribution is an explicit hierarchy for organizing and combining visual information in neural decoding. summary.tldr: ViEEG organizes EEG decoding around contours, objects, and scenes, improving zero-shot visual recognition through hierarchical representation alignment.

title: ViEEG: Hierarchical Visual Neural Representation for EEG Brain Decoding

abstract: Deep Research (DR) agents extend Large Language Models (LLMs) beyond parametric knowledge by autonomously retrieving and synthesizing evidence from large web corpora into long-form reports, enabling a long-horizon agentic paradigm. However, unlike real-time conversational assistants, DR is computationally expensive and time-consuming, creating an autonomy-interaction dilemma: high autonomy on ambiguous user queries often leads to prolonged execution with unsatisfactory outcomes. To address this, we propose IntentRL, a framework that trains proactive agents to clarify latent user intents before starting long-horizon research. To overcome the scarcity of open-ended research data, we introduce a scalable pipeline that expands a few seed samples into high-quality dialogue turns via a shallow-to-deep intent refinement graph. We further adopt a two-stage reinforcement learning (RL) strategy: Stage I applies RL on offline dialogues to efficiently learn general user-interaction behavior, while Stage II uses the trained agent and a user simulator for online rollouts to strengthen adaptation to diverse user feedback. Extensive experiments show that IntentRL significantly improves both intent hit rate and downstream task performance, outperforming the built-in clarify modules of closed-source DR agents and proactive LLM baselines.

paragraphs: Deep research agents can spend substantial time gathering evidence and writing reports, making an ambiguous initial request expensive to misunderstand. IntentRL trains an agent to clarify the user’s underlying intent before starting that extended work. The aim is to improve the direction of research early, when interaction can still shape what the system investigates and produces.

Because suitable open-ended research dialogues are scarce, the framework expands a small set of seed examples through a graph that progressively refines intent from shallow to deeper descriptions. Training then proceeds in two reinforcement-learning stages. The first uses offline dialogues to learn general interaction behavior efficiently. The second generates online interactions between the trained agent and a simulated user to improve adaptation to varied feedback.

Experiments report significant improvements in both intent hit rate and downstream task performance. IntentRL outperforms built-in clarification modules from closed-source research agents and proactive language-model baselines. The findings connect clarification quality with the usefulness of subsequent research, supporting explicit training for intent discovery as part of an autonomous research workflow.
summary.tldr: IntentRL trains research agents to clarify user intent before lengthy research, improving intent identification and downstream results.

title: IntentRL: Training Proactive User-intent Agents for Open-ended Deep Research via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Spatial reasoning from egocentric videos is inherently challenging because the observable evidence is constrained by the camera trajectory. Existing methods rely on single-turn inference, forcing models to resolve geometric ambiguity through semantic priors rather than verifiable evidence. We argue that spatial reasoning should be revisitable: conclusions formed under limited evidence should remain open to revision when complementary viewpoints become available. Building on this insight, we propose Reason, then Re-reason (ReRe), a training-free, inference-time framework with two phases: in the Reason Phase, an MLLM forms a spatial hypothesis from the original video; in the Re-reason Phase, it verifies or revises the hypothesis by observing a synthesized novel-view video. To enable effective cross-view revisiting, we design a Geometry-to-Video pipeline that renders strategically complementary novel views from predicted 3D geometry. These views feature an elevated, oblique perspective with scene-spanning coverage, while preserving the MLLM’s native video interface without architectural modifications. Extensive evaluations on VSI-Bench and STI-Bench demonstrate that ReRe substantially boosts open-source MLLMs to rival proprietary state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Spatial reasoning from first-person video is limited by where the camera travels and what it reveals. A single inference pass can leave a model resolving geometric uncertainty through semantic expectations. ReRe instead treats an initial spatial conclusion as something that can be checked and revised from another viewpoint.

The framework has two inference-time phases and requires no training. First, a multimodal language model forms a spatial hypothesis from the original video. It then examines a synthesized video from a complementary view to verify or revise that hypothesis. A Geometry-to-Video pipeline constructs these views from predicted three-dimensional geometry, using an elevated, angled perspective that covers the scene broadly.

The synthesized evidence remains a video, so the approach works through the model’s existing video interface without architectural changes. Evaluations on VSI-Bench and STI-Bench report substantial improvements that bring open-source models into competition with proprietary state-of-the-art performance. The result supports revisiting spatial judgments through complementary views. Those views are generated from predicted geometry, rather than supplied by an additional physical camera observation.
summary.tldr: ReRe improves spatial reasoning by letting models revisit initial conclusions using complementary videos synthesized from predicted 3D geometry.

title: Reason, Then Re-reason: Cross-view Revisiting Improves Spatial Reasoning

abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in agentic pipelines that depend on the model evaluating its own outputs without external verification. The reliability of these pipelines depends on an implicit assumption: that the model applies relevant concepts the same way when it generates an output and later evaluates that output. We propose a new measure, generator–evaluator self-consistency, to test this assumption directly and apply it to 10 frontier models across 491 concepts. We find, first, that there is substantial variation in self-consistency. Second, we find that in a clinical setting with physician-validated mistakes (Proniakin et al., 2025), across models, those with higher self-consistency are linked to greater vulnerability to mistakes. Thus, even when models consistently apply concepts they may not be safe to deploy. This is evidence of a consistency dilemma in LLMs: self-consistency is operationally useful, but models that are more consistent are also more prone to mistakes.

paragraphs: Agents that evaluate their own outputs depend on a model applying relevant concepts similarly when producing and reviewing an answer. This paper measures that assumption directly through generator–evaluator self-consistency. The measure concerns agreement between two roles played by the same model, which matters when a workflow lacks external verification.

The authors assess ten frontier models across 491 concepts and find substantial differences in self-consistency. They then examine a clinical setting containing physician-validated mistakes. Across models, greater self-consistency is associated with greater vulnerability to those mistakes. The reported relationship is an association across the evaluated models, rather than evidence that increasing consistency itself causes errors.

The resulting dilemma is that consistency can help a workflow operate coherently while still failing to establish that its decisions are safe. A model can apply concepts consistently during generation and evaluation yet remain vulnerable to mistakes. The findings challenge the use of self-agreement as a sufficient basis for trusting self-evaluating agents, particularly in the clinical setting studied.
summary.tldr: Models vary in generation–evaluation consistency, and higher consistency is associated with greater mistake vulnerability in the studied clinical setting.

title: The Consistency Dilemma in LLMs: Generator-Evaluator Agreement and Vulnerability to Mistakes

abstract: The task of temporal answer grounding in instructional videos (TAGV), which aims to locate precise video segments that respond to natural language queries, is increasingly important for direct video answer retrieval. This task remains challenging due to the need to comprehend semantically complex questions and to address the significant length mismatch between untrimmed videos and short target moments. Existing methods often suffer from sensitivity to irrelevant content or insufficient visual reasoning capabilities. To tackle these limitations, we propose a Candidate-Aware Causal Reasoning (CACR) framework. Our approach first employs a Visual-Language Pre-training based Candidate Selection (VBCS) algorithm to efficiently generate K candidate segments, then applies a temporal logic reasoning module enhanced by a rejection reward mechanism and optimized via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for robust inference. Extensive experiments on six benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU), providing a new perspective for reasoning-based retrieval in long videos.

paragraphs: Finding an answer inside an instructional video requires locating the particular moment that addresses a question. This is difficult when a long recording contains only a short relevant segment, especially if the question demands more than recognizing an object or action. Irrelevant footage can distract retrieval methods, while weak visual reasoning can prevent accurate selection.

CACR separates the task into candidate generation and reasoning. A selection algorithm based on visual-language pre-training first produces K possible answer segments. A temporal logic reasoning module then operates on those candidates. Its training uses Group Relative Policy Optimization and a rejection reward mechanism, combining a narrowed search space with an explicitly trained reasoning stage.

Across six benchmarks, the method achieves state-of-the-art mean Intersection-over-Union, which measures how well predicted segments overlap the target moments. The result supports the value of selecting plausible regions before reasoning about their suitability. For direct video answer retrieval, better overlap means that the returned interval more closely matches the part of the recording needed to answer the query.
summary.tldr: CACR combines candidate video segments with reinforcement-trained temporal reasoning to locate answer moments more accurately.

title: CACR: Reinforcing Temporal Answer Grounding in Instructional Video via Candidate-Aware Causal Reasoning

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are capable of emulating reasoning and using tools, creating opportunities for autonomous agents that execute complex scientific tasks. Protein design provides a natural testbed: although machine learning (ML) methods achieve strong results, these are largely restricted to canonical amino acids and narrow objectives, leaving unfilled need for a generalist tool for broad design pipelines. We introduce Agent Rosetta, an LLM agent paired with a structured environment for operating Rosetta, the leading physics-based heteropolymer design software, capable of modeling non-canonical building blocks and geometries. Agent Rosetta iteratively refines designs to achieve user-defined objectives, combining LLM reasoning with Rosetta’s generality. We evaluate Agent Rosetta on design with canonical amino acids, matching specialized models and expert baselines, and with non-canonical residues—where ML approaches fail—achieving comparable performance. Critically, prompt engineering alone often fails to generate Rosetta actions, demonstrating that environment design is essential for integrating LLM agents with specialized software. Our results show that properly designed environments enable LLM agents to make scientific software accessible while matching specialized tools and human experts.
