paragraphs: Protein-design machine learning methods achieve strong results but often focus on standard amino acids and narrow objectives. Agent Rosetta aims to support broader design workflows by connecting a language-model agent to Rosetta, physics-based software that can model non-canonical building blocks and geometries. The agent iteratively refines designs toward objectives specified by a user.

The central engineering contribution is a structured environment for operating the specialized software. It gives the language model a setting in which its reasoning can lead to usable Rosetta actions. The authors find that prompt engineering alone often fails to produce such actions, making environment design a substantive part of the agent's capability.

On canonical-amino-acid design tasks, Agent Rosetta matches specialized models and expert baselines. It also achieves comparable performance on non-canonical-residue tasks where the evaluated machine learning approaches fail. The results support using a carefully designed interface to connect general language-model reasoning with broad scientific software capabilities. In the studied tasks, this combination makes specialized tools accessible while retaining performance comparable to specialized systems and human experts.
summary.tldr: Agent Rosetta combines an LLM with a structured software environment to perform broad protein-design tasks at competitive quality.

title: Protein Design with Agent Rosetta: A Case Study for Specialized Scientific Agents

abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller student. In language modeling, the student is trained either on tokens sampled from the teacher (hard labels) or the teacher’s full next-token distribution (soft labels). Despite soft labels appear strictly richer, we find that mixing hard and soft labels consistently yields better results. Crucially, we show that this gain cannot be explained by closer teacher matching during training. Instead, it comes from reduced exposure bias—the mismatch between training and inference distributions. To explain this phenomenon, we introduce the Bridge–Garden Decomposition theory, which categorizes generation steps into two types: Bridges, where the next token must be exact, and Gardens, where it can be flexible. We show that hard-only KD excels in Bridges by avoiding risky deviations, while soft-only KD preserves diversity in Gardens. A hybrid strategy handles both cases and, as a result, reduces exposure bias across the sequence. Guided by this theory, we develop a family of Bridge–Garden hybrid supervision methods that adaptively balance hard and soft labels. Across seven teacher–student pairs (including Qwen, Llama, Gemma, and DeepSeek) and benchmarks in reasoning and coding, our approach outperforms divergence-based and on-policy KD baselines while reducing training cost by 9.7$\times$, enabling efficient model compression.

paragraphs: Language-model distillation can train a student using sampled teacher tokens, called hard labels, or the teacher’s full next-token probabilities, called soft labels. Although soft labels contain richer information, this paper finds that combining the two consistently works better. The authors attribute the benefit to reduced exposure bias, the mismatch between training and inference distributions, rather than closer teacher matching during training.

Their Bridge–Garden theory divides generation steps into those requiring an exact next token and those allowing flexibility. Hard-label training performs well at the exact steps by avoiding risky deviations, while soft-label training preserves diversity where multiple continuations are acceptable. A hybrid can address both demands across a sequence. The authors use this account to develop supervision methods that adaptively balance hard and soft labels.

Across seven teacher–student pairs and reasoning and coding benchmarks, the proposed methods outperform divergence-based and on-policy distillation baselines while reporting a 9.7-fold reduction in training cost. The findings explain why copying a richer teacher distribution is not by itself the whole objective: student behavior during its own generation also depends on where precision and flexibility are needed.
summary.tldr: Mixing hard and soft distillation labels helps students balance exact and flexible generation steps, reducing exposure bias.

title: The Bridge-Garden Dilemma in LLM Distillation: Why Mixing Hard and Soft Labels Works

abstract: Trajectory Inference (TI) seeks to recover latent dynamical processes from snapshot data, where only independent samples from time-indexed marginals are observed. In applications such as single-cell genomics, destructive measurements make path-space laws non-identifiable from finitely many marginals, leaving held-out marginal prediction as the dominant but limited evaluation protocol. We introduce a general framework for estimating the Kullback–Leibler divergence (KL) between probability measures on function space, yielding a tractable, data-driven estimator that is scalable to realistic snapshot datasets. We validate the accuracy of our estimator on a benchmark suite, where the estimated functional KL closely matches the analytic KL. Applying this framework to synthetic and real scRNA-seq datasets, we show that current evaluation metrics often give inconsistent assessments, whereas path-space KL enables a coherent comparison of trajectory inference methods and exposes discrepancies in inferred dynamics, especially in regions with sparse or missing data. These results support functional KL as a principled criterion for evaluating trajectory inference under partial observability. Code available here: https://github.com/eurecom-probai/functional-kl.

paragraphs: Trajectory inference reconstructs hidden dynamics from snapshots taken at different times. In settings such as single-cell genomics, destructive measurements prevent following the same sample through time. Finitely many snapshot distributions therefore do not uniquely determine the distribution of complete trajectories, and predicting held-out snapshots gives only a limited view of inferred dynamics.

The paper develops a data-driven estimator of Kullback–Leibler divergence between probability measures over functions. Applied to trajectories, this compares distributions over entire paths rather than only their values at individual times. The framework is designed to remain computationally tractable at the scale of realistic snapshot datasets, making this broader comparison usable in practice.

On benchmarks with analytic KL values, the estimates closely match those values. Experiments with synthetic and real single-cell RNA sequencing data find that existing metrics often disagree, while path-space KL offers a coherent comparison and reveals differences especially where observations are sparse or absent. These results support a stronger evaluation criterion under partial observability, without resolving the underlying non-identifiability.
summary.tldr: A scalable estimator of path-space KL compares inferred dynamics beyond snapshots and reveals discrepancies hidden by existing evaluation metrics.

title: Relative Entropy Estimation in Function Space: Theory and Applications to Trajectory Inference

abstract: Deploying multimodal models in real-world scenarios requires generalization to new environments where recording conditions differ from training, a challenge known as multimodal domain generalization (MMDG). Standard architectures employ separate encoders for each modality and a fusion module, training the system end-to-end by optimizing on the fused features. In this paper, we identify that such joint optimization causes encoders to exploit cross-modal co-occurrences, statistical relationships between modalities that arise from source-specific recording conditions, rather than learning domain-invariant features. We term this failure mode Fusion Overfitting. To address this, we propose Modality-Entropy Regularization for Domain Generalization (MER-DG), which maximizes the entropy of each encoder’s feature distribution to preserve feature diversity. MER-DG is architecture-agnostic and integrates into existing multimodal frameworks as an additive loss term. Extensive experiments on EPIC-Kitchens and HAC benchmarks demonstrate average improvements of ${\sim}5%$ over standard fusion and ${\sim}2%$ over state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Multimodal models often learn separate representations for each input type and then combine them to make predictions. This paper examines why that setup can struggle when recording conditions change. The authors identify fusion overfitting: joint training encourages encoders to exploit relationships between modalities that are specific to the training environment, rather than learning features that remain useful across environments.

MER-DG addresses this failure mode by maximizing the entropy of each encoder’s feature distribution. The aim is to preserve a diverse set of features within each modality, countering the narrowing associated with dependence on source-specific cross-modal patterns. The regularizer is added to the training loss and can be incorporated into different multimodal architectures.

Experiments on EPIC-Kitchens and HAC report average improvements of approximately 5% over standard fusion and approximately 2% over state-of-the-art methods. These findings support feature diversity as a useful intervention for multimodal domain generalization in the evaluated settings. The contribution includes both an explanation of a training failure and an architecture-agnostic way to address it.
summary.tldr: MER-DG preserves diversity in each modality’s features to reduce fusion overfitting and improve generalization to new recording conditions.

title: MER-DG: Modality-Entropy Regularization for Multimodal Domain Generalization

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as CLIP demonstrate strong zero-shot generalization, but their performance significantly degrades in cross-domain scenarios with scarce target-domain training data (Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning, CDFSL). In this paper, we focus on the target-domain few-shot finetuning in the CLIP-based CDFSL task. Prevailing finetuning paradigms uniformly align all image patch tokens with their corresponding textual embeddings. However, we find a counterintuitive phenomenon: actively pushing away certain low-similarity image tokens, termed “tail tokens”, from their textual embeddings consistently improves target-domain performance. We delve into this phenomenon and provide a novel interpretation: under great domain shifts and scarce training data, the model can hardly extract semantic information from visual inputs; therefore, the common belief of alignment is valid only for tokens already containing sufficient semantic information; for tail tokens, forcing the alignment would lead to excessive overfitting to the scarce training, while breaking the alignment is more useful. Motivated by this, we propose Adaptive Tail-Head Alignment (ATHA), a novel fine-tuning strategy for CLIP that transforms the conventional uniform alignment paradigm to an adaptive alignment paradigm, with both alignment strengthening and weakening. Extensive experiments on four challenging CDFSL benchmarks validate our state-of-the-art performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/shuaiyi308/ATHA.

paragraphs: CLIP can generalize without task-specific training, but adapting it to a substantially different domain with only a few labeled examples remains difficult. This paper examines the common practice of aligning every image patch token with its corresponding text representation. It finds that this uniform treatment can be counterproductive for some tokens.

The authors call low-similarity image tokens tail tokens and observe that pushing them away from the text embedding consistently improves target-domain performance. Their interpretation is conditional on large domain shifts and scarce data: some visual tokens lack sufficient semantic information, so forcing them into alignment can encourage excessive fitting to the few available examples.

Adaptive Tail-Head Alignment turns this observation into a fine-tuning strategy that can strengthen or weaken alignment as appropriate. It replaces a uniform objective with selective treatment of image tokens. Experiments on four challenging cross-domain few-shot benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance. The findings support adapting alignment to the information already present in a token, especially when limited target data makes indiscriminate alignment unreliable.
summary.tldr: ATHA improves few-shot CLIP adaptation by selectively strengthening useful image-text alignment and weakening alignment for low-similarity tokens.

title: Improving CLIP Adaptation by Breaking Tail Alignment for Source-Free Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning

abstract: Diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in generative modeling, yet how to effectively adapting large pretrained models to new tasks remains challenging. We revisit the reconstruction behavior of diffusion models during denoising to unveil the underlying frequency–energy mechanism governing this process. Building upon this observation, we propose FeRA, a frequency-driven fine-tuning framework that aligns parameter updates with the intrinsic frequency–energy progression of diffusion. FeRA establishes a comprehensive frequency–energy framework for effective diffusion adaptation fine-tuning, comprising three synergistic components: (i) a compact frequency–energy indicator that characterizes the latent’s bandwise energy distribution, (ii) a soft frequency router that adaptively fuses multiple frequency-specific adapter experts, and (iii) a frequency–energy consistency regularization that stabilizes diffusion optimization and ensures coherent adaptation across bands. Routing operates in both training and inference, with inference-time routing dynamically determined by the latent frequency energy. It integrates seamlessly with adapter-based tuning schemes and generalizes well across diffusion backbones and resolutions. By aligning adaptation with the frequency–energy mechanism, FeRA provides a simple, stable, and compatible paradigm for effective and robust diffusion model adaptation. Codes will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: Adapting a large pretrained diffusion model requires deciding how its parameters should change for a new task. FeRA approaches this through the model's behavior during denoising. The authors investigate how reconstruction progresses across frequency bands and propose aligning adaptation with that changing distribution of frequency energy.

The framework has three cooperating parts. A compact indicator summarizes how energy is distributed across bands in the latent representation. A soft router uses that information to combine multiple adapters specialized for different frequencies. A consistency regularizer encourages coherent adaptation across bands and stabilizes optimization, connecting the adapter updates to the same frequency-based description.

Routing remains active during inference, when the current latent's frequency energy determines the mixture of adapters. Thus, the adaptation mechanism responds to the representation being denoised rather than using one fixed mixture throughout generation. The authors report compatibility with adapter-based tuning and generalization across diffusion backbones and resolutions, presenting frequency-aware routing as a stable and broadly compatible approach to diffusion adaptation.
summary.tldr: FeRA adapts diffusion models by routing among frequency-specific adapters according to the latent representation's changing energy distribution.

title: FeRA: Frequency-Energy Constrained Routing for Effective Diffusion Adaptation Fine-Tuning

abstract: Diffusion Posterior Sampling (DPS) provides a principled Bayesian approach to inverse problems by sampling from $p(x_0 \mid y)$. While posterior sampling is valuable for capturing uncertainty and multi-modality, many classical and practical inverse problem settings ultimately prioritize accurate point estimation—most notably the MAP estimator, which has long served as a standard reconstruction objective in imaging and scientific applications. We introduce Local MAP Sampling (LMAPS), a new inference framework that iteratively solving local MAP subproblems along the diffusion trajectory. This perspective clarifies their connection to global MAP and DPS, offering a unified probabilistic interpretation for optimization-based methods. Building on this foundation, we develop practical algorithms with a covariance approximation motivated by Gaussian prior assumption, a reformulated objective for stability and interpretability. Across a broad set of image restoration and scientific tasks, LMAPS achieves state-of-the-art performance.

While posterior sampling is valuable for capturing uncertainty and multi-modality, many classical and practical inverse problem settings ultimately prioritize accurate point estimation—most notably the MAP estimator, which has long served as a standard reconstruction objective in imaging and scientific applications. We introduce Local MAP Sampling (LMAPS), a new inference framework that iteratively solving local MAP subproblems along the diffusion trajectory. This perspective clarifies their connection to global MAP and DPS, offering a unified probabilistic interpretation for optimization-based methods. paragraphs: Inverse problems reconstruct an unknown object from observations. Diffusion Posterior Sampling approaches this by drawing reconstructions from a conditional distribution, which is useful for representing uncertainty and multiple possibilities. This paper focuses on settings that prioritize an accurate single reconstruction, particularly the maximum a posteriori, or MAP, estimate.

Local MAP Sampling, abbreviated LMAPS, solves a sequence of local MAP subproblems along the diffusion trajectory. The authors use this viewpoint to explain connections with both global MAP estimation and Diffusion Posterior Sampling. It provides a probabilistic interpretation for optimization-based reconstruction methods and organizes the inference process around successive local estimation problems.

The practical algorithms include a covariance approximation motivated by a Gaussian prior assumption and a reformulated objective intended to improve stability and interpretability. Across image restoration and scientific tasks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance. The results support local MAP optimization along diffusion trajectories as an effective approach for the evaluated reconstruction settings where point-estimate accuracy is the central objective.
summary.tldr: LMAPS solves local MAP estimation problems along diffusion trajectories to produce accurate reconstructions for inverse problems.

title: Local MAP Sampling for Diffusion Models

abstract: Linear discriminant analysis (LDA) has been an active topic of research during the last century. However, the existing algorithms have several limitations when applied to visual data. LDA is only optimal for Gaussian distributed classes with equal covariance matrices, and only classes-1 features can be extracted. On the other hand, LDA does not scale well to high dimensional data (overﬁtting), and it cannot handle optimally multimodal distributions. In this paper, we introduce Multimodal Oriented Discriminant Analysis (MODA), a LDA extension which can overcome these drawbacks. A new formulation and several novelties are proposed: • An optimal dimensionality reduction for multimodal Gaussian classes with different covariances is derived. The new criteria allows for extracting more than classes-1 features. • A covariance approximation is introduced to improve generalization and avoid over-ﬁtting when dealing with high dimensional data. • A linear time iterative majorization method is suggested in order to ﬁnd a local optimum. Several synthetic and real experiments on face recognition show that MODA outperform existing linear techniques.

paragraphs: Linear discriminant analysis has restrictive conditions for optimality: Gaussian classes with equal covariance matrices. It also extracts at most one fewer feature than the number of classes and can overfit high-dimensional data. This paper proposes Multimodal Oriented Discriminant Analysis to address these difficulties, especially for visual data whose class distributions may contain multiple modes.

The authors derive an optimal dimensionality-reduction criterion for multimodal Gaussian classes with different covariances. The criterion permits more than classes-minus-one features. They also introduce an approximation to covariance intended to improve generalization in high dimensions. These changes broaden the distributional structure the method addresses and alter how much discriminating information its representation can retain.

For optimization, the paper proposes a linear-time iterative majorization method that finds a local optimum. This qualification distinguishes the optimization procedure’s result from the optimality of the derived criterion. Experiments on synthetic data and real face-recognition problems report better performance than existing linear techniques, supporting the proposed extension in those evaluations.
summary.tldr: MODA extends discriminant analysis to multimodal Gaussian classes with unequal covariances and reports gains on synthetic and face-recognition data.

title: Multimodal oriented discriminant analysis

abstract: We present the first algorithm for exact Bayes optimal classification from the hypothesis space of decision trees satisfying leaf constraints. Our contribution is that we reduce this problem to the problem of finding a rule-based classifier with appropriate weights. We show that these rules and weights can be computed in linear time from the output of a modified frequent itemset mining algorithm, which means that we can compute the classifier in practice, despite the exponential worst-case complexity. We perform experiments in which we compare the Bayes optimal predictions with those of the maximum a posteriori hypothesis.
originalAbstract: We present the first algorithm for exact Bayes optimal classification from the hypothesis space of decision trees satisfying leaf constraints. Our contribution is that we reduce this problem to the problem of finding a rule-based classifier with appropriate weights. We show that these rules and weights can be computed in linear time from the output of a modified frequent itemset mining algorithm, which means that we can compute the classifier in practice, despite the exponential worst-case complexity. We perform experiments in which we compare the Bayes optimal predictions with those of the maximum a posteriori hypothesis.

paragraphs: The paper presents an algorithm for exact Bayes optimal classification over decision trees subject to leaf constraints. The problem concerns predictions from this constrained hypothesis space, rather than simply selecting a single tree. The authors describe their method as the first exact algorithm for this setting.

Their key step is to reduce the classification problem to constructing a weighted rule-based classifier. A modified frequent itemset mining algorithm produces output from which the required rules and weights can be computed in linear time. This separates the final construction of the classifier from the potentially expensive work needed to generate the mining output.

The overall problem retains exponential worst-case complexity, so the linear-time claim does not apply to the entire procedure. Nevertheless, the reduction makes computing the classifier practical in the cases considered. Experiments compare its Bayes optimal predictions with predictions from the maximum a posteriori hypothesis. The abstract reports that comparison without asserting which approach wins, while the central contribution remains exact classification through the weighted-rule reduction.
summary.tldr: Exact Bayes optimal classification over leaf-constrained decision trees becomes practically computable through a reduction to weighted rules.

title: Bayes optimal classification for decision trees

abstract: We consider the problem of online selection of a bundle of items when the cost of each item changes arbitrarily from round to round and the valuation function is initially unknown and revealed only through the noisy values of selected bundles (the bandit feedback setting). We are interested in learning schemes that have a small regret compared to an agent who knows the true valuation function. Since there are exponentially many bundles, further assumptions on the valuation functions are needed. We make the assumption that the valuation function is supermodular and has non-linear interactions that are of low degree in a novel sense. We develop efficient learning algorithms that balance exploration and exploitation to achieve low regret in this setting.

We are interested in learning schemes that have a small regret compared to an agent who knows the true valuation function. Since there are exponentially many bundles, further assumptions on the valuation functions are needed. paragraphs: This paper studies repeated selection of bundles of items when item costs can change arbitrarily between rounds. The value of a bundle is initially unknown, and the learner sees only a noisy value for the bundle it actually selects. This limited feedback makes each decision serve two purposes: obtaining value now and learning what might be valuable later.

The number of possible bundles grows exponentially, so the authors impose structure on the valuation function. They assume it is supermodular and that its nonlinear interactions have low degree in a newly defined sense. Those assumptions are central to the setting in which efficient learning is developed; the approach does not address unrestricted valuation functions.

The proposed algorithms balance exploration and exploitation while estimating bundle values online. Their objective is low regret relative to an agent that already knows the true valuation function. The result shows how structural assumptions about interactions among items can make learning feasible despite noisy feedback, changing costs, and an otherwise enormous space of possible selections.
summary.tldr: Efficient online bundle-selection algorithms achieve low regret under supermodularity and a low-degree assumption on valuation interactions.

title: Bundle Selling by Online Estimation of Valuation Functions

abstract: This paper addresses the issue of model selection for hidden Markov models (HMMs). We generalize factorized asymptotic Bayesian inference (FAB), which has been recently developed for model selection on independent hidden variables (i.e., mixture models), for time-dependent hidden variables. As with FAB in mixture models, FAB for HMMs is derived as an iterative lower bound maximization algorithm of a factorized information criterion (FIC). It inherits, from FAB for mixture models, several desirable properties for learning HMMs, such as asymptotic consistency of FIC with marginal log-likelihood, a shrinkage effect for hidden state selection, monotonic increase of the lower FIC bound through the iterative optimization. Further, it does not have a tunable hyper-parameter, and thus its model selection process can be fully automated. Experimental results shows that FAB outperforms states-of-the-art variational Bayesian HMM and non-parametric Bayesian HMM in terms of model selection accuracy and computational efficiency.

We generalize factorized asymptotic Bayesian inference (FAB), which has been recently developed for model selection on independent hidden variables (i.e., mixture models), for time-dependent hidden variables. As with FAB in mixture models, FAB for HMMs is derived as an iterative lower bound maximization algorithm of a factorized information criterion (FIC). It inherits, from FAB for mixture models, several desirable properties for learning HMMs, such as asymptotic consistency of FIC with marginal log-likelihood, a shrinkage effect for hidden state selection, monotonic increase of the lower FIC bound through the iterative optimization. Further, it does not have a tunable hyper-parameter, and thus its model selection process can be fully automated. Experimental results shows that FAB outperforms states-of-the-art variational Bayesian HMM and non-parametric Bayesian HMM in terms of model selection accuracy and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Selecting a hidden Markov model involves deciding how much hidden-state structure is needed to explain sequential data. This paper extends factorized asymptotic Bayesian inference, previously developed for independent hidden variables in mixture models, to hidden variables that depend on one another over time.

The method repeatedly maximizes a lower bound on a factorized information criterion. It retains several properties of the mixture-model approach: the criterion is asymptotically consistent with marginal log-likelihood, a shrinkage effect supports hidden-state selection, and iterative optimization increases the lower bound monotonically. These properties connect model selection with the procedure used to fit the model.

The approach has no tunable hyperparameter, allowing its model-selection process to be automated. In the reported experiments, it outperforms state-of-the-art variational Bayesian and nonparametric Bayesian HMM methods in both model-selection accuracy and computational efficiency. The contribution is therefore both a theoretical extension to temporal dependence and an empirically effective procedure for choosing hidden-state structure without a separate hyperparameter-tuning step.
summary.tldr: Factorized asymptotic Bayesian inference enables automated HMM state selection and improves selection accuracy and efficiency in the reported comparisons.

title: Factorized Asymptotic Bayesian Hidden Markov Models

abstract: Estimating statistical models within sensor networks requires distributed algorithms, in which both data and computation are distributed across the nodes of the network. We propose a general approach for distributed learning based on combining local estimators defined by pseudo-likelihood components, encompassing a number of combination methods, and provide both theoretical and experimental analysis. We show that simple linear combination or max-voting methods, when combined with second-order information, are statistically competitive with more advanced and costly joint optimization. Our algorithms have many attractive properties including low communication and computational cost and “any-time” behavior.
originalAbstract: Estimating statistical models within sensor networks requires distributed algorithms, in which both data and computation are distributed across the nodes of the network. We propose a general approach for distributed learning based on combining local estimators defined by pseudo-likelihood components, encompassing a number of combination methods, and provide both theoretical and experimental analysis. We show that simple linear combination or max-voting methods, when combined with second-order information, are statistically competitive with more advanced and costly joint optimization. Our algorithms have many attractive properties including low communication and computational cost and “any-time” behavior.

paragraphs: In a sensor network, observations and computing resources are spread across multiple nodes. Estimating a statistical model therefore calls for methods that can work with this distribution of data and computation. The paper proposes a general approach based on combining local estimates constructed from components of the pseudo-likelihood.

The framework includes several ways to combine those estimates, rather than prescribing a single costly joint optimization. Its central finding is that simple linear combinations or max-voting methods can be statistically competitive with more advanced joint optimization when they incorporate second-order information. That qualification matters: the claim concerns these simple methods equipped with additional statistical information.

The authors provide both theoretical and experimental analysis. They also emphasize low communication and computation costs, along with anytime behavior that allows the algorithms to produce results during their operation. These properties make the approach relevant when coordination itself is expensive. The contribution is evidence that carefully combining local estimators can retain strong statistical performance without requiring the full expense of joint optimization.
summary.tldr: Combining local pseudo-likelihood estimators with second-order information can compete statistically with costlier joint optimization.

title: Distributed Parameter Estimation via Pseudo-likelihood
